title: De Engel, the angel on the factory chimney
summary: A three-metre concrete angel with six wings stands on the stump of an oil factory's chimney, fourteen metres up, above a 1950s church hall at the end of the Blankenstraat. It gave the building its name.
body:
Look up at the corner of the Blankenstraat and the Tweede Coehoornstraat: on top of a brick chimney stands an angel with six wings. The chimney belonged to the oil factory of N.V. Godol, which stood here until the site was cleared. When the Dutch Reformed Church lost its neighbourhood hall to Werkspoor's expansion, it got this plot, and the architect Marius Duintjer turned what was left of the factory into a new hall with a chalet-like glazed front and big dormers. The chimney, cut down to fourteen metres, was kept as a pedestal.

The sculptor Han Richters modelled the angel and it was cast in concrete on the spot. It is a seraph from Isaiah 6: two wings cover the face, two the body, two are for flying, at the moment the angel touches the prophet's lips with a glowing coal. It was placed on 11 October 1952, when the hall opened, and the building has been called De Engel ever since.

The hall later served as a community centre, a Moroccan neighbourhood centre and a set for the TV series Baantjer; in 2017 a daycare centre moved in. The angel is seen best from the street.

Look for:
- the six wings and the coal held out in front
- the glazed gable of vertical strips over the entrance, and the caretaker's bay window beside it
- the tall hall window on the garden side

title: Hulpbank van Lening, the pawnshop branch in the Czaar Peterbuurt
summary: In 1880 the city opened a branch of its pawnshop in the middle of a poor shipyard workers' quarter. When the blocks around it were pulled down in 1986, the pawnshop was the one building left standing.
body:
Amsterdam's municipal pawnshop, the Bank van Lening, dates from 1614. Besides its main house on the Nes it ran branches in the working-class districts, and this is one of them: Hulpbank van Lening no. 10, built in 1880 to a design attributed to W. Hamer. The Czaar Peterbuurt was full of men working in the shipyards and machine shops of the islands on low wages. Around 1900 the city received petitions asking for lower interest and for pawned clothes, blankets and tools to be handed back in hard winters. People pledged household goods here, down to their beds.

You can read the two functions in the building: two taller corner blocks and a low middle section, with wider doors for the store rooms. It was put up in two phases, which shows in the wall anchors.

In 1986 urban renewal flattened the first three blocks on the odd side of the Czaar Peterstraat. The block with the pawnshop was not rebuilt and the pawnshop alone was spared, so it now turns its back on a car park. A 2022 permit allows the building to be split into flats.

Look for:
- the low middle part between the two higher ends, and the different wall anchors of the two phases
- the bands of yellow brick sunk into the ground floor
- the back of the building, facing the square left by the demolition

title: Horse-tram depot of the Tweede Leeghwaterstraat
summary: From 1884 the horse tram to the Kadijksplein started here, and this low brick complex held the trams, a stable for 33 horses and a smithy for their shoes. Today it is a workspace for artists.
body:
In 1884 a horse tram began to run from the shipyard at the end of the Czaar Peterstraat, along the Oostenburgergracht to the Kadijksplein. Its depot was this complex, built the same year for the Amsterdamsche Omnibus Maatschappij, the private company that ran the city's horse trams from 1875. Its house architect, A.L. van Gendt, designed it: a shed for the cars, a stable for 33 horses in a double row with a hayloft above, and a smithy, where shoes and fittings were made. Each part has its own pitched roof, so you can still count the functions from the street. The line was electrified in 1906 and became tram 13.

Van Gendt's first depot, on the Overtoom (1876), is the oldest known surviving one in the country; those on the Amsteldijk and the Stadhouderskade were pulled down. This one is the next surviving link.

For decades the building was a youth centre, then it stood empty. Since 2018 it has been the Remise, a workspace for artists and small makers run by Urban Resort.

Look for:
- the separate roofs of tram shed, stable and smithy
- the wider stable block, built for two rows of horses
- the raised middle section on the Tweede Leeghwaterstraat side, where the staff room was

title: Czaar Peterbuurt workers' blocks
summary: After an 1873 inquiry into cellar dwellings, the city lent money, land and its own architect to build workers' flats here: long back-to-back blocks left open at the ends to let the wind through. Around them, private builders put up the cheapest housing they could.
body:
The Czaar Peterbuurt (named in 1878 after Peter the Great) was laid out on the Funen, a navy timber harbour and drill ground, under Kalff's extension plan. By 1882 it was nearly full of workers' housing.

Two kinds of builder are still side by side. In 1873 a health commission reported on the misery of Amsterdam's cellar dwellings, and in 1875 the Amsterdamsche Vereeniging tot het bouwen van Arbeiderswoningen was founded: the city supplied borrowed money, land and its architect Bastiaan de Greef, the association ran the homes. Between the Blankenstraat and the Kraijenhoffstraat De Greef built two blocks back to back, open at the ends for fresh air, with gardens in between. Each stair door served eight two-room flats; the front room had one box bed, the back room two.

Further north the private builders worked. A local master builder, H.P. Labohm, put up twenty houses in 1882 with a shop or workshop in every ground floor and one continuous beam round three streets. On block N47 W.F. Krol, owner, contractor and coffee-house keeper, built from his own rough drawings. The register calls one block the very cheapest speculative housing of the century.

Look for:
- the stepped and spout gables over every third window bay of De Greef's blocks
- the open ends of the blocks at the Cruquiusstraat
- the continuous shop beam on Czaar Peterstraat 173-189, Lijndenstraat 23-25 and Conradstraat 142-158

title: Volkskoffiehuis on the Kadijksplein
summary: A one-storey timber-framed coffee house of 1902, built by the People's League against Drink Abuse to keep dock workers away from gin: coffee and beer, cheap or for vouchers, but no spirits. Later restaurants moved in; the last, a pizzeria, closed in 2026.
body:
Around 1900 the Kadijken were poor, full of day labourers, and employers watched good workers go under to jenever (Dutch gin). The Volksbond tegen Drankmisbruik, the People's League against Drink Abuse (Amsterdam branch founded in 1876), answered with people's coffee houses: coffee and beer at reduced prices or for vouchers, but no spirits.

This one opened in 1902. It is a low hall of timber framing filled in with half-brick walls, one of the few examples of this light way of building in Amsterdam; a coffee house did not need more. The entrance is in the cut-off corner on the square. The side walls are plainer because they were hidden behind a wall that has since gone. Its near twin of the same year survives on the Cruquiuskade; most others were demolished once they were no longer needed.

Later restaurants moved in, one of them under the old name Koffiehuis van den Volksbond. The most recent, a pizzeria, went bankrupt in May 2026 and closed soon after, so for now you see it from the square.

Look for:
- the name of the Volksbond on the front
- the timber frame showing in the long wall: thirteen bays, three narrow ones in the corner
- the corner entrance facing the square

title: Zeemanshuis, the sailors' home on the Kadijksplein
summary: Built in 1856–1858 to keep stranded sailors off the streets, on the model of London and Liverpool, it began as a brick 'castle' with corner towers. It ran for 130 years until the subsidy stopped in 1985 and found some guests had lived there for eight years.
body:
In the mid-nineteenth century port cities began to build homes for sailors between ships, so they would not drift around the docks with no money and in the wrong company. London had the first, Liverpool a big one. In Amsterdam a private society raised the money, and slowly: the foundations were laid in 1854, the first stone of the building itself only in March 1856, and it opened around March 1858. The architect A.N. Godefroy gave it plain brick walls and heavy corner towers, more fort than hotel.

It was a success and kept growing: an extra floor in 1915, big rebuilds in 1921 and 1935 by the Baanders office, which lost the towers and the roofline. The nautical and electrotechnical schools used it too. After the port moved west, fewer sailors came, and refugees and drug users were housed here. On 1 January 1985 the state stopped the subsidy; at the closure some residents turned out to have been living in it for eight years. Shortly before, Joost Barbiers's statue Zeeman (Sailor) was put on the square in front.

The missionary organisation Youth With A Mission now uses the building; you see it from the square.

Look for:
- Barbiers's sailor on the square
- the 1923 leaded glass by the Haarlem firm Bogtman
- the symmetrical front, continued in the 1915 extension

title: Entrepotdok, the bonded warehouses behind a wall
summary: From 1827 to about 1900 this whole dock was walled off as the state's bonded store: goods waited here duty-free until sold. The triple warehouses still carry the names of Dutch and Belgian towns, and since the 1980s people live in them.
body:
Before the French period a merchant paid duty both bringing goods in and taking them out of Amsterdam. To win back the transit trade, the state opened the Algemeen Rijksentrepot here in 1827: goods could be stored without import duty until they went on the market. The whole complex was sealed off, with a wall on the Laagte Kadijk and a gatehouse on the Kadijksplein, built 1828–1830 to a design by city architect Jan de Greef. Warehouses were added; this row of triple warehouses dates from 1828–1829. Each carries the names of three towns: Nijmegen, Nijkerk, Ostende; Purmerend, Rotterdam, Roermond; Vlissingen, Venlo, Veendam, and so on. There are 84 such named warehouses along the dock.

Around 1900 the bonded store moved to a new site and the buildings stood half empty for decades. Because they were listed, they survived the demolitions on the islands around them. In the early 1980s the architect Joop van Stigt hollowed out the deep floors around inner courts, and from 1984 tenants moved into social housing, with a say in their own kitchens and bathrooms.

Halfway along the dock the lifting bridge of 1903 over the old lock still says who built it: Werkspoor.

Look for:
- the town names on every front
- the sandstone gate with its pediment on the Kadijksplein
- the 1951 harbour crane on the quay
- the Werkspoor plate on the posts of bridge 80

title: Werf 't Kromhout and the yard bosses' houses
summary: An 18th-century shipyard under an iron roof bought second-hand from a food exhibition, where the Kromhout engine was born. It still works as a museum, with the country's oldest surviving steam boiler, and the bosses' houses stand along the dyke in front.
body:
In 1757 the wife of the shipwright Doede Jansz Kromhout bought a plot behind the Hoogte Kadijk so her husband could build ships, and the yard kept his name. In 1867 the shipowner Daniël Goedkoop bought it for his seventeen-year-old son, who moved it to iron ships, installed steam drive in 1874 and in 1887 bought the riveted iron roof of a hall from an exhibition of foodstuffs held on what is now the Museumplein. The museum calls it the first covered shipyard in the Netherlands. A second roof followed in 1899. The Kromhout engine was born here before engine-making moved across the IJ in 1908.

The yard closed in 1967 and faced demolition. Volunteers opened a museum in 1973 and bought the site in 1975. Old Kromhout engines are started for visitors, and the riveted steam boiler of 1895 is the oldest in the country.

In front, no. 149 was the boss's house. No. 155 and the row 157–163 were built in 1875 for the yard and its staff; tradition has it that the union leader Jan van Zutphen, a tenant at 155, founded the Koperen Stelen Fonds in its attic, which paid for the Zonnestraal sanatorium.

The museum is open on Tuesdays and on the third Sunday of the month.

Look for:
- the two iron roofs over the slipways
- the yard roof poking into the office at the back of no. 149
- the name Sebbelee over the gate between nos. 159 and 161

title: Centrale Oost, the city's first power station
summary: Amsterdam's own first power station, opened in 1903 so the city could electrify its trams and harbour cranes. The boiler house and chimneys are gone; the machine hall on the Hoogte Kadijk still houses a high-voltage station.
body:
In 1900 the council decided, on a report by A.W. Ressing, that the city would make its own electricity. A main reason was that it wanted to electrify the trams and the cranes of the port, and those ran better on direct current. So the station on the Hoogte Kadijk, opened in 1903 under the name Centraal Station and later called Centrale Oost, made both: three-phase current for homes and firms, direct current for trams and harbour.

There were three long buildings side by side: this machine hall on the street, a boiler house with two chimneys, and a coal store on the Entrepotdok water where the coal came in by boat. The German firm AEG fitted out the machine hall, with five steam engines of 1000 hp from Stork in Hengelo. In 1908 the hall was doubled in length in the same style.

It generated power in full until 1931, then wound down. Most machines, boilers and the chimneys went in 1946; the boiler house and coal store were pulled down in the 1990s. A buttressed wall of the coal store was built into the new flats on the dock. The machine hall is still in use as a high-voltage substation, so you see it only from outside.

Look for:
- the brick front with stone springers and gargoyles
- the raised former office block at the east end
- the old coal-store wall in the flats behind, on the Entrepotdok

title: De Gooyer, the windmill that lost its wind to Napoleon
summary: The last of the corn mills that stood on the city's bastions. Napoleon's new barracks took its wind, so in 1814 it was moved onto the base of a demolished water mill. The brewery next door has it on its labels but nothing else to do with it.
body:
From the seventeenth century into the late nineteenth, a row of corn mills stood on the bastions along the outer canal, where they caught the wind at the edge of town. Around 1900 the last were pulled down, all but this one. The mill had already moved more than once: in 1725 it was rebuilt on the bastion where the Oranje-Nassau barracks now stand. When the barracks went up in 1810–1813 it no longer got enough wind, and in 1814 it was moved again, onto the stone base of a water mill demolished in 1812 on the Funenkade.

The city bought the rundown mill in 1928 for 3200 guilders and fitted it with more efficient streamlined sails. In the war, short of electricity, it ground corn again for private people. On 13 November 1972 those sails turned in a storm, the mill ran away, the upper shaft broke and the sails fell into the Nieuwe Vaart. A new shaft was cast at the Stork works nearby, and in 1976 the mill got old-Dutch sails again.

Stadsherstel owns it; it cannot be visited. Brouwerij 't IJ, in the former municipal bathhouse of 1911 next door, is not related to it, except that the mill is on its labels.

Look for:
- the two wooden octagons stacked on the tall square brick base
- the gallery round the mill, and the old gable stone in the base
- the bathhouse building of the brewery beside it

title: Oranje-Nassau Kazerne, Napoleon's barracks where the Artis lions slept
summary: Napoleon ordered a barracks for 2400 men and made Amsterdam pay for it. It was finished just as the French left, was condemned as too damp within twenty years, and in 1839–1840 housed the elephants, tigers and lions of the brand-new zoo across the road.
body:
After the Netherlands was annexed to his empire, Napoleon ordered a grand barracks here for 2400 men. Marshal Oudinot laid the first stone in 1810 of the Quartier Saint-Charles, designed by city architect Abraham van der Hart. The city had to pay: every householder was charged 5 per cent of his rent, and those who did not pay got French soldiers billeted on them.

It was ready in 1813, just before the French left. Renamed after the House of Orange, it got the Orange arms in place of Napoleon's, and its French eagles became Dutch lions. Damp and draughty, it was condemned around 1830. From 1839 to August 1840 the newly founded zoo Artis kept animals here, among them elephants, tigers and lions, while it waited for permission to build its own. Later it held army stores, the military pigeon post (from 1892) and again infantry.

The army left in 1987. Demolition was planned, but after protests by neighbours it was turned into about 150 social rented homes in 1990, with offices on the ground floor. Behind it, the 1920 office building of the barracks, with the engineers' office and the officers' mess, on the Louise Wentstraat, became homes too.

Look for:
- the Orange arms in the central pediment and the lions on the side ones
- the 1990 sculpture Timpaan by Wendela Gevers Deynoot on the west end
- a piece of the old barracks wall beside the 1920 office building on the Louise Wentstraat

title: Marineterrein, the navy yard behind the wall
summary: For 360 years the Admiralty and then the navy built and stored ships here behind a wall most Amsterdammers never got past. Since 2015 you can walk in: past a Stalpaert gate, a Cold War commander's bunker, and into the first official swimming spot of the centre.
body:
Around 1655 the Admiralty of Amsterdam moved its yards to Kattenburg, putting up the great sea store (now the Scheepvaartmuseum) and a long yard building. Tromp's flagship Hollandia and Van Speijk's gunboat were built here; iron ships followed from 1867. When warships grew too big for the locks and bridges to the sea, building moved to Den Helder; the yard closed in 1915 and the site carried on as the Marine Etablissement, a closed enclave. Vincent van Gogh lived here for a year in 1877–1878 with his uncle, the commandant, in a house that is gone.

From 1962 the west part was cleared for the IJ tunnel, and the navy rebuilt: a commander's house with a bunker meant to keep him in touch with the outside world in a Cold War emergency, a command building and an officers' building. These and an 1878 ship carpenters' workshop became municipal monuments in 2025 at the request of Heemschut. The wall on the Kattenburgerstraat, largely the back walls of vanished buildings, was listed in 2023.

The first part opened to the public on 1 April 2015. Defence still uses a corner. The inner harbour has been an official, unsupervised swimming spot since April 2025.

Look for:
- the 17th-century gate at Kattenburgerstraat 7, with pilasters and a carved pediment
- traces of old buildings in the wall along the Kattenburgerstraat
- the 1960s commander's house and the floating boardwalk round the swimming area

title: Mariniersbrug, Amsterdam's Chicago bridge
summary: A single steel bascule bridge of 1935 whose leaf tips back into a brick bastion, modelled on the bridges over the Chicago River. Sources still disagree on who designed it: Piet Kramer or Jan Leupen.
body:
The first bridge over the Dijksgracht, a swing bridge of 1878, had to leave a wide channel for ships heading to the yards on Oostenburg. By the 1930s traffic had grown, and the railway works of the time meant the road had to dip under a raised track, so a new, lower bridge was needed.

The result is unlike any other Amsterdam bridge: a bascule of the Chicago type, a single leaf 22 metres long that swings up around an axle hidden in the south pier, with its counterweight in a cellar below. The national register calls it the first of its kind in the Netherlands. Its steel trusses run above the deck as well as under it, and are rounded off where they sink into the bascule cellar when the bridge opens. The whole span, 876 tonnes with its counterweight, was built in Amsterdam-Noord and floated into place in September 1935; it opened that December.

The register and the Dutch bridge foundation name Piet Kramer as designer, and the south pier does look like his Amsterdam School work. The bridge historian Frank Smit names Jan Leupen of Public Works, inspired by bridges over the Chicago River, and a book on Kramer's bridges leaves it out.

Being listed, the bridge cannot be widened, though it is narrow for cyclists and walkers.

Look for:
- the abstract carving on the south pier
- the rounded truss ends by the bascule pier
- the glass bridge-keeper's cabin of 2000 by Hans Bloem

title: Old Kattenburg's last corner
summary: Between 1962 and 1968 every house on Kattenburg was demolished and the street plan wiped out. One short strip of the Kattenburgergracht escaped: a corner by Willem Kromhout with a round stair turret, a fire and police post in two old warehouses, and a girls' school of 1868.
body:
Kattenburg was a poor shipyard neighbourhood; before 1940 one house in eight already stood empty, condemned. Under the reconstruction plan of 1953 all its houses were pulled down between 1962 and 1968, its streets erased and replaced by flats. Unusually, the residents' committee backed the clearance and fought only for the right to return. What survived of the old island is one corner and the row next to it.

The corner building of 1897, where the Kattenburgerplein meets the Kattenburgergracht, is one of only three buildings in Amsterdam by Willem Kromhout, architect of the American Hotel. A round stair turret stitches its two fronts together: a shop with a house above on the square, a double house on the canal. The shop has long been a pharmacy.

At nos. 19–21 two warehouses, Ceres and Neptunus, were turned in 1880 into an auxiliary post for the fire brigade and the police, with paired round-arched windows and battlements in the style of assistant city architect Willem Springer, who designed the city's fire stations of those years.

Nos. 23–41 are the Parelschool of 1868 by Bastiaan de Greef, a public school for 200 girls with a teacher's house and a separate gym, its one big classroom split in two by a partition.

Look for:
- Kromhout's round stair turret on the corner
- the half-columns and battlements of the old fire post
- the school's three parts: classrooms, teacher's house, low gym

title: The gate to a church that is gone (Annakerk presbytery)
summary: The wide gate in this presbytery on the Wittenburgergracht was the only way into St Anne's church, which hid behind the houses with no front of its own. The church was demolished in 1978; the gate now leads to nothing.
body:
St Anne's parish began as a hidden Catholic church, set up in 1720 in the former wine warehouse of the merchant Ambrosius de Pool on what is now the Prins Hendrikkade, and nicknamed De Pool. Around 1900 it got a proper neo-Gothic church on Wittenburg by P.J. Bekkers, consecrated on 20 September 1900. The church stood right behind the houses of the Wittenburgergracht, with its back wall in the water of the Kattenburgervaart, and it had no entrance front at all: you reached it through a gate in the presbytery on the canal.

The church closed in 1970 and was demolished in 1978, when most of old Wittenburg went. Its Adema organ of 1916, built partly with material from the hidden church, went to the St Vincent's church in Volendam. The presbytery stayed, a narrow house of two window bays with an extra bay over the wide gate, and is still lived in.

The building is private; the point is what you see from the quay.

Look for:
- the broad gate that once led to the church
- the two steps up to the front door in the porch beside it
- the canal side behind, where the church stood in the water

title: Oosterkerk, the islands' church the city nearly demolished
summary: The shipwrights' church of 1669–1671, a Greek cross with a domed lantern, still strikes the hours on a Hemony bell and keeps the clockwork of the old Exchange tower on the Rokin. In the 1960s the city meant to pull it down; neighbours stopped it.
body:
In 1659 the city decided to build two churches for its new islands, first in wood. The stone Oosterkerk rose in 1669–1671 on Wittenburg: Daniël Stalpaert's design was approved in July 1669, but the church accounts of 1672 pay Adriaan Dortsman 500 guilders for "the architecture", and the stone-rich, livelier result looks like his. It is a Greek cross with low corner rooms and a lead-clad wooden lantern on the crossing. It opened on 4 October 1671.

The bell in the lantern was cast by Pieter Hemony in 1671, and its Latin rim says that with its strokes it divides time into equal parts; it still sounds the hours and half-hours. The clockwork below it came from the tower of Hendrick de Keyser's old Exchange, which stood on the Rokin.

The church closed in 1963, falling apart. The city took it over in 1969 and at first planned to demolish it as part of the islands' renewal; the residents prevented that and it was largely restored. From 1985 to 2012 social organisations used it; now it holds concerts, exhibitions, meetings and offices, and the Stichting Oosterkerk organises free concerts. The Van Oeckelen organ of 1871 is inside.

Look for:
- the lantern on the crossing of the hipped roofs
- the clock under it, from the old Exchange
- the stone entrance porch with its balustrade

title: Sluisdeurenloods, the wooden shed that moved for the IJ tunnel
summary: A timber workshop of 1882–1893 where the city made and repaired lock gates. In 1957 it was taken apart for the IJ tunnel and rebuilt 125 metres away. It is the last all-wooden 19th-century harbour building in the city, and now an art and event space.
body:
Amsterdam's lock gates were made and mended in this shed, built between 1882 and 1893 entirely of wood and at first open on two sides. Before 1952 the open sides were closed. Then the IJ tunnel came: in 1957 the shed was taken apart and rebuilt 125 metres to the north-east, on land newly made in the water. The frame of round timber posts and part of the original planking came along; the concrete base, the narrow-gauge rails, the sliding doors and the rooflight date from the move.

The city's bridges and locks department used it until 2014. The register values it as the only all-wooden harbour building of the nineteenth century left, and, with a 1930s double house for railway staff, the last relic of the old buildings on the Dijksgracht. The scars of all the changes are still readable in the frame and the planking. It became a municipal monument in 2022.

Since 2015 it has been used by Mediamatic, the art and science centre next door, for events; it can also be hired.

Look for:
- the round timber posts of the frame
- the narrow-gauge rails leading out of the shed
- the long rooflight on the ridge

title: Lifeboat shed on the Windroosplein
summary: A smithy of 1883 that became the Amsterdam base of the North and South Holland Lifeboat Society in 1896, with its own covered harbour on the Dijksgracht. The society's name in big black letters was a sight for train passengers for decades.
body:
The islands were lined with shipyards and the trades that served them. This was one of them: a smithy with a house over it, built in 1883 to a design by H.J. Amesz. In 1896 the architect C.B. Posthumus Meyjes rebuilt it for the Noord- en Zuid-Hollandsche Reddingmaatschappij, the lifeboat society, and the low shed was probably then lengthened towards the water of the Dijksgracht, so that it became a covered boatyard. The society painted its name in large black letters on a white field, both on the street front and on the back wall facing the Dijksgracht, which countless train passengers saw on their way into Centraal Station.

Lifeboats were stored and serviced here until 1995. The building was thoroughly done up after 1999 and became an event venue with its own inner harbour. After a sale it was rebuilt again and reopened in October 2026 as Amsterdam Wharf, a hall for business events, so most days you see it from the outside. The post-war rebuilding of Wittenburg cleared away all the other industry on the head of the island, so this is the last trace of it.

Look for:
- the society's name on the front and on the back wall seen from the Dijksgracht or the train
- the low boathouse with the taller house set across it
- the water gate on the Dijksgracht side

title: The VOC and Admiralty ropewalks
summary: Behind these two 1660 front buildings ran ropewalks half a kilometre long, where the East India Company and the Admiralty twisted the rope for their fleets. In 1673 a fire here was the first ever fought with Jan van der Heyden's new fire engines.
body:
On Oostenburg the Dutch East India Company (VOC) and the Admiralty of Amsterdam each built a ropewalk in 1660, side by side and separated only by an inner wall. The long sheds ran some 500 metres back from the canal towards the IJ, behind thick walls because of the fire risk of the tar kettles. The two buildings on the Oostenburgergracht were their fronts, used for storing rope and hemp and as offices. On 12 January 1673 fire broke out in the Admiralty ropewalk; it was put out with the fire engines designed by Jan van der Heyden, their first use.

The ropewalks closed in 1887 and were pulled down around 1920, except the fronts. In 1949–1950 Werkspoor, the last big industry on the island, had both restored by A.A. Kok and opened a company museum in them (1950–2011); Duintjer designed the modernist entrance building of 1952 between them, and Werkspoor won the city's architecture prize in 1958. The neighbouring office of the factory, from the late nineteenth century, housed its company school.

The VOC building was a sugar store into the nineteenth century, hence its nickname Suikerhuis (sugar house).

Look for:
- the VOC arms and the A VOC monogram in the pediment of the VOC building
- the two lions with swords and blue anchors on top of no. 81, once on the back of the ropewalk
- the 1947 plaque to Tsar Peter the Great, who may have stayed here in 1697

title: Werkspoor's halls on Oostenburg
summary: An order for 40 locomotives and 400 wagons from South Africa built these five brick halls in 1898–1905; the first cast-iron diesel ship engine came out of them in 1903. Nearby stand a riveted 'factory cathedral' of 1929 and a bridge the company built for itself.
body:
From 1660 Oostenburg was the VOC's yard; from 1827 it was a centre of engine-building. In 1891 the Nederlandsche Fabriek van Werktuigen en Spoorwegmaterieel restarted here, soon known by its telegram address, Werkspoor. When South Africa ordered 40 locomotives and 400 goods wagons, the works had to grow: A.L. van Gendt designed halls 1 to 3 (1898), hall 5 for locomotives followed in 1903 and hall 4 for turbines around 1905. Ship engines were built in them too, the first cast-iron diesel ship engine in 1903. In 1922 halls 4 and 5 partly burned and were rebuilt at once in the old style.

Next to them the shipbuilder NSM rented the north-west of the site from 1894; a small brick mess and washroom on the Conradstraat and a building of the old power plant (building A) are among the few relics. A footbridge without a city number crosses the Oostenburgerdwarsvaart; it is a private bridge, very probably made by Werkspoor itself. Further north stands Stelplaats 3 of 1929, a riveted steel hall so tall because finished ship engines were hoisted from it into ships lying in the Wittenburgervaart. Stork, as the firm became, closed here in 1990.

The Van Gendthallen are being converted for the Drift Museum and other tenants; you can see the outsides from the quays.

Look for:
- the cast-iron window frames and the 28-pane windows along the Wittenburgervaart
- the stepped friezes on the gable ends
- the height of Stelplaats 3 on the Oostenburgermiddenstraat

title: The Woning-Maatschappij houses, the islands' last old workers' street
summary: Workers' flats of 1874 by A.L. van Gendt, built by a company that pointedly refused to call itself a charity. In 1953 the city zoned all of Oostenburg for industry; they survived anyway, and are now the only old workers' housing left on the Eastern Islands.
body:
The first homes were handed over on 1 May 1874: two one-room flats at Nieuwe Oostenburgerdwarsstraat 9 and 11. The rest of the complex, three long blocks on the Nieuwe Oostenburgerstraat and its cross street and two small ones on the Oostenburgervoorstraat, had two-room flats with windows front and back. It was an early example of large-scale, decent housing for workers, and the N.V. Woning-Maatschappij insisted it was a business, not a charity, although its shares were bought by the same wealthy Amsterdammers who had funded philanthropic housing. Building so many homes in one go was new. The architect was A.L. van Gendt, who would later design the Werkspoor halls just across the Wittenburgervaart.

The reconstruction plan of 1953 zoned the whole of Oostenburg as industrial land so Werkspoor could expand. The company, still the owner, objected; the city replied that this did not mean demolition any time soon. In the 1960s and 1970s almost all other old housing on the islands was cleared, so these sober blocks are the only reminder of how the islands' workers lived.

The houses are lived in; see them from the street and from the far side of the water.

Look for:
- the Flemish gables over the middle and end stairwells
- the white keystones over the windows
- the backs of the blocks on the Wittenburgervaart, facing Van Gendt's halls

title: Tjerk Hiddesschool, the school children fought over and Constant's studio
summary: When this school opened in 1914, the Oostenburg children moved here were ambushed by Wittenburg children armed with sticks and had to be walked in by teachers and parents. Fifty years later the painter Constant took it over as his studio and worked here until his death.
body:
The city built this school of twelve classrooms in 1913–14 for public primary school no. 1, which had to leave the neighbouring island of Oostenburg to make room for the growing Werkspoor engineering works. It stands with its back to the water, where the Kattenburgervaart meets the Dijksgracht, its stair tower on the corner; the playground lay behind the wall on the street.

The move did not go quietly. According to the Haagsche Courant of June 1914, the children, most of whom lived on Oostenburg, were lain in wait for on Wittenburg by local children armed with sticks, and only reached their new school under the escort of teachers and parents. From around 1920 the building held the Almondeschool and the Tjerk Hiddesschool, until they closed from the late 1930s on.

After the Second World War it found other uses, among them a playground club and artists' studios. From 1964 until his death in 2005 the painter Constant Nieuwenhuys, of the CoBrA group and the utopian city New Babylon, worked here. It is not open to the public; see it from the street and from across the water.

Look for:
- the wall with its gate on the Derde Wittenburgerdwarsstraat, where the playground was
- the stair tower on the corner of the Kattenburgervaart and the Dijksgracht, seen from across the water

title: Kweekschool voor de Zeevaart, the school for the sons of Dogger Bank
summary: Founded in 1785 for the sons of sailors killed or wounded at the Dogger Bank. The boys lived in, rose at five, drilled on a ship in the courtyard and promised never to sail on a slave ship. Willem III laid the first stone of this building in 1878.
body:
In 1781 the Dutch fleet fought the British at the Dogger Bank. A patriotic fund, the Vaderlandsch Fonds ter Aanmoediging van 's Lands Zeedienst, opened a school on this spot in 1785 to train the sons of the dead and wounded as seamen, free of charge; when too few applied, the poorest boys of the city were taken in too. The city lent it a building, the former Willige Rasphuis. There were 150 places and nearly 400 applicants a year. Boys of twelve to sixteen lived in and wore a uniform, so no difference of creed or birth would show. They rose at five, had sewing lessons and practised on a real ship set up in the courtyard. Every pupil promised never to serve on a slave ship. A lazy boy ate at table number zero, the idlers' table, from what the others left.

Napoleon closed the school in 1811; King Willem I reopened it in 1814. King Willem III laid the first stone of this building, by Willem Springer and his son Jan, on 4 May 1878, and it was in use from 1880. In 1971 the school merged into the Hogere Zeevaartschool and later moved out. The building now holds offices and homes; you see it from the quay.

Look for:
- the relief of seafaring in the top of the central gable
- the gate with the stone Kweekschool voor de zeevaart and MDCCCLXXX
- the rounded corner on the Schippersgracht, where the telegraph office was

title: Oud Nico, the castle fire station on the IJ
summary: A fire station of 1889–1890 built like a little castle, with salamanders on the keystones. Its crews crossed to Noord by ferry. The brigade left in 1973; artists and former staff saved it from demolition, and Stadsherstel restored it in 2010–2011.
body:
In 1874 Amsterdam became the first Dutch city with a fire brigade made up entirely of professionals, after volunteers bungled a big fire near the Rembrandtplein in 1870. As the harbour grew east, a main station was needed near the IJ, and in 1889–1890 Willem Springer of Public Works drew this one like a small castle, with battlements and corner turrets, perhaps to give people faith in the new professional service. It had a signal room, a shed for the pumps, a stable, a canteen, and towers at the back for drying hoses and for climbing drills; dormitories above slept 44 firemen. When needed, the crews crossed to Noord by ferry. The station's predecessor in the Waag on the Nieuwmarkt was known by the letter N, which in the spelling alphabet is Nico, and the name stuck.

The brigade moved in 1973 to a new Nico by the IJ tunnel. Staff could keep their flats and artists took the rest. When the IJ banks were redeveloped and demolition threatened, the residents set up a foundation in 1992 and got the building listed. Stadsherstel took it over from the city in 2006 and restored it; it now holds a showroom, studios and homes.

Look for:
- the salamanders and firemen's gear carved on the keystones of the big arches
- the battlemented turrets on the corners
- the smithy of 1905 to the right, joined to the station by a wall with a gate

title: Steam diamond works on the Recht Boomssloot
summary: Seven storeys high counting the basement, exceptional in the Nieuwmarkt quarter: a steam-driven diamond-cutting factory of 1889 with the boiler in the basement and more than ninety mills on the floors. Since 1978 it has held homes.
body:
Count the floors: with the basement this corner block has seven, far more than anything around it on the Recht Boomssloot. It was built in 1889 to a design by C.A. Bombach for S.J. Boas as a steam diamond-cutting works. The boiler house, the engine room and the coal store were in the basement; the steam engine drove the cutting mills spread over the floors above, more than ninety of them. That is why all the storeys are the same height and every one has the same rows of large windows: cutters needed daylight at the mill. Bombach designed other cutting works in these years, among them one for J. Vigeveno round the corner on the Krom Boomssloot.

In 1978 the factory was converted into five homes, and it is private; the outside is easy to read from the quay and the Brandewijnsteeg.

Look for:
- the equal floors with their long rows of arched windows on both fronts
- the porch on the right with its iron gate and stone stoop of eight steps
- the side front on the narrow Brandewijnsteeg, seven bays long

title: Jan de Liefde school, now De Boomsspijker
summary: A Christian primary school of 1929–1930 in late Amsterdam School style, built by the society Tot Heil des Volks and named after the preacher who founded it. Since 1977 it has been the neighbourhood centre De Boomsspijker.
body:
The preacher Jan de Liefde (1814–1869) began with Bible readings in a house on the Goudsbloemgracht, now the Willemsstraat, and in 1855 founded the society Tot Heil des Volks (for the salvation of the people) to spread that work across the country, with schools among its means. In 1929–1930 the society built this Christian primary school on the corner of the Korte Koningsdwarsstraat and named it after him. The architect A. Ingwersen worked in a late Amsterdam School manner: two tall bays climb the front with ladder-like leaded windows that run round their corners, and the corner block rises above the rest under its own saddle roof. Inside were thirteen classrooms, a gym and two rooms for slöjd, school handicraft.

Since 1977 the building has housed the neighbourhood centre De Boomsspijker, founded in 1964.

Look for:
- the ladder windows of the two bays, turning the corners
- the strips of small-paned windows cut into the brick
- the tall chimney on the corner, running up past the eaves

title: Drijfhout's gold and silver works, on the site of café Victoria
summary: A stone front fit for a bank in the narrow Nes, built in 1912–1913 for the gold and silver firm H. Drijfhout & Zn. Its motto, Heb Durf En Zorg, spells the firm's initials. It replaced a café-chantant that staged wrestling matches; since 1988 it has been a hotel.
body:
The heavy rusticated stone front looks like a bank's, which is a lot for a street as narrow as the Nes. Joseph Herman designed it in 1912 for H. Drijfhout & Zn., gold and silver smiths founded in 1827 in Balk in Gaasterland, so the arms of Gaasterland hang beside those of Amsterdam. Over the door are the arms of Saint Eligius (Sint Eloy), the goldsmiths' saint, a cup and a ring, and two women's heads with necklace and diadem, which a newspaper report read as Luxury and Vanity. The motto reads Heb Durf En Zorg (have courage and care): its initials are those of H. Drijfhout En Zoon. In the basement an oven burned the dust swept from the workshops, and a good deal of precious metal came out of it.

The factory replaced, among other buildings, the café Victoria at nos. 13–15. From 1886 De Vic had its own theatre company and held wrestling matches for men and for women; it closed in 1906.

Drijfhout stayed until the end of 1988 and moved to Zuidoost, where the firm still is. Since then the building has been the Rho Hotel, and its lobby is the old public hall of the firm.

Look for:
- the motto and the name H. DRIJFHOUT & ZN over the door
- the year stones 1827 and 1912 in the frieze
- the rough-hewn stone blocks of the ground floor

title: Raamgracht 4, the charity office that became Vrij Nederland's
summary: An eighteen-year-old founded the charity Liefdadigheid naar Vermogen in 1871; in 1913–1914 it built this office with a relief of charity on its front. After the war the resistance-born weekly Vrij Nederland had its editors here until 2015.
body:
In 1871 Louis Blankenberg, aged eighteen, founded the society Liefdadigheid naar Vermogen (charity according to one's means) with his brother, his sister and a friend, inspired by the Charity Organization Society set up in London two years before. It helped the jobless find work, saw that children went to school, fought drink abuse, gave money to the old and sick and lent money where that helped. Blankenberg put the difference with the city's poor relief in an image: the city pasted an old newspaper over a broken window; his society put in a new pane and made sure it did not break again.

In 1886 the society bought this corner with donations, and in 1913–1914 the architect J.W. Hanrath built it a new office with bell gables, meant to sit easily among the old canal houses. In the 1940s it was renamed Zorg en Bijstand, and in 1975 it moved out.

After the war the weekly Vrij Nederland, which began as a resistance paper, had its editorial office here. One of its editors, Igor Cornelissen, called a volume of his memoirs simply Raamgracht 4. The paper left in 2015 and the building was turned into flats.

Look for:
- the stone over the first floor with three scenes of charity
- the stones ANNO and 1912, the year of the design
- the second bell gable, on the Kloveniersburgwal side

title: 't Schipblok, a liqueur distiller's shop with a warning against drink
summary: A Catholic politician's liqueur distillery left two buildings here: an Italianate office of 1879–1881 on the canal and a stepped-gabled shop of 1902 on the corner, crowned by lions with drinking jugs and carrying a saying against drinking too much.
body:
J.B. van Dijk owned the liqueur distillery 't Schipblok and was a leading Catholic: a city councillor from 1901 to 1907 and a member of parliament from 1918 to 1929. In 1879–1881 G.C.E. Rademaker built him a large office on the Oudezijds Achterburgwal, Italian in manner with a low mezzanine floor above the cornice, and the liqueur was probably distilled there.

In 1902 Jan Stuyt and Jos Cuypers gave him a shop, probably with a tasting room, on the corner of the Oude Hoogstraat, built like a sixteenth-century Dutch house with stepped gables, red tiles and small panes. A newspaper of the day welcomed the old Dutch style. On top of each gable a lion holds a shield with a flapkan, a lidded drinking jug, gilded on the street side and silvered on the canal. A stone shows an old ship over the name 't Schipblok, and below it runs a saying that warns against drinking too much: on a liqueur shop.

The office later housed the editors of De kleine kapitalist, a financial paper, and in the 1990s, for a time, Henk Schiffmacher's tattoo museum. Both buildings are seen from the street.

Look for:
- the two lions with their flapkan
- the ship stone and the warning under it
- the year anchors 1902 on the canal side of the corner shop

title: Feldmann's tobacco warehouse, later the Bhagwan disco
summary: A brick warehouse of 1914–1915 built for tobacco traders, with goods doors below and a bay-windowed office floor for receiving clients. It went on to hold carpets, a radio shop, a dance bar, the Bhagwan movement's disco Zorba the Buddha and now a Bulldog hotel.
body:
W. Noorlander designed this sober brick warehouse in 1914–1915 for the tobacco traders Feldmann & Co. The bales went in through the two wide arched doors at street level and up to the hoist doors in the two gables. The first floor, behind the two bay windows, held the offices, the sample room and the room where clients were received. The firm was founded in 1904 and went into liquidation in 1934.

After that the building had a run of tenants that reads like a history of the street. In the 1950s a dealer in Persian carpets used it; in the 1960s it was a store of the state's Domeinen department and a radio shop moved in. Then came a bar-dancing, The Toyshop, and from about 1983 to 1992 Zorba the Buddha, the disco of the Bhagwan movement. In 2001–2002 the coffeeshop chain The Bulldog renovated it, and it is now a Bulldog hotel.

Look for:
- the two goods doors with the four barred round-arched windows between them
- the two different bays of the office floor, one square, one three-sided
- the hoist beams in both gable tops

title: Sibbelwoningen, the dyke houses saved by squatters
summary: Two long rows of mirrored workers' houses on the Hoogte Kadijk, from the early 19th century and about 1828, with front doors on the dyke and basement homes below. Squatters and neighbours stopped their demolition; restored for a symbolic euro, they then smelled of rotten fish.
body:
Two long rows of identical small houses line the Hoogte Kadijk, built in mirrored pairs under one long roof. They are dyke houses: a short stoop leads up to the living floor on the dyke, while steps go down beside it to a basement home at the level of the Laagte Kadijk behind. The row at nos. 84–106 dates from the early nineteenth century; the one at nos. 112–150 was built around 1828 to a design by G. Moele, J. Moele and Gerrit Moele. They were workers' homes, for people from the Rapenburgergracht (now the Entrepotdok) and for men of the brewery De Gekroonde Valk.

After a century and a half they were worn out and demolition loomed. In the 1970s squatters moved in and neighbours fought for them; in 1984 all forty were listed one by one. In 2002 the housing corporation De Key bought them for a symbolic euro and restored them house by house, held up for years by a court fight with the residents over moving out. They were handed back on 28 April 2011. In 2015 Het Parool reported that the restored houses had smelled of rotten fish for four years.

Look for:
- the gable stone Van de dijk af (Off the dyke) by Hans 't Mannetje on the east end
- the bottle-shaped mural De brouwers (2023) by Gino Bud Hoiting on a side wall
- the 1990s flats at nos. 108–110 filling the gap between the two rows

title: Salerno, one of the first model blocks for workers
summary: The first block of the Vereeniging Salerno, founded in 1853 to give working families healthy homes. Jan Leliman had seen model workers' housing at the 1851 Great Exhibition in London and built 48 flats on the sewer and the water mains, with no money left for ornament.
body:
In 1853 the merchant Simon Wolf Josephus Jitta, the doctor E.C. Büchner and others founded the Vereeniging Salerno, one of the first societies in the country set up to improve working people's housing. This is its first block, built in 1854–1856. The architect Jan Leliman, then in his twenties, had visited the 1851 Great Exhibition in London and been struck by its models of workers' homes. His 48 flats were new for their time: they were connected to the sewer and the water mains, and each flat was meant to be as independent as possible. There is almost no ornament, because, Leliman wrote, the money had to be spent sparingly.

The front block on the street has sixteen two-room and sixteen one-room flats on four floors, reached by stairs. The narrow projections that run up the front and end in points held the privies. Passages two metres wide lead from the street to the yard behind, where more homes stood back to back. In 1856 the Algemeen Handelsblad went to look and praised the architect for avoiding anything that felt like an institution. Salerno went on building; Leliman also designed its block of 1872 in the Pijp.

Look for:
- the stone Salerno 1854 and the memorial stone dated 1853
- the pointed projections of the privies
- the bands of yellowish mortar that zigzag towards the top floor

title: Militair Hospitaal, the army hospital where the cancer hospital grew up
summary: The garrison hospital of 1868–1870, where the Antoni van Leeuwenhoek cancer hospital lived from 1929 to the 1970s; its banner now says nescio. Beside it, the army's clothing store and the state medicine depot, which had its own gate in the railway fence.
body:
Along the inner side of the Singelgracht the War Department built a row of buildings for the garrison city. The largest is the Military Hospital of 1868–1870, with about 250 beds, on the old Diemen bastion. The architects' society wrote to the minister in 1868 to complain: the site lay near a cemetery, the Rhine railway and factories, and the building looked like nothing the capital deserved. Work went on, and in February 1871 the first patients came in. When Amsterdam lost its garrison after the First World War the building half emptied, and in 1929 the Netherlands Cancer Institute and its Antoni van Leeuwenhoek hospital moved in. They left for Slotervaart in the 1970s. Ten years later the building became about eighty homes, the Nesciohuis: the banner over the middle door that said Militair Hospitaal now says nescio.

To the east stand the army's clothing store of 1873–1875, with the state arms in its pediment, and the State Medicine Depot of 1889, which made and stored medicines for the colonies, the garrisons, the navy and the prisons; a movable section in the railway fence let its deliveries in. Since 1998 it has been the head office of the housing corporation Stadgenoot.

Look for:
- the word nescio on the banner, and Da van Daalen's bronze relief with the first line of Nescio's De uitvreter
- the gilded inscription anno rijksmagazijn van geneesmiddelen 1889 in the courtyard
- the painted state arms in the pediment of the clothing store

title: Physisch Laboratorium, where Van der Waals worked
summary: The university's physics laboratory of 1880–1882, where Johannes Diderik van der Waals worked from about 1883; his successor Pieter Zeeman outgrew it and got the new lab next door in 1923. The lecture hall rises straight out of the canal. Now private flats.
body:
When Amsterdam's new city university started in 1877, Johannes Diderik van der Waals became its first professor of physics. His first laboratory was in the Handboogdoelen; around 1883 he moved into this one, built in 1880–1882 on the Plantage Muidergracht to a design by B. de Greef and W. Springer of Public Works. At the back a wide block rises straight out of the water. That was the big lecture hall, with a glass roof and blinds so it could be made dark for experiments with light, and round its frieze ran the names of eighteen physicists, Archimedes, Huygens, Newton, Faraday and Maxwell among them. Van der Waals won the Nobel Prize for physics in 1910.

In 1908 Pieter Zeeman, a Nobel laureate himself, succeeded him as director. He found the building too cramped for his magnetic and optical work and had to wait until 1923 for the new laboratory next door, now named after him.

The university left in 1990. In 1995 the building was divided into nine flats, under the name Villa Einstein; it is private.

Look for:
- Natuurkundig Laboratorium on the frieze over the columned door
- the lecture hall standing in the canal, seen from across the Plantage Muidergracht
- the balustrade with vases along the roof edge

title: Huis met de Vazen and its coach house
summary: A villa of 1874 on the corner of the Plantage Middenlaan, named for the zinc vases on its front, with zinc statues in its niches. In its back garden stands a coach house of 1907–1909, one of the last designs of Kropholler and Staal before they split in a quarrel.
body:
The Plantage calls this corner villa the Huis met de Vazen (house with the vases), after the big zinc vases set on brackets in its front. Willem Springer and his son Jan designed it in 1874 for J. Coninck Westenberg, a former alderman for finance and a stockbroker. The front folds in and out: the middle bay is pulled far back, so the walls on either side stand forward like three-sided bays, and in the niches above the vases stand zinc statues. Much of what looks like stone, the bands, cornices and window frames, is cast from Portland cement. Jan Springer added the low wing on the Middenlaan in 1893.

In the back garden on the Plantage Lepellaan stands a coach house with a stable and a coachman's home, dated 1907 over the door. It was one of the last designs of A.J. Kropholler and J.F. Staal, who parted in a quarrel in 1910. A long garden fence of 1874, wrought iron on brick piers, joins the two. Both buildings are private and seen from the street.

Look for:
- the zinc vases and the statues in the niches of the Lepellaan front
- the stepped gable of the coach house, with Ao 1907 over the door
- the wrought-iron fence running between the two

title: The horse-tram director's villa (Plantage Middenlaan 60)
summary: The Amsterdamsche Omnibus Maatschappij, which ran the horse trams, built this villa in 1878–1880 for its director Karel Schadd, who also co-founded Elsevier. Later a retired central bank president lived here, then the city's tax collectors moved in.
body:
The Amsterdamsche Omnibus Maatschappij ran the city's horse trams, and in 1878–1880 it had G.B. Salm build this villa as the home of its director, Karel H. Schadd. Schadd, a bookseller, had founded the company in 1872 with a handful of neighbours, among them the Artis director Westerman and the man next door at no. 62. In 1875 the company had put up a long stable for its tram horses inside this same block, also by Salm. In 1880 Schadd was one of the founders of the publishing house Elsevier. He moved away in 1899.

From 1912 until his death in 1917 the retired president of De Nederlandsche Bank, N.P. van den Berg, lived here. The city, which owned the villa after taking over the tram company, then turned the ground floor into a branch office for municipal taxes until 1923. In 2011, together with no. 62, it briefly housed Henk Schiffmacher's tattoo museum.

Look for:
- the small balcony on lion-headed scroll brackets over the door
- the paired little square windows of the mezzanine under the cornice
- the plaster scored with grooves to pass for stone

title: Hodshon and Van Limmik, two Reformed homes in the Amstelhof garden
summary: Two homes for old Reformed people built in the garden of the diaconate's old people's home, now H'ART. In the Hodshon house of 1878 couples had to have their own income, so a widow had to move out when her husband died.
body:
Behind the Nieuwe Keizersgracht lay the garden of the Reformed diaconate's home for old men and women, the Amstelhof (now H'ART Museum), and two charities built in it. The Magdalena Hodshon Stichting of 1877–1878, by P.J. Hamer, has a taller middle house for the warden and four one-room flats, and low wings with eight homes for old couples. It was paid for from the estate of J.F.A.M. Witsen baron Straalman, who died in 1865, left his fortune to the Reformed church and asked for the home to carry his mother's name. Couples had to have an income of their own, and that rule bit when the breadwinner died: the widow had to leave, for the Hilmanshofje in the Nieuwe Looiersstraat. Later nurses of the Amstelhof lived here; since 2008 it has been supported housing for young people.

Next door, at no. 1, the Van Limmikstichting of 1894–1895 by C.B. Posthumus Meyjes had room for twelve old couples and about twenty single old men, all Reformed. The family of the deacon N.J. van Limmik paid for it; his sister chose half the residents and the diaconate the other half. In the 1970s it became part of the Amstelhof nursing home.

Look for:
- VAN LIMMIK STICHTING carved under the middle window
- the wall anchors shaped like Latin crosses on the Hodshon house
- the Vredeman de Vries style gable with vases on the Van Limmik house

title: Huidekoperstraat, the showpiece of the first housing association
summary: Seventy-two workers' homes of 1869–1870 behind a front as stately as a row of merchants' houses. They were built by the first housing association in the Netherlands, which wanted its rent on time and put drunks out on the street.
body:
In 1852 a group of well-off Amsterdammers, among them the former mayor Pieter Huidekoper, founded the Vereeniging ten behoeve der Arbeidersklasse (association for the benefit of the working class), the first housing association in the Netherlands. Each member put in 2,000 guilders for at most 3% interest. The homes were meant for respectable families: that meant paying the rent promptly and taking in no lodgers, and drunkenness or indecent behaviour meant eviction.

Its first large block, on today's Planciusstraat (1856), was a plain model; this L-shaped block of 1869–70, on the street named after Huidekoper, was its showpiece. Pieter Hamer, who designed several of its blocks, put 72 homes and two corner shops behind one symmetrical front, 28 windows wide, with white plastered strips marking each stair entrance and rounded corners at both ends. It hardly fell short of the fine houses going up at the same time on the Westeinde and Oosteinde, opposite the Paleis voor Volksvlijt. At the back, each home had a small extension for the kitchen and the privy.

The city took the association over in stages from 1962, and almost all of its houses are now let by the housing corporation Ymere. Look from the street.

Look for:
- the 28-window front, mirrored around its centre
- the richer middle bays with a balustrade between the dormers
- the rounded corners on the Weteringschans and the Falckstraat
- photographer Jacob Olie's house across the street at no. 19

title: The villas on the Weteringschans, facing the Rijksmuseum
summary: A row of freestanding villas with towers, spires and lion-head gargoyles on the strip between the Weteringschans and the Singelgracht, a rare sight inside the old city line. Their neighbours by the Museumbrug were knocked down for two offices nicknamed Peper en Zout.
body:
Villas are a rarity inside the Singelgracht, the outer canal that once marked the city limit. This strip of land between the Weteringschans and the water, opposite the Rijksmuseum, is the exception: between 1878 and 1884 a row of freestanding houses went up here, and four of them survive, each with a fence of its own.

The oldest, no. 24 (1878–1880, by P.F. Laarman), has a round corner tower topped by a balustrade and a flagpole; from 1934 it also served as an office of the life insurer NILLMY. J. Daverman designed the triple villa at 10–14, which ends in two towers with spires, and the double villa at 20–22, where the brackets under the cornice carry women's heads, lions' heads and fluting in turn. N. Vos gave the white double villa at 16–18 a stricter, classical front.

Near the Museumbrug, older villas of the row were demolished for two office blocks by Frans van Gool, nicknamed Peper en Zout (pepper and salt). The city listed those as municipal monuments in 2022, against the owner's wishes.

The villas are private: look from the pavement or from across the Singelgracht.

Look for:
- the round stair tower of no. 14 with eight lion-head gargoyles
- the women's and lions' heads under the cornice of 20–22
- the iron fence of arrowheads and pine cones at 20–22
- the gate with a name plate in the fence of no. 14

title: Barlaeus Gymnasium and its palace of classics
summary: A school that traces itself to a Latin school of 1342 moved here in 1885, into a building dressed in the classical learning it taught, with ancient thinkers on the front. Until 1926 it was the only gymnasium in Amsterdam.
body:
The school traces its roots to a 'Hoofdschool' of 1342 that became the Latin school. Amsterdam's two Latin schools, at the Oude Kerk and the Nieuwe Kerk, merged in 1678 and moved to the Singel; in 1847 the school became the city gymnasium. By the 1880s the old building was too small, badly lit and poorly ventilated, and in 1883 the council decided to build a new one at the edge of the city, between the Weteringschans and the Zieseniskade.

Willem Springer and his son gave it classical forms meant to reflect the classical schooling inside: stone corner pavilions with portrait medallions and trophies, and on the central bay a sculpture group by Bart van Hove above the words ANNO GYMNASIUM 1885. It opened on 22 December 1885. Until the Vossius Gymnasium was founded in 1926 it was the city's only gymnasium; in 1927 it took the name of the 17th-century scholar Caspar Barlaeus. W.F. Hermans published his first piece, aged eighteen, in its school paper.

In 2002–2004 it was joined to the former girls' industrial school next door, and the main entrance moved there. It is a working school: look from the street, with Paradiso opposite.

Look for:
- Van Hove's group on top of the central bay
- the portrait medallions on the corner pavilions
- the female herm between the top windows of the central bay
- the old front door, no longer the way in

title: Bensdorp's chocolate office on the Amstel
summary: A turreted head office of 1899 for the chocolate maker Bensdorp, with tile panels, a carved woman's head and an empty canopy where a woman with a basket of cocoa beans once stood. The old chocolate works are now a hotel.
body:
Gerardus Bensdorp learned the confectioner's trade in cities such as Brussels, Paris and Vienna, came back to Amsterdam in 1840 and opened his first factory on the Amstel in 1849. In 1899 the firm had A.J. Joling build this head office in a style close to the Nieuwe Kunst, the Dutch Art Nouveau. The front follows the old, jagged plot line and turns a rounded corner that grows into a small tower with a spire.

Joling kept working for the firm: in 1911 he turned the hayloft into offices and bridged the Wapen van Delftsteeg, and in 1912 the courtyard got a glass roof. In 1906 the Amsterdam works employed 150 men and 100 girls. The Amsterdam factory closed in 1926 and production went to Bussum, where Bensdorp cocoa was made until 2000. The old Amsterdam complex now houses the Eden Hotel.

At the corner of the former Suykerbakkerssteeg (sugar bakers' alley) a bracket under a small Gothic canopy marks the spot where a statue of a woman in a headscarf, carrying a basket of cocoa beans, once stood. She has gone; the canopy is still there.

Look for:
- the empty canopy at the corner of the old alley
- the woman's head carved beside the doors
- the arms of Amsterdam in the leaded glass of the rounded corner
- tiles in the arches over the upper windows

title: Metz & Co, the New York building and Rietveld's glass room on the roof
summary: Built in 1891 for an American life insurer and still monogrammed NY, this corner became Metz & Co, the country's leading store for modern design, where Rietveld put a glass showroom on the roof in 1933. In 1941 its Jewish owner lost the business.
body:
The American Life Insurance Company had this corner of the Leidsestraat and the Keizersgracht built in 1891 to a design by Jac. van Looy and named it New York: the intertwined letters N and Y appear all over the fronts, among eagles and caryatids, and the domed corner tower has clock faces on three sides. From 1908 it housed Metz & Co, a firm that went back to Moses Samuels from Metz, who traded French silk in the Jodenbreestraat from around 1740.

Joseph de Leeuw, partner from 1896 and sole owner from 1910, made it the leading Dutch store for modern furniture and fabrics, with work by Oud, Rietveld, Le Corbusier and Breuer. In 1933 Gerrit Rietveld set a round room of glass and steel on the roof to show tubular steel furniture, with METZ on its railing in his own lettering. In 1926–1927 Metz had H.A. van Anrooy build a workshop with shops round the corner at Kerkstraat 45–49.

In 1941 the business was taken from De Leeuw because he was Jewish; he was deported and died in Theresienstadt in 1944. The store left this building in 2012 and closed in 2013; other shops have used it since. Look from the street.

Look for:
- the NY monograms and the eagles on the fronts
- the clock faces on the corner tower
- Rietveld's glass drum with the METZ letters on the roof
- the grid of concrete-framed windows at Kerkstraat 45–49

title: Keizersgracht 461, the corner where Fahrenheit taught
summary: A brick office of 1909–1910 with a copper bell-shaped helmet on its corner tower. The 17th-century house it replaced was where Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit, the man behind the temperature scale, taught statics and optics.
body:
Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit (1686–1736), born in Danzig (Gdańsk), settled in Amsterdam in 1717 to make barometers, altimeters and thermometers. He was the first to make thermometers with truly identical tubes, so that they agreed with each other, and he set the zero of his scale at the coldest temperature of the hard winter of 1708–1709 in his home town. From 1718 he gave lectures in Amsterdam, and in the corner house of 1675 that stood on this spot he taught statics and optics. He died penniless in The Hague in 1736.

His house was pulled down for the present building, put up in 1909–1910 for the firm Disconto Effecten to a design by W. Hamer, in a sober style touched by Art Nouveau. Above the diagonal entrance a round bay window rests on a stepped base; over it the walls rise into a tower that narrows from square to octagon under a bell-shaped copper helmet. Green bricks run through the frieze. The Amsterdamsche Bank later altered the attic and the ground floor, and since 1972 the ground-floor shop runs through into the neighbouring houses on the Leidsestraat.

With Metz & Co opposite, it is one of the corner buildings that frame this crossing. Look from the street.

Look for:
- the copper helmet on the corner tower
- the round bay with slim columns over the entrance
- green bricks in the frieze
- the domed Metz corner across the Leidsestraat

title: The Javasche Bank and the Indies banks of the Keizersgracht
summary: Two Keizersgracht offices of banks run from Batavia. The Javasche Bank printed the Indies guilder and was turned into Bank Indonesia in 1953; a few doors up, the Escompto bank kept its Dutch head office until 1960.
body:
The Javasche Bank, founded in 1828 with its head office in Batavia (now Jakarta), was the bank of issue of the Dutch East Indies: it printed the Indies guilder, and it also lent money for profit. It opened an Amsterdam office in 1891 and from 1906 worked from the 17th-century double house Zeerust on this spot. In 1937–1939 C.B. Posthumus Meyjes junior and J. van der Linden replaced that house with the present bank of stone and dark brick, traditional with a touch of neoclassicism; a gable stone in the new front still recalls Zeerust. After independence Indonesia bought out the shareholders, and in 1953 the Javasche Bank became Bank Indonesia, which was still altering floors here in 1954.

A few doors up, at no. 575, the Nederlandsch-Indische Escompto Maatschappij, founded in Batavia in 1857 to lend to trade and industry, had J.A. van Straaten join two canal houses into one office in 1909–1910, behind a front of four giant Ionic pilasters under a pediment. It was the bank's Dutch head office from 1910 until 1960, the year its Indonesian side was nationalised.

Both are offices; look from the street.

Look for:
- De Javasche Bank on the transom over the door of 666–668
- the Zeerust gable stone in the same front
- the lanterns on either side of its central bay
- the Ionic pilasters and pediment of no. 575

title: Heinemann's bakery house, where Van Arkel changed style
summary: A lopsided house of 1894 for the baker W.J. Heinemann, the design with which Gerrit van Arkel dropped historical styles for a sober Art Nouveau. The bakery that later worked from here was known for its Haagsche beschuit.
body:
Gerrit van Arkel began his career mixing neo-Gothic and neo-Renaissance. With this rebuild of 1894 for the baker W.J. Heinemann he switched to a sober kind of Jugendstil (Art Nouveau), and from then on his many shop-houses got bay windows, loggias, off-centre balconies, turrets and little domes. The house is an early example of the Nieuwe Kunst in Amsterdam, and it has survived almost unchanged.

The front is deliberately lopsided. The stoop and the main door are on the right, a wide three-part window on the left, and over that window a wooden bay runs up through two floors, with panels painted ochre. A stone balcony on brackets sits over the door, and the dormer breaks through the cornice like a Flemish gable, with the hoisting gear still on it.

From 1927 and for a long time after, the firm W.J. Heinemann occupied the building: a bakery known for its Haagsche beschuit (Hague rusks) that called itself a French and German 'pain de luxe' bakery. In 1947 the ground floor became a shop with offices and storerooms. It is private; look from the canal side.

Look for:
- the two-storey wooden bay with its ochre panels
- the stoop of seven steps set sideways to the front
- the stone balcony on brackets over the door
- the hoist on the dormer

title: The milk factory with a children's bacchanal
summary: Only the front is left of a dairy of about 1890 by Eduard Cuypers: neo-Renaissance below, a Swiss chalet gable with a turret on top, and over the gateway a frieze of children holding a bacchanal with milk.
body:
Around 1890 the company Amsterdamsche Melkinrichting (AMI) had Eduard Cuypers design a milk factory here. He mixed two styles that rarely meet: a stone and red-brick neo-Renaissance front, and on top a gable in the Swiss chalet style, with carved bargeboards, an oriel set across the corner and a little turret with a weathervane.

The best part is over the big arched gateway. The Flemish sculptor Emil van den Bossche carved a long frieze of children holding a bacchanal, the drinking feast of the wine god Bacchus, only with milk. On the corners, abstract carved friezes flank it. The listing values the front not only as architecture but as a reminder of how Amsterdam's milk supply was improved.

In 1989–1990 the building behind was demolished and replaced by an office called Koningsveste. Only the front was kept, and only the front is listed. Look from the canal.

Look for:
- the milk bacchanal over the gateway
- the abstract carved friezes on the corners beside it
- the corner oriel and the turret with a weathervane in the gable
- the iron hoisting beams between the top windows
- the ceramic tiles under the eaves

title: Gebouw De Fakkel, the newspaper printers' front
summary: A stone front of 1900 by Willem Kromhout, who went on to build Hotel American, for the Amsterdamsche Courant and the steam printers De Fakkel. The paper's name still runs across it in an Art Nouveau tile frieze hung with grapes.
body:
In 1900 Willem Kromhout rebuilt an existing house here as a printing works with a shop and offices for the newspaper Amsterdamsche Courant and the steam printers De Fakkel (the torch). It is one of his early Amsterdam works and, with Hotel American on the Leidseplein, stands for that first period, with echoes of Berlage's sober style and of Art Nouveau.

A city rule tied the height of a front to the width of the street, so on the narrow Reguliersbreestraat the fourth floor had to be set back. Below it the front is flat and clad in stone. Between the first and second floors a long, unsigned tile frieze spells out Amsterdamsche Courant among vines and bunches of grapes. Two balconies on open iron brackets have wrought-iron railings, the upper one more outspoken in its Art Nouveau curls. Of the first shopfront only the big three-part arched fanlight is left. Later rebuildings linked the works to the back of Muntplein 9, and in 1922 the shop was joined to the printing works behind.

Look up above the modern shopfront.

Look for:
- the Amsterdamsche Courant tile frieze with grapes
- the railings of the two balconies on iron brackets
- the arched three-part fanlight of the old shopfront
- the heavy stone balustrade crowning the front

title: Singel 512, from vaudeville theatre to painters' studio
summary: Built as a vaudeville theatre, refronted by Isaac Gosschalk in his first work with a little satyr's head as a nod to its past, then crowned with a glass studio for a photographer that later housed the International Painters' Studio.
body:
This building began as a vaudeville theatre, commissioned by the Amsterdamsche Bouwvereniging in 1856. What you see now is mostly Isaac Gosschalk's design for an office building, his first work. He drew the terracotta parapets himself and put a small satyr's head on a bracket in the middle of the front, as a reference to the vaudeville days.

In 1880 G.B. Salm raised the building for J.C. Marx with a studio flat on top: a floor that is almost all glass, with a row of slanting windows in the roof. That was the light a photographer needed, and the studio was to be taken by 'photographie M. Büttinghausen', a reminder of the early days of photography. In 1910, on the initiative of Mrs Mesdag-van Calcar, the Internationaal Schildersatelier (international painters' studio) moved into the top floor. The building is also remembered for the Amsterdamse Joffers, a circle of women painters, through Coba Ritsema. The floors below stayed offices.

It stands on the Singel by the flower market; look past the stalls to the upper floors.

Look for:
- the satyr's head on a bracket above the paired middle windows
- the glazed top floor of the studios
- the row of eight slanting roof windows
- the neo-Renaissance plaques under the side windows

title: Telegraaf building, the newspaper fortress on the Nieuwezijds
summary: A printing works with a tower, built in 1928–1930 for De Telegraaf. After the war the resistance papers took over its presses, and in 1966 furious building workers overturned and burned its vans outside. Stone newsboys still shout from the top of the spire.
body:
For most of the 20th century the Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal was Amsterdam's newspaper street, and this was its loudest building. Jan Frederik Staal and G.J. Langhout designed it for De Telegraaf: presses on the ground floor, offices above, typesetting on the fourth floor, paper stores at the top. The two iron doors on the right hid platform lifts that took the heavy paper rolls down to the cellar. The tower holds the lift shaft and two water tanks, and its lead-clad spire has a flagpole that can be lowered into it.

Because the paper's owner had worked with the occupier, De Telegraaf was banned in 1945, and the resistance papers Het Parool and Trouw were given its building and presses. In June 1966 building workers, angry at a report about a colleague who had died during a protest, besieged the building. They overturned and burned the vans and set paper rolls alight; staff got the shutters down in time. Days of rioting followed, and the mayor had to resign.

De Telegraaf left for Sloterdijk in 1974. The bank KAS BANK moved in in 1985; since 2021 the game studio Guerrilla Games works here. You see it from the street.

Look for:
- Hildo Krop's four shouting newsboys at the top of the spire (replicas)
- the dark glazed brick, the bronze window frames and the glass blocks
- the two iron doors of the paper lifts

title: Gebouw Helios, a photographer's sun palace on the Spui
summary: A German portrait photographer had this art nouveau block built around 1900 with his name in mosaic on the front. Its bronze medal came from the Paris world fair; later tenants included a gambling den, Albert Heijn's tea room and Madame Tussaud's.
body:
Max Büttinghausen came to Amsterdam from near Düsseldorf in 1873 and became a well-known portrait and press photographer. On this corner he had Gerrit van Arkel build him a shop with studios and a home on top. He called it Helios, after heliography, a printing process he used. Van Arkel sent the design to the architecture competition of the 1900 world fair in Paris, where it won a bronze medal.

The tenants make a story of their own. On the Voetboogstraat side a beer cellar called Barbarossa opened in 1900; within a few years it was a notorious den for illegal gambling. From 1910 the ground floor was the tea and lunch room Maison Ledeboer. In 1923 the grocer Albert Heijn took it over and made it Formosa, an English-style restaurant with Sunday concerts, which closed in 1969. Then Madame Tussaud's wax museum moved in, with its entrance on the Kalverstraat, until it left for the Dam in 1991. Shops and a café followed.

Look for:
- "M. Büttinghausen Fotografie Artistique" in mosaic over the ground floor
- "Gebouw" and "Helios" either side of carved sunflowers at the top
- the reliefs of women reaching for a fruit tree around the doors
- the mosaic "Zum Barbarossa" in the Voetboogstraat
