title: De Drie Fleschjes, the liqueur distillery behind the Nieuwe Kerk
summary: The name of Amsterdam's oldest tasting room is carved in stone two doors along: here its owner, the liqueur distiller Bootz, rebuilt his distillery in 1887–1888 with mosaics and lion heads. The tasting room itself still pours.
body:
In the alley behind the Nieuwe Kerk stands proeflokaal De Drie Fleschjes (the three little bottles) at no. 18, the oldest tasting room in the city. At the end of the 19th century it was run by the liqueur distiller J.H.G. Bootz, and in 1887–1888 he had the building at no. 14 turned into a proper distillery, designed by J.P.F. van Rossem and W.J. Vuyk. Inside, iron galleries ran around a glass roof light.

The front was made to be seen: a stone frieze carved LIKEURFABRIEK DE DRIE FLESCHJES DISTILLEERDERIJ, round-arched windows with mosaic in the arches and lion heads as keystones, sculpted heads on the brackets under the gutter, and an iron hoist beam at the top. The register calls it one of the few traces of industry left in the old centre.

Around 1950 the distillery moved to the Keizersgracht, and from 1957 to 1969 a clothing factory worked here. Since the mid-1980s it has been a hotel. The tasting room at no. 18 is open Monday to Saturday from 14.00, with a drinks organ of fifty casks behind the bar.

Look for:
- the carved frieze with the firm's name
- the mosaics and the lion heads over the first-floor windows
- the heads under the gutter and the iron hoist beam in the gable

title: Kettner's piano shop, with its wares in tiles
summary: A piano dealer's shop of 1906–1907 that still announces PIANO'S, ORGELS and VLEUGELS in tiles over its windows. Kettner sold Steinways and Bechsteins here and had a special room for pianos that played themselves.
body:
The piano firm C. Kettner had a shop on the Kalverstraat before it asked Alexander Kropholler and Jan Staal for a building of its own. They gave it a late, straight-lined art nouveau front in grey Vecht brick, with two pointed gables, coloured tiles at the corners and three tile panels that spell out the stock: PIANO'S, ORGELS, VLEUGELS (pianos, organs, grand pianos). The firm's name was set in the railing along the roof ridge, between two tall chimneys.

When it opened in April 1907 a newspaper reported electric light, a lift and three floors of showrooms. Kettner was the main Dutch agent for Bechstein and Steinway, and had just become agent for Erard of Paris. There was a separate room for self-playing instruments such as the Angelus and the Mignon. The grand pianos stood on the first floor; repairs were done in the attic.

In 1936 Kettner merged with a rival into Kettner & Duwaer, which kept the shop going until the early 1970s. The pianos are long gone; you see the building from the street.

Look for:
- the three tile panels over the ground-floor windows
- the coloured tiles on the corners of the window frames
- the ridge railing between the two chimneys

title: Stähle's model bakery on the Spuistraat corner
summary: In 1898 a baker opened his 'model bakery' in this turreted corner house by Gerrit van Arkel, with Rozenburg tiles of the baking trade on the shop walls and an old 1748 gable stone with a rhyme set in the new front. It has been a bakery ever since.
body:
Fred. C. Stähle, son of a baker from Prussia who had a bakery round the corner in the Raamsteeg, opened his luxury bakery here in July 1898. Gerrit van Arkel designed the building and fitted out the shop too. The papers called it a model bakery: tile panels from the Rozenburg pottery showing scenes from the bakery trade, brass display cases, doors of cut glass, an onyx counter, and electric light even in the hot-air ovens behind the shop. On the outside, too, decorations refer to baking bread. When it was finished it was the tallest building in this part of the block, with a round oriel ending in a pointed roof on the corner.

Into the new front Stähle had an old gable stone set, dated 1748, with a rhyme: laid out in troubled times, finished in peaceful times, and trusting in God for everything. Stähle went on to lead the national bakers' association and sat on the city council from 1919 to 1923.

The shop has stayed a bakery: since 1990 the Egstorf firm. The tiles are in the shop, which is open in shop hours.

Look for:
- the gable stone of 1748 with its rhyme
- the round corner oriel and its pointed roof
- inside, the Rozenburg tile panels of bakers at work

title: The Lloyd building, the "gilded coffin" on the Prins Hendrikkade
summary: A shipping line grew rich in the First World War carrying emigrants to South America and spent 4.5 million guilders on this stone palace, over the objections of the city's design panel. Within two years it had left again; Amsterdammers called it the gilded coffin.
body:
The Koninklijke Hollandsche Lloyd made large profits during the First World War, when many people from Eastern Europe sailed on its ships to South America. In 1917–1921 it built this head office on the corner of the Martelaarsgracht, all in natural stone, to a design by E. Breman. Its director is said to have wanted nothing to do with modern architecture, and the firm stayed out of the Scheepvaarthuis, where most shipping lines had their offices.

The city's design panel rejected the historicising plan: a modern shipping line ought to have a modern office. The mayor and aldermen approved it anyway, reasoning that it stood mostly on the firm's own land. It cost 4.5 million guilders, and its ironwork was gilded, so Amsterdammers called it "de vergulde doodskist", the gilded coffin.

From 1920 the line ran into trouble. The building was never fully used and was abandoned in 1923. The city rented it for the head office of its electricity company in 1932–1939; later the land registry sat here. Since 2013 it has been a hotel.

Look for:
- the domed turret over the round corner
- over the Prins Hendrikkade entrance: a lifebuoy, a globe, an anchor, ships, dolphins and Mercury's staff
- the wrought-iron Dutch arms over the door on the Martelaarsgracht

title: Kas-Associatie, two cashiers' banks and an elephant clock
summary: Amsterdam's oldest cashiers' firm, the Associatie Cassa of 1806, put its founding year on its Herengracht front; the Kas-Vereeniging, which swallowed it in 1952, sat in a sculpted bank on the Spuistraat. That bank's glass-roofed hall is now a hotel restaurant you can walk into.
body:
Kassiers (cashiers) held money and securities for merchants and settled their payments. The Associatie Cassa, founded on 10 March 1806, moved to the Herengracht in 1818. In 1900–1902 C.B. Posthumus Meyjes replaced its 17th-century house with a 38-metre stone front, with the founding year MDCCCVI in one gable and MCMII in the other.

Across the Singel, F.W.M. Poggenbeek built a bank for Labouchère, Oyens & Co. in 1906–1908, rich with carving by Lambertus Zijl. From 1914 the Kas-Vereeniging worked here, and in 1932 the building was extended to the Paleisstraat. In 1952 the Kas-Vereeniging took over the Associatie Cassa and became the Kas-Associatie, later KAS BANK. The bank sold the Spuistraat building to a hotel group in 2013 and moved into the old Telegraaf building.

The Spuistraat bank is now part of the W Amsterdam hotel, and its hall, under a glass roof painted with the arms of cities where the first bank had offices or partners, is the restaurant The Duchess. The register also lists a bronze clock on three elephants by C.A. Lion Cachet and a tile panel of the cashiers' successive offices.

Look for:
- the animals and heads carved into the Spuistraat front, and KAS-ASSOCIATIE on the 1932 wing
- at Herengracht 179, MDCCCVI and MCMII in the gables and keystones of an owl, eagle, pelican and rooster

title: The Raadhuisstraat gallery and 't Binnenhuis
summary: When the Raadhuisstraat was cut through the canals, an insurance company built a whole curving side of it at once: eighteen shops under a glass-roofed gallery over the pavement, crowned with dragons and fabulous beasts. Across the street it housed Berlage's design shop.
body:
In 1897 the contractors Staal and Haalmeijer, acting for the life insurer De Utrecht, asked to buy sixteen plots on the new street at once. The city preferred them to other bidders because they would fill the whole south side between the Herengracht and the Keizersgracht with one building. The Van Gendt firm designed eighteen shops with homes above, behind a three-metre gallery on seventeen stone pillars, built out over the pavement and partly roofed with glass. Its roof is the balcony of the first-floor homes, and the front follows the curve of the street. Stones with gilded letters at both ends date it to 1898.

Across the street, at nos. 46-50, De Utrecht had Kropholler and Staal build an office in 1906–1907 with a shop for 't Binnenhuis, the firm H.P. Berlage had founded in 1900 to sell furniture and household things designed by artists. They proved too dear for ordinary buyers; 't Binnenhuis left in 1922. A piano dealer followed, and today it is a fashion shop.

The gallery shops are open; the homes above are private.

Look for:
- the beasts after Gothic gargoyles on the gables, and the dragons and shields at the gallery's ends
- the round corner tower and the carved rooster at the Keizersgracht end
- 'T BINNENHUIS in tiles high on the front of no. 46

title: The Assurantiehuis, with kangaroos for insurance
summary: An insurance broker rebuilt this canal house as offices in 1918–1919 and had its front carved with what insurance promises: lifebuoys, anchors, pelicans and kangaroos with a joey in the pouch. In the 1930s a bank here ran a fraud worth millions.
body:
Around 1900 the canal belt filled with offices. This house of 1910 got a completely new stone front only eight years later, when P.H. van Niftrik rebuilt it for F.A. Sorel, head of a company that let office space. It became "Het Assurantiehuis", home to several small insurance companies, with the name in large letters over the ground floor.

The sculpture explains the trade. Between the first and second floors square reliefs show lifebuoys, anchors, pelicans and kangaroos with a joey in the pouch, all images of protection. Between the first-floor windows a medallion shows Arion with his harp on a dolphin: in the Greek story a dolphin saved the singer from drowning.

From 1930 a small securities bank had its office here. It promised private savers high interest if they left their securities in its care. The interest was paid; the securities were never seen again. Its two directors were arrested in 1938 and jailed in 1939 for a fraud of millions.

You see it from the quay.

Look for:
- the kangaroos with their young among the reliefs over the first floor
- Arion on his dolphin
- the house number 213 carved over the door

title: The city telephone exchange on the Singel
summary: Amsterdam ran its own telephone service, and in 1917–1919 it built this exchange, where operators put through 500 calls a minute. Hildo Krop carved telephone poles with wires on the front, in his first big job for the city. The building now stands empty.
body:
Until 1940 the telephone in Amsterdam was a city service, the Gemeentetelefoon. Its central exchange, the Centraal Bureau Centrum, was built in 1917–1919 by the Public Works architects G.J. Rutgers and P.L. Marnette, in a severe version of the Amsterdam School style, and taken into use in 1921. It ran through to the Herengracht, where the management sat; that front was replaced in 1955.

The exchange was semi-automatic: subscribers had no dial yet, so operators made the connections. At opening the newspaper De Tijd counted 24 operators putting through about 500 calls a minute in the busy hours, and batteries that could keep it running for two days if the power failed.

The sculpture was Hildo Krop's first big commission from the city. At the entrance are farmers, miners and building workers; the capitals of the brick pilasters are telephone poles with their wires, between the arms of Dutch cities.

In 1940 the service was taken over by the state PTT. Around 2020 its successor KPN no longer needed the exchange and left it empty; there are plans to turn it into offices. You see it from the canal.

Look for:
- the telephone poles with wires at the top of the pilasters
- Krop's farmers, miners and builders by the door
- the heavy rough-hewn stone base with barred windows

title: The first home of the Vrije Universiteit
summary: The Vrije Universiteit, founded in 1880 by Abraham Kuyper's circle, got its first building of its own here in 1884: a canal house with lecture rooms below and rooms for 37 students above. It stayed the main building until the move to Buitenveldert in the 1960s.
body:
The Vrije Universiteit (Free University), a Protestant university founded in 1880 outside state control, began in borrowed rooms, among them the building that is now the theatre De Kleine Komedie. In 1884 its society bought this 17th-century canal house, remodelled in the 18th century, and gave it a new neoclassical front designed by J.W. Meyer, on behalf of its director W. Hovy. The 18th-century house behind was left as it was.

It was main building and hospitium (a student hostel) in one. A newspaper described the plan: meeting room, library and offices on the main floor, lecture rooms above, and on the top two floors about 37 small rooms where students would each have a sitting room and a study. It reopened in January 1885. The university later added nos. 160, 164 and 166, and Abraham Kuyper, one of its founders and later prime minister, lived at no. 164 around 1900. Its 18th-century main room became the senate room, with a painted ceiling of the four seasons.

The VU left for Buitenveldert in the 1960s. The Salvation Army used the house from 1969, and since 1985 it has been eight apartments; the interior is private.

Look for:
- the lions' heads over the door and the window beside it
- the pediment with its iron weathervane at the top

title: Breitner's studio on the Prinseneiland
summary: The painter and photographer George Breitner sketched this double studio himself, and a builder put it up for him in 1898 on a bend of the Prinseneiland. Breitner worked here until 1914; his pupil, the builder's son, kept the other studio until 1967.
body:
George Hendrik Breitner (1857–1923) painted Amsterdam as a working city: building sites, horses, wet streets. In 1898 the contractor C.J. Maks built this double studio-home on the south-west bend of the Prinseneiland. Breitner supplied the sketches for its design and layout and took the larger of the two studios. Between the studios was a small changing room for the model.

Breitner worked here until 1914. His studio then went to the painter Kees Maks (1876–1967), the builder's son and Breitner's pupil, who worked there until his death. The smaller studio was used in 1932–1936 by the architect Auke Komter.

The national register calls it the first purpose-built studio-home in Amsterdam and probably in the country; Amsterdam op de kaart points out an older one of 1871 on the Stadhouderskade. Either way it was built for work: the big studio windows face the back, into the bend, away from the street. It sits a few metres back from the building line, perhaps to allow the street to be widened. It is private; you see it from the quay.

Look for:
- the two wooden entrance porches running out to the street, with pediments over the doors
- the blind windows upstairs on the right

title: Hana's model homes, the oldest workers' housing still standing
summary: Twelve trial homes of 1853 by the first housing association in the Netherlands, built on cleared slum plots in the Jordaan to test its ideas before the big Planciusblok. Its very first block, on Oostenburg, is gone, so these are the oldest left.
body:
In 1852 the Vereeniging ten behoeve der Arbeidersklasse (Society for the Working Class) was founded, the first housing association in the Netherlands. Its members wanted decent homes for workers at a fair rent, partly, as they said, to keep them out of the street and the pub. Its first block, on Oostenburg, was ready in 1853; it was sold to the Werkspoor factory in 1917 and has gone.

On this corner the society bought twelve run-down plots, cleared them and had the architect Hendrik Hana build a second, small trial: two houses, each with three pairs of homes, twelve in all. Here it tried out its ideas before the large model block on the Planciusstraat. The block is plain and symmetrical, with two bays with cut-off corners that hold the stairs; behind the broad windows were the twelve living rooms. The three homes on the Passeerdersstraat were added in 1933–1934, and the whole was renovated in 1991.

It is still housing; you see it from the street.

Look for:
- the cast-iron wall anchors shaped like rosettes
- the cut-off corners of the two stair bays, followed by the overhanging cornice
- the original glazing bars in the windows and fanlights

title: Bouwonderneming Jordaan, an experiment that proved a point
summary: In 1896 a group of wealthy Amsterdammers tore down 131 slum homes to prove that good workers' housing could pay its way without subsidy. The blocks are fine; the experiment failed, because almost none of the old tenants could afford the rent.
body:
The Bouwonderneming Jordaan, founded in December 1895 with 280,000 guilders from three tobacco planters, set out to show that decent homes for workers in the old city could be built and let on a commercial basis. If it worked, others could follow. The architect Jan Ernst van der Pek chose a block of 131 slum homes between the Lindengracht and the Goudsbloemstraat; they were bought and demolished, and on 26 September 1896 the first 92 new homes were ready.

On the Lindengracht came 32 two-room homes with a kitchen and a toilet with running water, shops and workshops on the ground floor and storage lofts under the deep eaves. Behind them, on the Goudsbloemstraat, one-room homes stand round small courtyards so each gets light and air. Louise Went, trained in England under Octavia Hill, collected the rent every week and checked how the homes were kept.

Only 9 of the 103 families who had lived here moved back: most could not pay rents from 1.70 guilders a week, and the company wanted tenants with a steady income. Without subsidy, the experiment showed, it could not be done. The homes are now let by the housing corporation Ymere.

Look for:
- the lintels on the Lindengracht honouring eight building trades, each with its tools
- the faces carved on the ends of the gutter brackets under the overhang
- on the Goudsbloemstraat, the hoist hatches in the dormers

title: Koning Willemshuis, a club for the people of the Jordaan
summary: A neighbourhood hall of 1863–1864 where a temperance preacher's society held Bible readings and language lessons at night, partly to keep the men out of the pub. Its dates over the doors, 1813 and 1863, mark fifty years of the kingdom.
body:
In 1863 a Christian neighbourhood society for this part of the Jordaan built itself a hall, designed by J. van Maurik. Its driving forces were C.S. Adama van Scheltema, preacher at the Westerkerk and a leading campaigner against drink, and G.H. Crone. In the evenings adults came for Bible readings and language lessons, partly to keep the men out of the pub; children learned drawing and needlework, skills that could help them find work. The Algemeen Handelsblad called it a "sociëteit voor het volk", a club for the people. Other groups could use it too, as long as their aim was the people's morals and wellbeing.

The dates over the doors are 1813, when the Netherlands regained its independence, and 1863. On 17 November 1863, a national holiday for that jubilee, the mayor laid the first stone on behalf of King Willem III, who had given money; hence the name.

The society also founded the nursery school next door in 1889. After the Second World War the hall was mostly a club for the elderly. Since 2018 it has held five apartments; you see it from the street.

Look for:
- 1813 and 1863 over the two doors
- the small stone dated 17 November 1863, just above the plinth
- the nursery school next door

title: Bombs on the Blauwburgwal, May 1940
summary: On the second day of the German invasion, bombs fell on this corner and killed 44 people. The disaster was all but forgotten until 2016; the office on the gap was built for a coffee firm that had been forced to drop its Jewish name, and one bomb still lies in the canal.
body:
On 11 May 1940, the second day of the German invasion, a German bomber dropped four bombs of 250 kilos on the corner of the Blauwburgwal and the Herengracht. One hit the houses, two exploded in the water and the fourth sank without going off; it is still in the mud of the Herengracht. Forty-four people died and 79 were wounded. The plane had probably been hit by anti-aircraft fire on its way to Schiphol and dumped its load.

Newspapers hardly reported it, and the bombing of Rotterdam a few days later pushed it out of memory. Only in 2016 did a volunteer researcher trace the names of the dead through their death certificates. Since 11 May 2020 a plaque on the Blauwburgwal side lists them with their ages.

The gap was filled in 1952 by an office for the coffee firm Matagalpa. It was founded in 1919 as the Koffie Handelmaatschappij van Cohen Bendiks; in 1941 it had to take a non-Jewish name and chose a Nicaraguan coffee town. A critic found the result "as un-Amsterdam as it gets". Across the water, the baker's house at Blauwburgwal 22 of 1667 was badly damaged and repaired.

Look for:
- the plaque with the 44 names, Blauwburgwal side
- the 1952 opening stone on the Herengracht side, and the paper mill gable stone
- the loggia on the roof and the windows getting smaller upwards
- the raised bell gable of Blauwburgwal 22 opposite

title: Torensluis, the bridge that carried a tower
address: Singel at the Oude Leliestraat and Torensteeg
summary: At 42 metres the Torensluis is one of the widest bridges in the city, because a tower with a prison stood on it. The tower went in 1829; its cells are still inside the bridge, and its outline is laid out in the paving.
body:
The Torensluis of 1648 is the oldest bridge in Amsterdam to survive in its original state, and at 42 metres one of the widest. The width is explained by the Jan Roodenpoortstoren, a tower that stood on it until 1829, with cells beneath it. When the bridge was designed, there was a plan to line it with little shops, as on the Rialto in Venice, so the rents would pay part of the cost. It was dropped because of the heavy traffic expected, but a painting of 1829 shows that small houses had been built against the tower after all; they went with it. The bridge also served as a market.

The cells under the tower are still in the bridgehead. They have been restored and opened up, and have been used for exhibitions and events. Since 2003 the outline of the tower's foundations has been marked in the cobbles. In 1987 a bronze bust of the writer Multatuli by Hans Bayens was set up on the bridge.

Look for:
- the tower's outline in the cobbles
- the Multatuli bust
- the view along the Singel to the dome of the Ronde Lutherse Kerk

title: Twentsche Bank archive, five fronts that are one building
summary: On the Bergstraat this looks like a row of five small houses. It is one bank archive of 1939–1941, built where a Catholic church called Het Torentje had stood since 1720, and later a depot of the city's street cleaners.
body:
In 1939 the Twentsche Bank, one of the forerunners of ABN Amro, had C.B. Posthumus Meyjes jr. design an archive and office here. It replaced four plots on the Singel and five on the Bergstraat. One of them, Singel 156, held the Catholic church Het Torentje, which had stood there from 1720 until 1937. The bank's head office was across the water, where the P.C. Hooftgebouw now stands.

The wholesale demolition of canal houses for offices drew a storm of criticism, and the architect tried to fill the gap rather than make a statement. On the Bergstraat he broke the long front up so that it reads as five separate little houses; on the Singel, four wide gateways led into a ground floor used for bicycles and cars, with the archive on the floors above. A stone over the Singel door gives the year 1940.

In 1964 the bank merged into the Algemene Bank Nederland. In 1966–1967 the city took this building and the head office in exchange for the land under the bank's new head office on the Vijzelstraat, and used it for a while as a post of the Stadsreiniging, the street cleaning service. Today it holds homes and offices.

Look for:
- the five "house fronts" on the Bergstraat
- the 1940 stone over the Singel entrance
- the varnished doors with slanted boards

title: Amsterdams Welvaren, a nursery school paid for by a captured ship
summary: The first nursery school in Amsterdam was founded in 1828 with money a Quaker could not keep: insurance paid out on a Dutch merchant ship that British privateers had captured and lost. The ship still sails over the door.
body:
In 1781 the English captured the Dutch merchant ship Amsterdams Welvaren. Her cargo was valuable, and the captors promptly insured it at Lloyd's. When the ship sank, the new owners received a large sum from the insurers. One of them was John Warder, a Quaker, whose pacifist faith did not allow him to own spoils of war. He and his heirs set the money aside for a good cause.

That cause became this bewaarschool (a day nursery for small children), founded in 1828 as the first in the city, for children aged two to six. In 1864 the architect P.J. Hamer replaced the run-down first building with the present one, in the Willem II Gothic style, an early, romantic form of neo-Gothic that is rare in Amsterdam. Later a Christian school association used it; in 1922 the flat upstairs was taken into the school and in 1937 a classroom was added in the attic. The front survives intact; the building is now a home.

Look for:
- the sailing ship in relief over the door, under the name Amsterdams Welvaren
- Warder's monogram JW on the stones beside it
- the stone "in de berestraat" with a bear
- the ship on the top of the gable

title: Keizersgracht 316, a bicycle-hub importer's office that kept a gable
summary: In 1935 an importer of Torpedo bicycle hubs had old canal houses pulled down for a new office, but its architect stored one of their neck gables and rebuilt it on the Rechtboomsloot three years later. The new building tried hard to look old.
body:
William Koch & Co imported Torpedo bicycle hubs and F&S ball bearings. In 1935–1936 the firm built an office here with warehouses, sample rooms and a caretaker's flat, designed by A.A. Kok in the Delft School style. Kok wanted to build "with a system of proportions as our forefathers did". He had the existing houses on the corner measured before they were demolished, kept one neck gable in storage and, after three years, had it put up again at Rechtboomsloot 39-41.

Kok turned the roof so that its ridge runs along the canal, which put the wavy stepped gable on the Berenstraat. The windows get lower floor by floor, as on an old canal house. The Haarlem sculptor J.M. Veldheer made the carving: two gable stones for industry (designing and making) and trade (receiving and distributing), an imperial crown on a capital on the canal side, bears on the Berenstraat side, and a head of Hermes, god of trade, on the corner. The original weathervane showed two figures on a high stoop, one falling and losing hat and suitcase, for the firm's hard early years; the present vane has the city's arms. It is still an office.

Look for:
- the Hermes head on the corner
- the crown and the bears on the capitals
- the initials A.K. and 1935 in the door frame, and W.K. in the grille
- the wall anchors that spell 1935

title: De Transvaalsche Boer, a cigar shop from the Boer War craze
summary: In 1900, with the Netherlands cheering on the Boers in South Africa, a cigar shop opened on this corner under the name De Transvaalsche Boer. A carved Boer still stands on the corner of Gerrit van Arkel's tall art nouveau building.
body:
During the Boer War, South Africa and its Boers were hugely popular in the Netherlands. In October 1900, four months after the building contract was let, a cigar shop called De Transvaalsche Boer (the Transvaal Boer) opened on this corner of the Gasthuismolensteeg and the Herengracht. The figure of a Boer on the corner, by the sculptor Johann Zeitz, recalls it.

The architect was Gerrit van Arkel, who signed his work on the alley side. He built in the Nieuwe Kunst, the Dutch art nouveau, with a teak shopfront and an unusual height; the building originally had a tall pointed roof. The floors above the shop formed one home. On the Herengracht side, a gable stone reading "in de Wijck tot Maestricht" was taken over from the house that was pulled down for it.

The cigar shop was gone by 1902. An art dealer called Gerard Dou followed, then around 1915 a shoe and boot shop, and in 1919 the shop was joined to the shoemaker at no. 18. It is still a shop.

Look for:
- the Boer figure on the corner
- the inscription "G. van Arkel / Architect" on the alley side
- the teak shopfront
- the gable stone "in de Wijck tot Maestricht" on the canal side, third floor

title: Raadhuisstraat bridges, with fauns, crows and frogs
address: Raadhuisstraat over the Herengracht and the Keizersgracht
summary: When the Raadhuisstraat was cut through the canal belt as a tram route to the west, its old humpbacked bridges had to go. Piet Kramer's replacements of 1925 carry Hildo Krop's bearded fauns between crows and frogs, and one is named after a founder of the COC.
body:
In the 1890s the Warmoesgracht was filled in and a new street was broken through between the Herengracht and the Keizersgracht, to give Amsterdam-West a road to the centre: the Raadhuisstraat. Its arched bridges were soon too much for the traffic, and trams in particular struggled with them. Piet Kramer, bridge architect of the city's Public Works, drew new ones in the Amsterdam School style around 1921–1922, but price rises after the First World War held up the work until 1925.

Over the Herengracht lies bridge 22, the Warmoesbrug, named after the old canal, with three openings. Over the Keizersgracht lies bridge 106 with two, and here Hildo Krop carved the grey granite on the middle piers: twice a faun's head with a long beard between groups of three crows, with two frogs' heads below. Both have Kramer's wrought-iron railings; on bridge 106 they were made by H.J. Winkelman. Both became national monuments in 2001.

In 2002 bridge 106 was named after Niek Engelschman (1913–1988), actor, wartime resistance member and, as "Bob Angelo", a founder in 1946 of the COC, the Dutch gay and lesbian association. The Homomonument lies beside it.

Look for:
- the fauns, crows and frogs on the piers of bridge 106, seen from the quay
- the wrought-iron railings fixed to the stone pylons
- the name plate of the Niek Engelschmanbrug

title: Joes Kloppenburgbrug, a bridge against senseless violence
address: Singel, between Raamsteeg and Oude Spiegelstraat
summary: In 1996 Joes Kloppenburg, 26, was kicked to death in the nearby Voetboogstraat after he told a group of men to stop beating someone up. Twenty years later the city named this old bridge over the Singel after him.
body:
A bridge has crossed the Singel here, between the Raamsteeg and the Oude Spiegelstraat, since at least about 1599, when Pieter Bast drew a drawbridge on his map. The present low bridge, with three openings and granite brackets, dates from 1910–1911, when it was renewed together with the next bridge over the Herengracht. It was never officially named; people called it the Raambrug, or the Appelmarktbrug after an apple market once held nearby. It was thoroughly renovated in 2013.

On 17 August 1996 Joes Kloppenburg came out of a café in the Voetboogstraat, a few minutes' walk away, and saw drunk men kicking a young man in the alley. He shouted at them to stop ("Kappen nou!"), and they turned on him. He died in hospital a few hours later, aged 26. His death became a byword for zinloos geweld (senseless violence). A year later a memorial was unveiled in the Voetboogstraat, and his father and friends set up a foundation called Kappen Nou! On 5 July 2016 the city named bridge 5 after him, as a sign against senseless violence; the name plate went up in September 2017.

Look for:
- the name plate
- the granite brackets under the deck
- the memorial in the Voetboogstraat, close by

title: Papiermolensluis, the paper mill bridge
summary: A single stone arch of 1781 over the Brouwersgracht, named after the sign of a paper dealer on the corner. It was also known as the Oliekoekensluis, after the women who fried and sold oliekoeken and pancakes from stalls here.
body:
Where the Prinsengracht meets the Brouwersgracht, boats from the Westerdok and the IJ come into the canal belt, which makes this one of the busiest water crossings in the city. The Papiermolensluis carries the east quay of the Prinsengracht across the Brouwersgracht. Sluis here is the old word for a stone bridge, though there was once a lock as well. A stone bridge was built here in 1781.

The name comes from a signboard: a paper dealer on the corner house of the Brouwersgracht hung out a board reading "de Papiermolen" (the paper mill). The bridge was also called the Oliekoekensluis, after the bakers of oliekoeken (fried dough balls) and pancakes who once had their stalls here.

In 1946 the city's Public Works looked at the 160-year-old bridge and found it could still take the traffic. Money for bridges was short after the war, and a new bridge might spoil the character of the neighbourhood, so it stayed. In 1976 it was strengthened with a concrete span inside, and in 1991 it was adjusted again. It shares its southwest quay wall with the Lekkeresluis over the Prinsengracht.

Look for:
- the single, fairly narrow arch
- the bridge number on the top stone of the arch
- the Lekkeresluis next to it, at the same corner

title: Herengracht 14, the sunflower house and its hidden church
summary: Behind a sober 1767 front with a sunflower carved in the pediment, Catholics met in secret in the 1650s, and the Reformed church council noted with alarm that they played music at Mass. Later the house was a Jesuit residence.
body:
In 1656 the Reformed church council had a list drawn up of the places where Catholics gathered for their forbidden services. One entry is this house, then owned by the widow of the merchant Pieter Dablijn: "a large gathering, where instruments are played and many people come". The priest was named as Van der Linde, probably the Jesuit Henricus van der Linden. Organ music was still hotly disputed at the time, so the music made it worse.

The widow's heirs sold the house in 1661 to a rich Catholic lawyer, and from 1663 it served as the residence of the head of the Catholic mission in Holland.

What you see now is a later disguise. In 1767 two buyers paid 18,429 guilders for the house, rebuilt it and sold it a year later for 62,000. They gave it a four-window sandstone front in the new Louis XVI style, with a large triangular pediment, possibly the first time such a pediment returned to a canal front. In the wooden pediment are a sunflower between two palm leaves, which gives the house its name, De Sonneblom.

It is a private house; only the front can be seen.

Look for:
- the sunflower and palm leaves in the pediment
- the stoop, once a double flight; the left one went when a basement door was cut
- the narrower, lower houses at 16 and 18 beside it: when the plots were redivided in 1614, 14 and 20 got the gardens behind them

title: Vita Brevis dormers (Herengracht 6–8)
summary: Two 1883 town houses share one motto, split over their dormers: Vita on the left, Brevis on the right. The first half, Ars longa, is left for you to supply.
body:
Look up at these two houses at the start of the Herengracht and you can read half a Latin proverb. The left dormer says Vita, the right one Brevis: the end of Ars longa, vita brevis, "art is long, life is short".

The houses that stood here were bought at auction in March 1882 by Levy Speelman, a broker from the Nieuwmarkt. He tried to sell them on at another auction a month later, without success, and new houses went up instead in 1883. The design was by J. Daverman, a builder of whom almost nothing is known. The city's monument description says, unusually bluntly, that his coarse and lavish decoration shows a rather unrefined taste.

The first residents were a merchant from the Zaan region at number 6 and a notary at number 8.

Both are private homes; the motto is on the street side.

Look for:
- Vita and Brevis in the two dormers
- the heavy, busy ornament on the fronts that earned the architect his verdict

title: De Drie Traancoopers, the house that turned to face the canal
summary: In 1632 this corner house was rebuilt with its front moved from the alley to the Herengracht, which had just been widened from a ditch into a canal. Its step gable and leaning upper floor survive from that rebuild.
body:
This corner house began life facing the other way. Its address was in the Korsjespoortsteeg, the alley beside it, and the Herengracht behind it was only a narrow ditch on the edge of town. Around 1612 that ditch was widened into a proper canal, and suddenly the canal side was the better address. When Jan Gerritsz Backer had the house rebuilt in 1632, he moved the front to the Herengracht: the house was given a quarter turn.

The rebuilt house has a brick step gable with bands of natural stone, and the first floor juts out over the ground floor on carved beam ends. Small lean-to rooms called pothuizen (literally pot houses) stand against both the front and the side. The side wall on the alley is plastered white.

The earliest known residents, at the end of the 16th century, were a leather tanner, a shoemaker and a cutler; later came a tar trader, a surgeon and a carpenter. A traan is train oil (whale or fish oil), and a traancooper someone who traded in it. The doorway dates from around 1800. Hendrick de Keyser Monumenten bought the house in 1958 and restored it five years later. It is let as a home; you see it from the canal and the alley.

Look for:
- the step gable with stone blocks in the arches over the windows
- the first floor overhanging on carved beam ends
- the pothuizen against both walls

title: Gebouw De Koophandel, a coal office with the Exchange on its front
summary: A 1906 office for lignite briquette traders, built where an alley once led to a Mennonite church. On its front a stone shows Berlage's Exchange and the Westerkerk under a motto: fortune favours the bold.
body:
Five storeys high, with no raised basement and an off-centre gable, this is not a canal house but one of the first purpose-built offices on the canal. The NV Bruinkolenbrikettenhandel, a firm trading in lignite briquettes, had it built in 1906 to a design by A.J. Joling, a pupil of Cuypers best known for the Peek & Cloppenburg store on the Dam. It came with electric light, a lift and central heating.

Until 1906 two shallow 17th-century houses stood here, and between them a passage just over two metres wide led to the Mennonite church De Toren behind the block.

Joling kept the rhythm of three window bays and a heavy base, so the office would not shout among the houses. The name Gebouw de Koophandel (commerce building) is written over the door in gold. Between the two narrow windows on the first floor a carved stone shows a staff of Mercury between a horn of plenty, Berlage's Exchange and the Westerkerk, with the motto Audaces fortuna juvat. The stone is signed by the sculptor Rien Hack; a bronze Mercury, god of trade, has been added to the front.

It is an office building; the front is what you see.

Look for:
- the stone with the Exchange and the Westerkerk
- the stained glass with Amsterdam buildings in the wide first-floor window on the left
- the huge carved brackets under the balcony over the door

title: Huis Bartolotti and the White House next door
summary: Two rich men, two famous fronts. Bartolotti's house bends with the canal and got its name from an inheritance with strings attached. Next door, Michiel Pauw, who bought a slice of New Jersey and named it after himself, built what is called Amsterdam's first neck gable.
body:
Willem van den Heuvel grew rich by inheriting from a childless uncle by marriage, the Bolognese merchant Giovanni Battista Bartolotti. The will had a condition: he had to call himself Bartolotti. Around 1617–1620 he built this house. Two painted mottos under the top explain the fortune differently: by ingenuity and hard work, and by religion and honesty.

The front kinks twice to follow a bend in the Herengracht, where the old town moat curved around a bastion. The top of the gable, stripped in the early 1800s, was rebuilt in 1968–1971, hence the date 1971. Since 2026 the house, owned by Hendrick de Keyser Monumenten, is a recognised museum, with period rooms and a deep garden.

Next door, number 168 was built in 1638 by Philips Vingboons for Michiel Pauw, a director of the West India Company. In 1630 Pauw bought land on the Hudson from the Lenape for his own colony, Pavonia (Latin for pauw, peacock). His company went on to become one of the great slave traders of the Atlantic. Its pale sandstone gave the house its name, the White House; it is called the oldest neck gable in the city.

Huis Bartolotti is open several days a week; book a timed ticket.

Look for:
- the two Latin mottos high on the Bartolotti front
- the two kinks in the Bartolotti front, where the outer bays turn with the canal
- on 168, Pauw's arms held by two Venetian lions in the neck of the gable

title: The two Van Brienen houses
summary: A merchant family with two houses on one canal: a grand modern one at 182 and, at 284, a wedding present for the son. A French prince gave the second away in 1933 on one condition: it had to carry his mother's maiden name.
body:
In 1772 the merchant Arnout Jan van Brienen gave his 17th-century house at Herengracht 182 a new face. His Brussels-trained architect, Ludwig Friedrich Druck, used the latest Louis XVI style: a tall sandstone front with fluted strips, a balustrade with a crowned coat of arms and the year in Roman numerals. Behind the balustrade he hid a mansard roof, an early example in Amsterdam. Since 1894, when the Raadhuisstraat was cut through the canal wall, you can see that roof from the back.

In 1781 Van Brienen bought a second house at number 284 at auction, and a year later gave it to his newly married son Willem Joseph, later mayor of Amsterdam under King Louis Napoleon. Its sandstone front and rich interior date from 1728, when the Mennonite merchant David Rutgers and his two sisters rebuilt it to live in together. David died during the works; one sister lived on alone until 1743.

In 1933 Thierry, prince de Hénin, whose mother was born a Van Brienen, gave it to Hendrick de Keyser Monumenten, on condition that the interior was kept and the house was named after his mother's family.

Number 284 is hired out for meetings and weddings; 182 became an office in 1935. Both are seen from the street.

Look for:
- at 284, the carved sandstone middle bay and the door
- at 182, the crowned arms on the balustrade and the Roman date in the frieze
- the mansard roof of 182, seen from the Raadhuisstraat

title: Office of the American funds (Herengracht 255)
summary: A slice of northern France on the Herengracht: an 1894 office in brick and soft sandstone, built for a company that managed Dutch money in American railways. Look for the stone frog that swallows the drainpipe.
body:
This office was built to look after American securities held in Amsterdam. In 1894 three Amsterdam stockbroking firms had this office built for their joint company, the Maatschappij tot beheer van Amerikaansche fondsen, which looked after securities such as shares in American railway companies. Stables and coach houses made way for it.

The architect F.W.M. Poggenbeek, otherwise a fairly modern designer, here borrowed from the late Gothic and early Renaissance of northern France: red brick striped with pale sandstone, an asymmetrical front, and a steep roof with a stone dormer over the projecting bay. The city's monument description calls the style unique on the canal belt. The carving is said to follow designs by Lambertus Zijl, the sculptor of Berlage's Exchange. Because a soft sandstone was used, much of it is badly weathered.

The Van Gendt brothers extended the building to the left in 1933. It has been a hotel since 1975, rebuilt inside, so the front is what remains of the office.

Look for:
- the corner block shaped as a frog, with the rainwater pipe running through it
- the relief over the main door: a ship loaded with barrels
- animal figures carved in the window brackets of the ground and first floor
- the stone dormer with its steep pediment high on the right

title: Gas mantle factory with rooster tiles (Herengracht 267)
summary: A six-storey workshop and warehouse of 1898, squeezed onto a vanished alley between two canals. Tiles with crowing roosters still announce KANTOOR and MAGAZIJN (office and warehouse), although it has been flats since 1986.
body:
Among the houses on this stretch of the Herengracht stands something that looks like a warehouse, because it largely was one. J.J. van Bork had it built in 1898 for his factory of gas mantles, the little glowing fabric hoods that made gas lamps shine bright. The ground floor was the workshop, the first floor the office, the floors above storage. To fit six storeys and an attic in, the building was partly put on the Koksteeg, an alley that ran from here to the Singel.

The architect J. van Looy based it on 17th-century warehouses: three window bays, the middle windows larger than those at the sides. But he did not leave it plain. Art nouveau tile panels with roosters spell out what each floor was for. After the Second World War a branch of a paper merchant sat here until around 1970; in 1986 the building was converted into flats.

It is private; everything worth seeing is on the front. The Treeftsteeg runs along its side.

Look for:
- the tile panels with roosters and the words KANTOOR and MAGAZIJN
- the original glazed doors with small round-arched fanlights at street level
- the trefoil window in the pointed top

title: The other Mart Stam's office (Herengracht 303)
summary: A rare piece of Amsterdam School on the canal belt, with stirrup-shaped dormers and folding bay windows. It is by Mart J. Stam from Wormerveer, not the famous modernist of the same name, and it replaced a house that the new telephone exchange next door had shaken loose.
body:
In 1919 the building of the old telephone exchange beside it left the house that stood here, known as the Wapen van Swoll or the Trompetter, so weakened that it had to come down. What replaced it is one of the few buildings on the canal belt in the Amsterdam School style, and an early one.

The designer was Mart J. Stam (1886–1957), of a building firm in Wormerveer, mostly active in the Zaan region. He is easily confused with Mart Stam (1899–1986), the modernist of tubular steel chairs, and the city's monument description warns against exactly that. Unlike De Klerk or Kramer, this Stam let the concrete show: the bay windows on the upper floors are tied together with plain concrete posts and slabs, trimmed with ceramic drops and sawtooth bands.

His firm built it as its own office, went bankrupt, and in 1921 the building was sold at auction. The first user, a stockbroking firm, at once put in a strongroom and rented out safe-deposit boxes there until 1965. Unusually, the side wall on the Oude Spiegelstraat was designed too.

It is an office; you see it from the canal and the Oude Spiegelstraat.

Look for:
- the dormers shaped like stirrups, typical of the early Amsterdam School
- the angled bay windows, stacked and linked by concrete
- the carved front door set in a field of small orange tiles

title: Proeflokaal A. van Wees in a coach house with a turret
summary: An 1889 stable for a private carriage, with a turret built over a vanished alley and its classical orders upside down. Since the 1970s it has been a genever tasting room, still pouring spirits from the family's own Jordaan distillery.
body:
In 1889 a well-off couple from the Keizersgracht had this coach house built, with stabling below and a home for the coachman above. It replaced a neck-gabled house called the Koning van Portugal, and unusually on the canal belt the new building is lower than the old one: two storeys instead of four. The narrow right-hand part with the little tower stands on the site of the Vlasbloemsteeg, an alley it was built over.

The designer, J.F. van Hamersveld, also drew the Doelen Hotel. His neo-Renaissance front has a quirk the city's monument description points out: the Ionic order is on the ground floor and the Doric above, the wrong way round, and the plain wall anchors sit on the main floor while the fancy ones are up in the attic.

After the First World War a bottling plant and wine trade moved in. Later a family distilled liqueur here under the name De Admiraal, a business taken over by the Van Wees brothers, who opened a tasting room in 1973. Now Proeflokaal A. van Wees, it pours 17 genevers and over 50 old Dutch liqueurs from the family's own distillery in the Jordaan, and serves food from 10.00.

Look for:
- the wide arched carriage entrance
- the little tower with its eight-sided zinc spire and the date stone 1889
- Ionic capitals below, Doric pilasters above
- inside, the old pump from the distillery built into the bar

title: Cromhout houses and the neighbour who would not sell
summary: Four matching sandstone gables by Philips Vingboons, built for one rich merchant in 1660–1662. A timber dealer next door held out until the plans were finished, so his small house ended up swallowed inside number 368.
body:
The merchant Jacob Cromhout had Philips Vingboons design four houses side by side in 1660–1662: one to live in himself (366) and three more. Vingboons, often called the inventor of the Amsterdam neck gable, gave all four the same sandstone front with a triangular top, oval windows with wings, festoons and fruit along the shoulders. Over Cromhout's own door a stone shows a crooked piece of wood: krom hout.

The timber merchant Cornelis Kerfbijl, whose house stood on the plot of 368, agreed to sell only when building was about to start. The drawings could no longer be changed, so the plan of his little house, with its kitchen of 1623, was built into the new one. That is why 368 has no back house and 366 a double-width one.

In 1718 Cromhout's grandson hired the young painter Jacob de Wit for the ceiling of the great hall: his earliest ceiling painting, signed on the archer's quiver. From 1887 the Netherlands Bible Society used 366 and propped up the cellar with cast-iron columns to bear the weight of its Bibles; the Bible Museum followed, until 2020. Stadsherstel then bought 366 and 368 and restored them; they are now let as business premises. The fronts are seen from the canal.

Look for:
- the crooked wood on the stone above the door of 366
- the date 1662 in Roman numerals on three of the gables
- the empty or hacked-off coats of arms in the shoulders

title: Huis Nienhuys, a tobacco château that keeps the war archives
summary: A Loire château on the Herengracht, paid for with Sumatra tobacco. Its first owner's old house burned down in a freezing January night in 1888. Since 1997 it has held NIOD, the Dutch institute for war, Holocaust and genocide studies.
body:
Jacob Nienhuys was the first Dutch tobacco planter in Deli, on Sumatra, arriving in 1863, and in 1869 a founder of the Deli Maatschappij, whose plantations ran on contract labourers recruited in China and Java; from 1880 a worker who broke his contract could be punished as a criminal. Back in Amsterdam, rich, he bought Herengracht 382 in 1887 and had it done up. On Sunday 15 January 1888 a fire broke out during the drying of the works. Firemen fought it in wind and frost; by morning the ruin was hung with ice.

Nienhuys bought number 380 as well, pulled both down, and let Abraham Salm, who had studied in Paris, build him a palace in the style of Francis I, with the châteaux of Blois and Chenonceau and W.K. Vanderbilt's mansion on Fifth Avenue as models. The style is all but unknown elsewhere in Amsterdam. Inside, almost every room had its own style, from a Moorish bathroom to a Louis XVI billiard room, and the house made its own electricity.

He moved in in 1891 and sold to the Deli Maatschappij in 1909. Later owners included a bank and the Ministry of Finance. Since 1997 NIOD has been here, with the archives of the Second World War. Its study room is open on weekdays.

Look for:
- the architect's signature on the front: A. Salm GBzn Architect
- Mercury and Minerva, portrait medallions and lilies in the sandstone
- the railing on the stoop and its two lanterns

title: Grachtenmuseum (Museum of the Canals)
summary: A Vingboons double house of the 1660s that now explains how the canal belt was planned and built, with scale models, projections and a dollhouse brought to life with a Victorian stage trick.
body:
The canal belt became UNESCO World Heritage in 2010, and in April 2011 this museum opened to explain it. It sits in a double house that Philips Vingboons built in 1663–1665 for the businessman Karel Gerards: five bays wide, with pilasters and a pediment over the middle.

The house itself shows how canal houses changed over time. At the end of the 18th century the banker Jan Willink had the windows enlarged, and the festoons under them disappeared. Around 1875 the double stoop was removed and the entrance moved down to street level, with a staircase inside. The 18th-century period rooms on the first floor survive; the back room has wall paintings of idealised Dutch landscapes by Jurriaen Andriessen from 1776.

The permanent display tells how the belt was laid out in the 17th century, with scale models, animations and projections. A dollhouse shows the rooms of a canal house using Pepper's ghost, the 19th-century theatre trick of reflected glass. Since 2022 there are also temporary shows, including solo exhibitions by young Amsterdam artists, and there is a canal garden at the back.

Look for:
- the pediment over the slightly projecting middle of the front
- the big 18th-century windows that replaced the 1660s ones
- the entrance at street level where the stoop used to be

title: Tower on the Beulingsloot (Herengracht 395)
summary: An 1882 corner house with a step gable and a round stair tower rising from the water, by the two men who would go on to design Carré. It was built for a firm of butter and cheese exporters.
body:
Where the Beulingsloot meets the Herengracht, a round tower with a spire rises straight from the water. It belongs to a house built in 1882 as the premises of Broekman & Henny, exporters of butter and cheese. The designers were J.P.F. van Rossem and W.J. Vuyk, best known for Carré, the circus theatre on the Amstel.

They dressed it in neo-Renaissance, with a step gable that was already out of step with its neighbours when it was built. The idea was to fit the old, late medieval look of this side of the canal, which was built up before the canal belt itself. The city's monument description adds a dry note: a tower like this would very rarely have been seen in that 16th-century strip. Both fronts, on the canal and on the water, are treated as equals, and the tower has two doors, one at street level and one up a curved stone stair.

The front was refurbished in 2013 and became much lighter. It is private; the bridge over the Beulingsloot gives a good view of the tower.

Look for:
- the round tower turning octagonal at the top, with small round windows
- the lion's head on the corner of the step gable, with a hoisting anchor in its mouth
- the doors curving with the tower

title: Groenlandse Pakhuizen (the whale-oil warehouses)
summary: Three step-gabled warehouses of the 1620s where Amsterdam's whalers stored their oil. When they were turned into flats in the late 1970s, builders found sixty brick oil pits under the floors, and the oil-soaked walls kept spoiling the paint for years.
body:
The Noordse Compagnie, the Dutch whaling cartel founded in 1614, hunted whales off Spitsbergen and boiled the blubber into oil there, at stations such as Smeerenburg on the island the Dutch named Amsterdam. Some of its partners bought this plot in 1620 and built a row of five warehouses for the catch; the company also met here. The cartel lost its monopoly in 1642, and from 1685 storing whale oil was allowed only on the Nieuwe Teertuinen on the western islands.

Three of the five survive, nicknamed De Drie Gevels (the three gables). The oil was kept in brick pits on the ground floor, each holding about 10,000 litres, and in barrels in the lofts. Step gables are rare on Amsterdam warehouses, which usually have plain spout gables. The other two, with homes attached, burned in the 19th century and were pulled down in 1875 for a school, itself since replaced by flats.

A paper wholesaler, Bührmann, restored the three in 1922. In the late 1970s they became nineteen apartments, and the builders found sixty filled-in oil pits, twenty per warehouse. They are private homes, seen from the quay.

Look for:
- the three step gables, each topped with a little pilaster
- the stacked loading doors with a window on either side
- the hoist beams under their small roofs
- just south, bridge 54 from the Herenstraat to the Prinsenstraat, named the Noordsche Compagniebrug after the whaling company; its number is over the middle pier

title: The old De Zaaier on the Keizersgracht, the church that became a wrestling gym
summary: Behind a gable that lost its top hides an 1837 Catholic church, built on the spot of a 17th-century attic church. After the faithful left in 1929 it became a distillery store, then the training hall of a wrestling club whose bar stood where the altar had been.
body:
In the 17th century, when Catholics could not worship in public, they met in the attic of a warehouse on this site, called De Zaaier (the sower). Once Catholics had won equal rights, the Catholic architect and contractor Johannes van Straaten built a proper church here in 1837, in a sober classical style. Officially it was dedicated to St Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits; the name De Zaaier came from the earlier building.

The congregation left in 1929 for a larger church on the Rozengracht, and the building was sold. Demolition was considered; instead it was adapted. From 1949 it served as a warehouse for a distillery. Later the wrestling club Hercules trained in it, among them the former champion Bert Kops, and the club's small bar stood in the old altar space. After the wrestlers came an exhibition space and other uses; now a clothing label is based here.

The front lost its top gable and roof, and the entrance doors became windows, but the church structure behind it is still largely there. It is not open to the public.

Look for:
- the classical sandstone front, now cut off flat
- the frame of the old main doorway, kept when the doors were replaced by windows

title: Rode Hoed, the biggest hidden church in the country
summary: In 1630 the Remonstrants, banned from worshipping in public, pulled down a hat workshop and built a church in the middle of the block, with no door onto any street. It is the largest and oldest hidden church left in the Netherlands, and since 1990 a debating hall.
body:
The Remonstrants, a Protestant group at odds with the official Reformed church, were not allowed to profess their faith in public. In 1629 a wine merchant and a doctor bought a hat-maker's workshop here for them; it was pulled down, and in 1630 the hidden church Vrijburg rose in its place. It stood in the middle of the block, ringed by houses, with no access from any street. The congregation bought or rented almost all the houses around it to keep the site safe.

For a hidden church it is big: a hall with two tiers of galleries on Tuscan wooden columns, arched windows and even a small rose window. It was much rebuilt in the 19th century, when it got its skylight, and the entrance wing on the canal dates from 1876. The organ case is of 1719. The Remonstrants used it until 1957.

In 1989 the theologian Huub Oosterhuis found it empty and set up his student congregation and a debating centre in it, opened in 1990. Sonja Barend's talk show and Het Lagerhuis were recorded here. You get in for debates, lectures and concerts; it is also hired out for weddings and meetings.

Look for:
- the 1876 entrance wing with round-arched windows and an arched frieze under the gable
- how the church itself stays out of sight: only the entrance wing touches the canal

title: Huis met de Hoofden (House with the Heads)
summary: Six stone heads on a 1622 canal house. Legend says a maid beheaded six burglars one by one with a meat cleaver; they are in fact Roman gods. Comenius lived here as a guest, and today it is a museum of esoteric books, the Embassy of the Free Mind.
body:
The house was built in 1622 for Nicolaas Sohier, a rich dealer in stockings and a lover of art, on two extra-wide plots. Its front is attributed to Hendrick de Keyser, who died in 1621, and was probably finished by his son Pieter. Shortly after Sohier moved in, his wife and two daughters died, and in 1634 he sold the house to the arms dealer Louis de Geer, whose family kept it for four generations. Laurens de Geer let the Czech educator Jan Amos Comenius live here.

The six heads at the height of the main floor gave the house its name. The legend: six robbers crept in, and the kitchen maid cut off their heads one by one with a meat cleaver. The busts are Apollo, Ceres, Mercury, Minerva, Bacchus and Diana, three men and three women, each with an attribute, and were added by De Geer. Mercury (trade) and Minerva (wisdom) flank the door.

Later it housed a school, the conservatory (1909–1931) and the city's monuments office (from 1983). In 2006 the collector Joost Ritman bought it, and since 2017 it holds his library of hermetic philosophy as the museum Embassy of the Free Mind, open Wednesday to Sunday.

Look for:
- Ceres with ears of corn, Bacchus with grapes, Diana with a crescent moon
- the 1622 date stone in the step gable
- the little gate on the right, with a room above it for the coachman

title: Keizersgracht 143, the room that moved to The Hague
summary: From the street an ordinary 18th-century canal house. Until 1931 its front room held a complete painted salon of about 1710, with tapestries of a dream forest; the whole room now stands in the Kunstmuseum in The Hague.
body:
The house dates from about 1624 and was rebuilt around 1700; the front and the carved stoop are 18th-century, the door and straight cornice 19th. Around 1710 the front room, the sael, was fitted out as a painted salon. Its ceiling opens onto a painted sky in which Minerva (wisdom) and Justitia (justice) float, and the walls were hung with tapestries by Alexander Baert, a weaver from Oudenaarde working in Gouda and Amsterdam, showing an imaginary wooded landscape with water, birds and buildings.

From the 1860s the Boissevain family lived here and ran their insurance office from the house; the classicist Ursul Philip Boissevain lived here from 1911 until 1930. In 1931 the salon was taken out complete and moved; it is now shown as the Gobelinzaal in the Kunstmuseum Den Haag.

The house has its own wartime story: Betje Cohen, a Jewish resident, was taken from here and died in Auschwitz in 1942; two children who still lived at home survived. Later came a post-war restitution office and university institutes, and now apartments. A ceiling painting is still in a side room, but the house is private: you see the front, and the room itself in The Hague.

Look for:
- the carved 18th-century stoop
- the 19th-century door under the straight cornice

title: Astoria, a life insurer's tower on the Leliegracht
summary: One of the first office towers in the Netherlands, built in 1904–1906 for a life insurance bank, with a guardian angel in mosaic and the bank's initials in gilt on the roof ridge. Greenpeace International was run from here for fifteen years; a chocolate empire began next door.
body:
The Eerste Hollandsche Levensverzekerings-Bank had its head office built on this corner in 1904–1906 to designs by Gerrit van Arkel and H.H. Baanders, in the sober Dutch version of art nouveau called Nieuwe Kunst. Seven storeys and 37 metres high, on a reinforced-concrete frame in the French Hennebique system, it counts as one of the first office towers in the country. In 1966 it was extended on both sides in exactly the same style. The register calls it the expression of the canal belt turning into offices.

The insurer also invested in property and kept using Baanders for it. He designed the shop fronts of Leliegracht 24 (1895), which he signed on the right pier, and Leliegracht 22 (1899). At number 22 Casparus van Houten started a chocolate mill in 1815, the forerunner of the Van Houten cocoa factory that moved to Weesp in 1850.

Greenpeace International had its headquarters in Astoria for fifteen years from its founding in 1989. It is offices now; the interior is not open.

Look for:
- the mosaic of a guardian angel high on the Keizersgracht side, with a clock above it
- the letters EHLB in gold in the iron ridge railing on the copper roof
- the open octagonal turret on the Leliegracht side
- "H.H. Baanders architect" carved in the right pier of Leliegracht 24

title: Coymanshuis, Jacob van Campen's first known design
summary: Before he built the town hall on the Dam, now the Royal Palace, Jacob van Campen drew this classical front for two merchant brothers in 1625: his earliest known design. A family that ended at the Gold Coast owned it later; now Amnesty International works behind it.
body:
In December 1624 Balthasar Coymans bought the plot, and in 1625 Jacob van Campen designed the front: the first architectural design of his that is known, decades before his town hall on the Dam. It is eight bays wide, with Ionic pilasters on the main floor and composite ones above. In 1631 the front and plan were published in the book Architectura Moderna. Balthasar and his brother Johan lived here with other members of the Coymans trading firm.

The house changed a good deal. The cross windows became sash windows around 1780, which cost the first-floor windows their pediments; in 1876 the low attic was replaced by a full storey when the house became a secondary school, and the back wall collapsed in 1931. After the last Coymans died in 1759 it went to Jan Pieter Theodoor Huydecoper, who died at Elmina on the Gold Coast, and then to his nephew. The city bought it in the 19th century; until the 1980s it held the Ir. Lely Lyceum. Since 2003 Amnesty International Netherlands has its office here, so you see it from the quay.

Look for:
- the two orders of pilasters, Ionic below and composite above
- the full top storey of 1876 that replaced Van Campen's low attic

title: Moeder Godskerk (Church of Our Lady), Syriac and Catholic
summary: A neo-Gothic church of 1852–1854, built in among the canal houses for the Redemptorist fathers. When they left in 1985 the Syriac Orthodox bought it, and they still share it with Catholic congregations; once a year a procession walks the canals.
body:
The Redemptorist fathers had this church built in 1852–1854, right beside their monastery at number 218. The architect, Theo Molkenboer, then the leading church builder in the north of the country, based it on the Redemptorist church in Mons in Belgium. It is a cross-shaped basilica with clustered piers and rib and star vaults; the vaults are not stone but plastered wood. The register calls it the first Dutch church in the manner of French High Gothic; nl.wikipedia says it was the first true neo-Gothic church outside Brabant and Limburg, not in the whole country. Built in on three sides, it shows the canal only its front.

The Redemptorists left Amsterdam in 1985 and the Syriac Orthodox Church bought the building, calling it the Moeder Godskerk, the church of the Mother of God. It stayed open to others: a Dutch Catholic community served by Opus Dei priests and a Surinamese Catholic community also hold services here. Since 1868 the church has kept a copy of the icon of Our Lady of Perpetual Help. Since the 150th anniversary in 2004 a procession along the canals on Corpus Christi has become a tradition.

You can go in for the services.

Look for:
- the tall Gothic front squeezed between the canal houses
- the Syriac inscription on a wall inside

title: Offices that ate the Keizersgracht
summary: Between 1912 and 1955 five firms tore down canal houses on this stretch to build offices, and each architect had to answer the same question: how do you fit a modern office into a 17th-century canal? Two of the answers, both of 1955, face each other across the water.
body:
Around 1900 the canal houses filled up with offices, and soon firms wanted purpose-built ones. At Keizersgracht 307 (1912) P.H. van Niftrik built one on the Wolvenstraat corner that only just passes as a canal house. Next door at 313 the Rotterdam firm R.S. Stokvis had two old houses demolished in 1913 for a 13-metre-wide warehouse with sample rooms, for sanitary ware and for chandeliers, designed by J. Verheul, known for the Witte Huis on the Raadhuisstraat. At 369-371 a whole row, once used by the Reformed orphanage, went in 1938 for the office of ANIEM, an electricity company in the Dutch East Indies; the architect, A.J. van der Steur, wrote a long defence of it.

In 1955 two offices went up almost at the same time, facing each other. At 271-275 the Nederlandse Crediet Maatschappij demolished three houses for a quiet brick office by A.J. Westerman; in the following decades its row grew to five buildings and swallowed seventeen houses, amid a storm of criticism. Across the water, at 298-300, C. de Geus and J.B. Ingwersen chose an openly modern front that still keeps the old window rhythm and the high stoop.

All are offices; you see them from the quays.

Look for:
- the 1955 pair, 271-275 and 298-300, facing each other across the canal
- the foundation stones on the NCM row, dated 1955, 1967, 1974, 1980 and 1983
- the high stoop in front of the modernist glass front of 298-300

title: Roode Huys, where Han van Meegeren lived on his fake Vermeers
summary: In 1943 the painter Han van Meegeren bought this 17th-century house with money from forged Vermeers, one of which had ended up with Hermann Göring. Arrested here as a collaborator in 1945, he saved himself by proving he had painted it.
body:
The house was built in the first half of the 17th century with a step gable of finely ground brick with very thin joints. Around 1740 it was raised, which damaged the gable. Because the front was plastered for a long time, the brickwork survived well; the plaster came off in 1958.

In the autumn of 1943 Han van Meegeren bought it. A painter scorned by the critics, he had turned to forging Vermeers, and during the occupation the trade went well: his Christ and the Adulteress was sold, through a dealer, to Hermann Göring. After the war the Allies found it among Göring's loot, and the trail led to Van Meegeren, living in luxury here. Since he could not explain where the painting came from, he was arrested as a collaborator in May 1945. To escape that charge he confessed he had painted it, and, at first disbelieved, painted one more "Vermeer" under supervision. In November 1947 he was sentenced to a year for forgery, but died of a heart attack before he began it. His widow lived here until 1954; the contents were auctioned in the house in 1950.

Later the Dutch timber federation and then the Dutch architects' association had offices here. It is private; you see it from the street.

Look for:
- the brick front with big relieving arches over the windows
- the cornice of about 1800 where the step gable once rose

title: Keizersgracht 318, the gutted rococo house
summary: A canal house of about 1765 with rare rococo window frames. In 2017 a builder was caught tearing out its listed interior; the works stopped, squatters moved in in 2020, and only after their eviction in 2025 could the repairs begin.
body:
The front dates from the third quarter of the 18th century, around 1765, with a storey and roof added in the 19th century. Caspar Philips drew it around 1768 for his Grachtenboek, the canal book of house fronts, and it has changed little since: a stone basement front, a stoop up to the main floor, one floor of living rooms and two storage floors with loading doors. The window frames are carved in rococo style, which is rare on the canals. Inside are marble mantelpieces.

In 2017 the owner started a renovation, and the city's heritage department found the contractor demolishing parts of the listed interior. The Vereniging Vrienden van de Amsterdamse Binnenstad, the inner-city preservation society, got involved and the works were halted. The delay left the house empty, and in 2020 it was squatted. In 2024 the society reported that it was decaying, still squatted and still unrepaired. By February 2025 it had been cleared, and the restoration could start under Architectenbureau Vroom; in spring 2026 the front was wrapped in blue sheeting.

It is private; you see it from the quay, a few doors from Felix Meritis.

Look for:
- the carved rococo frames around the windows and door
- the stone basement front behind the stoop

title: Felix Meritis, from Enlightenment club to Communist HQ
summary: Built in 1788 for a society of art and science, its oval hall was Amsterdam's best concert room. Then came a sweatshop printing works and, from 1947, the Dutch Communist Party, which in 1956 beat off a furious crowd by pelting it with lemonade bottles from the roof.
body:
The society Felix Meritis (happy through merit) was founded in 1777 by well-to-do Amsterdammers to practise music, drawing, physics and literature. Its building, by Jacob Otten Husly after an international competition, opened on 31 October 1788, a temple-like front with Corinthian columns and a separate room shaped for each discipline. Women and Jews were not admitted as members until far into the 19th century. Until about 1830 the oval concert hall was the city's main music room: Clara and Robert Schumann, Brahms and Saint-Saëns played here, and Beethoven's Ninth had its Dutch premiere here.

The society folded in 1888. The printers Holdert & Co moved in, notorious for child labour: boys of 13 slept in hammocks between the presses. A fire in 1932 destroyed the upper floors. From 1947 to 1981 it was the head office of the Communist Party of the Netherlands and its daily De Waarheid. On 4 November 1956, the day Soviet tanks entered Hungary, thousands besieged the building, smashing windows and ramming a door; the defenders answered from the roof with bottles of lemonade that burst with loud bangs and seas of foam.

In 1969 Ramses Shaffy opened a theatre in it, the Shaffy theatre. After a renovation it reopened in 2020 as a cultural centre with talks, debates and performances, so you can get in.

Look for:
- the sandstone front with half-columns and a carved pediment
- the balustrades along the top of the front

title: Liefde is 't Fondament, the 'papist' hofje
summary: In 1618 Claes Reiniersz founded a hofje for Catholic women here, to the annoyance of the Reformed preachers. It survived, was rebuilt in 1912–1914 with little step gables, and still belongs to the Catholic poor relief that has run it since 1866.
body:
In 1618 Claes Reiniersz founded an almshouse court here for Catholic women of some means: after paying an entrance sum they could live in one of its eighteen small houses. That it was a "papist hofje" was a thorn in the side of the Reformed preachers, but it carried on, and in 1866 its management passed to the Roomsch Catholijk Oude Armen Kantoor, the Catholic poor relief office, which still runs it.

In 1912–1914 the office had it completely rebuilt to a design by J.N. Hendrix, a contractor, city councillor and later senator. He kept the spirit of the old hofjes: a sober street building on the canal, and behind it five little houses in a U around a garden, in Dutch neo-Renaissance with step-gabled dormers, bands of sandstone and many-paned sash windows. The old name and the founder's coat of arms, with a star, went back over the door. Single elderly women no longer live here; after a spell of student housing it is now all offices, one of them the poor relief office itself. The garden, with a long pond, was redesigned by the landscape architect Arend-Jan van der Horst, and the old lintel was set at the end of the pond.

Look for:
- LIEFDE IS HET FONDAMENT over the left-hand door, with the founder's arms below
- the long passage from that door to the court

title: Schouwburgpoort, the gate of the first city theatre
summary: This sandstone gate of 1638 once led to Jacob van Campen's city theatre, opened with Vondel's Gijsbrecht van Aemstel. The theatre burned down in 1772 with sixteen dead; the gate survived and now leads to a luxury hotel.
body:
From 1617 a wooden playhouse stood behind this spot. On 3 January 1638 the first stone city theatre of Amsterdam, designed by Jacob van Campen, opened here with Joost van den Vondel's Gijsbrecht van Aemstel, the start of a theatre tradition that lasted for centuries. The gate on the canal, with three openings, Ionic pilasters and a triangular pediment, was its entrance. It once carried Vondel's lines: "De weereld is een speeltoneel, elck speelt zijn rol en krijght zijn deel" (the world is a stage, each plays his part and gets his share).

The theatre was rebuilt in 1665. On 11 May 1772 it went up in flames, and sixteen people died, among them regents and their wives. Two years later a new theatre opened at the Leidsepoort, by today's Leidseplein. On the courtyard behind the gate the Catholic poor relief office, the R.K. Oude-Armenkantoor, built a new house in 1772–1773. In 1999 that was turned into a hotel, now The Dylan.

The gate is the only part of the 1638 theatre left. You can look through it into the forecourt; the hotel and its restaurant are open to guests.

Look for:
- the three arches with their railings and the pediment above
- through the gate, the 1773 poor office front with its lantern over the door

title: Huis Marseille, a map of Marseille on a canal house
summary: A French merchant who made his fortune on one ship from Marseille set a stone map of the port in the front of his new house around 1665. Since 1999 the house has been the first Dutch museum given over entirely to photography.
body:
The house was built around 1665 for Isaac Focquier, a French merchant. A ship he had freighted in Marseille, which brought him to Amsterdam, made him rich, and he had a stone with a plan of the French port set in his classical front. For some years he sat on the city's College van Commercie, which advised on trade, and he made it into the top circles of the city.

Three centuries on, the 17th-century layout of front house, courtyard, back house and garden is largely intact, with painted ceilings, stucco and marble.
