In the garden room hangs a ceiling of 1730 painted for the house by Jacob de Wit, with Apollo enthroned among Minerva and the nine Muses; it spent years in the Rijksmuseum and came back in 2004. When the museum took in number 399 next door in 2011–2013, a room of the early 18th century turned out to have scarlet mouldings under its cream paint, a red found almost nowhere else in a Dutch period room, and it was restored to that colour.

Since 1999 the house has been Huis Marseille, the first museum in the Netherlands devoted entirely to photography, with exhibitions over five floors, a photo library and a canal garden with a garden house. It is open daily from 10.00 to 18.00, on Thursdays until 21.00.

Look for:
- the stone with the map of Marseille in the front of number 401
- the sandstone neck gable with round windows
- the decorated stoop and its 18th-century railing

title: Huis Fuld, a banker's palace in prefab ornament
summary: On the spot where the sculptors carved the statues for the new town hall on the Dam, a city palace went up in 1685. In 1860 a Frankfurt banker had it remade by the architect of the Amstel Hotel, with some of the first factory-made ornaments on a canal house.
body:
Until the canal belt was extended to the Amstel in 1662–1663, the city's stone yard stood here, where among other things the sculpture for the new town hall on the Dam, now the Royal Palace, was made. When the canals were dug through, the yard was pulled down and moved. In 1685 the builder Pieter Adolfse de Zeeuw put up a city palace on the corner for Joannes Vinckel.

In 1859 it was bought by Elias Jacob Fuld, a Jewish banker from Frankfurt am Main who had settled in the Netherlands in 1853. In 1860–1861 he had it rebuilt by Cornelis Outshoorn, architect of the Paleis voor Volksvlijt and the Amstel Hotel: a new plastered front in an eclectic style, rich stucco ceilings and a grand staircase, and the coach house turned into the office of his bank, Becker & Fuld. It was one of the first canal houses with prefabricated ornament: terracotta on the outside instead of carved stone, and cast zinc on the stair rail instead of carved wood, cheaper and quicker at a time when skilled carvers were scarce and dear. In 1892 the lawyer and politician Cornelis Jacob den Tex had Eduard Cuypers enrich the interior once more.

It is let as offices and is not open; you see the fronts on the Keizersgracht and the Molenpad.

Look for:
- the stuccoed corner fronts under a carved cornice
- the sandstone ground floor with a balcony

title: Multatuli's birth house and museum
summary: The author of Max Havelaar was born in this alley house in 1820, though he believed almost to the end that he was born on the Haarlemmerdijk. His admirers started planning a museum in 1910; it took them until 1975 to open it here.
body:
Eduard Douwes Dekker, who wrote as Multatuli, was born here on 2 March 1820, according to his birth certificate. He himself believed until shortly before his death that he had been born on the Haarlemmerdijk. His novel Max Havelaar (1860) showed how the Dutch colonial government ruled Java through the local aristocracy.

In 1910 a committee of admirers, among them Floor Wibaut and Ferdinand Domela Nieuwenhuis, met at the Krasnapolsky hotel to plan a lasting tribute, including a museum. It did not come off: the Multatuli papers were stored at the Stedelijk Museum and from 1926 at the university library. In 1943 a member of the Multatuli society bought this house, and in 1957 the city bought it, on condition that he and his wife could stay. Then the tenant of the ground floor refused to leave, despite offers from the city, until 1963. The museum finally opened on 1 March 1975, at first by appointment only. A sister museum opened in 2018 in Rangkasbitung on Java, where Douwes Dekker lived through the events he described in Max Havelaar.

The house is an alley house shaped like a canal house, with a bell gable. The museum keeps a permanent collection and holds exhibitions; it opens on a few days a week, so check before you go.

Look for:
- the cartouche between the windows: Douwes Dekker "Multatuli" werd in dit huis geboren, 2 maart 1820
- the stone stair set along the front, moved there when the museum was made

title: Langestraat 3-19, one office that swallowed a row
summary: From 1894 to 1912 one client, O.W.G. Briegleb, bought up and joined the houses of this stretch one after another into a single office, latterly for the French paint firm Le Ripolin. The fronts still look like separate houses, but share one cornice.
body:
The Langestraat, laid out around 1610 as the Bredestraat between the Singel and the Herengracht, was a street of craftsmen and barge skippers, criss-crossed by alleys. Around 1900 the canal belt filled with offices, as colonial trade, industry and banking boomed, and many homes were converted.

This row shows how that went, one house at a time. In 1894 O.W.G. Briegleb had the architect W. Hamer, otherwise a builder of workers' housing, turn numbers 3 and 5 into an office. In 1897 number 7 was added, in 1899 numbers 9, 11 and 13, each time knocked through inside. The last part, numbers 15-19, followed in 1912 to a design by J.W.F. Hartkamp. By then the office belonged to the paint dealer Le Ripolin. Hamer kept repeating the same elements, so the separate fronts read as one: the same doors, window frames, floor heights and brickwork, and one moulded cornice over the shop fronts running from number 3 to number 15. Numbers 15-19 differ in width, detail and designer.

The office has since been split into homes again; the passages between some of the houses remain. You see it all from the street.

Look for:
- the moulded cornice running unbroken over the ground floors of 3 to 15
- the same ironwork in the doors, porch and windows of 5 and 9
- where the pattern breaks at numbers 15-19

title: Boldoot's coach house (Langestraat 47)
summary: A coach house and workshop of 1897 for Boldoot, the Amsterdam eau de cologne maker that supplied five royal courts and had one of the city's first telephones. Amsterdammers also gave its name to the night-soil cart.
body:
Boldoot began in 1789 as a pharmacy on the Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal, where Jacobus Cornelis Boldoot sold powders, ointments and a remedy of his own based on alcohol. Around 1865 production moved to Singel 92 and 94, and the firm grew into the country's best-known eau de cologne maker: purveyor to the courts of the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Portugal and Italy, one of the first firms with a telephone (1881) and a gas engine (1882). At its height it used sixteen buildings on the Singel and in the Langestraat. In 1897 it had this building put up by H.J. Amesz, probably as a coach house and workshop, on a plot backing onto the Singel premises; the firm owned Langestraat 47 to 57 as well. Production moved to the Haarlemmerweg from 1902 and to Sloterdijk in 1938.

The name stuck in the language: in Amsterdam and Drenthe the cart that collected night soil was called the Boldootkar.

The building is little changed. It is private; you see it from the street.

Look for:
- the big dormer with a spout gable, hoist beam and round window, breaking through the cornice
- the arched double doors for carts in the middle of the ground floor
- the two single doors with round-arched fanlights
- round the corner at Singel 94, part of Boldoot's property, the front of 1876 with a richly carved roof house that poses as a neck gable

title: The tailors' saint (Langestraat 78)
summary: A 17th-century house that was a tailor's workshop for generations carries a gable stone of St John the Baptist with the Lamb of God, patron saint of tailors. Restored in 2014, it now shines in red, blue and gold.
body:
In 1610 the house belonged to a tailor, Hendrik Jacobsz; his heirs sold it in 1628 to a hatter. In 1663 another tailor, Tieleman Broens, bought it, and the deed of sale says the tenant, also a tailor, could take away his shop sign and his cutting table. For many years the tailoring trade went on here.

The gable stone is first mentioned in 1749, when the deacons of the Reformed church sold "a house with Sint Jan Baptist in the front". Its niche-like frame suggests it is older, perhaps from the first quarter of the 17th century, and St John the Baptist was the patron of weavers, dyers, tailors and furriers, which fits the trade in the house. He stands in a camel-hair cloak, pointing at the Lamb of God at his feet; instead of the usual cross-staff or book there is a sword with a little cross-banner. In 2014 the stone was examined and restored with help from the society of friends of Amsterdam gable stones, and painted.

The house still looks like a workshop, with a wooden ground-floor front and a central double door. It is private.

Look for:
- the stone between the first-floor windows: S. JAN BAPTISTA
- the old loading opening between the second-floor windows

title: Potgieter's house, with the poet on the front
summary: The writer E.J. Potgieter lived here from 1855 until his death in 1875. His friends and admirers paid for a life-size marble bust of him on a pedestal of books, set over the door in 1882 in a new front designed by a fire-brigade officer.
body:
Everhardus Johannes Potgieter lived and worked in this house from 12 May 1855 until his death on 3 February 1875. In January 1879 a memorial stone with those dates was placed in the front.

In 1881 the house was thoroughly rebuilt for its owner, C. Gautzch, and got a whole new front in Dutch neo-Renaissance style, designed by J.W. Meijer, a fire-brigade officer who was entitled to call himself architect and engineer. The old stone was damaged in the works. In May 1882 friends and admirers paid for a new one, gold letters on black marble with the same text, and for a life-size bust of white marble by Henri Teixeira de Mattos, just back from Rome, standing on a pedestal of books in a niche over the door. The house was auctioned in 1918 and again in 1929, and in 1949 the courtyard was roofed over for a warehouse.

It is private; you see the bust from the street.

Look for:
- the marble Potgieter on his books, over the door with Corinthian half-columns
- the balcony on three brackets on the first floor
- ANNO 1881 in gilt in the scrolls of the top gable

title: Molenpad, from carriages to cars, and a copied corner
summary: A path to a mill older than the canal belt, lined with the coach houses of the Amsterdamse Rijtuig Maatschappij that became garages around 1930, a girls' school of 1883 on the site of a French refugee church, and a 17th-century corner house that was rebuilt from scratch in 1971.
body:
The Molenpad was there before the canal belt: a country path to a mill near today's Raamplein, swallowed by the city in the 17th century.

Numbers 6-8 are a 19th-century coach house with a home above. In 1928 the Amsterdamse Rijtuig Maatschappij, the carriage company, had them converted into a garage by Izaäk Blomhert, and in 1930 it had him build a new garage with four flats above at 10-16. It is still a garage: Parking Molenpad, where staff park your car. Number 6-8 later served the public library, whose head office was round the corner on the Prinsengracht.

On the corner, Molenpad 15-17 stands where the city fencing school was turned into the Nieuwe Walenkerk, a church for French refugees. In 1883-1884 the city built a public school for girls of the fourth class, the dearest kind, with a fee of 70 guilders: the Agatha Dekenschool. The school left around 1901, other schools followed, and from 1937 came a sound-film studio, a sculptor's studio and a physiotherapy practice.

Across the Molenpad, Prinsengracht 663, a listed 17th-century corner house, was demolished to the ground in 1971-1972 and rebuilt as a copy by the architect Anton van Es, with its two lily-shaped wall anchors.

Look for:
- the garage doors and round fanlights of 10-16
- "Openb. School v.m.u.o.o.v. Meisjes" in the frieze over the school door
- the wedge-shaped corner of Prinsengracht 663, widening towards the top

title: Van Brienenhofje, an almshouse on a brewery
summary: Behind a long Prinsengracht front with a little clock tower lies a hofje. It was built from 1804 on the site of the De Star brewery, for Catholics living in deep poverty.
body:
The brewery De Star stood here until Aernout Jan van Brienen, lord of De Groote Lindt, bought it with a house and a warehouse and had them pulled down. In their place he and his wife Sophia Maria Half-Wassenaer had a hofje built, an almshouse round a garden, meant for poor Catholics. The design was by the city architect Abraham van der Hart, building began in 1804 and the first residents moved in around 1806. The official name still recalls the brewery: Van Brienens Gesticht De Star.

The family ran it privately until a foundation took it over in 1841. Since 1995 the buildings have belonged to the housing association Het Oosten, and people still live here.

The layout is unusual for a hofje: a free-standing main building on the canal, two wings of homes along the courtyard, and another separate building at the far end. Over the canal front sit dormers with clock faces and a small bell tower. The courtyard is a residents' garden; if the gate is open, go in quietly.

Look for:
- the clock faces in the dormers and the bell tower on the roof
- the memorial stones and the framed doorway of the main building
- the long courtyard behind, glimpsed through the gate

title: Zon's Hofje, on the site of a Mennonite church
summary: An ordinary front door on the Prinsengracht opens on a courtyard where a Mennonite church once stood. From 1765 it housed Mennonite women of fifty and over; since 1967 its residents have been young women students.
body:
The name is a leftover. On this spot stood a Mennonite church, De Kleine Zon (the little sun). After mergers of congregations it was no longer needed by 1752, and in 1764 the plan for an almshouse was made. In 1765 the first women moved in: Mennonites aged fifty or more. In the 19th century two houses on the canal, numbers 173 and 175, were added, one with the regents' room and the overseer's home, and in 1893 the hofje was enlarged and rebuilt for 32 residents.

In the 20th century fewer older women wanted to come; a modernised Mennonite hofje elsewhere was more popular. Rooms went to young Mennonite women and social workers, and when the last elderly resident left in 1967 it became a students' hofje for young women.

The main building has three storeys under a hipped roof. Above the door to the upper homes is a stone of Noah's ark with the animals going in two by two under a shining sun, a date stone of MDCCLXV (1765), a verse and a sundial. It is a home, so be quiet and respectful.

Look for:
- the stone "De Arke Noach" with its beaming sun
- the date stone and the sundial above it
- the clock face on the main building

title: The meat hall on the old Westerkerk graveyard
summary: A plain brick hall of 1814 beside the Westertoren is one of only two old market halls left in the city. It exists because Louis Napoleon had the weigh house on the Dam pulled down.
body:
In 1808 King Louis Napoleon had the weigh house on the Dam demolished. The weighing moved into the 17th-century meat hall on the Westermarkt, and the butchers needed a new home. So in 1814 the city architect Abraham van der Hart built this sober hall of twenty stalls on a corner of the Westerkerk graveyard, which had just been closed. He offered a wooden version on a stone base and a brick one; the brick one was built, budgeted at a little under 9,400 guilders.

It did not stay a meat hall for long. By 1832 the land register calls it a city stable and store. Later it was the gym of a secondary school on the Keizersgracht, and after the Second World War, for decades, a stonemason's workshop. Around 2000 it became a restaurant, and modern extensions were added on the side and back.

The register calls it a rare survivor: of the city's covered market halls, only this one and the much altered Sint Pietershal on the Nes remain. You see it from the Prinsengracht, under the tower.

Look for:
- the single low storey under a saddle roof, with stepped brick edges on the gables
- the long run of windows down the side
- the open space around it, once the graveyard

title: Homomonument, three pink triangles
summary: The world's first free-standing monument in public space to gay men and lesbians persecuted for who they were. Three pink granite triangles, one dipping into the Keizersgracht, together form a triangle 36 metres a side.
body:
In 1970 two young activists tried to lay a wreath for persecuted homosexuals at the National Monument on the Dam on 4 May. They were arrested and the wreath was destroyed. After the national remembrance of 1979, Bob van Schijndel asked why Jews and Roma had their own memorials and gay people did not. A foundation followed within months, the council chose the Westermarkt that summer, and Karin Daan won the design competition. Money came in slowly until governments more than doubled it. The monument was unveiled on 5 September 1987, a hundred months after the first call.

The pink triangle was the badge the Nazis made men imprisoned for homosexuality wear in the camps; the movement took it over in the late 1960s. Each triangle has a meaning. The one on street level, carrying Jacob Israël de Haan's line "Naar vriendschap zulk een mateloos verlangen", stands for the past and points to the Anne Frank House. The raised one, for the future, points to the old COC office on the Rozenstraat. The one in the water, for the present, points to the Dam.

It is in daily use: flowers on the triangle in the water, a commemoration every 4 May at 8 pm, parties on King's Day and during Pride, and protests. The tram stop has been called Homomonument since 2017.

Look for:
- De Haan's line cut into the street-level triangle
- the triangle that lies half in the canal
- the Pink Point kiosk beside it

title: Huize Labor, the office that founded a heritage society
summary: For this wine merchant's office of 1919–1921 a 17th-century double house on the corner of the Westermarkt was demolished. The outcry led to the founding of the Vereniging Hendrick de Keyser, which has been buying and saving old houses ever since.
body:
On this corner stood a fine 17th-century double house with twin step gables. In 1918 the wine merchant H.W.C. Würdemann had it pulled down for a large office, partly for his own firm and partly to let; he lived in it too and called it Huize Labor. There was no heritage law yet. All that was needed was the consent of the Commissie voor het Stadsschoon, the city's beauty committee, and its member Gerrit van Arkel was the architect of the new building.

The protest was fierce. In the journal De Gids the client was called a man without taste or feeling, the builder of a new "sky-scraper". Würdemann answered in De Telegraaf that he had bought a ruin with a revolting advertising wall and would be proud to be the founder of Huize Labor. Out of the protest came the Vereniging Hendrick de Keyser, founded in 1918, which buys threatened houses and keeps them by letting them. It now owns houses all over the country, among them Huis Bartolotti on the Herengracht.

The building itself is a sober, symmetrical design with Amsterdam School touches, and it can be seen from far along the Raadhuisstraat. It is an office building; you see it from the square.

Look for:
- the main entrance on the Westermarkt and the second one on the Keizersgracht
- the Homomonument at its feet

title: Raadhuisstraat, a tram street cut through the canals
summary: In 1895 the city filled in a canal and knocked a bend through the canal belt to run a tram from the Dam to the new west. The fronts that rose along the gap, from 1897 to 1935, show the old residential canal belt turning into offices and shops.
body:
The Raadhuisstraat got its name on 27 February 1895. To make it, the Warmoesgracht between the Singel and the Herengracht was filled in, and between the Herengracht and the Keizersgracht a breach was cut through the blocks. Because the streets on either side did not line up, it came out as an S-bend. George Hendrik Breitner photographed and painted the breakthrough. A horse tram ran here from 1896.

The north side filled with new buildings. No. 20-22 (1897) was an office for an insurer founded in 1771, which stayed until 1959; its architect, Louis Rieber, was better known as a writer. No. 44 (1903, F.M.J. Caron) housed an office giving free advice on insurance, and no. 42 (1910, Jac. Duncker) was designed as its partner; from 1913 a firm there sold projectors for "salon cinemas". Nos. 36-40 (1935) replaced an annex of a Catholic orphanage.

Across the street, no. 15 (1891) was built for the coffee trade, with a sample room facing north so the beans could be judged in even light; the coffee futures market met there until 1973.

All are shops and homes or offices, seen from the street.

Look for:
- the two Jugendstil fronts of nos. 42 and 44, side by side
- the neo-Renaissance gables and iron balcony railings of no. 20-22
- the oak oriel of the coffee sample room on no. 15, and G. van Arkel's name carved under the corner oriel of nos. 52-54 (1902)

title: Singel 250, the colonial bank robbed by speedboat
summary: A stone palace of 1910–1912 on the corner of the Raadhuisstraat, built for a bank that lent to firms in the Dutch East Indies. Later the city's giro office worked here, and in 1976 robbers got away across the canal in a speedboat.
body:
The Nederlandsch-Indische Handelsbank, founded in 1863, lent money to businesses in the Dutch East Indies. In 1910–1912 it built this office on the new Raadhuisstraat, designed by J.P.F. van Rossem and W.J. Vuyk, with fronts of bluestone and sandstone and two storeys of giant Corinthian pilasters. A newspaper of 1912 said it recalled the palace on the Dam. In 1926–1927 A.D.N. van Gendt enlarged it by seven bays, the part left of the entrance. Inside, according to the register, are leather wall hangings with maps of the Netherlands and the Indonesian archipelago, a list of the bank's branches, and stained glass with the bank's initials.

After Indonesian independence the bank's holdings there were nationalised, and in 1960 it was taken over. From 1963 the building was the head office of the Gemeentegiro, the city's own payment bank. In 1976 robbers raided it and escaped over the canal by speedboat; they were never caught. From around 1990 it was the main post office. Today it holds offices; you see it from the street.

Look for:
- the carved arch over the main door on the Singel
- the vases on the corners of the roof
- the posts and hanging chains round the building

title: De Dolphijn, home of the Night Watch captain
summary: Two step gables pushed into each other make up the double house the poet Hendrick Laurensz Spiegel built around 1600. Frans Banninck Cocq, the captain in Rembrandt's Night Watch, lived here while the painting was made.
body:
The poet Hendrick Laurensz Spiegel had this house built between 1599 and 1602, to a design by Hendrick de Keyser. A drawing of De Keyser's design survives, but the front was built plainer, without some of its classical pilasters and cornices. It is a house with a side house, a forerunner of the double canal house: a normal house of three bays with a narrower one of two bays beside it. Its two step gables are each designed wider than the space allows, so they overlap.

In 1609 Volckert Overlander bought it, and in 1630 he left it to his son-in-law Frans Banninck Cocq, who lived here when Rembrandt painted his company of civic guards, the painting now called The Night Watch (1640–1642). Between 1655 and 1679 the house was split in two: De Vergulde Dolphijn on the left and De Kleyne Dolphijn on the right. In 1863 the right gable was replaced by a flat cornice, and in 1966–1967 it was rebuilt from old pictures such as a view by Abraham Storck. The split into two houses remains. Both are private homes.

Look for:
- the masks and sandstone ornament on the fronts
- the two step gables, the right one a 1960s reconstruction
- the Empire-style doorway of no. 142

title: Necofa, an Amsterdam School clothing factory on the Singel
summary: A dark-brick corner block of 1918–1920 that the register itself calls out of tune with the canal. It was built for a Jewish clothing firm that did not survive the war; in 1976 squatters moved in.
body:
In 1918–1920 Adriaan Moen designed this office, workshop and store for the clothing factory A. Cohen & Co., which made clothes for women, men and children. Moen knew the firm through the Gerzon fashion chain, which Cohen supplied and for which he had worked. He wrote that he wanted to keep what was beautiful of the old house: the carved oak staircase, the doors and the back front on the Roomolenstraat. That 18th-century front is still there, now the side of the rear wing.

The firm went bankrupt in 1922 but carried on, from 1926 as Necofa, short for Nederlandsche Confectiefabriek. Like many Jewish businesses it came to an end in the Second World War. After the war the national postal savings bank used the building; in 1976 it was squatted, and today it houses small businesses.

The register is frank: in size it fits the canal, but in style it is a dissonant, with its stressed corner and its odd balance of window and wall, typical of the Amsterdam School. Moen, it adds, was almost forgotten when he died in 1950.

Look for:
- the triangular bay window over the door
- the brickwork rising to a crest at the corner
- round the corner, the old canal-house front with its carved cornice and stoop railing

title: Huis met de Neuzen (the House with the Noses)
summary: A neck-gabled house of about 1750 with three grotesque heads on its front, hence its name. The wing pieces beside the neck are of an unusual design too.
body:
This neck gable of the mid-18th century carries three caricature heads, faces with exaggerated features, which gave it its name, Huis met de Neuzen, the house with the noses. The national register dates the gable to about 1750 and singles out its wing pieces, the carved stone side pieces of the neck, as being of a particular design.

The doorway below is later, in the Empire style of the early 19th century. The house is private; you see it from the Singel quay or from across the water.

Look for:
- the three caricature heads on the gable
- the carved wing pieces on either side of the neck
- the Empire doorway

title: Centraal Beheer's first office, an old house inside a new front
summary: In 1916 the insurer that became Centraal Beheer merged a canal house of 1769 with two new-built neighbours behind one brick front. The old house's door, basement height and window rhythm decided the whole design.
body:
The insurer behind this front began as the Centrale Werkgevers Risico-Bank, which handled the 1901 Accident Act for employers. In 1905 it moved here from the Damrak into an old canal house, no. 130, and in 1909 it joined two farm and market-garden insurers under the name Centraal Beheer. In 1916 it took in nos. 126 and 128, had them demolished and rebuilt in concrete, and put one new brick front across all three. The firm moved to Apeldoorn in the 1970s.

The architect, H.J.M. Walenkamp, was one of the young reformers of the Architectura group who fought the 19th-century revival styles, though not a successful builder himself. Here he kept parts of the house of 1769 and let it set the pattern: the place of the door, the height of the basement and the width of the bays. He then simply added three more bays on the right. The register calls the combination of 18th-century interiors and his work unique. The interiors are not open; the front is seen from the Singel.

Look for:
- the three bays of the old house to the left of the door and the three new ones to the right
- the high basement and the stoop

title: The one-of-a-kind cable box in the Langestraat
summary: A cast-iron electricity cable box from shortly after 1913, when the city took over the power company. It carries the logo of the municipal electricity works, and no other box of this model is known.
body:
Around sixty historic cable boxes survive in Amsterdam, from the years when the city was wired for electricity. The best known are the Amsterdam School ones with three ribs over the top and front. This one is different. It probably dates from just after 1913, the year the city took over the private N.V. Electra, and it carries the logo of the Gemeente Electriciteitswerken, the municipal electricity works. It was cast by the Amsterdam iron foundry Zimmer.

As far as the city register knows, no other box of this model exists. That is why it was listed as a municipal monument in 2013: an early reminder that electricity became a city service. It stands on the pavement and is still in use.

Look for:
- the logo of the municipal electricity works
- the founder's name, Zimmer

title: Nieuwe Suykerhofje, a Catholic hofje with a fake organ
summary: Through a door in an 1895 house front lies a hidden former hofje of 1755 for elderly Catholic women, with its own chapel. Inside the chapel, says the register, is an organ made entirely of stucco.
body:
The Nieuwe Suykerhofje was founded in 1755 for 54 elderly Catholic women. It lies inside the block, out of sight: three buildings of flats, three storeys high, grouped along a narrow passage and its side arm, with the chapel across a courtyard at the back. The chapel, dated 1755, has three round-arched windows, the middle one framed in bluestone. According to the national register its interior keeps its stucco decoration, an altarpiece and a remarkable imitation organ, modelled in stucco rather than built of pipes. The homes still have 18th-century casement windows with small panes.

The way in is the right-hand door of Prinsengracht 383, a house rebuilt in 1895 for a pharmacist who lived here with his family until 1900. That door was once an open gateway to the courtyard. The house itself is a neat piece of 1890s neo-Renaissance, with a little tower on its dormer and a bay window on a shell-shaped console.

The hofje is private; from the canal you see the gateway house.

Look for:
- the right-hand door of no. 383, the old gateway
- the turret on the dormer and the bay window on its shell console

title: Te Huis, a Christian lodging house for women travelling alone
summary: A narrow canal front of 1901 with tile panels on its bay was a hostel for women and girls travelling alone, run by a Reformed society. Ladies paid up to 1.50 guilders a day for full board at the front; housemaids slept at the back.
body:
The Vereeniging tot Verbreiding der Waarheid, a Reformed Christian society, already ran a lodging house for women here when it had this building rebuilt in 1900–1901. The architect was Tjeerd Kuipers, best known for the more than fifty Reformed churches he designed across the country.

The newspaper Het Nieuws van den Dag described it in June 1901. The front house was for ladies: room and full board for 1.50, 1.25 or 1 guilder, with a shared conversation and dining room behind the big bay window looking out over the canal, and space for seventeen. The back house was for housemaids, who paid 50 or 75 cents a day for a small but bright room with everything included; there was room for thirty, with their own dining room and hall.

The front still shows its purpose, the register says, in the tile panels on the bay. It keeps its original look almost entirely, down to the recessed balconies. You see it from the canal.

Look for:
- the tile panels on the bay window of the second floor
- the recessed balconies higher up
- the shallow roof that hides a flat one behind it

title: Van Bottenburg's bookshop, where Trouw was printed in secret
summary: For more than a century this canal house held a Reformed theological bookshop and publisher. In the war it hid a resistance base: early issues of the underground paper Trouw were printed here, and in 1944 Radio Oranje was recorded upstairs.
body:
In 1897 Hendrik Arnold van Bottenburg opened a theological bookshop, publishing house and antiquarian business here, of Reformed signature. It grew into an influential firm, above all in the 1920s and 1930s.

The founder died suddenly in 1941. His son Arnold and Arnold's wife Hilly carried on the business and joined the resistance. Students of the Vrije Universiteit met here in secret, because the occupier had banned student societies. The underground paper Trouw, started in 1943 by orthodox Protestant resistance people, had early issues printed here. From May to October 1944 its editors ran a listening post on an upper floor: broadcasts of Radio Oranje from London were recorded on gramophone records and typed out elsewhere for the paper. Arnold van Bottenburg was betrayed, arrested and sent to a concentration camp. He survived.

Hundreds of Trouw's makers were arrested, and 23 men were shot at Camp Vught. After the war Trouw became a national daily, as it still is.

The bookshop stayed until 2010; from 1986 to 1992 the national school students' action committee LAKS had its first office here. The house, mid-18th century and raised in the late 19th, is seen from the canal.

Look for:
- the business rooms in the basement and on the raised ground floor
- the line where the 18th-century front meets the later top

title: The poor-relief bakery on the burned theatre's site
summary: Down an alley off the Prinsengracht stands the former bakery of the Catholic poor relief office, with a time verse of 1787 in its front. It was built on the grounds of the city theatre that burned down in 1772.
body:
On 11 May 1772, at the end of a performance, a rope caught fire on stage and within minutes the whole city theatre on the Keizersgracht was ablaze. More than fifteen people died; the ruins were sifted for gold and jewellery. The grounds, which reached back towards the Prinsengracht, were bought by the R.K. Oude Armenkantoor, the Catholic office for poor relief. On the Keizersgracht side it built its new office behind the old theatre gate, now the hotel The Dylan. On this side stands its bakery.

The bakery's front carries a time verse dated 1787 in a bluestone frame. In a time verse, or chronogram, certain letters are also Roman numerals and add up to the year. The ground floor keeps windows and fanlights with small panes.

The building stands back from the canal. A nameless alley beside Prinsengracht 495 leads to it.

Look for:
- the time verse in its bluestone frame
- the small-paned windows and fanlights on the ground floor
- on the Keizersgracht, the theatre gate on the other side of the same grounds

title: The frog stone of Prinsengracht 535
summary: Beside the front door hangs a tiny blue tile with a frog and a Latin line from Ovid: 'though they are under water'. It remembers the people who hid in this house in the war, and their habit of gossiping in hiding.
body:
In 1941 the archaeologist and art historian Annie Zadoks-Josephus Jitta went into hiding in this house. More than eight people hid here during the Second World War. She escaped when the hiding place was cleared in 1942 or 1943, bought the house after the war, and her son later gave the stone that is now beside the door.

It is a small blue tile with a frog in relief and the words QUAMQUAM SUNT SUB AQUA, "though they are under water". The line is from Ovid's Metamorphoses, where the goddess Latona turns the peasants of Lycia into frogs; even under water they go on slandering. Only the first half is quoted. The people in hiding here gossiped a lot, and the comparison was made as a joke; "under water" also points to onderduiken, the Dutch word for going into hiding, literally diving under.

The house itself is an 18th-century canal house with a raised cornice of the early 19th century, as the national register has it. It is private; the stone is small and easy to miss.

Look for:
- the blue frog tile beside the front door
- the Latin words above and below the frog

title: De Nederlander, a biscuit factory with three step gables
summary: A neo-Renaissance shop front of 1895 hid a whole biscuit works behind it, with ovens, stables and some forty workers. It was designed by Tjeerd Kuipers, an architect known for churches, for the baker B.J. Lindeboom.
body:
In 1895 Barend Jan Lindeboom, who had just split from his partner in a bread and rusk bakery, had this building put up for his biscuit and pastry factory De Nederlander. His architect was Tjeerd Kuipers, better known for more than fifty Reformed churches. In front was a shop with homes above, one of which Lindeboom lived in for a while. Behind, through a long passage from the gateway on the left, lay the works, reaching into the gardens of the neighbours: ovens, workshops, a carriage house, stables, an office and a packing room. In 1895 some forty people worked here, making spiced cake, butter biscuits and the like. The firm was known for its picture albums and puzzles given away as advertising; it probably lasted until about 1920.

After that came a rubber, leather and oilcloth trader, from 1986 a piano dealer, and now an antiques dealer. The step gable was once richer, with scrolls and finials; the plainer top dates from after 1962. The register singles out the stone shop front with its carriage gateway and the porch with its decorative glass as rare in the inner city.

Look for:
- the stone shop front and the gateway on the left
- the step gables on three sides
- the small carved details on the plinths

title: The old central library that pretended to be canal houses
summary: Behind this front of 1973 stood the biggest textile factory in Amsterdam; then an office block was designed in its place, broken up to look like a row of canal houses. From 1977 to 2007 it was the city's central public library.
body:
From the 1870s a textile company spread across this block between the Prinsengracht and the Keizersgracht. Its sewing machines were driven by a steam engine, and until 1900 it was the largest textile factory in the city. A German competitor bought it in 1968 and closed it a year later, and developers wanted offices on the huge plot.

The firm of G. de Klerk, with Rob Nord as designer, drew an office building here in 1973, and almost all of the factory was demolished; only an 1897 front on the Keizersgracht was kept. A modern office front was out of the question: a large bank on the Vijzelstraat had just caused a storm of protest. Nord broke the wide front into brick blocks about as wide as canal houses, of differing heights, divided by narrow strips of wood and glass. Before it opened, the design was strengthened, piles and all, to carry the weight of books: from 1977 the public part of the central library was here. Even a society of preservationists praised it. The register calls the front a milestone, one of the first steps towards small-scale building in the old city.

The library moved to the Oosterdok in 2007, and the building was turned into a hotel.

Look for:
- the brick blocks of different heights, each roughly one house wide
- the recessed strips of wood and glass between them

title: Runstraat 14-18, Pegasus on a 1934 row
summary: Three shop houses of 1934 that look like three old ones. The gable top with the winged horse Pegasus, dated 1730, and the stone 'De Stadt Zutphen' were saved from the houses that stood here before.
body:
In 1934 four old houses on this side of the Runstraat were replaced by three new ones, built as a single project. The city's chief building inspector, Eelke van Houten, was involved; he argued for reusing good old parts in new buildings, and some two hundred houses in the city are counted as Van Houten houses. Here the sandstone gable top of old no. 14, with its scrolls and a Pegasus of 1730, went onto the middle house, no. 16, and the gable stone De Stadt Zutphen came from old no. 20, which has gone.

The architect, A. van der Vlugt, let the middle house step forward under its neck gable, so the row reads as three separate houses. The register praises how complete it is: shops below, homes above, two of the three shop fronts with their original leaded fanlights, and almost all the doors and windows from 1934. No. 14 has been the left half of café De Doffer since the 1970s.

Look for:
- Pegasus in the round pediment at the top of no. 16
- the gable stone De Stadt Zutphen lower down
- the leaded fanlights over the shop fronts

title: The fishmonger's house on the Amstel
summary: A red brick house of 1893 built for a fishmonger, and it says so: fish on the keystones, two fish and a net in the gable, and a sea god on a bracket who has lost his trident.
body:
The building runs right through the narrow block between the Reguliersbreestraat and the Amstel, so it has two fronts. Both were designed in 1893 by Van Rossem and Vuyk, the architects of Carré, for C. Saur, who kept a fish shop here. They chose a lively neo-Dutch Renaissance style and let the carving tell you what was sold downstairs.

The Amstel side is the better one. Above a wooden bay window with a balcony, a large figure stands on a carved bracket halfway up the front, probably Neptune; his trident has gone. Over him hangs a canopy and a garland with the year 1895. The stepped gable is crowned with a relief of two fish in a net, and fish appear again on the keystones of the third-floor windows. On the Reguliersbreestraat side, look up for a carved man's and woman's head in the cornice and little dolphins curling round the corner pinnacles.

Both ground floors were rebuilt long ago for shops; the upper floors are flats. Everything worth seeing is above the shop fronts.

Look for:
- the sea god without his trident and the 1895 garland above him, Amstel side
- two fish and a net at the top of the Amstel gable
- fish on the third-floor keystones
- the dolphins on the corner pinnacles, Reguliersbreestraat 11-13

title: De Kleine Komedie
summary: Amsterdam's oldest working theatre began as a French playhouse where Louis Napoleon came to watch. It was a Scottish mission church, a hall for freethinkers and a wartime bicycle shed before it became the country's best-known cabaret stage.
body:
The city architect Abraham van der Hart built this theatre on the Amstel in the 1780s as the Théâtre Français sur l'Erwtemarkt. King Louis Napoleon and later King Willem I were regulars. It then became a German theatre, and from 1856 the Scottish mission church; for a few years after 1880 the newly founded Vrije Universiteit rented rooms here for lectures. Between about 1908 and 1935 it was a meeting hall for both right-wing Protestants and left-wing freethinkers. During the war it served only as a bicycle shed.

In 1947 it reopened as De Kleine Komedie. The fire brigade condemned it in 1973 and it stood empty until private money reopened it in 1978. When the city cut its subsidy in 1988, a public campaign led by the comedian Youp van 't Hek saved it, and under director Joost Nuissl it grew into what the Dutch call the temple of cabaret. Big names still play runs of several nights here, and many TV recordings are made in the 503-seat hall.

It is open on performance nights; the programme is mostly Dutch-language cabaret and music.

Look for:
- the round-arched doors on the ground floor
- the Empire-style framed windows above them
- the dormer set in the roof over the front of the building

title: Café De Kroon and its painted lobsters
summary: A café-restaurant of 1898 on the Rembrandtplein with a corner tower and a crown on top. Look up at the bay window: painted lobsters and butterflies, and sunflowers running up the corner pilaster.
body:
De Kroon (the crown) opened in 1898 on three old plots on the north side of the Rembrandtplein, with a second part on the Amstel behind it. It was designed by Gerrit van Arkel, who around this time moved from historical styles to a sober Jugendstil, and it came just as the square was changing from shops to places to go out.

The square front is all white plaster now; Van Arkel's design had more colour. What colour is left is in the paintings: lobsters and butterflies over the windows of the bay, a crown at the top of the corner tower and sunflowers on the pilaster at the right. The leaded glass in the bay and in the fanlight over the main door is original, and so is the ironwork balcony on the second floor. The ochre Amstel front, with its fanciful gable, was also a café.

It is still a café-restaurant on the first floor, turning into a club with DJs at night, so you can go up and sit in the bay.

Look for:
- the painted lobsters and butterflies over the bay windows
- the crown painted at the top of the corner tower
- sunflowers on the right-hand corner pilaster
- the yellow back front on the Amstel, Amstel 82

title: Swigtershofje
summary: Behind a carved gateway of 1756 on the Amstel lies one of the smallest hofjes in town, with a row of houses and a rococo chapel that is now let as a guest suite for two, the bed under the altar.
body:
Between the Rembrandtplein and the Amstel, Amstel 88-98 is a hofje, an almshouse court, known as the Swigtershofje. The national register lists three parts: a small gateway carved by Pieter Pantel in 1756, a row of dwellings, and a chapel with galleries, a stucco ceiling and a stucco altar wall with an altarpiece, from the third quarter of the 18th century.

The gateway is the part you can see from the street. The chapel survived, restored in 1979 with the rest of the hofje, and has become a hotel room: Private Mansions lets it as The Hidden Church, a suite for two with the bed beneath the stucco altar wall and its cherubs. Only guests get in.

Look for:
- the carved gateway of 1756 in the Amstel front
- the row of small houses behind it, numbers 88 to 98

title: Wertheim & Gompertsz, a bank for American railway shares
summary: One of the first buildings in Amsterdam designed as a bank, put up in 1871 for a firm that administered shares in American railways. Eleven years later another architect doubled it by copying the front.
body:
In 1871–1872 the firm of Wertheim & Gompertsz built an office on the Amstelstraat to run its business in American railway shares. It is one of the earliest buildings in the city designed specifically as a bank: offices grouped round a central light well, a director's room, a caretaker's flat and the archive upstairs. The firm hired Cornelis Outshoorn, architect of the Amstel Hotel and the Paleis voor Volksvlijt, who gave it a rich classical front, unusual in the old centre.

In 1882 Isaac Gosschalk added a second half to the left, and simply repeated Outshoorn's five window bays, so the front now reads as one symmetrical palace with two centres. By the 1920s the bank had gone: part of the ground floor was joined to the stage of the Flora theatre next door, and the rest became furniture shops. When the city listed it in 2004 it held restaurants, a café and a nightclub upstairs.

Look up past the shop fronts.

Look for:
- the two identical halves of the front, each with a raised centre bay
- the wide window framed by two narrow ones under a broken pediment in each centre
- garlands over the first-floor windows

title: The Amsterdamsche Bank and its thrifty animals
summary: Twenty-four houses came down for this bank of 1926–1932 on the Rembrandtplein, with paternoster lifts and room for 1,250 staff. Over the Herengracht door Lambertus Zijl carved the bank's ideal customers: bees, ants, beavers and squirrels.
body:
To build its new head office the Amsterdamsche Bank had twenty-four houses demolished, taking up the whole end of the block between the Herengracht, the Utrechtsestraat, the Rembrandtplein and the Amstelstraat. H.P. Berlage worked on it with B.J. and W.B. Ouëndag; the facades were probably his, though his exact share is not clear. Inside it was thoroughly modern: climate control, double glazing, nine ordinary lifts and two paternosters, vaults over two basement floors and space for 1,250 people.

The building looks deliberately closed, a safe stronghold for savings, with a base of rough granite and barred windows. The city's design committee wanted shop windows; the display windows along the Utrechtsestraat only came later. On the square Berlage placed a slim tower, not on the corner itself but where the building steps down two floors.

The sculptor was Lambertus Zijl, who had worked with Berlage on the Beurs. Above the main entrance on the Herengracht he carved industrious and thrifty animals. The building is now offices called The Bank, with restaurants on the ground floor.

Look for:
- the bees, ants, beavers and squirrels in granite between the windows over the Herengracht entrance
- the bronze grilles and lanterns at the three entrance porches
- the tower on the Rembrandtplein corner
- the yellow glazed tiles in the gallery on the Utrechtsestraat

title: Blauwbrug
summary: A showpiece bridge of 1883, built to impress visitors to the Colonial Exhibition, with ship-bow piers, red granite columns and imperial crowns. Critics found it far too pompous for Amsterdam. In Yiddish it is the Bloubrik.
body:
The Blauwbrug (blue bridge) is named after its wooden predecessors, which had blue railings. In the 1880s the city wanted a bridge the tram could cross, and one to show off during the International Colonial Exhibition of 1883. The city architects Bastiaan de Greef and Willem Springer designed a monumental fixed bridge of blue limestone, with balustrades of polished white stone, eight columns of polished red Swedish granite, sixteen lanterns and piers shaped like the bows of ships. The Amsterdam Omnibus Company paid half the cost. When it opened, many found it too grand for the city.

It was the way into the old Jewish quarter, and in Yiddish it was the Bloubrik, a name that turns up in many sayings about never escaping where you come from. On 30 April 1980, the day Beatrix was crowned, squatters and riot police fought here; A.F.Th. van der Heijden turned it into the novel De slag om de Blauwbrug.

Piet Kramer replaced the iron girders with concrete in 1938–1939 and changed the look; a restoration in 1999 undid his changes and brought back the blue.

Look for:
- the imperial crowns, painted in colour, on top of the granite columns
- the ship's prow and the animal figures halfway up each column, holding the lanterns
- the piers shaped like ship bows, best seen from the Amstel quay

title: Hamburger's lead works and the triangular house
summary: An 18th-century brewery became a lead works in 1900, and its name is still spelled out under the cornice. Next door stands a house on a triangular plot less than four metres deep at its deepest, all window.
body:
From about 1768 to 1787 the brewery De Drie Roskammen (the three curry-combs) stood here, and the site went on brewing until the late 19th century. In 1900 A.D. Hamburger of the Koninklijke Nederlandse Lood- en Zinkpletterijen, a lead and zinc rolling mill in Utrecht, had the architect M.H. Ligthart turn it into a lead works: a shop, a warehouse and flats on the Amstel, and the foundry itself on the inner court, reached through a passage to the Wagenstraat. Oven and casting tray on the drawings suggest they made sheet lead there.

Number 194-196 is the robust part: red brick, two wide arches, heavy balconies, and the firm's full name in relief under the cornice. Stone bump-blocks at the right-hand gate show where the carts went in. Number 198, in Art Nouveau, sits on a triangular plot less than four metres deep, so its front is one tall bay window to win a little floor space. Its piers carry a relief of plants that look like hops, perhaps a nod to the brewery. When the city listed it in 2004 the ground floor was a diamond dealer's shop and showroom; the upper floors are homes.

Look for:
- KONINKL.NED. LOOD EN ZINKPLETTERIJEN v/h A.D. HAMBURGER under the cornice of 194-196
- the letters ADH and UAR forged into the grille of the wide right-hand door
- the stone bump-blocks beside the cart gate
- the red bay window and the hop-like reliefs on number 198

title: Huis met de Bloedvlekken (the house with the bloodstains)
summary: A stately sandstone house of 1671 where Coenraad van Beuningen, six times mayor and the Republic's star diplomat, ended his days. Ruined and convinced the end of the world was near, he painted Hebrew or kabbalistic signs on the front; legend says in his own blood.
body:
The house was built in 1671–1672 for Gijsbert Dommer, probably to a design by Adriaan Dortsman: a double house with a sandstone front three windows wide, a balcony on columns in the middle carrying the year MDCLXXI, and a carved balustrade on top.

Its fame comes from a later resident. Coenraad van Beuningen was the Dutch Republic's most experienced diplomat and mayor of Amsterdam six times between 1669 and 1684. In 1686 he married his neighbour, Jacoba Bartolotti, and moved in here. In 1688 he lost half a million guilders speculating in VOC shares. He wrote letters to the church authorities about the coming end of the world and went out into the street to paint Hebrew or kabbalistic signs on his house. After he named the city of Amsterdam his heir he was put under guardianship, and he died in 1693, shut up in a house on the Amstel, leaving little more than a bed, a desk, a mirror and a portrait of an old man by Rembrandt. Amsterdam calls this the house with the bloodstains: the story goes that he wrote in his own blood.

It is a private house; the front is what you can see.

Look for:
- the reddish-brown signs at eye level either side of the front door
- MDCLXXI on the middle section, above the balcony on its two columns
- the carved balustrade on the cornice
- the early 19th-century stoop posts and chains

title: Six Collection, Amstel 218
summary: Rembrandt's portrait of the mayor Jan Six still hangs in the home of his descendants, in an ordinary-looking canal house on the Amstel. The eldest son of the eldest son lives there, and visitors come only by appointment.
body:
Rembrandt painted Jan Six (1618–1700) in 1654. The portrait never left the family. It is the best-known piece in the Six Collection, which also holds family portraits by Frans Hals, Paulus Potter, Gerard ter Borch and others, and paintings by Cuyp, Ruisdael and Saenredam. Until 1915 the collection was in the family's double house at Herengracht 509-511. When the Vijzelstraat was widened that house was demolished; the panelling went to Amstel 218, and so did Jan Six VI, the professor who in 1922 set up a family foundation so the collection could never be split. Since then the eldest son of the eldest son has lived here with it.

The state supports the foundation on condition that the collection stays together and can be seen, on introduction. It owned the house from 1957 until a new agreement in 2008, after years of legal dispute and poor upkeep, gave it back to a family foundation. After a restoration the house reopened in 2012.

The house itself dates from 1662–1668, refronted in the late 18th century. You can visit only on personal request through the collection's website: art-history students give free tours of about an hour on weekday mornings, in Dutch or English, for up to four people per request, aged ten and over. No photos, and bags stay in the cloakroom.

Look for:
- the carved double stoop with eight bottle balusters
- the entrance, door and fanlight, all from the time it was built

title: The Amstel-end bridges and the men who laid out the canals
address: Amstel, at the Herengracht, Keizersgracht and Prinsengracht
summary: Where the Herengracht, Keizersgracht and Prinsengracht run into the Amstel, three 18th-century stone bridges carry the names of the men behind the canal ring: a city carpenter, a surveyor and a mayor. Date stones on the river side give their years.
body:
Each of the three great canals ends at the Amstel under an arched stone bridge, and each now carries the name of one of the planners of the canal ring's third extension. Hendrick Jacobsz. Staets was the city carpenter, Lucas Jansz Sinck the surveyor and Frans Hendricksz. Oetgens a mayor; together with Hendrick de Keyser they prepared and carried out the plan.

The Herengracht bridge, the Staetsbrug, has two stones reading "Anno" and "1728" either side of its middle arch. It had to be fairly high because the quay of the Weesp ferry lay behind it. The Keizersgracht bridge, the Sinckbrug, dates from 1769 according to a stone in the north quay wall. The Prinsengracht bridge, the Oetgensbrug, has two badly worn stones reading "Anno 1773" on the river side, and patches of later repair brickwork that do not match the old. All three look old but were strengthened inside with concrete in the 1970s.

They are ordinary public bridges along the Amstel walk; the date stones are best seen from the quay.

Look for:
- Anno and 1728 on either side of the middle arch of the Herengracht bridge
- the 1769 stone in the quay wall by the Keizersgracht bridge
- the weathered 1773 stones and mismatched repairs on the Prinsengracht bridge

title: Reguliersgracht, the seven bridges and the canal they nearly filled in
summary: Stand on the Herengracht and look down the Reguliersgracht: seven arched bridges line up one behind the other. In 1901 the city wanted to fill the canal in for the electric tram; a protest saved it. One of the bridges is named after Tante Saar, the Rembrandtplein flower seller.
body:
The Reguliersgracht was dug in 1664. It was meant to run on to the Amstel, but buying out the houses in the way would have cost more than the new plots brought in. Its first stretch, now the Thorbeckeplein, was filled in during the 17th and 18th centuries. In 1901 the city planned to fill in the rest for the electric tram. The new history society Amstelodamum, the educator Jan Ligthart and the painter Jan Veth protested and won.

Bridge 38 over the Keizersgracht was sagging in 1901, but the city held off repairs while it considered a roundabout here; in 1905 cracks closed it to all but pedestrians. In 1907 the city decided against filling, and in 1908–1909 the three bridges at that crossing were rebuilt a little flatter. De Telegraaf wrote that they would no longer be the terror of Amsterdam's horses.

The bridge at the Herengracht end is the Tante Saarbrug, named in 2016 after Sara Bachrach (1887–1982), who sold flowers on the Rembrandtplein for decades, survived several concentration camps in which she lost children and grandchildren, and became an honorary citizen. The Kerkstraat bridge of 1780 is nicknamed the Ronde brug: in still water arch and reflection make a full circle.

Look for:
- the seven arches in a row, seen along the canal from the Herengracht
- the Tante Saar name plates and the Anno 1734 stone in the Herengracht quay
- the Anno and 1780 stones on the north side of the Kerkstraat bridge

title: Amstelkerk, the temporary wooden church
summary: In 1668 the city put up a wooden preaching barn on the Amstelveld, leaving room for a proper stone church later. The stone church never came, and the wooden one is still here. Vincent van Gogh sat through his uncle's sermons in it.
body:
Daniël Stalpaert designed the Amstelkerk in 1668–1670 as a temporary wooden preaching barn: a square of 100 by 100 feet, the same size as his Oosterkerk. It was set against the Reguliersgracht side of the Amstelveld so that a stone church could one day be built in the middle of the square. That never happened. Originally the pine walls were painted ox-blood red and inside you looked at the bare back of the planks. From 1837 the interior was remodelled in neo-Gothic style by Springer, and in 1843 J. Batz & Co. built the organ.

From 1855 to 1883 the minister was Johannes Paulus Stricker, an uncle by marriage of Vincent van Gogh. During his stay in Amsterdam in 1877–1878 Vincent faithfully attended his Sunday services while Stricker prepared him for studying theology.

The church was used by the Reformed Church until 1985. Since 1986 it has belonged to Stadsherstel Amsterdam, which has its office here and rents it out for gatherings, receptions and weddings; there is a restaurant in the basement on the south side, and since 2006 a congregation holds Sunday services again. The square around it has a flower market on Mondays.

Look for:
- the square wooden body of the church with its brick annexes and fence
- the rare left-lapping roof tiles on part of the church and on the little building beside it
- the Monday flower market on the Amstelveld

title: Huis Willet-Holthuysen and its plantation money
summary: A canal house left to the city in 1895 by a collector couple, on condition it became a museum under her name. In the 18th century a banker ran a Surinam office here, lending against plantations and the enslaved people on them.
body:
The house was built in 1685–1687 for Jacob Hop, the city's pensionary; its front dates from about 1739. About ten families lived here before Abraham Willet and Louisa Holthuysen, collectors of silver, glass, ceramics and paintings. Louisa left the house and everything in it to Amsterdam in 1895, on condition that it became a museum bearing her name. Its first curator, until 1931, was the writer Frans Coenen. It is run by the Amsterdam Museum and since 2022 is called Huis (house) rather than Museum Willet-Holthuysen.

The wealth behind the house is the subject of the exhibition Plantage aan de gracht (16 October 2026 to 4 April 2027). The banker Willem Deutz (1697–1757) ran a Surinam office here and developed the negotiatie, a form of credit in which plantations, and the enslaved people on them, served as security. The next resident, the merchant Fredrik Berewout, owned plantations himself, among them Jagtlust, where 125 enslaved people were recorded in 1786.

Inside you see the 19th-century salons, the dining room, the kitchen in the basement and a formal French-style garden laid out in 1972. The museum is open daily.

Look for:
- the richly carved doorway and the sandstone ornament under the windows
- the decorated stoop with its bottle baluster
- the garden, from inside the museum

title: Saint Michael on the party wall
summary: Two canal houses share one 17th-century front, built as a single double house. The statue of Saint Michael and the dragon that crowned its centre now stands exactly on the line between the two properties.
body:
Herengracht 579 is one half of what was built in the third quarter of the 17th century as a single double house. The two halves were later split into separate houses, but they still sit behind one shared front, with a projecting centre section, corner pilasters and garlands from the time it was built.

In the middle of that centre section stands a statue of Saint Michael fighting the dragon. Now that the house is two, the archangel stands right on the dividing line between the neighbours.

The rest is a catalogue of later centuries: a 19th-century cornice and dormer, an 18th-century stoop with three Louis XIV balusters, and an Empire door, fanlight and glazing bars from around 1800. It is a private house, seen from the canal.

Look for:
- Saint Michael and the dragon in the middle of the shared front
- the 17th-century garlands
- the stoop with three Louis XIV balusters

title: Huis met de Kolommen, the mayor's residence
summary: Built in 1672 for a West India Company director with four warehouse doors at street level, this has been the official home of Amsterdam's mayor since 1927, when a banker gave it to the city on that condition. Its garden opens on a few days a year.
body:
Paulus Godin, merchant and director of the West India Company, had this double house built in 1671–1672, probably to a design by Adriaan Dortsman. At street level it had four warehouse doors, with the front door in the middle under a small balcony on two columns. In 1791 the city architect Abraham van der Hart remodelled it: the warehouse doors became windows and cellar lights, the entrance got a marble balcony, and at the back a balcony on four Doric columns was added.

In 1912 the banker C.J.K. van Aalst bought it, just as he became president of the Nederlandsche Handel-Maatschappij. In 1927 he gave it to the city on condition that it became the mayor's residence, and Willem de Vlugt moved in that July. Not every mayor has lived here, but several have; Eberhard van der Laan died in the house in 2017.

It is not open to the public, except on Open Monumentendag and during the Amsterdam Tulip Days, when you can see the garden with its copper beech and the coach house at the far end, which opens on to the Keizersgracht.

Look for:
- the marble balcony over the front door
- six stoop posts in front
- the Empire door and fanlight with its lantern

title: The Incassobank's Mercury and its Paris corner
summary: One bank, two faces on the same stretch of canal: a sober classical front of 1902 that later got a big relief of Mercury, and on the Vijzelstraat corner a stone building of 1923 that looks lifted from a Paris boulevard.
body:
The Incassobank, founded in 1891, built its first office at Herengracht 535-537 in 1902–1903, to a classical design by J.P.H. de Man, a villa architect from Hilversum. It kept growing sideways: number 533 in 1906 and 531 in 1915–1916, both by H.A.J. Baanders in the same style, which threw the front out of symmetry. In 1919 a large relief of Mercury, god of trade, was set in the front of 533, above a frieze of open account books.

In 1923 the bank went further up the canal. At the corner of the Vijzelstraat H.G. Jansen built Herengracht 519-525 on the site of four houses: clad entirely in stone, with a Doric colonnade at street level, balconies running all the way round and a curved mansard roof. The city register calls it a rare case of French Belle Époque style in the Netherlands, closer to the Paris boulevards than to the canal ring. The entrance is in the cut-off corner. It later housed the population register, and is now the Banks Mansion hotel.

Both are seen from the street.

Look for:
- Mercury between the first-floor windows of number 533
- the reliefs of banking and the open ledgers in the friezes of 533-537
- the colonnade, balconies and the dormer with odd scrolls over the corner of 519
- round the back at Reguliersdwarsstraat 90, the bank's modern office of 1928 by J. Gratama, on the site of the coach house and stable of no. 537

title: KattenKabinet, the cat museum
summary: A museum of cats in art, from Rembrandt and Picasso to Toulouse-Lautrec posters, on the bel-etage of a Golden Bend house. It was founded in memory of a red tomcat called John Pierpont Morgan. Long before, John Adams came calling here.
body:
The house was built in 1667 together with its neighbour for the brothers Willem and Adriaen van Loon; Willem got number 497 by drawing lots. Later residents included the mayor Jan Calkoen, and when the city pensionary Engelbert van Berckel lived here he was visited by John Adams, then the American envoy and later the second president of the United States.

After a restoration in 1985, Bob Meijer turned the bel-etage, the grand first floor, into the KattenKabinet in 1990, in memory of his red tomcat John Pierpont Morgan (1966–1983), his headstrong companion for life. The collection shows the cat in art and culture over the centuries: paintings, drawings, sculpture and posters, with work by Rembrandt, Picasso, Toulouse-Lautrec, Corneille, Sal Meijer and Théophile Steinlen, among others. You walk through five period rooms, and the formal garden with its garden house runs back to the Reguliersdwarsstraat. There are temporary exhibitions too.

It is open Tuesday to Sunday, 12:00 to 17:00; tickets are sold on the museum's website.

Look for:
- the six-bay front with its pediment over the centre
- the KattenKabinet name at the door
- the garden and garden house, from the back rooms

title: Herengracht 458, Goudstikker's art dealership
summary: From 1927 the leading art dealer of the Netherlands, Jacques Goudstikker, sold old masters from this Golden Bend house. He fled in May 1940 and died at sea; his stock of 1,113 works passed to Göring and his associate Miedl. A black notebook later proved what had been his.
body:
In 1927 the art dealer Jacques Goudstikker moved his family firm from the Kalverstraat into this double house of about 1670, which had a ceiling painted by Gerard de Lairesse. He turned the firm into the country's leading dealership, introduced Dutch collectors to early Italian painting and had a client list that included Daniël George van Beuningen, Hearst and Thyssen. He also brought in panelling, chimneypieces and ceiling paintings from other canal houses for his showrooms.

After the German invasion, on 14 May 1940, he and his wife and son got aboard the cargo ship Bodegraven at IJmuiden. Two days later he was found dead in the hold, having fallen in at night. He left behind a stock of 1,113 recorded works. Through dubious transactions it passed into the hands of Hermann Göring and Alois Miedl, who in July 1940 also bought this house, the firm's name and Nijenrode Castle. A photograph of 1941 shows Göring leaving the building. After the war much of the collection went to the Dutch state; the heirs negotiated for years to get it back. The inventory his widow kept, a small notebook with a black leather cover, was key evidence.

The house is private; the front is what you see.

Look for:
- the 1875 front with sandstone corner pilasters and a curved pediment with two vases
- the high stoop, rebuilt in 1903

title: Gouden Bocht, five double houses and their owners
summary: On the Golden Bend the mayors pushed buyers to take double plots, and the richest families obliged. Five of their houses tell the stretch's story: a governor-general's retirement home, a facade reused and stretched, and a coat of arms that replaced a pediment.
body:
When the Herengracht was extended after 1663, the canal got a kink at the Nieuwe Spiegelstraat and the plots on the south side became deeper. They were sold between 1664 and 1668, and the mayors encouraged buyers to take two at a time. The result was a row of wide stone town palaces, the Gouden Bocht (Golden Bend).

Huis De Vicq, number 476, was built in 1670 for the physician and regent François de Vicq, with Corinthian pilasters already out of fashion by then. Around 1730 Dirk van Lennep swapped its pediment for a carved balustrade with his family arms by Ignatius van Logteren, then lost heavily on speculation and left for Utrecht. The occupier requisitioned it in 1943; from 1974 to 1981 anti-squat guards lived in it. Number 450, attributed to Philips Vingboons and built for the banker Joseph Deutz, was bought in 1710 by Joan van Hoorn, former governor-general of the Dutch East Indies; a storey added in 1922 spoiled its square front. At number 466 a late 18th-century stone front was reused in 1894 and widened with two new bays. Number 475, Huis De Neufville, is often called the finest house on the bend. Number 448 has an unusual sandstone front with garlands on the piers.

You see them from the canal.

Look for:
- the Van Lennep arms in the balustrade of 476
- the extra floor above the cornice of 450
- the two added bays either side of the old front of 466

title: Vijzelstraat bridges, SPQA and two women
address: Vijzelstraat, over the Keizersgracht and Herengracht
summary: Piet Kramer's two Vijzelstraat bridges carry a joke in stone: SPQA, for the Senate and People of Amsterdam. Since 2016 they carry the names of two women, a 19th-century financier who kept the NHM afloat and the archivist who knew the city's houses better than anyone.
body:
When the Vijzelstraat was widened from 1911, Jo van der Mey designed three matching bridges for it, but the work went in phases and around 1919 Piet Kramer was asked to redo them. Over the Herengracht (bridge 30, 1922) he kept Van der Mey's structure and added his own wrought-iron railings and granite year stones. Over the Keizersgracht (bridge 41, 1923) he designed a new bridge with four stone columns cut with SPQA, his joke on Rome's SPQR, read as the Senate and People of Amsterdam. Both were taken apart and rebuilt in 2020–2021; the last tram left them in December 2023. Bridge 30 is one of the lowest the canal boats pass under, and in 2020 its new girders were set 2.6 cm too low and damaged boats, so they were raised again.

In 2016 bridge 41 was named after Johanna Borski-van de Velde, a 19th-century financier born on the Vijzelstraat, co-founder of the Nederlandsche Handel-Maatschappij, which she rescued several times; its later head office, De Bazel, stands beside the bridge. Bridge 30 was named after Isabella Henriette van Eeghen, archivist and historian at the city archives, which moved into De Bazel in 2007. A few metres west of bridge 41 runs the Poentunnel of 1974, a foot tunnel for bank staff.

Look for:
- SPQA on the four columns of the Keizersgracht bridge
- the year stones Anno 1922 and Anno 1923 on the piers
- Kramer's wrought-iron railings

title: Leidsestraat bridges and Krop's fable beasts
address: Leidsestraat, over the Herengracht and Keizersgracht
summary: Four granite fable animals by Hildo Krop guard each of the two tram bridges in the Leidsestraat. They were designed in 1916, but the First World War pushed up prices, and the bridges were only built in 1921–1922, with the trams squeezing past on one track.
body:
The Leidsestraat bridges over the Herengracht (the Koningssluis, bridge 29) and the Keizersgracht (bridge 43) had trouble long before they were rebuilt. In 1889 the wooden blocks between the tram rails on bridge 43 swelled in the rain and burst out of their bed, making it impassable. In 1916 the city chose the Leidsestraat, rather than a filled-in Leidsegracht, as the main road to the southwest, and set money aside for new bridges designed by Jo van der Mey. Hildo Krop designed the sculpture that same year, and the stone firm of Johan Polet carved it. Then the war drove up material prices, and only after the budget was doubled in 1920 could work begin. Piet Kramer, by then the city's bridge man, adapted his teacher's designs, adding wrought-iron railings but keeping Van der Mey's corbels on the piers. Trams kept running during the works on a single track, and a hard winter slowed things further.

Since 26 July 1971 the Leidsestraat has been closed to traffic except trams and deliveries; on the bridges you can only cross from quay to quay.

Look for:
- Krop's four fable animals in grey granite on the wing walls of each bridge
- the stepped piers ending in stone corbels
- Kramer's wrought-iron railings

title: Singelkerk, the Mennonite church you cannot see
summary: Between the Singel and the Herengracht hides a Mennonite church of 1639, reached through what look like ordinary houses. It was named Bij het Lam after a brewery's gable stone down the street, and women once paid a stuiver to rent a folding chair.
body:
From about 1530 the Mennonites of Amsterdam met in private houses, as they were not allowed churches of their own. Once they were tolerated in the early 17th century they could build meeting houses, but these still had to stay out of sight. In 1607 Harmen Hendriksz. van Warendorp bought a plot on the Singel and put up a barn for the Flemish Mennonites. It was called Bij het Lam (by the lamb), after the gable stone of a brewery a few doors along. In 1639 a larger church replaced it, set back towards the Herengracht. In 1839 it got a new roof and its present Herengracht front.

Originally you came in through the half-round doors of Singel 454. Inside, women used to pay a stuiver for a folding chair from the porch and set it down in the middle of the church, while the pews were rented to richer members, and the poor and the children of the De Oranjeappel orphanage sat in the upper gallery. In the corridor hangs the old seminary library table, into which graduates carved their names.

The Mennonite congregation still worships here, and for its acoustics the church is often hired for concerts and recordings.

Look for:
- the plain Herengracht front behind its forecourt and iron fence
- the house fronts on the Singel at 452 and 454 that hide the church
- the stone posts in front of the Singel side

title: Koningsplein, the rag-trade square
summary: A short, widened street that around 1900 was lined with clothing stores. One architect designed four rival fashion houses here in four different styles, and one shop sold outfits for the colonies.
body:
The Koningsplein is hardly a square: it is the stretch between the Singel and the Herengracht where a canal was filled in in 1663. From the late 19th century its north-west side filled up with fashion and textile stores, Meijer (there since 1841), Herbermann, Nieuw Engeland and Broekmans, with glass shopfronts, sales floors upstairs and sewing workshops and offices above them.

Between 1904 and 1915 the shop architect Alphons Jacot designed all four, and no two look alike. Nieuw Engeland, on the Singel corner, is traditional. Broekmans, on the Herengracht corner, is strikingly plain and modern for 1904. P.M. Broekmans sold hunting clothes and kit for the East and West Indies; in 1892 he had Gerrit van Arkel build him a shop-house at Leidsestraat 24, just over the bridge.

Across the square, the corner tower of Kosmos was built in 1890-1891 for the insurance bank of that name; in 1929-1930 Harry Elte gave its jewellers' shop a black granite front. Students squatted the empty upper floors in 2007, ran a gallery and held poetry afternoons, and were evicted that November. At the Herengracht end, facing Broekmans, the corner house of 1891 still has its rich original shopfront.

Look for:
- the plain grid of Broekmans, Koningsplein 16-20
- Elte's black granite shopfront under the Kosmos tower, Koningsplein 1
- the cast heads on the shopfront of Koningsplein 15
- the bay window of 1898 on Leidsestraat 24
- Nieuw Engeland's rounded corner on the Singel (1899)

title: Senembah's office on the Leidsegracht
summary: A 1913 office that dresses up as a 17th-century merchant's house, built for a company that grew tobacco on Sumatra. The sober front was meant to look trustworthy.
body:
In September 1913 the city let De Senembah Maatschappij pull down Leidsegracht 13 and 15 and put up one building with offices and a caretaker's flat. Senembah grew tobacco in Deli, on Sumatra, and had its Amsterdam offices here.

The architect, J.W.F. Hartkamp, had given an office on the Damrak a showy art nouveau front in 1904. Here he did the opposite. The front borrows from the strict Dutch classicism of the mid-17th century: a stone base, plain red brick, sharp-cut windows with their old sashes, a cornice on brackets and a steep slate roof with two chimneys. He kept the height level with the narrow neck-gabled houses either side. It was a new kind of building, an office designed as an office, wearing the clothes of a patrician house, and that calm and discreet look was what banks and trading houses wanted.

The middle bay carries the show: a double door with glass panels behind iron grilles, between two stout Doric columns that hold up a stone balcony with ball finials.

You see it from the street; it is not open to visitors.

Look for:
- the Doric columns and balcony over the door
- the small dentils cut in the stone above the windows
- the stoop with its bollards

title: Kerkstraat, the back street of coach houses
summary: The one street of the canal belt with no canal was laid out for the canal houses' coaches and horses. Carriage builders, a saddler and a farrier followed, and you can still read their trades in the fronts.
body:
