When Daniël Stalpaert drew the 1663 extension of the canal belt, he added a street between the Keizersgracht and the Prinsengracht so the canal houses could have a back entrance and a coach house. It was also meant to link four planned churches, two of which were never built; hence the name. About 45 former coach houses still stand along it.

The horse trades came with them. At Kerkstraat 28-30, Van Rossem and Vuyk, later the architects of Carré, built a carriage and saddle store in 1882 for Schutter & Van Bakel, and the name is still in relief over the ground floor, which is now a garage. Number 75 was a carriage warehouse of 1882 with flats above; in 1925 it got an Amsterdam School shopfront. The three big doors of 67-69 (1890) led to a stable and coach house, later a garage for the Oud Bussum dairy. At 174 a farrier shod horses on the ground floor. Isaac Gosschalk built 425-427 in 1876 as two coach houses with flats, later the city health service's garage. On the Nieuwe Spiegelstraat corner, a plain coach house with offices upstairs survives from about 1855.

Look for:
- SCHUTTER & VAN BAKEL in relief, Kerkstraat 28-30
- the colourful tile panels of Kerkstraat 32
- the three wide doors of 67-69
- the Amsterdam School shopfront of 75
- at the Utrechtsestraat end, no. 383 (1879–80, A.L. van Gendt), shops with flats that hid a stable, a coach house and a hayloft

title: De Gruyter's shop and its three farm workers
summary: A chain store of 1927 in travertine and Labrador granite, with statues of ploughing, sowing and harvesting on a shopping street. The city's beauty committee objected; the firm's director won.
body:
In 1927 the firm P. de Gruyter en Zoon of Den Bosch opened a shop here, designed by its house architect, W.G. Welsing of Arnhem. Amsterdam's Schoonheidscommissie (the committee that vets new fronts) objected to, among other things, the mix of polished Labrador granite below and Cannstatt travertine above. Director P. de Gruyter wrote back that every shop of the firm was built in one house style meant to look representative. Because the company mattered to the city's economy, the objections were dropped.

The result stands out among the brick fronts of the Leidsestraat: a pale stone face with four tall window slots filled with white leaded glass, set into the wall like shallow bays. The piers between them read like columns, the lintel like a frieze, and the travertine slabs, laid with their grain upright, hint at a pediment. Three bronze figures by Theo van Delft stand at the foot of the piers: a ploughman on the left, a sower in the middle and a reaper on the right, probably after the Book of Amos, where the ploughman shall overtake the reaper. It is an early Dutch example of a shop chain with a corporate look.

The shopfront itself has been modernised; the upper floors are flats.

Look for:
- the ploughman, the sower and the reaper
- the lobed granite corner piers with wavy cut brackets
- the upright grain in the travertine

title: Keizersgracht 453, Uncle Cor's bookshop
summary: Vincent van Gogh's uncle Cor sold books from this 1669 canal house for over thirty years. Vincent visited the shop, and in 1882 his uncle paid him for two series of views of The Hague.
body:
Cornelis Marinus van Gogh (1826–1908), "Oom Cor", had worked for his brothers' art and book businesses before opening his own bookshop in 1849. After a spell in the Leidsestraat he moved it in 1871 to this neck-gabled house of 1669, and it stayed here until about the time of his death.

His nephew Vincent visited the shop in 1877-1878. In 1882 Uncle Cor paid Vincent for two series of townscapes of The Hague.

After the bookshop the house was split up into flats, offices and a shop. A typewriter dealer advertised from here in 1919, the film studio Lumina had an office here in 1934, and in 1932 Anton Dunselman, the lawyer of Otto Frank, had his office or flat here.

It is still flats and offices, so you see it from the canal.

Look for:
- the 1669 neck gable

title: De Zwaan, an auction house since 1913
summary: A narrow canal front of 1913 built for an auction house, which still holds its sales here more than a century later. The wide double door was for the lots.
body:
In 1913 the auctioneers N.V. De Zwaan had the architect Jos Hegener rebuild this house as sale rooms, an office and a caretaker's flat. More than a century on, De Zwaan still auctions here: art, antiques, ceramics and design, with sales in 2026.

Hegener is best known for his Jugendstil work, such as Haarlemmerstraat 83, but on the Keizersgracht he chose something calmer: a classical build-up of base, upper floors and heavy cornice, with the classical details pared down into flat, almost abstract shapes. The pale yellow plaster makes it stand out in the row.

The ground floor is clad in hard Belgian limestone, and the wide double door in it was plainly made for carrying lots in and out. The windows beside it still have their original roller shutters. Above, fluted strips run up the side walls, the window bays sit back as dark bands, and a row of small round windows in the frieze lights a low mezzanine under the cornice.

Viewing days before each sale are open to the public, so you can go in.

Look for:
- the wide double door for the goods
- the original roller shutters on the ground floor
- the round windows in the frieze

title: Pakhuis Sparreboom, a timber merchant's warehouse
summary: One of seven near-identical warehouses a 17th-century trading family built behind its Herengracht house. Named after the spruce it stored, it survived a fire in 1952 and became a KLM miniature.
body:
Andries Pels inherited his father's house at Herengracht 438 and, between 1680 and 1685, built a row of seven almost identical warehouses at the back of the plot, on the Keizersgracht (today 483 to 489). His family firm, Guillaume & Jean Pels, imported coffee, tea, cotton, silk, sugar and spices from the East Indies. Only two of the seven survive as warehouses: Palmboom at 483 and this one.

Sparreboom means spruce tree. It first held timber and building materials from the trade with Scandinavia and the Baltic; later it was a coffee store. The design, six metres wide and thirty deep under a pointed gable with scrolls, is by Pieter Adolfse de Zeeuw.

From 1908 part of it belonged to the Amsterdamsche Rijtuig Maatschappij, the city's cab company. On 13 June 1952, when the antiquarian booksellers Swets & Zeitlinger had it, a big fire hit the front. In 1994 KLM made it one of its Delft blue miniature houses. It is flats now, seen from the canal.

Look for:
- the pointed gable with its scrolls
- Pakhuis Palmboom two doors along at 483

title: Keizersgracht 516, Bodon's glass bookshop
summary: In 1932 a Hungarian-born architect cut the bottom two floors out of a canal house and glazed them in thin steel for a bookshop. Two well-known galleries followed.
body:
From the first floor up this is an ordinary early 19th-century house under a straight cornice. Below that, in 1932, the Hungarian-born architect Alexander Bodon turned the ground and first floors into a bookshop for Schröder & Dupont, following the rules of the Nieuwe Bouwen (Dutch modernism). He replaced most of the front with glass in narrow steel frames, set the base back behind a barred cellar window, and stuck a canopy out over the pavement. On the right is a recessed entrance with a steel display case and a steel door with a round window.

Inside, the shop is one white space two floors high, with a narrow gallery with steel tube railings along the walls at first-floor level.
From 1969 the influential gallery Collection d'Art of Cora de Vries was here. Wiel Arets restored the interior, keeping Bodon's elements, and BorzoGallery opened in it in 2006. Borzo moved to Keizersgracht 321 in 2021; since then the hall has been hired out now and then for short exhibitions, so with luck the door is open.

Look for:
- the steel-framed glass across two floors
- the canopy over the pavement
- the door with the round window in the entrance recess

title: Huis Geloof and the painted coach house
summary: Faith, built as a trio with Hope and Love next door. Its owner's rococo coach house on the Kerkstraat was painted in 1772, and that painting later served to restore it.
body:
Keizersgracht 524 was built together with 522 and 520, and the three were named Geloof, Liefde and Hoop: Faith, Love and Hope. Faith has an 18th-century front under a straight cornice, a decorated stoop, a carved Louis XV door and a fanlight with a lantern.

Its owner Nicolaes Doekscheer had a grand coach house and stable built in 1758 at the far end of his garden, on the Kerkstraat (number 61). Its garden front is a showpiece with statues in niches, Hercules among them. In 1772 Hendrik Keun painted the view from the house across the garden to the coach house; the panel is now in the Rijksmuseum. Restorers later used it to restore the coach house's cornice, which made it into a Polygoon newsreel. Beside it stands a low one-storey garden house, also listed.

The garden side is private and cannot be seen from the street. From the canal you see the front of Faith and its neighbours; on the Kerkstraat, the back buildings at number 61.

Look for:
- the carved Louis XV door and the stoop of 524
- its siblings Love and Hope at 522 and 520
- Keun's painting in the Rijksmuseum (SK-A-3831)

title: Keizersgrachtkerk, Kuyper's breakaway church
summary: The 'cathedral of the Doleantie', built in 1888 for Abraham Kuyper's breakaway Calvinists, with their school behind it on the Kerkstraat. In 1944 its sexton and a minister were shot in the street outside.
body:
In 1886 Abraham Kuyper led a group of strict Calvinists out of the Dutch Reformed Church, a split known as the Doleantie. In Amsterdam the new congregation bought a double house on the Keizersgracht with its coach house on the Kerkstraat, meaning to build behind it. The city refused: a bylaw of 1663 kept the inner gardens free of building. So the canal house came down, and in its place G.B. and A. Salm, father and son and neither of them of the faith, built a pointed-arch church for 1,600 people, flanked by two low towers. It opened on 4 November 1888. J.W. Meijer designed the school on the Kerkstraat, School No. 1 for Calvinist primary education. Across the canal at number 495 stands the congregation's gymnasium of 1891, one of the city's first Protestant grammar schools, known for preparing pupils for the Vrije Universiteit.

On the night of 12 to 13 September 1944, five days after weapons were found in an annexe, German occupiers shot the sexton Sieberen van der Baan and the minister Taeke Ferwerda in the Kerkstraat. Memorial stones are set in the walls on both sides.

Today it is an open, ecumenical Protestant congregation with a Sunday service; it hosts the Pride church service each August.

Look for:
- the memorial stones on the canal and Kerkstraat sides
- the plain school front at Kerkstraat 109-111
- the brass hand-shaped knocker on the door of Keizersgracht 495

title: Lippmann, Rosenthal & Co., the bank whose name was stolen
summary: A respectable Jewish private bank of 1859 on the Nieuwe Spiegelstraat. In 1941 the occupiers borrowed its good name for a fake branch on the Sarphatistraat that robbed the Dutch Jews of their money and possessions.
body:
Leo Lippmann and George Rosenthal merged their banking businesses in 1859. The firm moved to Nieuwe Spiegelstraat 6, where Cornelis Outshoorn built it an office in 1869 with a coach house below. In 1881 Isaac Gosschalk added this long front, a sober brick palace with colossal pilasters, ball finials and dormers shaped as serliana windows, chosen to look solid rather than picturesque. The street, leading straight onto the Golden Bend, had become a small financial district.

In the war the bank was taken from its Jewish owners and put under a German administrator. The occupiers then opened a separate "branch" under the same name on the Sarphatistraat, meant to win trust. Jews were forced to deposit their money, shares, jewellery and art there; the robbery bank, known as Liro, handled an estimated 300 to 400 million guilders, part of which paid for the camps at Westerbork and Vught.

The real bank resumed after 1945, but the stolen name clung to it; in 1974 the Hollandse Koopmansbank took it over. Through the first-floor windows you can still see the wood panelling of the old directors' rooms. Other businesses use the building now.

Look for:
- the serliana dormers over the old main entrance
- the wider left corner, the extension of 1925
- across the Amstel at Sarphatistraat 47–55, the Amsterdamsche Bank branch of 1928 that housed the Liro robber bank in the war, now a hotel, with a plaque of 2003

title: 'T Huys te Bieseling, the gable stone that hid its caption
summary: A 17th-century gable stone of a castle-like country house whose caption vanished behind a later shopfront until building work in 1993. In 2021 a street artist put a tiny Bob Ross on a scaffold in front of it, painting.
body:
This neck-gabled house dates from the second half of the 17th century. Its gable stone shows a castle-like country house with a flight of steps, a guardhouse and a stable by the water. For years its caption was hidden: a later shopfront had been fixed so that it covered the text. Building work in 1993 brought it back: 'T Huys te Bieseling.

The city's old deeds name a Joannes Bieseling, a surgeon, who bought part of a plot on the Nieuwe Spiegelstraat in 1687, kept his surgeon's shop here and sold the house in 1693. His father, Matthijs Jansz, a furniture maker from Rotterdam, never used the name, but worked for mayor François de Vicq, who lived round the corner on the Golden Bend. The name probably points to Biezelinge in Zeeland, though no such country house is known there.

In June or July 2021 Street Art Frankey, known for small additions to the city's walls, fixed a miniature builder's scaffold against the stone, with a little Bob Ross on it, the soft-spoken painter of the American TV show The Joy of Painting, brush raised as if he is touching up the stone.

Look for:
- the caption under the gable stone
- Bob Ross on his little scaffold in front of the stone

title: Van Houten's recycled gables
summary: Two 1930s houses that look much older, because the city's chief building inspector wanted new building on the canals to fit in and had old carved stone reused in their gables.
body:
In the early 20th century Amsterdammers grew worried that demolition and new building were eating away at the canal belt. In the 1930s the answer was often new houses in an old style, and one of its keenest champions was E. van Houten, chief inspector of the city's building department, who also pushed for reusing valuable old fragments. Such buildings are still called Van Houten houses.

The corner of the Keizersgracht and the Amstel shows it best. Number 826, built in 1938, has a bell gable on the Amstel side with late 17th-century sandstone parts: the scrolls at its foot, fruit hanging down its neck and the curved pediment on top. The rest gives the date away: modern sash windows instead of mullioned ones, and a brick bond the 17th century did not use. Across the canal, a near twin of about 1940 also carries a reused 17th-century top, so the pair frames the canal's mouth.

On the Nieuwe Spiegelstraat, number 55 was rebuilt between 1935 and 1940 from an 18th-century bell-gabled house: a storey higher, with a shop below, and the old springer stones probably put back in the new gable. Its shopfront is original.

Look for:
- the carved fruit on the neck of the Amstel gable of 826
- its twin on the opposite corner
- the reused springers of Nieuwe Spiegelstraat 55

title: Museum Fodor, a coal trader's gift, now Foam
summary: A coal merchant left the city his art on condition it got a museum in his warehouse. The gilded MUSEUM FODOR is still over the door of what is now Amsterdam's photography museum.
body:
Carel Joseph Fodor (1803–1860) grew rich in the coal trade and collected contemporary art. When he died on Christmas Eve 1860 he left the city 161 paintings, 877 drawings and 302 prints, with conditions: the museum had to be in his own buildings on the Keizersgracht, the conversion could cost no more than 60,000 guilders, and it had to be called Museum Fodor. The city accepted, a little grudgingly, since the best works could not go to the Rijksmuseum.

The warehouse chosen was known as Het Spook (the ghost). City architect Willem Springer found the brief too limited and declined; Cornelis Outshoorn gave it an Italianate sandstone front, and the work was let for just under 40,000 guilders. King Willem III came to look in 1862, and the museum opened on 18 April 1863, Fodor's birthday.

Interest faded with the taste for 19th-century art. From 1948 it was an annex of the Stedelijk Museum, and Museum Fodor closed in 1993. After the design institute came Foam, the photography museum, in 2001. You can go in daily; Foam is preparing a sustainability renovation, so check before you go.

Look for:
- MUSEUM FODOR in gold letters in the door arch
- the date stones ANNO and 1861 beside it
- the little candelabra columns at the middle first-floor window

title: Museum Van Loon and its coach house with false windows
summary: Twin houses of 1671 whose first tenant, the painter Ferdinand Bol, took his landlord to court. Behind the garden, the coach house has fake windows so the servants could not look out at the family.
body:
Adriaan Dortsman built these twin stone houses in 1671-1672 for the Flemish merchant Jeremias van Raey, who meant to live in 674 and let 672. Four gods stand on the roofline: Minerva, Mars, Vulcan and Ceres. The first tenant of 672 was the painter Ferdinand Bol, and we know because he went to court: he was paying rent for stables that had not been built. Van Raey went bankrupt five years later, and several owners after him ended in bankruptcy or prison.

The Van Loon family, whose history runs back to the East India Company, bought 672 in 1884. Maurits van Loon restored it and opened it as a museum in 1973. Exhibitions there have looked at the family's ties to the VOC, the West India Company and the plantations.

Walk through the house and the garden, laid out after a drawing of 1679, to the coach house on the Kerkstraat. Its garden front of 1775 has a bust of Apollo over the door and statues of Flora and Silenus with Bacchus. The first-floor windows are false, so the staff could not watch the garden. The museum bought it back in 2009, and the family carriages stand inside again. The house is open most days with a ticket.

Look for:
- the four gods on the roofline
- the brass stair rail with the initials of a 1750s owner
- the copper beech planted in 1884
- the blank windows of the coach house

title: Nieuwe Waalse Kerk, now a museum of illusions
summary: The Huguenots' church of 1856, whose folding chairs were cast iron painted to look like wood. It became a baptist pool, a dance school and an ad agency, and since 2025 a museum of optical illusions.
body:
Amsterdam's Walloon congregation, swelled by Huguenot refugees, opened a second church in 1719 in an old bell foundry on the Prinsengracht; it was shut by royal decree in 1808. In 1841 the congregation bought a canal house of 1671 here, designed like its Van Loon neighbours by Adriaan Dortsman, to pull it down. Building only started in 1854, and the first service was held in 1856.

A.N. Godefroy mixed styles, a classical stone front with rusticated base and a Romanesque arched frieze and five little turrets on top, and new technology: gas chandeliers that could all be lit at once, galleries on cast-iron columns, and folding chairs of cast iron given a wood-grain finish. In 1861 fire brought the roof down; the iron chairs survived, and Godefroy rebuilt it.

In 1959 the Seventh-day Adventists took over and built a six-sided baptismal pool. From 1989 it was the arts centre Artemis, with dance studios on a new inserted floor, which cost much of the old interior; later an advertising production company used it. Since July 2025 it has been the Museum of Illusions, so you can go in, ticket required.

Look for:
- the five turrets on the gable
- the round-arched windows and the arched corbel frieze
- the foundation stone of 1855 by the pulpit stair inside

title: Het Huis, Eduard Cuypers' design workshop
summary: A red brick workshop of 1904 where architect Eduard Cuypers had rattan furniture and copperwork made for the modern home, and showed it in his own magazine.
body:
In 1903 the architect Eduard Cuypers added a decorative arts workshop to his office, Het Huis (The House), and in 1904 he built it this home on the Kerkstraat. The workshop made mostly rattan furniture and copperwork, and Cuypers showed its designs in a magazine of the same name, which he founded. The workshop closed in 1912.

The building is wider than the plots around it, two tall storeys and an attic behind a steep zinc roof. The red brick front is nearly symmetrical, banded with plaster, with four almost identical openings on the ground floor under segmental arches; the left one is the entrance. It has hardly been altered since it was built, so what you see is Cuypers' design.

It is not open to visitors; you see it from the street.

Look for:
- the four arched openings on the ground floor
- the plaster friezes under the wooden cornice
- the steep zinc front roof

title: Het Falckshuis, a home for widows disguised as two houses
summary: A 1905 home for respectable Protestant widows and single women, dressed up as two old stepped-gable houses of different heights. There is only one front door.
body:
The Falckshuis was founded in 1873 at Keizersgracht 715 to give one-room homes to Protestant widows and unmarried women of small means but good standing. In 1905-1906 the architect C.B. Posthumus Meyjes replaced two older houses and a coach house with this building.

From the canal it looks like two old narrow stepped-gable houses, one with five steps and one with seven. It is in fact one long building under one roof running parallel to the canal, with a single entrance: architectural mimicry. Stepped gables were almost extinct on this part of the canal belt by 1905, and they rarely topped houses this tall. Posthumus Meyjes, who had moved from neo-Renaissance to modern work, used honest brick and sandstone rather than plaster.

Inside the plan was made for its purpose: bed-sitting rooms for the residents, a shared sitting room and dining room, a regents' room, rooms for the matron and a sickroom. Even the zinc drainpipes are placed symmetrically. The stoop and its railing may be 18th-century, kept or reused from elsewhere.

You see it from the canal.

Look for:
- the two stepped gables of five and seven steps
- the single front door with its fan-shaped fanlight
- the stoop railing

title: Plancius, the dairy that moved to the Keizersgracht
summary: In 1895 rumours about dirty milk drove a dairy out of the Planciusstraat. It built a model factory on one of the grandest canals, with its own 100-metre well and a laboratory, behind a front that looks like a smart office.
body:
The Melkinrichting en Roomboterfabriek Plancius, a milk and butter plant, had been in the Planciusstraat since 1885. In 1895 persistent rumours about poor hygiene forced the directors to find a new home, and they chose a plot on the Keizersgracht for a model plant using the most modern methods of treating and purifying milk. A.L. and J.G. van Gendt designed it; a factory on one of the city's main canals was rare.

Milk was received and distributed on the ground floor; tools were cleaned in the courtyard behind; a well in the garden drew water from 100 metres down; and in the rear building a laboratory tested milk samples. The offices were on the mezzanine and a home above.

Perhaps because of the address, the architects dropped the plain round-arched style usual for works buildings. The lower two floors are dressed up with expressive brick arches and stone accents, and the front mixes neo-Renaissance with the fretwork of the Swiss chalet style. The frieze above them once carried the firm's name; the wide gates and the windows above were once filled with flowing Jugendstil woodwork and leaded glass, since changed. You see it from the canal.

Look for:
- the two original side doors with their curving lines
- the stone accents on the piers
- the empty frieze where the name was

title: The bitters seller's little stepped gable
summary: A tiny one-storey house of 1911 between taller neighbours, rebuilt with a stepped gable because the old one had one. It was a shop for a distiller whose specialities included Rins Maagelixer and Sam Pickwick Punch.
body:
Among its taller neighbours this house is a dwarf: one storey and an attic under a stepped gable. In 1911 P.J.A. Crispijn had an existing house rebuilt here as a shop with storage above. Crispijn ran a liqueur distillery, wine business and bitters factory at Rechtboomsloot 28, whose specialities were Rins Maagelixer (a stomach elixir), Nassaubitter and Sam Pickwick Punch, and his drinks were most likely sold here.

The old house had a stepped gable, so the new one got one too, with stone copings on the steps and a cast-iron hoisting beam in the top. The wooden canopy over the shop was added in the same year and is still there, as are most of the ground-floor windows. The cross windows with shutters upstairs have been replaced. It is a home now, but the front still reads as a small shop with a store above.

You see it from the street.

Look for:
- the wooden canopy of 1911
- the cast-iron hoist beam in the top
- how the gable sits far below the cornices next door

title: Kapel Immanuël, Amsterdam's first Pentecostal church
summary: A church hall tucked under three floors of flats, built around 1910 for Amsterdam's first Pentecostal congregation. It set a pattern for churches hidden inside housing; Russian Orthodox worshippers used it until the mid-2000s.
body:
From the street it looks like a block of flats with a wide, oddly churchy ground floor. That is exactly what it is. Around 1910 C. de Groot, of a Hilversum building family better known for villas, built an evangelisation hall with flats above for the Pentecostal movement. It was the first Pentecostal church in Amsterdam, and it became the model for a type: a church built into a housing block.

The prayer hall is really the concrete frame that carries the flats. Walls and round columns hold up the floors above a double-height space with a gallery running round it; at the back an octagonal lantern lit the spot where the baptismal font stood. Outside, two shallow porches either side of a wide window, behind which was a consulting room, led into the church, and three round-arched leaded windows on the first floor lit the gallery. The word Immanuel above the central window was probably added later.

From 1995 the Russian Orthodox parish of St Nicholas of Myra worshipped here, until it moved out in the mid-2000s. It is no longer a church.

Look for:
- IMMANUEL above the central window
- the two porches with their painted walls and granito floors
- the round windows lighting the flats' stairs

title: Prinsengrachtziekenhuis, the hospital for the well-to-do
summary: Amsterdam's oldest private hospital, opened in 1857 for paying patients while the poor went to the Binnengasthuis. It also trained nurses, all of them women until 1978. On the Kerkstraat side the old sisters' house still says ZIEKENVERPLEGING in gold.
body:
After a cholera epidemic, a Protestant society for nursing the sick, the Vereeniging voor Ziekenverpleging, was set up in 1843. In 1854 it began a hospital on the Prinsengracht, on the plots of three canal houses that had burnt down, and in June 1857 the doors opened. It was meant for the comfortable middle class; poorer Amsterdammers were sent to the Binnengasthuis. The national register calls it the oldest private hospital in the city built on medical and nursing grounds rather than as poor relief. It was also a school for professional nurses, and until 1978 only women could nurse here.

J.H. Leliman designed the nine-bay core. A sisters' house followed on the Kerkstraat in 1872, and wings were added on the canal in 1890 and 1902-1903. Among those who died here were the Flemish painter Rik Wouters, in 1916, and Mayor Arnold Jan d'Ailly, in 1967.

After a merger with the OLVG in 1994 the last beds went in 1996, the outpatient clinic closed in 2014, and since 2019 the building has been offices. You see it from the street only.

Look for:
- the round-arched entrance with its pediment, in the middle of the oldest part
- the stepped gable and gold letters ZIEKENVERPLEGING over the door at Kerkstraat 126
- the tile friezes between the floors of the sisters' house

title: Deutzenhofje, a widow's almshouse with a lesson for the rich
summary: An almshouse court on the Prinsengracht, built in 1694-1695 with money left by Agneta Deutz. Her verse stone says it is a comfort to the poor and an example to the rich; the story goes she also wanted to keep her money from a spendthrift son.
body:
Agneta Deutz bought the ground and chose the regents herself; when she died, her estate paid for the hofje, an almshouse court, founded in 1692 and built in 1694 and 1695 by Pieter Adolfse de Zeeuw. It was for elderly maidservants and poor relations. Over the entrance her stone reads "Agneta Deutz laat hier haar liefde en godsdienst blijken / Den Armen tot een troost, tot voorbeeld aan de rijken" (here Agneta Deutz shows her love and faith, a comfort to the poor, an example to the rich). The story goes that she was just as keen to keep a large inheritance from her wasteful son, Jan Meerman.

On the canal stand three double houses under one roof. Only the middle one, the gatehouse with its door at street level, belongs to the hofje proper; the two outer houses were let and their rent went to the almshouse. Behind it, three wings of small homes surround the courtyard, and opposite the gate a Tuscan portico carries a carved clock. The hofje had 19 homes; in 1964 four houses on the Kerkstraat were added, bringing it to 31. Older women still live here, so the courtyard is their home: look from the canal.

Look for:
- the verse stone of 1695 over the entrance
- the two putti and the coats of arms of Agneta Deutz and her two husbands
- the sandstone door surround and festoon of the gatehouse

title: Prinsengracht 703-705, the smithy that signed its front
summary: Two shopfronts of 1897 for a firm of smiths and ironmongers, and above them a strip of glazed brick that still spells out 703 SMEDERIJ MAGAZIJNEN 705: smithy, warehouses. The builder was a contractors' leader who sat in the council and the Senate.
body:
In 1897 the smiths and iron dealers Harm en Zonen had their storerooms on the Prinsengracht turned into shops, with two new shopfronts designed by J.N. Hendrix. In 1905 Hendrix rebuilt the front above them and joined the two houses inside; older parts are probably still in there. The ground floor is still shops, with homes upstairs.

What makes people stop is the lettering. Along the top of the shopfronts runs a frieze of glazed bricks set into the wall: 703 SMEDERIJ MAGAZIJNEN 705, smithy and warehouses, with the two house numbers as bookends. The rest of the front is careful brickwork too: mosaics of brick in the arches over the windows, bands of glazed brick, and a row of paired arched windows on the top floor that are all original.

Hendrix was not an ordinary builder. He ran his own technical office from 1886 to 1929, co-founded the Dutch contractors' union and chaired it from 1903 to 1919, set up an arbitration board for the building trade, sat on the city council from 1903 to 1919 and ended his life in the Senate. The register suspects he knew where to find good bricklayers.

Look for:
- the glazed lettering 703 SMEDERIJ MAGAZIJNEN 705
- the cast-iron beams and brackets carrying the shopfronts
- the small balcony on the second floor of the left half

title: Knegt's insurance office and its carved front
summary: In 1925 an insurance broker gave his canal office a limestone front carved with a car, a ship, a farmer, a sailor and two Black figures, an early piece of branding in stone. The name of the firm is still over the door.
body:
On 6 May 1925 the city allowed J.C.J. Knegt & Zonen, brokers in insurance, to join two houses at Prinsengracht 917-919 into an office with two flats on top. The architect was B. van den Nieuwen Amstel jr. Upstairs the front is almost bare brick; downstairs he put a tall office front of grooved Belgian limestone, full of carving, with the firm's name in the lintel above the door.

The carvings show a car, a ship, a farmer and a sailor, a Black man killing a snake and a Black man carrying an elephant's tusk. The register thinks they may stand for the kinds of risk the firm insured, and reads the front as an example of a trend of the 1920s: in a booming, competitive insurance trade, firms used eye-catching buildings, symbols and name plates to make passers-by think of their product. The colonial images are part of that sales pitch.

Next door, at no. 921, stands a richly decorated house in Dutch neo-Renaissance style that E. Breman designed in 1891, with a bay window and dormers modelled on the prints of Vredeman de Vries.

Look for:
- the carved figures in the limestone of the ground floor
- J.C.J. Knegt en Zonen in the lintel over the entrance
- the bay window and ornate dormers of no. 921

title: Elizabeth Wolffschool, a public school for paying girls
summary: Amsterdam once sorted its public schools into four price classes. This one of 1882 was a girls' school of the dearest class, one of only six in the city: more room per pupil, paid for by higher fees, and a front heaped with sandstone carving.
body:
In the 1880s Amsterdam's public primary schools came in four classes, set by the school fee. The Elizabeth Wolffschool, built in 1882 by the city's public works department, belonged to the most expensive class, and it was a school for girls: there were only six girls' schools of this class in the whole city. The register says the floor plan was the same as in cheaper schools. The difference was space, with much more room per pupil, and show: a rich neo-Renaissance front in orange brick and sandstone.

The building is a typical corridor school: classrooms on the street and on the courtyard, a playground between the front and back blocks, and a gym, compulsory for every class of school since 1862, in the back wing. Only the entrance has been modernised. When the register described it, the former public school was still a school, run privately.

Look for:
- the cartouche with the name Elizabeth Wolffschool under the first-floor windows
- the city's coat of arms above the entrance
- the little carved heads at the corners of the frieze and the ornament after Vredeman de Vries round the top window

title: Prinsengracht 1011-1017, where the Mennonite orphans lived
summary: From 1677 the Mennonite orphanage stood here, with a house for old women behind it. In 1867 the congregation had G.B. Salm put up four matching houses in its place. Round the corner, an 18th-century doorway on the Kerkstraat still leads to the old women's house.
body:
From 1677 these plots, running through to the Kerkstraat, held the orphanage of the Mennonites (Doopsgezinden), with separate parts for girls and boys that ran on across the back yard. By the end of the 18th century there were homes for elderly Mennonite women here as well. The orphanage let out the five identical houses next door, Prinsengracht 1001-1009, and probably the small houses on the Kerkstraat too. The Mennonites left the orphanage in 1811.

In 1867 the congregation had G.B. Salm build four houses on the canal as one symmetrical design, the outer two stepping forward under their own roofs. The register points out the irony: the same house type went up in the new working-class districts, with the same details as in the Pijp; here the luxury was only in the height and size of the rooms. In the early 20th century no. 1015 housed a society that ran evenings, courses and a library for young girls, and nos. 1015-1017 later became a hotel.

Look for:
- the two outer houses projecting under their cross roofs
- the matching cornices running level across all four fronts
- on the Kerkstraat, the 18th-century doorway of no. 310, which leads to the long building that was probably the old women's house

title: Cineac, Duiker's newsreel cinema
summary: Opposite Tuschinski's exuberant art deco stands its opposite: a steel and glass box of 1934 by Jan Duiker, built to show the news on film nonstop. The canopy sheltered the queue, and heaters outside kept it warm.
body:
Cineac was a French chain of cinemas that showed newsreels in a continuous loop, usually tied to a local paper. The Amsterdam branch, opened in the Reguliersbreestraat in 1934 for NV Cineac of the Algemeen Handelsblad, was first known as Cineac Handelsblad. The architect Jan Duiker, a pioneer of the Nieuwe Bouwen, Dutch functionalism, gutted a café of 1919 and set a steel frame into it, with a hall for over 600 seats laid diagonally across the corner plot.

Everything shows how it works. The projection booth sits in the corner on the second level; a folded concrete canopy, once with eleven glass panels in it, runs along both streets to keep the queue dry, and Duiker even put heaters outside for people waiting to buy tickets. The walls of the hall were sprayed with asbestos for the sound. Inside, the blue-lacquered steel windows sat in long bands, and the walls were clad in grey steel plates.

In 1992 Cineac reopened as the first riksbioscoop in the Netherlands, showing older films for 2.50 guilders; it was restored in 1994, became a normal cinema in 1996 and then a restaurant, event venue and, from 2007, a club co-owned by DJ Tiësto. Only the outside is protected.

Look for:
- the sloping concrete canopy over the corner
- the projection booth window at the corner, one floor up
- the stepped balcony level showing in the upper windows

title: Reguliersgracht 57-59, a medieval house of 1879
summary: Overhanging storeys and a wooden top gable, as if from the Middle Ages, but built in 1879 by Isaac Gosschalk, with neo-Renaissance trimmings, a wooden shopfront and colours you will not find on the neighbours.
body:
It looks centuries older than it is. It was built in 1879 by the architect Isaac Gosschalk as a business building, listed under the name of the firm Deenik en Zoon, and he gave it a front in the medieval manner: storeys that overhang, a wooden top gable, but with details borrowed from the Dutch Renaissance. The national register singles out the unusual wooden shopfront and its colours, which differ from the usual canal palette.

Gosschalk designed the house at Reguliersgracht 63 a few doors along three years later. You see the house from the street.

Look for:
- the floors stepping out over each other
- the wooden top gable
- the colours and woodwork of the shopfront

title: Schiller, the painter-hotelier's hotel
summary: A brewer's son who painted built this hotel on the Rembrandtplein in 1912-1915, and filled it with his own pictures and his artist friends. In 1927 a cabaret star and his wife were shot dead outside after dinner here.
body:
George Schiller, a brewery owner, opened a café on the Damrak in 1886 and a second one on the Rembrandtplein in 1892. After his death in 1907 his children Frits, Hein and Elsa bought nos. 28-32 and had M.J.E. Lippits and N.H.W. Scholte build a hotel-restaurant, opened on 6 August 1913 and finished in a second phase in 1914-1915. In 1921 the same architects added a narrow, much plainer brick building to the right, and a hotel bar with its own entrance opened at no. 24A: today's Café Schiller.

Frits Schiller (1886-1971) painted too: his friends called him the greatest painter among hoteliers and the greatest hotelier among painters. In the 1920s and 1930s Jan Sluyters, George Hendrik Breitner, Herman Heijermans, Nap and Fien de la Mar and Louis Davids were among the regulars, and his portraits of them hang in the hotel along with over 350 of his works. On 26 November 1927 the cabaret artist Jean-Louis Pisuisse and his wife Jenny Gilliams left a dinner here and were shot dead in the garden behind the Rembrandt statue by her jealous former lover, who then killed himself.

The family sold the hotel in 1970; it has run as NH Schiller since 2000. The café next door has its own entrance.

Look for:
- the two stone bay windows rising four floors
- the tower-like block with cut corners on the roof
- the meander patterns in the brick of the 1921 building

title: Rembrandtplein 44, an Amsterdam School front for a night out
summary: In 1918 a café-restaurant on the Rembrandtplein got a front in the newest style in town, the Amsterdam School, almost unheard of in the old centre. The restaurant was on the first floor and its kitchen up in the attic.
body:
Shortly after 1900 three houses at Rembrandtplein 44-48 came down for a café-restaurant by J.H. Lesmeister, with a large billiard room on the ground floor, meeting rooms above and two flats on top. In 1918 an architect named Van Schaik rebuilt it for the restaurant trade and gave it a new face in the Amsterdam School style, the expressive brickwork that Michel de Klerk had only just introduced around the Spaarndammerplantsoen. On the Rembrandtplein, already turning into the city's entertainment square, the client clearly wanted to be noticed.

The plan was as odd as the front. A huge kitchen with four storerooms went into the old attic to serve the restaurant on the first floor, and the flat on the third floor, probably the manager's, had a dining room but no kitchen of its own: meals came from the restaurant.

The register notes that the original window frames have all survived and that the ground floor is still whole in its structure, while the interior has almost entirely gone. Look at it from the square.

Look for:
- the sculpted, symmetrical brick front
- the original window frames on every floor
- the ornamental brickwork in the upper floors

title: Thorbecke, the statue The Hague would not have
summary: The father of the Dutch constitution was meant to stand by the parliament in The Hague, until a minister vetoed it. Amsterdam offered a square, renamed it after him in 1876 and moved Rembrandt partly to make room.
body:
Johan Rudolph Thorbecke (1798-1872) chaired the committee behind the constitution of 1848; the national register calls him the founder of the Dutch system of government as it still stands. When he died a national committee raised money for a statue and gave the commission, without a competition, to Ferdinand Leenhoff, a sculptor living in Paris.

The statue was meant for the Binnenhof in The Hague, then for the Plaats nearby; after years of objections the minister, Jan Heemskerk, vetoed it, which led to questions in parliament. Amsterdam, Assen and Zwolle all offered a site, and in 1875 the committee chose Amsterdam. It was unveiled on 18 May 1876 on the Reguliersplein, also called the cheese square, which the mayor renamed Thorbeckeplein at the unveiling. The Rembrandt statue, until then on the butter market by the Reguliersdwarsstraat, was moved, partly to make way, to the middle of what became the Rembrandtplein.

Thorbecke leans on a Greek column, for democracy, and holds a scroll of law. He looks out over the Reguliersgracht; when the square was redone in 2010-2011 local businesses wanted him turned to face it, but he went back as before.

Look for:
- the four inscriptions on the pedestal, including OPRECHT VOLKSVRIEND, TROUWE DIENAAR der KROON
- Leenhoff's signature in the bronze base
- the low wrought-iron fence round it

title: Singel 428, the modern canal house rejected fourteen times
summary: A canal house of concrete panels by Abel Cahen, designed from 1963. The city's design panel turned it down fourteen times, pushing for something old-looking, until younger members got it through at the fifteenth hearing.
body:
In the early 1960s the young architect Abel Cahen got a rare chance: his then father-in-law bought an empty plot on the Singel so that Cahen could show what he could do. With Patrice Girod he drew a frankly modern canal house, but the welstandscommissie, the city's design review panel, would have none of it. Getting approval took more than two years and fourteen rejections, each time with attempts to steer the design towards a historical look. Only at the fifteenth hearing, thanks to some younger panel members, above all Frans van Gool, was it passed.

What stands here is a building of precast concrete elements between two brick side walls, three windows wide, with French balconies in the middle. At the top the concrete rises on the left like a lopsided gable, with a roof terrace beside it. The glass of the outer windows is glued straight onto the concrete. The register sees the influence of Aldo van Eyck's orphanage. Inside are a business space in the basement, three flats and a maisonette on the top two floors, around a round stairwell with a lift.

For the register it marks the moment in the 1960s when the cultural avant-garde wanted to live in the old centre again. It is private; look from the canal.

Look for:
- the concrete gable rising on the left, with the roof terrace on the right
- the French balconies on the middle axis
- window glass set straight into the concrete

title: De Krijtberg, the Jesuits' church squeezed between canal houses
summary: Jesuits have said Mass here since 1654, first in a hidden church in a house called Crijtberg. In 1881-1883 Alfred Tepe fitted a tall neo-Gothic church onto the narrow plot, and a bust in it holds the heart of a Jesuit superior general.
body:
In 1654 the Jesuits started a schuilkerk, a hidden Catholic church, in a house on the Singel called Crijtberg (chalk mountain), and they have served this spot ever since. In 1881 they began a real church, designed by Alfred Tepe and consecrated in 1883. Tepe had to fit a big church onto a small plot hemmed in by canal houses, with only one side on a street. So it does not face east, the side aisles are narrow and carry galleries, and most windows sit as high as possible to catch the light. As the rest is hidden, the front got two stair towers to make a show on the canal.

Inside, artists of the St. Bernulphus guild, Friedrich Wilhelm Mengelberg among them, did the furnishings, and the national register calls the very tall, intact interior a key document of neo-Gothic as that guild saw it. There is also a bust holding the heart of Jan Philip Roothaan, the 19th-century superior general of the Jesuits.

The church is open for services: Mass is said every day at 12.30, with more services at the weekend.

Look for:
- the two stair towers flanking the front
- the brick front squeezed between the canal houses
- inside, the galleries over the narrow aisles and the bust with Roothaan's heart

title: Singel 458, the Mennonite nurses' house
summary: A narrow house of 1901 with a big bay window, built as a home for the nurses of a Mennonite district-nursing society. Its architect was also the society's administrator, so he was his own client. Today it is a hotel.
body:
Around 1900 the Vereeniging Doopsgezinde Wijkverpleging, a Mennonite society for nursing the sick at home, needed a house for its nurses. The design came from M.H. Ligthart, who was also the society's administrator, so he was in effect his own client. He built it in 1901 on the Singel, next to the Odeon.

The house is two windows wide, and Ligthart made the most of it with an off-centre front: a narrow bay on the right and, on the left, a heavy bay window over two floors, topped by a balcony reached through a door on the third floor. The red-brown brick is livened up with glazed bands and with green and orange brick mosaics in the window arches, typical of around 1900. The curve over the balcony door returns in the little gable above.

When the city listed it, it was a hotel. You see it from the canal.

Look for:
- the big bay window with the balcony on top
- the green and orange brick mosaics over the windows
- the curved gable on the left

title: Odeon, from brewery to concert hall to gay disco
summary: A brewery that appears in a famous civic guard painting, then a merchant's house by Vingboons, a concert hall opened by King William I where the Schumanns played, the city's first municipal shop and, in the cellar, DOK, the biggest gay dance hall of postwar Europe.
body:
Around 1593 the brewery 't Witte Lam stood here; Bartholomeus van der Helst painted its front into his civic guard banquet of 1648. In 1661 the merchant Gillis Marcelis pulled it down and had Philips Vingboons build a new house, called Nuerenburg, with a lamb on the gable in memory of the brewery. Joan Geelvinck, a VOC director, lived here later in the century.

In the 1830s Eduard Croese had the inside rebuilt as a concert hall and renamed it Odeon; the relief of Nuremberg in the gable stone gave way to the word ODEON, though Nuerenburg still runs round the rim. King William I opened it with a ball on 17 October 1838, and Clara and Robert Schumann performed here in 1853 and 1855. Then it was a cinema, in 1919 the city's first municipal shop, selling cheap cloth and clothes, and after the war an auction house.

In 1952 the gay rights group COC opened a club in the cellar, De Odeon Kelder, or DOK. Run from 1954 by Lou Charité, it grew into the largest gay dance hall in postwar Europe and closed in 1989. A fire on the night of 14-15 August 1990 gutted the building; the front survived and it was restored. Since 2015 it has housed a club-restaurant and bars.

Look for:
- the gable stone reading ODEON, with Nuerenburg in the rim and the year 1662
- the neck gable with three round windows
- the Empire-style doorway

title: The Carlton crash and the gap it left
summary: On the night of 26-27 April 1943 a burning RAF bomber came down behind the Carlton Hotel, then a Luftwaffe office. The fire razed the block to the Singel. A modern savings bank and a disguised car park now fill the gap.
body:
The Carlton opened in 1929 as Grand Hotel Centraal, designed by G.J. Rutgers on land freed by the widening of the Vijzelstraat, with a ballroom bridging the Reguliersdwarsstraat. English investors gave it its name, and Louis Armstrong played here in 1933. In the war the Germans took it over for their air force command.

In the early hours of 27 April 1943 a Halifax bomber on its way to Duisburg, hit by a German night fighter, circled the city in flames and crashed at 2.34 behind the hotel. All seven crew died, with six civilians and three German soldiers. The fire destroyed nearly everything between the Singel, the Reguliersdwarsstraat and the Geelvincksteeg, including Philips Vingboons' house for Joan Huydecoper at Singel 548; its front was taken down and stored, and never rebuilt. Anne Frank mentions the fire in her diary.

The site lay empty until 1958. Then K.L. Sijmons built the Spaarbank voor de Stad Amsterdam (1958-1964), deliberately open rather than a fortress, faced in travertine he expected to turn green; it stayed beige. In 1994 thieves had themselves locked in overnight and emptied 500 safe-deposit boxes. Across the street Sijmons added a car park (1966-1968) behind shopfronts so neat that passers-by still do not notice it.

Look for:
- the glass and travertine grid of Singel 542-548
- the hotel's ballroom bridge over the Reguliersdwarsstraat
- the 1960s shopfronts of the car park, Reguliersdwarsstraat 50-64

title: Vijzelstraat, the street they widened by tearing down one side
summary: To get traffic to the Pijp, the city knocked down the whole west side of the Vijzelstraat from 1917. What rose in its place includes a block of flats that partly collapsed in 1955 and was replaced by a terraced bank tower.
body:
Around 1900 the city wanted a wide road to the new Pijp district. A plan to fill in the Reguliersgracht met a storm of protest in 1900-1901, so in 1907 the council chose to widen the Vijzelstraat instead, in the end to 22 metres, by pulling down only its west side, canal houses included. Demolition began in 1917 between the Singel and the Herengracht, reached the Keizersgracht in 1918 and the Prinsengracht in 1926. The council insisted it stay a shopping street, and Karel de Bazel drew a master plan with arcades; after his death in 1923 Berlage took over.

On the Herengracht corner G.J. Rutgers built a large block in 1928 with shops and restaurants downstairs and flats above, its canal side kept deliberately calmer than the lively Vijzelstraat front.

Between the Keizersgracht and the Prinsengracht rose a block of flats, the Vijzelflat, in 1926-1928. During repairs on 3 March 1955 a pillar gave way and part of it collapsed. It was demolished in 1962, after years of haggling between the city and the ABN bank, which wanted the land. In 1969 M.F. Duintjer and J. Trapman finished the bank's office here, stepping back in terraces towards the canals; in 1974 a 50-metre tunnel under the street linked it to De Bazel opposite.

Look for:
- the terraced setbacks of the bank building towards both canals
- Rutgers' quieter Herengracht wing beside his busy Vijzelstraat front
- the width of the street itself, compared with the Leidsestraat

title: De Bazel, the trading company's striped fortress, now the city archives
summary: The head office of the Netherlands Trading Society, 1919-1926: ten floors, a hundred metres long, striped like a layered cake and nicknamed De Spekkoek. Three colonial governors stand over the door. Since 2007 it houses the city archives, open to the public.
body:
The Nederlandsche Handel-Maatschappij (NHM), founded to trade with the Dutch East Indies, built its new head office on the widened Vijzelstraat between 1919 and 1926. Karel de Bazel designed it; when he died in 1923 his office and A.D.N. van Gendt, who had engineered the concrete frame, finished it. At ten storeys it towers over the canal houses, and its bands of brick and granite earned it the nickname De Spekkoek, after the layered Indonesian cake. The city wanted shops along the street; the NHM refused, threatened to leave town and got away with display cases with no shops behind them.

High above the entrance stand Jan Pieterszoon Coen, Herman Willem Daendels and Jo van Heutsz, three governors-general of the Dutch East Indies, a gift of the Amsterdam Chamber of Commerce in 1924. Lower down, Mendes da Costa carved Asia and Europe beside the bronze doors. Inside, two light wells run the full height.

After the NHM came the ABN and ABN AMRO, which left in 1999. The city bought the building, and since 2007 it has housed the Stadsarchief, the city archives, open to the public, with the café-restaurant De Bazel at no. 30 since 2016.

Look for:
- the three governors over the main entrance
- Asia and Europe beside the bronze doors
- on the Keizersgracht side, the old safe-deposit entrance with a guardian beast's head

title: Eenhoornsluis and Hudde's sea-dike stone
address: Korte Prinsengracht at Haarlemmerstraat and Haarlemmerdijk
summary: The lock where Haarlemmerstraat becomes Haarlemmerdijk hides a 17th-century marble stone with a groove that marked how high the sea dikes had to be. Eight were set around the city; this is the only one still in its place, and the Dutch national water level descends from them.
body:
The Eenhoornsluis (Unicorn lock) was planned in 1618 with the canal belt, to link the new canals with the IJ and keep the tide out. It is named after a brewery, De Eenhoorn, that stood nearby; a unicorn on Korte Prinsengracht 19 recalls it.

After a storm in 1675 broke dikes across Holland, burgomaster Johannes Hudde, a mathematician, had the height of the IJ measured every day. The city then fixed its sea dikes at nine feet five inches above city level, and Hudde had marble stones with a groove at that height built into eight sea locks. In 1876 six were left. The one in the Eenhoornsluis is the only one still in its wall; a second turned up in 2013 when the Nieuwe Brug on the Damrak was taken down. Hudde's city level, the Amsterdams Peil, became the national standard in 1818 and lives on as NAP.

The lock still works as part of the city's flood defence: one big lock chamber with three pairs of flood doors and a smaller sluice to the east. It is public; you cross it on the bridge.

Look for:
- the marble stone, inscribed "Zee dyks hooghte zynde negen voet vyf duym boven stadtspeyl", in the lock wall at the north-east corner
- the white wooden capstans that open the doors
- a tiny bronze raised finger on the south-west abutment, for Nel de Jager, who ran the Haarlemmerbuurt shopping street (stolen in 2021, replaced in 2023)

title: West-Indisch Huis (West India House)
summary: A meat hall of 1617 where the West India Company's directors met, ordered a fort on Manhattan in 1625 and stored Piet Hein's captured Spanish silver in the cellars. Later an inn, an orphanage and old people's home; it nearly burned down in 1975.
body:
The building went up in 1617 as a meat hall with a guardroom for the civic militia upstairs. In 1623 the new West India Company (WIC) rented it, and until 1647 its board, the Heren XIX, met here. In this house they gave the order in 1625 to build a fort on the island of Manhattan, the start of New Amsterdam and so of New York. When Piet Hein captured the Spanish silver fleet in 1628, the loot was stored in the cellars, and crew members stormed the building to demand their pay.

After losing Dutch Brazil the company moved out in 1647. The house became an inn, from 1825 an orphanage and old people's home of the Restored Lutherans, and from 1954 a textile wholesaler's. On 16 December 1975 a fire, probably started by a stray firework, gutted the stock-filled attics. A foundation restored it from 1978 to 1981.

Today it holds offices, the John Adams Institute for Dutch-American exchange and rooms for weddings and events. The courtyard can sometimes be seen during events and open days.

Look for:
- the plastered front on the Haarlemmerstraat with its carved pediment
- in the courtyard, a bronze Peter Stuyvesant by Hans Bayens on a fountain
- in the courtyard paving, the line that divided the men's and women's sides of the old people's home

title: The insurance angel of Haarlemmerstraat 2
summary: A three-metre angel stands on the corner where the Haarlemmerstraat meets the Singel. An insurer from Brabant hoisted it up around 1920 as its logo, moved out in 1937 and left the angel, its shield and its lettering behind.
body:
The corner house was built in 1895 to a design by Emanuel Marcus Rood for the bookshop of Joh. G. Stemler, here since 1832, which sold and published books on navigation, building, steam engines and electricity. At 23 metres and five storeys it rose well above the old canal houses around it. Rood put his name in the plinth.

Around 1920 the life insurance company Noord-Brabant, from Waalwijk, opened a branch office here and later rebuilt the top. A pointed ornament made way for an angel, the company's emblem, by Gabriël Parentani and his brother: three metres tall, it was lifted into place by crane. Lettering panels went up between the floors, and a shield with the arms of Noord-Brabant and the year 1843, when the insurer was founded. In 1937 the company moved to the Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal. The angel stayed. Angel, shield and lettering were restored in 2014.

The building has a shop downstairs and homes above; everything worth seeing is on the outside.

Look for:
- the angel on top of the corner bay
- the 1920s lettering of the Noord-Braband company between the windows
- the shield with the arms of Noord-Brabant and 1843 on the corner
- the architect's name in the stone plinth

title: Ghost signs of the Haarlemmer shopping street
summary: Along the Haarlemmerstraat and Haarlemmerdijk, shopfronts still advertise trades that left long ago: a textile store named after a king, a grocer's coffee and cocoa tiles, a pastry baker's hanging pretzels and the blue tiles of a vanished grocery chain.
body:
The Haarlemmerstraat and Haarlemmerdijk have been a shopping street for centuries. A handful of shopfronts from around 1900 still carry their first owners' names and wares, whatever is sold inside now.

At no. 65, on the corner of the Binnen Wieringerstraat, Th. Berger's textile store Magazijn Willem III had its front rebuilt in 1880–1881. It went bankrupt in 1935, but the frieze over the shop window still lists its stock. At no. 60 a grocer had a new shop built in 1898 by A.W. Weissman with three rows of tiles: coffee, tea and cocoa, then fruit, then poultry. At no. 51, built in 1896 by F.M.J. Caron, the name of the butter, cheese and grocery trader J.J.F. Möllmann is set in green letters on yellow.

Further along the dijk, no. 63 was built in the late 1930s for De Gruyter, the grocery chain, framed in its trademark blue tiles from De Porceleyne Fles in Delft. At no. 158, the 1930s shopfront of J.G. Beune keeps its name and two hanging signs shaped like krakelingen, the Dutch pretzel biscuit.

Look for:
- lingerie, confectie, mantels, stoffen, Willem III, manufacturen on the frieze of no. 65
- Koffie, Thee, Cacao on the lowest row of tiles at no. 60
- the date stones "Anno 1736" on Caron's 1896 front at no. 51
- the blue tiles round the corner shop at Haarlemmerdijk 63
- the two krakelingen over the curved windows of Haarlemmerdijk 158

title: Posthoorn church and its Catholic island
summary: Cuypers' first Amsterdam church rose so tall because it had no room to spread. Around it the parish built a little Catholic world: a presbytery with Our Lady on its stair tower, three schools and a convent for the teaching sisters.
body:
The Posthoornkerk replaced a clandestine church called De Posthoorn on the Prinsengracht. P.J.H. Cuypers designed it in 1860; nave, transept, choir and crossing tower were built in 1860–1863, the two front towers in 1887–1889. Because it could not stand free between the houses, it was built extra high, with galleries over the aisles. The national register calls it one of the first churches with brick of different colours inside.

Cuypers also designed the presbytery on the Haarlemmer Houttuinen, his first design for Amsterdam together with the church. Next to it the parish put up school buildings in 1875 and 1890, and in 1891 A.C. Bleys added a convent, probably for the teaching staff. In 1893 F.M.J. Caron built the St. Antonia school for girls on the Haarlemmerstraat; sisters taught there, including German, French and English.

The church closed in 1963, was listed in 1972 and faced demolition plans until 1987. It is now used by businesses and hired out for events. The presbytery, schools and convent became homes around 1990; the girls' school houses De Vinse School.

Look for:
- the statue of Our Lady crowning the round stair tower of the presbytery, Haarlemmer Houttuinen
- the stone "St Antonia Gesticht 1872-1890" and the iron cross on the convent's stepped gables
- the tile panel with Gothic lettering on the girls' school, Haarlemmerstraat 132
- the church towers seen from across the railway, on Bickerseiland
- the parish's school of 1910 at Korte Prinsengracht 15–21, a unicorn's head in its right gable

title: The hidden Old Catholic church behind Brouwersgracht 132
summary: Behind a 19th-century front on the Brouwersgracht stood an Old Catholic house church, reached through a covered alley, that served its congregation from about 1664 until 1953. Its galleries and light dome survive inside, hidden by a later floor.
body:
The church of Saints John and Willibrord was probably founded in 1664 by Justus Mödersohn, for the Old Catholics, Catholics who later broke with Rome. Like other non-Reformed churches of the time it stood out of sight, on the back plot. A broad double house on the canal had a covered passage in the middle leading to it.

In 1876 the front house, a presbytery with a second home, was rebuilt to a design by C. Blok; its front is still there in altered form. In 1953 the church was sold and turned into homes: a floor was put in at gallery height. Above it four gallery columns, the clerestory with a plastered vault and a light dome are still there. The city register calls a 19th-century presbytery with a house church behind it very rare in Amsterdam.

Part of the furnishings went to the Old Catholic church on the Ruysdaelstraat in De Pijp, including two 18th-century statues of the patron saints and a 16th-century alabaster Mary.

The building holds private homes; only the canal front can be seen.

Look for:
- the rough rusticated middle bay with garlands over the door, where the passage to the church used to run
- the 1950s garage doors on either side of it

title: Tromsø and Hammerfest, the stockfish warehouses
summary: Two warehouses on the Brouwersgracht are named after Norwegian harbour towns, and the names can still be made out on their fronts. They were built in 1891–1892 for A. Smit & Zoon, importers of stockfish and cod-liver oil from Norway.
body:
A. Smit & Zoon traded in stockfish (wind-dried cod) and cod-liver oil from Norway. The firm already owned the corner warehouse at Brouwersgracht 162, called De Twee Stokvissen (the two stockfish), and in 1891–1892 it put up a double warehouse next door on two old plots. It named the halves after the Norwegian ports it traded with: no. 160 Tromsoe, no. 158 Hammerfest.

The two parts are clearly one project, in brick with yellow accents, the right-hand one a little taller, under one broad overhanging cornice. Above the ground floor the fronts are unchanged, though the loading doors have become windows. The buildings now hold a business space with homes above.

Together with the corner warehouse they are a reminder of the trade that once filled the Brouwersgracht's warehouses.

Look for:
- the names Tromsoe and Hammerfest, partly legible on the two fronts
- the small round-arched windows, still with their original frames
- the corner warehouse De Twee Stokvissen at no. 162

title: Van Houten's rescued gables in the Haarlemmerbuurt
summary: Two 1930s buildings here wear 18th-century gable tops taken from the houses they replaced. A building inspector saw to it that carved tops were saved from the rubble, and the national register protects one of these houses only for its top.
body:
When slum clearance got going under the Housing Act, many old houses were demolished and their carved stone gable tops went into the rubble barges. Worried by this, the Amstelodamum society asked the building inspectorate to save them; tops were stored in the garden of the Stedelijk Museum, and inspector E. van Houten made sure many were put back on new fronts. Such "Van Houten houses" are known by an old top over plain new brickwork.

At Binnen Oranjestraat 11-13 two condemned houses made way for a new front by H. van Saane, later a well-known builder of housing blocks. The left half got a reused bell-gable top. The national register lists no. 11 for the sandstone parts of that top; no. 13, designed as one with it, is not on it.

At Haarlemmerstraat 150, on the corner of the Korte Prinsengracht, the old corner house had lost the support of its neighbour by the late 1930s and was leaning, propped up with beams. In 1939 Simon Switzar jr. rebuilt it for the Algemeene Waarborgmaatschappij, reusing its cleaned old top.

Both are private homes and shops, seen from the street.

Look for:
- the 18th-century bell-gable top on the left half of Binnen Oranjestraat 11
- the old top and the stones "Anno 1939" on Haarlemmerstraat 150, facing the Eenhoornsluis
- the tuff-stone shopfronts of no. 150

title: Droogbak, the railway company's palace
summary: When it went up in 1882–1884 as head office of the Holland Iron Railway Company, the Droogbak shut off what had been the open harbour front. Stone children over the door act out the railway, and the keystones show heads that are probably its own staff.
body:
Until the station islands were made for Centraal Station, the street called Droogbak lay on the open harbour. In 1882–1884 the Hollandsche IJzeren Spoorweg-Maatschappij, the company that ran the line to Haarlem, built its administration building here, in exuberant neo-Renaissance by C.B. Posthumus Meyjes, around the time its tracks were joined up with the new central station. It closed off the view of the water. Nobody is sure where the name Droogbak comes from: a place for drying herring or dyed cloth, or a slipway are among the guesses.

Over the entrance runs a three-part frieze of putti acting out the railway business, by Emil Van den Bossche. The keystones carry heads in the clothes of the day, according to the national register probably railway employees.

The company left; the Land Registry was here from 1922 to 1973, and later the Netherlands Architecture Institute and a college. In the 1970s a four-lane road was planned through the site; the council dropped the plan in 1978. The building was restored as offices in 1999–2000, with a glass roof over the courtyard. It is not open to the public.

Look for:
- the frieze of children over the windows of the first floor, one of them dressed as Mercury
- the heads on the keystones of the front
- the octagonal tower with lantern on the north side

title: Harm Smeenge school for skippers' children
summary: In 1925 the city opened a school here for the children of inland boatmen, in Amsterdam School brick with big windows away from the trains. Since 1989 it has been a day centre for drug users, after a fight that went to the Council of State.
body:
In the 1920s room had to be found for the schooling of thousands of children who lived on barges. The city's Public Works department built this school in 1924–1925; P.L. Marnette designed it in a sober Amsterdam School style. It opened on 1 October 1925 and was named after Harm Smeenge, a politician who stood up for inland boatmen, who came to the opening. It held a day school and an evening school for skippers' children and a trade school for boatmen.

The windows tell you where the trains are: small on the north side, along the busy railway, and large on the south, where the playground was. The rounded corners and wavy top edge are typical of the style.

The school lasted until the late 1960s. When the city proposed a day centre for drug users here in 1988 there were protests, and the case went to the Council of State; at the end of 1989 Blaka Watra of De Regenboog opened its doors. It is still here: a walk-in centre for its own visitors, not a place to look around. See the building from the street.

Look for:
- the wavy top edge of the walls and the rounded corners
- the rows of small square windows on the railway side against the wide classroom windows facing the city
- the entrance in the narrow east front, beside a broad stone pier

title: Francisca and Petrus, a widow's warehouses
summary: Two small warehouses in the Buiten Vissersstraat carry the first names of a dairy trader and his widow. She ran the family business after his death, and her son, a pupil of Cuypers, designed both buildings twenty years apart.
body:
Petrus Hegener kept a dairy business on the Droogbak and died in 1875. His widow, Francisca Antonia Gersteling, carried on the firm P. Hegener & Zoon with her children. In 1878 two sister houses went up for the firm at Droogbak 7-8, designed by A.A. Swenger, a carpenter.

In 1884 she had a warehouse with a smokehouse built at Buiten Vissersstraat 4, designed by her son Jos Hegener, who had trained in the office of P.J.H. Cuypers and at the academy in Antwerp. It got her name in stone. In 1904 he built the extension next door at nos. 6-8 and named it after his father. Twenty years on his style had changed: Francisca is round-arched and symmetrical, Petrus angular and lopsided, with a stepped bay around the hoist.

The warehouses were made into homes in 1978 and 1995; all three buildings are private and seen from the street. Buiten Vissersstraat is a short side street between the Haarlemmerstraat and the Droogbak.

Look for:
- the name stone Francisca and the stones Anno 1884 around the arched doorway of no. 4
- the stone Petrus and the date stone 1904 on nos. 6-8
- the original iron bars in the ground-floor windows of no. 4
- the bunches of grapes on the keystones of Droogbak 7-8

title: Havengebouw, Dudok's tower that lost its partner
summary: Dudok designed his port office on the IJ as half of a pair, with helicopters landing on the roof in his sketches. The second block was never built, and at the opening in 1960 he said parts of the tower made no sense without it.
body:
In the 1950s the city wanted offices and high-rise in the inner city, and this was one of the few places where it could open up to the IJ. In 1952 W.M. Dudok drew a whole group: office tower, hotel, flats and a post office building. A second design followed, with only the tower and a seven-storey block for the Chamber of Commerce along the water. Only the tower and a low annexe were built. Dudok's sketches show helicopters landing on the roof.

The building has thirteen storeys, made largely of prefabricated parts, and the top two held a staff canteen and a restaurant. It opened on 14 May 1960, when Dudok said some parts could only be understood once the second building stood. It never came, and the tower stands a little oddly alone by the water.

Dudok's touch shows in the tiling: dark tiles on the columns, cream ones on the parapets, light balcony frames against dark walls. The Port of Amsterdam has its head office here, alongside other offices and homes. Admire it from the IJ side or from the ferries.

Look for:
- the steel columns standing free of the walls on the stepped-back top floors
- the contrast of dark and cream tiles on the long fronts
- the open balcony zone in the middle of the short ends

title: Roeraade's fish shop and the bakery next door
summary: On the Haarlemmerdijk a fishmonger's front of 1896 has an octopus and a seal in tiles and wall anchors shaped like eels. Four years later a pastry bakery for her husband's family went up two doors along, with peacocks in its tiles.
body:
In 1896 the fish and fruit trader Neeltje Roeraade had a new shop built at Haarlemmerdijk 39, designed by F.M.J. Caron, who signed it. The front tells you what was sold: a tile panel with an octopus clutching fish, another with a seal with a fish, and iron wall anchors shaped like eels. Her name is still cut in the stone arch, between two creatures that some see as cats and others as dragons. The carved wooden figure was added after 1981.

Around 1900 Caron also rebuilt no. 43, as the pastry bakery of the Dake family; Neeltje had married into it. Her three-year-old son laid the first stone on 22 September 1900 with his grandfather Roeraade. The porch tiles, from the Holland tile works, show peacocks. Three weeks later smoke poured from the half-built house; it was only a heap of smouldering wood shavings.

Caron designed no. 37 as well. All three are shops with homes above, seen from the pavement.

Look for:
- the octopus and the seal in the tile panels of no. 39
- the iron wall anchors in the shape of eels
- Caron's name on the right side of the arch of no. 39
- the peacock tiles and the first stone of 1900 on no. 43

title: The Movies, Amsterdam's little Tuschinski
summary: A cinema has run behind this house front on the Haarlemmerdijk since 1912. Its art deco interior earned it the nickname little Tuschinski, and for about eight years A Clockwork Orange was its regular late-night film.
body:
The building opened in 1912 as Bioscoop Tavenu, designed by P.J. van Doorn and C.H. Hagedoorn, and from 1914 ran as Cinema Hollandia. In 1971 it was sold and renamed The Movies. Its art deco interior was kept, and the entrance hall got an art deco look of its own in the rebuild, which earned it the nickname Klein Tuschinski (little Tuschinski). For about eight years A Clockwork Orange was its night film.

It calls itself the oldest cinema in Amsterdam still in use, a title De Uitkijk on the Prinsengracht also claims. It is in any case one of the very few early picture houses in the city still showing films.

After a long renovation, paid for partly by crowdfunding, it reopened on 13 March 2023 with four screens. There is a bar and restaurant, so you can step inside without buying a ticket.

Look for:
- the plain plastered front of about 1860 under a straight cornice: the cinema hides behind an ordinary house
- the name The Movies over the door
- inside, the art deco foyer and bar, open to anyone

title: Willem Drees's birthplace
summary: Willem Drees, the prime minister who gave the Dutch their state pension, was born in this plain 18th-century house on the Haarlemmerplein in 1886. The memorial stone unveiled for his centenary in 1986 drew a counter-demonstration.
body:
Willem Drees was born here on 5 July 1886, or at least spent his first days here. As prime minister from 1948 to 1958 he led the post-war rebuilding of the Netherlands, and his name is tied to the state old-age pension: older Dutch people still talk about "trekken van Drees", drawing from Drees.

The house itself is a modest one with a neck gable from the second quarter of the 18th century, protected for the gable rather than for Drees. For his centenary, residents of the Willem Drees nursing home took the initiative for a memorial stone, and mayor Ed van Thijn unveiled it on 3 July 1986. Not everyone came to celebrate: there was a counter-demonstration over the wars in Indonesia fought under his governments, and some demanded a memorial for Hans Kok, a squatter who had died in a police cell the year before.

The stone was then over a door; after 2011, when the house got a new shopfront, it moved down to the plinth. Look from the square.

Look for:
- the commemorative stone for Drees in the plinth
- the neck gable with richly carved sandstone side pieces and crest
- the city gate at the end of the square, which Drees would have seen from his door

title: Haarlemmerpoort and its fire station
summary: The city gate of 1840 was built for a king who rode in the day before his inauguration. It became a toll house, the first point to buy dune water by the bucket, a fire station and a police post, was nearly demolished, and was saved by squatters.
body:
The fifth gate on the road to Haarlem, officially the Willemspoort, was finished in 1840 to a design credited to Cornelis Alewijn and largely the work of Bastiaan de Greef. On 27 November 1840 King Willem II rode into the city through it, the day before his inauguration; an inscription on the city side recalls it.

It was a toll gate: excise men and soldiers checked the goods coming in, until the city excise was abolished in 1866. In 1853 the Duinwater-Maatschappij opened its first water point here, where people bought clean dune water by the bucket. From 1877 a fire engine stood in the middle passage. The council decided to demolish the gate in 1889 and changed its mind in 1900. A police post was here until 1961.

Squatters moved in in 1978 and campaigned for its restoration; homes were made in it by 1986. It now holds a café-restaurant and homes. Across the square, the fire brigade built a separate auxiliary station in 1896–1897.

Look for:
- the eight Corinthian columns of Bentheim sandstone
- the inscription on the city side
- the former fire station of 1897 at Haarlemmerplein 48, on the north side of the square

title: Korte Marnixkade 4, the house a nine-year-old started
