summary: A builder's showpiece of 1893–1894 in the bend of the Korte Marnixkade, covered in coloured brick, glazed tiles and carved heads. His nine-year-old son laid the first stone, and the boy's name is in the front.
body:
In 1893 the builder and estate agent J.W. van Tubergen had a house with two upper flats built in the bend of the Korte Marnixkade, looking out over the Singelgracht. The design is by H.H. Baanders and Gerrit van Arkel, in the mix of styles the Dutch call transitional architecture, the years between the neo-styles and modernism.

The builder clearly wanted to show what his trade could do. The dark brick front is loaded with ornament: bricks of different colours and shapes, glazed tiles in the arches over the windows, stained glass, carved stone consoles with heads under the balcony, and wrought iron on the railings, doors and balcony.

On 12 September 1893 the first stone was laid by his son Johan Willem, then nine years old. His name and the date are cut in the front, and above them, between two mouldings, the name H.H. Baanders.

It is a private home; everything is visible from the quay.

Look for:
- the first stone with the boy's name
- the name H.H. Baanders above it
- the colourful relief tile panel in the porch
- the carved heads on the consoles under the balcony

title: Willemsbrug, where a tram fell into the canal
address: Haarlemmerplein and Nassauplein, over the Singelgracht
summary: Piet Kramer's Amsterdam School bridge of 1928–1929 carries the road out of the old city towards Haarlem. Its predecessor had no overhead wire, trams had to take a run at it, and in 1924 one went over the railing into the Singelgracht.
body:
A bridge was needed here after the Westerkanaal was dug in 1877, and it was named after the nearby Willemspoort, the Haarlemmerpoort. Trams crossed it, but when the lines were electrified in 1906 the bridge got no overhead wire. Coming off a slight bend from the Nassauplein, drivers had to build up speed so the tram would coast across without power.

On 2 January 1924, in snow and ice, motor car 9 of line 18 jumped the rails just before the bridge, rammed the balustrade and ended up in the Singelgracht. Crew and passengers got away with a fright. It took the fire brigade until the next day to hoist the tram out.

The present bridge was designed by Piet Kramer in 1925 and built in 1928–1929, this time with overhead wires. Trams ran over it until 1955, when a bus took over; bus 22 still crosses.

It is a bascule bridge, opened for the boats that pass on the Singelgracht. Look at it from the Haarlemmerplein side.

Look for:
- the bridge-keeper's house in Amsterdam School brick
- Kramer's carved stone and brick details on the abutments
- the Haarlemmerpoort at the city end, which gave the bridge its name

title: Sloterdijkerbrug, the last old double drawbridge
address: Sloterdijkstraat and Galgenstraat, over the Prinseneilandsgracht
summary: The double wooden drawbridge between the Sloterdijkstraat and Prinseneiland looks like a postcard of old Amsterdam. Its look-alikes nearby are 1980s reconstructions; this one was kept as it was, twice saved from becoming a fixed bridge.
body:
A bridge has crossed the Prinseneilandsgracht here since before 1649, when Blaeu's map shows a wooden bridge. In 1880 it was due for renewal, at a time when the city was replacing drawbridges with fixed ones. City architect Bastiaan de Greef pushed to keep this double drawbridge as it was, and it was rebuilt in 1881 to the old model.

In 1952 it was in effect built anew, again to the old design; it came close to being replaced by a fixed bridge, until the head of Public Works, G.F. Janssonius, stood up for it. In 2005 heavy building traffic knocked the leaves and frames out of true and the bridge had to be fixed shut; a year later it was restored to its old state.

The bridges at the Petemayen, the Zandhoek and the Drieharingen look much the same, but they are reconstructions from the 1980s. This is the only double wooden drawbridge in the area still in its original state.

The name has two explanations: a house called Sloterdijk on the street, or the view over the fields to the village of Sloterdijk, which the railway embankment blocked at the end of the 19th century.

Look for:
- the two wooden frames with balance beams over the two leaves
- the view along the gracht to the warehouses of Prinseneiland

title: Bickerseiland renewal housing
address: Grote Bickersstraat, Bickersgracht and Kleine Bickersstraat
summary: Where the city once allowed huge office blocks, two architecture students drew an alternative: homes slotted plot by plot into the old island. Their puzzle of narrow houses, light wells and passages became an early model for renewing the city without clearing it.
body:
Bickerseiland was for centuries an island of shipyards and workshops. In the 1950s the city earmarked it for large businesses, and around 1965 much of the run-down north of the island was demolished for office blocks; the Walvis went up in 1965 and the Narwal in 1973. Two architecture students, Paul de Ley and Jouke van den Bout, drew an alternative plan with homes instead, and housing association Lieven de Key took it on.

It was their first built work. Between 1972 and 1982 they fitted homes into the small, irregular old plots on the Grote Bickersstraat, the Bickersgracht and the Kleine Bickersstraat, plot by plot rather than block by block. The city register calls it a clever puzzle of different home types, semi-public passages and outdoor spaces, with unusual proportions, bay windows for the view and light wells to bring daylight deep inside.

It became an early example of building with the historic fabric of the city rather than against it, and De Ley went on to design many more renewal projects in Amsterdam. Both parts became municipal monuments in 2025.

The homes are private; walk the streets and the public passages.

Look for:
- the narrow fronts that follow the old plot widths
- the bay windows facing the water of the Bickersgracht
- the passages through the blocks, and the original colours

title: Bickerseiland's last workshops
summary: Three buildings keep the island's industry in view: a steam-engine works whose name runs along its front, an iron firm with an art nouveau tile panel, and the office and gate of the last shipyard on the island.
body:
For centuries Bickerseiland was a working island of shipyards, timber yards and metalworks. Today it is almost all homes, but three buildings close together still say what was made here.

On the corner of the Bickersgracht stands the factory that G. van Arkel built in 1908–1909 for Hk. Jonker & Zoon, makers of steam engines and machinery, a family firm founded in 1806. When it turned 150 in 1956, the square in front, then the Bickersplein, was renamed Hendrik Jonkerplein. The building became homes in 1982.

Round the corner, at Grote Bickersstraat 15-17, Van Rossem and Vuyk built De IJzerstaven (the iron bars) in 1904 for the iron and steel firm Van Vlietjonge. Its tile panel from the De Distel pottery is still complete.

Further north, at no. 48, the firm Lalk built an office with stables and a service house in 1881. The brick gate beside it once led to the slipway of the shipyard De Hollandsche Tuin, which Jacob Olie photographed in the early 1860s. It was the island's last link to shipbuilding.

All are private homes, seen from the street.

Look for:
- "Naaml. Venn. Fabriek van Stoom en Andere Werktuigen Hk Jonker & Zoon" along the front of the Jonker factory
- the 1644 stone with a crown, a hammer and nails in its side wall
- the Jugendstil tile panel signed Distel on De IJzerstaven
- the brick gate next to Grote Bickersstraat 48
- Zeilmakerstraat 15–19, the Van Vliets' office and house of 1879–80

title: Planciusblok, the workers' homes built to be seen
summary: In 1856 the first housing association in the Netherlands put up its first big block of workers' flats here, alone in a park on the old ramparts, so that everyone could see that decent homes for workers were possible.
body:
In 1852 a group of Amsterdam merchants, doctors and a former burgomaster founded the Vereeniging ten behoeve der Arbeidersklasse (Society for the Working Class), the first housing association in the Netherlands. Members put in money at a capped interest of 3 percent. This long, narrow block by Pieter Johannes Hamer was its first large project, finished in 1856, after a small first block on Oostenburg.

It was meant as a model. The society deliberately built it on a conspicuous spot: on its own, in a park laid out on the former city ramparts, with the west front as its face. It held 104 homes of one, two or three rooms, most of them back to back. Each had its own privy, a sewer connection and water from the dune water main, then only a few years old. Washing was not to be dried in or around the homes; every household got a screened corner in the attic. The three-room homes proved too dear for the tenants and were split, which brought the total to 120.

The park disappeared in 1875–1876 for the Westerkanaal, and the block got neighbours. In 2006 it was restored, with new foundations and its original colours back. It is still housing; look at it from the street.

Look for:
- the plain fronts, divided only by slightly projecting bays
- the grey frames with green windows and doors
- the long side along the Houtmanstraat, the block's old back

title: Planciusschool, the school the parents occupied
summary: A stern brick school of 1916–1917, built because the railway took the old school's site. Sixty years later, with two classes left, parents occupied it for four days to keep a primary school in their own neighbourhood.
body:
In 1914 the city found that the Western Islands needed a new school: the old double school on the Houtmankade had to make way for the doubling of the railway line. Warehouses on the Nieuwe Teertuinen were pulled down, and the city's Public Works department designed this school with twelve classrooms, a drawing room and a gym. It opened for the school year 1917–1918 as the Bickersschool and only later took the name Planciusschool, from an older school further along the quay that had closed.

By January 1977 only two classes were left, and the alderman for education wanted to merge them into the Hudsonschool across the Zoutkeetsgracht. Parents occupied the building in protest. After four days they ended the occupation and turned to other means. The school closed in the following years.

Today the building holds a day nursery and workshops. The wrought-iron name sign and the original doors are seen from the street.

Look for:
- the iron sign "Openbare School voor Gewoon Lager Onderwijs" with "Planciusschool"
- the iron date "1916" beside the door
- the gate with the city arms in front of the entrance
- the low side building with its pointed roof, once a storeroom

title: Komter's flats that pretend to be canal houses
summary: After a department store burned down on this corner in 1940, the site lay empty for more than a decade. In 1954–1956 Auke Komter filled it with modern flats whose front on the canal is cut up to look like a row of separate old houses.
body:
On this corner stood a branch of the Vroom & Dreesmann department store, built by F.M.J. Caron. In 1940 a fire gutted it. V&D wanted to rebuild, but the war came in between, and in 1953 a newspaper called the corner one of the sore spots of the old city for more than 13 years.

The architect Auke Komter, who had worked for Le Corbusier and belonged to Groep '32, then built 32 flats over shops here (1954–1956). His problem: flats are horizontal and alike, a canal front is vertical and every house is different. On the Korte Prinsengracht he therefore split the block into narrow bays that alternate between brick fronts with old-style windows and open bays with loggias and roof terraces, crowned by concrete parapets with round holes. Two old fronts at the Brouwersgracht end were rebuilt in the same brick, two storeys taller; one gable is largely Komter's own invention. Because the quay slopes up to the Eenhoornsluis, he put the shops behind an arcade of white columns.

The city register calls it a very early, perhaps the first, example of new building carefully fitted into the historic city. The shops now hold an organic supermarket.

Look for:
- the arcade on the Korte Prinsengracht
- the concrete parapets with round holes over the roof terraces
- the four angled white bay windows on the Haarlemmerstraat

title: Femina Muller's crèche in the Vinkenstraat
summary: Babies from six weeks old were cared for here from seven in the morning to half past eight at night. Femina Muller opened the crèche in 1872 to show that childcare could be clean; her name has been over the door for more than a century.
body:
In the 1860s Amsterdam's day nurseries for the children of working parents were notorious: a city doctor, Samuel Coronel, wrote a damning report on them in 1864. In 1872 Femina Muller (1826–1909) and a group of women took over the Vereeniging tot Verbetering der Kleine Kinderbewaarplaatsen (society for better day nurseries) and opened their own in the Vinkenstraat, much cleaner than the crowded ones elsewhere. Children from six weeks old could stay from 7 am to 8.30 pm. Queen Sophie visited in April 1873. The society went on to open nurseries in the Warmoesstraat, the Eerste Van Swindenstraat and the Van Ostadestraat.

In 1903 the building was rebuilt to a design by Coenraad Wiegand, with a flat for the head. The crèche closed in 1936. The city then lent the building to an association of unemployed men, and after the war it housed a canning factory and later a maker of piezo-electric parts. In the early 1980s it became homes and a neighbourhood room, after a fight by the local residents' committee to save it.

It is private housing; the front is seen from the street.

Look for:
- the art nouveau style tile panel with the crèche's name over the door
- the row of round coloured panes in the big window
- the 1984 stone below the window for the committee's fight

title: Korte Marnixstraat, a farrier's horseshoes and a boy's first stone
summary: A 70-metre street on the site of a razed bastion, almost all of it built around 1900 by one carpenter-builder. A farrier's tools are carved beside one door, and a nine-year-old's first stone sits in the front next door.
body:
The Korte Marnixstraat got its name in 1894. Its namesake, the Marnixstraat, runs for nearly 2.5 kilometres; this one for about 70 metres, between the Bullebak bridge and the Haarlemmerplein. It was laid out where the bastion Sloterdijk of the 17th-century city walls had stood, after the defences were pulled down from 1876. Most houses were designed between 1894 and 1901 by W.J. Appel, a carpenter and contractor, recognisable by his wide wooden bay windows.

The shops below were working businesses. At no. 7 the farrier Johannes Albertus Slisser, trading as Slesker, had his workshop and lived above it with his family; his son ran the business until it went bankrupt in 1916. No. 5 opened with a tapster. At no. 3, built for the shopkeeper Johannes Zegger in 1901, his eldest son, then nine, laid the first stone. On the corner with the Haarlemmerplein, a pastry shop became a café in 1929, and the architect Fred. Huisman jr. gave it a front in Amsterdam School style, rare in the old city.

The whole street was renovated in 1996 and is housing; all of it is seen from the pavement.

Look for:
- reliefs with a horseshoe and farrier's tools on the piers of no. 7
- the stone "De eerste steen gelegd door Johannes Nicolaas Zegger oud 9 jaar 15 maart 1901" on no. 3
- the yellow and green glazed brick piers of no. 3
- the granite café front at Haarlemmerplein 31

title: The excommunicated apostle's church on Prinseneiland
summary: A merchant's house and chicory warehouse that became a church in 1892 for a congregation led by a German preacher who called himself an apostle. It was later a car store and a warehouse; since 2019 it holds flats.
body:
Friedrich Wilhelm Schwartz (1815–1895), born in Germany, was excommunicated in Hamburg and came to the Netherlands in 1863, where he founded a new congregation, the Apostolische Zending (Apostolic Mission). He went through life as "apostle". His flock already had a church on the Prinseneiland when, in 1892, Schwartz had this merchant's house with a chicory warehouse rebuilt as a new church, to a design by F.J. Krop.

It was consecrated on Christmas Day 1892, with the congregation's choir En-Gedi singing. A newspaper noted that the building had been paid for mostly by the members' voluntary gifts, and that the congregation tried to worship as the first Christians had. The church used it until about 1926, by which time there were three other Apostolic church buildings in the city.

In 1928 it became a store for cars, with lofts, and the owner moved in himself. From about 1950 the ground floor was a warehouse again, on an island that was all trade. In 2019 it was turned into flats, with an extra roof storey in old style. It is private; the front is seen from the street.

Look for:
- the plain plastered front with incised fake joints and corner pilasters, unlike the brick warehouses around it
- the wide central door between two narrower ones

title: De Roogans, the low tar shed among tall warehouses
summary: On an island set aside in the 17th century for timber and tar, a one-storey shed with a swaying gable crouches between tall warehouses. A painted board under the roof still says RooGans Anno 1687.
body:
When the Prinseneiland was laid out in the 17th century, it was meant for storing timber and tar. Tar stayed part of the Western Islands for centuries: they had tar-boiling works where ships' hulls, sails and nets were preserved, and tar was stored in their warehouses.

This shed on the corner of the Galgenstraat is the odd one out. Its neighbours are tall warehouses; it has one storey and an attic, with a broad brick gable that swings in and out. It dates from 1865–1870, probably a rebuilding of an older building. The city register calls it a former tar-boiling works; it was in any case a building of the tar trade. The text on its boarded-up attic window, "RooGans Anno 1687", refers to the year the business was founded.

The long side wall on the Galgenstraat is unchanged, with its iron wall anchors and original window pattern. It is private; everything worth seeing is outside.

Look for:
- "RooGans Anno 1687" on the middle attic window
- the curving gable, finished with a row of upright bricks and a moulding
- the old Dutch roof tiles on the Galgenstraat side

title: 't Seepaert, a wartime warehouse with a modern secret
summary: Built in 1943 on the plot of a burned warehouse, this one wears two traditional spout gables, one of them a mirror copy, with a startlingly modern concrete wall in between. Squatters moved in in 1980.
body:
In the middle of the war, in 1942, the owner of a burned-out warehouse plot on the south-east corner of the Prinseneiland asked the Amsterdam architect A.J. Westerman for a new building with workshops, storerooms and an office. It went up in 1943.

From the Bickerseiland it looks like a row of old warehouses. Look again at the south side: Westerman took an existing spout gable and copied it in mirror image on the corner, and between the two he put a plain concrete wall. The city register calls that wall a very early piece of modernism in the old city, and thinks the aesthetics committee let it pass because the island still counted as an industrial area.

In 1980 the building was squatted, and it has been housing ever since. It is private; the fronts are best seen from across the Bickersgracht and the Eilandsgracht.

Look for:
- the gable stone "'t Seepaert" with a carved horse in the water
- the two matching spout gables with round windows in their tops
- the concrete wall between them

title: De Atlas, the steam-powered mirror factory
summary: A frame-maker who started in a city-centre alley in 1857 moved here in 1890 and built a steam-driven, electrically lit mirror and frame factory that traded as far as Hong Kong. One workshop and a warehouse on the next island survive.
body:
Johannes van Vorstenberg opened a frame-making business in the Barndesteeg in 1857. Via the Lange Niezel and the Nieuwendijk it came in 1890 to the Realeneiland, on part of the site of a defunct machine factory called De Atlas, whose name it took over. The new factory ran on steam, and it was lit by electricity that its own steam engines generated. In 1891 it became a company, the Spiegel- en Lijstenfabriek De Atlas (Atlas-Works). It did much business with the colonies, and also with the Philippines and Hong Kong. In 1919 it closed, and a warehousing firm took over the site.

The building on the Vierwindenstraat is the survivor of a complex that reached to the Taandwarsstraat. Downstairs frames were varnished and glass was silvered; upstairs lived staff, among them the factory's machinist. Across the water, the double warehouse Liefde en Eendracht on the Prinseneiland, which had housed a steam mill for grain and pulses from 1883, got a frame workshop in 1894, probably part of De Atlas.

Both are now flats, seen from the street.

Look for:
- the lively gable on the Vierwindenstraat with brick pilasters and stone vases
- the patterned brickwork over the upper windows and the decorative wall anchors
- Liefde en Eendracht on the corner of the Prinseneiland, with its two small round-arched attic windows

title: Rederij Goedkoop, the tug company's office in the IJ
summary: A slim modernist office of 1960 that stands largely on piles in the IJ, so the tug dispatchers on the top floor could watch the harbour. The city's aesthetics committee was furious that it blocked the view of the water, and it was built anyway.
body:
Rederij Goedkoop, founded in 1807, ran tugs and salvage in the port and on the North Sea Canal. For a new head office it held a closed competition; F.J.E. Dekeukeleire and J.H. Grolle won. The harbour authority pushed the plans far ahead before telling Public Works, and the aesthetics committee was angry because the building closed off a long stretch of the view over the water. It was approved anyway because the shipping firm mattered to the city.

There was only room on the dike for an access road, so most of the building stands on a concrete platform on piles in the IJ. Three floating jetties formed a little harbour for the tugs. The design follows Lever House in New York: a low slab with a tower set off-centre on top. The slab held four staff flats with terraces on the water, converted to offices after about ten years; the tug service sat on the top floor, with the best view of the port.

Goedkoop was taken over by Wijsmuller in 1979 and left in 1994. The outbuildings have gone; the main building now holds offices and is seen from the Westerdoksdijk and the Stenen Hoofd.

Look for:
- the tower set off-centre on the lower slab
- the stair tower with its concrete grid between bands of blue glazed brick
- the dark, set-back ground floor under the overhanging first floor

title: De Kruiwagen, the herring buyer's double house where the Singel starts
summary: One of the oldest and widest stepped gables in the city, put up around 1606–1611 by a herring buyer on land just won from the IJ. A later owner named Cruywagen set a wheelbarrow (kruiwagen) in the front, and the IJ side was once the Buiksloot ferry house.
body:
Where the Singel begins at the Droogbak stands one of the broadest stepped gables in Amsterdam. The land here was made by dumping earth into the IJ in the city's expansion after 1585, and the plots were auctioned in 1601 and 1602. In 1606 the herring buyer Jan Loots bought two of them and built this double house: two homes with a warehouse between them behind a single front. It already appears on a city profile of 1611, which makes it one of the oldest houses in the city.

By 1641 it belonged to Hendrik Jansz. Cruywagen, who set his name in the front as a picture: a stone with a wheelbarrow, a kruiwagen. Until 1662 the ground floor on the IJ side served as the ferry house for the boat to Buiksloot across the water. People also call it the Spanish House, though it has nothing to do with Spanish times: when the Spanish left, this was still open water.

A fire in 1925, started while ropes were being dipped in tar, gutted the top floors. The restoration of 1953–57 by Ysbrandt Kok rebuilt the wooden ground floor as it looked in the 17th century. The house is private.

Look for:
- the stone with the wheelbarrow above the first floor
- the wide stepped gable with brick dentil bands
- the wooden ground floor rebuilt in 17th-century form

title: Sint Andrieshofje
summary: The oldest surviving hofje in Amsterdam after the Begijnhof was a Catholic almshouse at a time when Catholic foundations were not allowed. It never had a founding deed, stayed in one family for a century and has been run from the Begijnhof since 1699.
body:
Behind a plain doorway on the Egelantiersgracht lies the oldest hofje (almshouse round a courtyard) still standing in Amsterdam, the Begijnhof aside. The money came from Ivo Gerritszoon, a cattle farmer who left almost everything he owned for the purpose in his will of 1614. His nephew Jan Jansz. Oly gave a piece of his land on the canal. Because Catholic institutions were forbidden in the Republic, the hofje has no founding deed: for the whole 17th century it was simply family property. A chapel opened in 1623, and the chaplain of the Begijnhof came on Fridays to say mass there until the 1960s.

The last family regent, Anna de Magistris, was herself a beguine. When she died in 1699 she left the hofje to two mistresses of the Begijnhof, and it has been run from there ever since. The chapel gave way to more housing in a restoration in the 1980s. The houses are let to single women and are private homes.

Look for:
- the low wings of 1617 round the courtyard, with doors and coupled windows on the ground floor
- an old gable stone set into the wall of the former chapel wing
- next door, a re-set gable stone, In Den Koning van Bohemen, saved from the convent that stood at nos. 143–159 until the early 1960s
- round the corner at Tweede Leliedwarsstraat 3–9, the row of four shops with flats that the hofje's board built in 1896 as an investment

title: Claes Claesz. Hofje (Anslo's Hofje)
summary: A cloth merchant's almshouse of 1616 stood empty after 1945 and was set to be demolished. One man's stubbornness, a deathbed letter and three regents found by genealogists saved it, and the fight became a turning point for the whole Jordaan.
body:
In his will of 30 March 1616 the cloth merchant Claes Claesz. and his wife Griet Jans had five little houses built behind the Egelantiersstraat, reached by a narrow alley. Twelve poor women lived there, two to a room. The name Anslo, also the old name of Oslo, only turns up from 1626 and was probably made up.

After 1945 the damp houses stood empty, and Amsterdam, short of homes, planned to clear the block. Geurt Brinkgreve of the Diogenes foundation wanted it for art students; his letter of 1960 reached the last regent on his deathbed. The province then refused to let Diogenes take over, because the founders' will said their descendants should run it, so genealogists traced three new regents, who were appointed by the Crown. In 1965 a new foundation took over the Anslo's Hofje and the neighbouring Zwaardvegershofje; the work ran from 1968 to 1973. The struggle is remembered as the moment Amsterdam began to see the Jordaan as worth keeping.

The house and gate on the Egelantiersstraat were rebuilt from an old drawing. The homes are let to artists and students.

Look for:
- round the corner in the Tuinstraat, the gable stone of 1971 by Hans 't Mannetje: a woman playing an organ made of planks, behind a red and white windbreak
- across the street at no. 29, a mid-17th-century step gable on a wooden front, one of the last houses with only an attic above its tall main floor

title: Hofje Venetiae
summary: A VOC cashier who traded with Venice built this hofje in 1650 and gave it the city's name. In the 1970s the regents forced open a 60-kilo iron chest that had sat in a shed for decades, and found the archive everyone thought was lost.
body:
Over a plain door in the Elandsstraat the word VENETIA is cut in big letters. Behind it lies a hofje built in 1650 by Jacob Stoffels, a merchant and cashier of the Dutch East India Company (VOC) who traded a lot with Venice. His thirteen houses were for poor widows and elderly unmarried women. Around 1709 the regent Gerrit van Maarloop added seventeen more, and for a while it was known as Van Maarloop's hofje. In 1685 it was freed from city taxes for as long as it took in Huguenot refugees, widows and single women driven out of France for their faith.

Since the 17th century the hofje has owned an iron archive chest of more than sixty kilos. In the mid-1970s the regents needed the founding deed and had the rusted chest opened. Inside was the hofje's archive up to 1824, including a parchment of 1709 that served as the deed. That parchment, by its own terms, must stay in the chest forever, so it was asked back from the city archive.

Women live round the courtyard and men in the street houses. The houses are private.

Look for:
- VENETIA over the door, and inside the passage the text Vrede zy met dezen Huize (peace be with this house)
- Liefde is het Fondement (love is the foundation) on the east wing
- the back entrance at Lauriergracht 97, a house of 1903 by A.P. Timmers with the passage to the hofje behind its porch

title: Hof van Parijs
summary: Behind a wrought-iron gate in the Elandsstraat, a tidy U of workers' flats of 1903 stands where one of the Jordaan's most notorious slums used to be, an inner court of thirty hovels reached through an alley called the Boerengang.
body:
In the 19th century the Hof van Parijs (court of Paris) was a courtyard of some thirty hovels behind the Elandsstraat, reached through the so-called Boerengang. It was a notorious slum, home to the poorest of the poor, and crawling with vermin. The name is said to come from a 17th-century inn sign for French refugees that hung at the entrance.

In 1858 the businessman C.P. van Eeghen bought the slum and had it patched up, but it stayed a slum: a dozen houses tucked inside the block, reached through two covered passages. In 1902 the building company Concordia, founded from the property of Van Eeghen and H.S. van Lennep, pulled the lot down. In 1903 P.J. Hamer built a new court of 36 flats in its place, a U open to the street, with the double house on the left built at the same time.

The city took over Concordia's homes in 1917, and in 1984 the complex was renovated. It is still rented housing.

Look for:
- the wrought-iron railing between brick posts that closes the court off from the street
- the alternating red and dark brown brick of the blocks
- little tile mosaics in the arches over the windows of the red blocks
- the open stepped gable on the dormer at the far end of the court

title: Hofje van de Weduwe Roosen
summary: A hofje without a courtyard: four little 18th-century houses under one front, where eight women lived rent-free with 150 guilders a year besides. A plaque gives the widow's name, and the canal side is a blank wall.
body:
Most hofjes hide a garden behind a gate. This one has none. The Hofjen van de Weduwe Roosen is simply four small houses from the second half of the 18th century, built two by two and coupled into upstairs and downstairs homes behind one shared front, with the points of their four roofs poking up above the cornice.

The foundation dates from 1820 and paid for itself from a fund. Eight women lived here free of rent and got an allowance of 150 guilders a year. A house in the Lange Leidsedwarsstraat, for three more women, once belonged to the same foundation. Little else is known about it.

The houses survived the clearances that took away most of the old buildings of this street late in the 20th century, and in 1990 their numbers went up by a hundred, from 24–30 to 124–130. They belong to the Diaconie (welfare board) of the Protestant Church in Amsterdam and are let as ordinary homes.

Look for:
- the plaque with the name, Het Hofjen van de Weduwe Roosen
- the four roof peaks rising above the straight cornice
- the old glazing bars in all the windows
- the corner house on the Passeerdersgracht, half built in, with a wall without a single window on the canal side

title: Fort van Sjako gable stones
summary: Two painted stones of 1999 mark the spot where the robber Jaco is said to have holed up in a lawless 'fort'. The house block of 1886 that replaced the slum is real, and so is its odd first stone, laid by a boy of three. The fort itself was a story invented in 1901.
body:
Amsterdam loves the tale of Jaco, or Sjako: an 18th-century gang leader who ruled a thieves' republic in a maze of alleys behind the Elandsgracht, where no officer of the law dared go. On 15 October 1999 two gable stones were unveiled in no. 73 to remember him and his Fort van Sjako, carved and painted by Jan Hilbers.

The man was real. Jacob Frederik Muller, born in Königsberg around 1690, was sentenced to death in Amsterdam in 1716 for seven crimes, none of them committed in the city, and executed in 1718 after appeals to two higher courts. The fort is another matter. It first appears in a book of 1901 by Justus van Maurik, who said he had it from a man in the street who had it from his grandfather. The historian Frans Thuijs found in 2007 that none of it holds up. What did stand here was a cluster of houses on alleys behind the canal, demolished in 1886.

In their place the Hemker family built the big block of flats with shops that is still theirs today. The register still counts several of its doors and shopfronts as original.

Look for:
- the two coloured gable stones in no. 73: the fort and Jaco himself
- in the stone base, the line Eerste steen gelegd door C.W. Hemker oud 3 jaar 9 juni 1886 (first stone laid by C.W. Hemker, aged 3, 9 June 1886)

title: Bullebak (bridge 149)
summary: The Marnixstraat bridge over the Brouwersgracht is named after a water spook that lurked under the old sluice and dragged careless children into the canal. Residents fought off a concrete replacement in 1977; the bridge rebuilt in 2020–2023 kept its old look.
body:
Ask an old Amsterdammer what a bullebak is and you may hear about a bogeyman. Here it was a water spook. According to an old superstition it lay in wait between this bridge and the vault that joined the Lijnbaansgracht to the Singelgracht, ready to pull passers-by and children who came too close into the water. The bridge has carried its name ever since, and so, confusingly, does a second bridge further along the Marnixstraat, the Bullebakssluis.

A bridge has crossed here since at least 1625. The present double bascule bridge dates from around 1889. Horse trams ran over it from 1892, and in 1900 it was strengthened for the first electric tram line in Amsterdam. In 1977 the city wanted to swap it for a concrete slab that could be lifted out. Some 25 houseboat households protested, and neighbours put posters in their windows reading Houdt onze Bullebak open (keep our Bullebak open).

In 2019 cracks and rotting piles closed it to heavy traffic. Between August 2020 and June 2023 it was rebuilt from the ground up, with the old railings and stonework restored and put back, and barriers in place of the old gates.

Look for:
- the name plate on the railing, which runs on far along the quay
- on the west side, the sculpture Bullebak by Martie van der Loo: brick from the old bridge on curved Corten steel plates

title: Tetje de Jongbrug and its sister bridges
summary: Three little bridges of 1927 where the Lijnbaansgracht meets the Looiersgracht and Passeerdersgracht, from Piet Kramer's office. Since 2020 the middle one carries the name of Tetje de Jong, the first woman in the Netherlands to be a paid police commissioner.
body:
In 1913 the city wanted to fill in the Looiersgracht and the Passeerdersgracht and run a broad road through the canal belt here. The plan was dropped, the canals stayed, and in 1927–1928 the old bridges were replaced by three new ones from the office of Piet Kramer, the bridge architect of the Amsterdam School: bridge 100 over the Looiersgracht, its twin bridge 99 over the Lijnbaansgracht, and bridge 98 over the Passeerdersgracht.

On 25 May 2020 bridge 100 was named after Tetje de Jong (1918–1999). She joined the Amsterdam police as a typist during the war, finished her law degree in 1948 and in 1964 became a commissioner of police, the first woman in the country to reach that paid rank. In 1974 she became deputy chief of the force, again the first woman to do so. Her bridge lies between two police buildings, on the Elandsgracht and on the Lijnbaansgracht.

Just south of bridge 98 the Lijnbaansgracht stops dead at the Raamplein. Its water runs on underground, through a culvert under the Nieuwe Passeerdersstraat to the Singelgracht.

Look for:
- the brick abutments and quay ends in Kramer's Amsterdam School style
- the cast-iron railings with granite balusters on bridge 100
- the name plate of the Tetje de Jongbrug

title: Koekjesbrug (bridge 170)
summary: Nobody knows for sure why the bridge over the Singelgracht at the Nieuwe Passeerdersstraat is called the Biscuit Bridge. Under its east end, a 93-metre culvert brings in the water of the dead-end Lijnbaansgracht.
body:
The Koekjesbrug (biscuit bridge) has carried its name since at least April 1886, when it turns up in the Algemeen Handelsblad. Three explanations do the rounds: a biscuit seller who worked the area, chocolate biscuits sold at a cocoa mill nearby, or a market gardener called Pannekoek (pancake) who owned a patch of land by the bridge. None has won. The children's theatre De Krakeling (1978) and the building De Makroon (2015) beside it borrowed the joke.

Until 1879 there was no bridge here, only a ferry. A wooden footbridge followed in 1884 and an iron one in 1896–1897; when that grew too small, its ironwork and piers were reused in 1911 for another bridge over the Singelgracht. The present bridge of 1911, partly designed by the engineer Wichert Arend de Graaf, rests on iron trestles. Its western slope is built into the Nassaukade, which is why that quay is not level here.

Look for:
- in the east abutment, the mouth of the culvert: 93 metres long and three metres wide, carrying water from the end of the Lijnbaansgracht under the Nieuwe Passeerdersstraat
- the cross-braced iron trestles under the deck
- the steep slope up from the Nassaukade

title: Rozengracht bridges and the tram to Zandvoort
summary: When the Rozengracht became the road to the west, its three bridges were rebuilt as one Amsterdam School set. The outer one is named after a village swallowed by the Haarlemmermeer, and on it a stub of unused third rail remembers the tram to Zandvoort.
body:
Around 1885 the city chose the Rozengracht, not the Westerstraat, as the main road from the centre to the new west. The canal was filled in in 1889 and its bridges had to grow. In the 1920s all three got a new look from the bridge office of Piet Kramer: bridge 63 over the Prinsengracht (built 1925), bridge 117 over the Lijnbaansgracht (widened in the winter of 1927–1928) and bridge 167 over the Singelgracht (1927).

Bridge 63 is the Nieuwe-Wercksbrug, after the Nieuwe Werck, the old name of the Jordaan when it was laid out. Bridge 117 was known as the Jordaanbrug until 2016, when the city scrapped all unofficial bridge names. Bridge 167, the Rijckerbrug, is named after the bastion Rijck, itself named after Rietwijk, a village that disappeared in a storm in the Haarlemmermeer in the 17th century.

Until 1 September 1957 the tram to Zandvoort used these bridges on a three-rail track, with one rail shared by the city tram. When the track was renewed in 1985, a short length of third rail was laid on the Rijckerbrug as a reminder, and it came back again in 2018. For the Oranje Loper works, 167 was renovated and 117 rebuilt behind its old stone; it partly reopened in October 2026.

Look for:
- on the north-east parapet of bridge 167, a fire-breathing dragon and a fireman by Frans Werner (around 1932), a nod to the old fire station
- the stub of third rail on bridge 167

title: Bridge 102, the wooden footbridge of the Looiersgracht
summary: A footbridge already drawn on Blaeu's map of 1649, set on fire during the Jordaan riot of 1934, and still made of wood: steps up, a timber deck and timber piers, with separate ramps for bikes.
body:
Most Jordaan bridges went over to brick and iron long ago. Bridge 102, which carries the Eerste Looiersdwarsstraat over the Looiersgracht, is still wooden. A bridge already appears here on Joan Blaeu's map of Amsterdam of 1649. The wooden bridge of about 1795 had to be renewed in 1885. The work was held up because the Hollandsche Gasfabriek did not feel like removing its gas pipes, so in the end the city took them out itself, and the new bridge was ready around the turn of 1886–1887.

In July 1934, when the Jordaan rose against cuts in unemployment benefit, residents broke up streets, built barricades and tried to burn bridges. This one was set alight. It was renovated in 1960 without changing its look.

It is really a footbridge, with steps at either end; cyclists have ramps of their own.

Look for:
- the timber piers under the deck, a rare survival
- the steps up from both quays and the separate bike ramps

title: Bloemstraat's buildings for the poorest
summary: At the end of the Bloemstraat, a school of 1853 for 'ragged children' and a Mennonite block of 1871 with one-room flats and a shared dormitory of eighteen beds. The architects were teacher and pupil.
body:
In the 1850s the Jordaan was overcrowded and poor, and the well-off began to build for those at the bottom. On the corner of the Bloemstraat and the Lijnbaansgracht the Inrigting voor havelooze kinderen (institution for ragged children) pulled down a factory called De Zwaan and laid the first stone of its new school on 13 November 1852. The architect was Hendrik Hana. The stone over the corner reads Eben-Haëzer: hitherto hath the Lord helped us. It was rebuilt in 1914 as a Christian school with a separate teacher's house; by 1966 a trimmings factory had moved in.

A little further east, in 1871, the Mennonite congregation answered a report that urged the churches to build almost free homes for the very poorest. Its architect was G.B. Salm, once Hana's pupil. On each floor he drew six one-room flats, back to back round two staircases, and one floor, probably the attic, was a dormitory of 18 beds behind partitions. The attic and the stepped gables have gone, but the paired sash windows and the doors with cast-iron grilles are original.

Both are seen from the street.

Look for:
- the Eben-Haëzer stone and the tall gable on the cut-off corner of no. 191
- at nos. 129–145, the yellow brick round the windows and the original doors
- between the two, no. 189 of 1765, whose gable stone of an angel with a trumpet, a swan and a man with a book still has no explanation

title: Bloemgrachtkerk
summary: A church of 1880 squeezed into the canal front in place of two warehouses, in a Gothic style already old-fashioned when it was built. Its little tower was taken down in 2019 for fear it would fall, and has not come back.
body:
In 1880 two shabby warehouses on the Bloemgracht made way for a church of the Christian Reformed congregation, which had worshipped since 1836 in a converted house on this canal. The congregation built it itself, and the church took the canal's name. Its front, all pinnacles and pointed arches, is late Willem II Gothic, a style of the 1830s to 1850s, and closely follows the Catholic church of 1854 at Keizersgracht 220.

In the mid-1920s, as the city grew westward and the Jordaan lost people, the congregation moved to a new church in the Staatsliedenbuurt. From 1927 the Hersteld Apostolische Zendingkerk (Restored Apostolic Mission Church) used the building. It is no longer a church.

In May 2019 the city had the tower in the middle of the front removed: rust had parted it from the columns that carried it. It was put into storage. An investor bought the building in 2020 with plans for offices or a gym, but in January 2026 the business magazine Quote reported that it was for sale again without any restoration having taken place.

Look for:
- the stone pilasters, each ending in a pinnacle
- the round window and the three arched windows, the side ones smaller copies of the middle one
- the empty spot at the top of the front where the tower stood

title: Theo Thijssen school
summary: The Jordaan's school named after Theo Thijssen, the teacher who wrote Kees de jongen, sits in a 1920s Amsterdam School corner building next to a school of 1874. It moved here in 1987 and brought along its 1947 portrait stone of the writer.
body:
Theo Thijssen (1879–1943), born in the Jordaan, was a teacher and the author of Kees de jongen (1923), the Dutch classic about an Amsterdam schoolboy with a vivid imagination. Several schools carry his name. This one got a stone portrait of him by Fred Carasso in 1947, and when it moved into these buildings in 1987, the stone came along.

The corner building is a school of 1924 by the city's Public Works department, in the Amsterdam School style. Because of the corner plot it is V-shaped: two corridors at right angles meet at a staircase in the bend, the classrooms face south for the sun, and the toilets and storerooms face the street. That is why the street fronts look so closed, with long bands of windows. Next door stands a school of 1874 by A.L. van Gendt, which only got architecture on its street front; the newer building swings out round the corner as if trying to escape the street wall.

It is a working primary school, so visit from the street.

Look for:
- the rounded entrance with its varnished door and the windows with V-shaped glazing bars beside it
- the stepped roof line and the curving brickwork on the corner
- the portrait stone of Theo Thijssen

title: Eelke van Houten's second-hand gables
summary: Look up in the Laurier streets: dozens of old gable tops sit on houses of the 1930s. A city building inspector saved stone tops from condemned houses and had them put back on new fronts, and the national register lists many of these houses only for those stones.
body:
The national register says it plainly: Eerste Laurierdwarsstraat 3 is listed "because of the sandstone parts of the gable neck". The rest of the house is from 1935.

That is the work of Eelke van Houten (1872–1970), head inspector at the city's building department. After the Housing Act of 1901, many condemned houses came down. Van Houten wanted their carved stone gable tops kept. From the 1920s he had them stored and, when a condemned house was rebuilt, set on the new brick front. These Van Houten houses give themselves away by slightly awkward proportions and plain 1930s brickwork under an 18th-century top.

The streets round the Lauriergracht hold the thickest cluster. Lauriergracht 62, rebuilt in 1933–34 under the top saved from no. 65, is one of the first, its modern brickwork plain to see. In the Laurierstraat a building company, NV Assur, bought up whole runs of slum houses and rebuilt them, putting old tops back on. The houses are private.

Look for:
- the stone necks and bell gables of Eerste Laurierdwarsstraat 3 and 50
- Lauriergracht 62, its crested top rising above its neighbour, and no. 50, with two stones of 1936 recording the rebuild
- the run of bell gables at Laurierstraat 8–53, no. 27 with a date where the hoist beam should be
- at Eerste Rozendwarsstraat 13, a gable stone with a gilded double chandelier, there since 1725
- Prinsengracht 382, rebuilt in the early 1930s under a bell top of about 1720

title: Hoppe's wine house on the Egelantiersgracht
summary: A bunch of grapes carved over a double door is all that tells you this canal house of 1889 belonged to P. Hoppe, the wine merchants later better known for their gin and liqueurs. Their warehouse of 1891 still stands round the back.
body:
In 1889 the wine merchants P. Hoppe, who already owned nos. 12 and 14 and three warehouses behind them, rebuilt no. 16 as offices with a home above. The firm later became better known as a distiller of jenever (Dutch gin) and liqueur. The house kept almost everything from that year: the double door under a round arch with smaller side doors, the original wooden doors with wrought-iron grilles, the carved brackets under the cornice and a wooden dormer with a hoisting beam.

Round the corner in the Egelantiersstraat, the firm built a warehouse in 1891 at nos. 21–23. It looks like two warehouses following the old plot lines, but it is one building behind a twin gable. Most of its loading doors have become windows and doorways, but the wall anchors and hoisting beams are still there.

Both are seen from the street.

Look for:
- the bunch of grapes on the carved keystone over the double door of no. 16
- the fan of glazing bars in the fanlight above it
- at Egelantiersstraat 21–23, the twin gable, the hoisting beams and the bands of grey brick in the red

title: Berlage's narrow canal house
summary: Early in his career, the architect of the Beurs, H.P. Berlage, drew this tall, narrow front on the Egelantiersgracht in 1890, dressed up in Dutch Renaissance finery like the leading architects of the day. Only the front is his.
body:
H.P. Berlage is best known for his Exchange (Beurs) on the Damrak. In 1890, early in his career, he drew this front for C. van der Bijl, and at that time he still worked the way his leading colleagues Bleys, Cuypers and Gosschalk did, borrowing from the Dutch Renaissance and the late Middle Ages.

The house is only two windows wide, and its tall top makes it look even narrower. Bright red brick in cross bond is lifted by stone bands and decorative wall anchors. The windows sit deep in rich surrounds, with relieving arches filled with brick and stone ornament, and the brickwork steps forward at each floor to deepen the shadows. The top, with balls, scrollwork and a pediment, follows the style of the 16th-century designer Vredeman de Vries.

The front has survived remarkably intact, apart from the first-floor window frames. The house behind it was not designed by Berlage. It is a private home.

Look for:
- the two front doors tucked into a shallow niche on the right
- the white-painted rusticated ground floor
- the bead of moulded brick lining each window

title: Papeneiland and the Lekkeresluis
summary: A brown café in a corner house of 1641 with stepped gables on both street sides, a rare double show-front, beside a stone bridge of 1754 whose name is said to come from the bakers who sold their wares on it. Locals also call it the Papeneiland bridge.
body:
Where the Prinsengracht runs into the Brouwersgracht, the corner house at Prinsengracht 2 shows a stepped gable to both canals, something few Amsterdam houses do. It dates from 1641, and its fronts are dressed with horizontal stone bands and big stone blocks in the window arches. Café 't Papeneiland, which fills the ground floor, says it has been on this corner since 1642. It is open as a café, so this is a monument you can sit in.

The bridge in front of it, bridge 59 over the Prinsengracht, is the Lekkeresluis. A bridge appears here on Blaeu's map of 1649; the present one of three brick arches was built in 1754. The name is said to come from bakers who praised their goods on the bridge. A less common nickname is the Papeneilandbrug, after the café. It still carries cars: it was strengthened with reinforced concrete in 1976 and again in 1991. For a while the western arch was closed off and used for storage.

Look for:
- the two stepped gables of the café, one to each canal
- on the north side of the bridge, two stones reading Anno and 1754 on either side of the middle arch, and the bridge number cut into its keystone
- the little stair down to the water on the same side
- from the bridge, the view down the Prinsengracht to the Westertoren

title: Karthuizerhof, the city's widows' court on a monastery site
summary: The biggest hofje in Amsterdam was built by the city itself in 1650: 104 small homes for poor widows and unmarried women, on the ground of a Carthusian monastery. Its old graveyard next door became a playground with schools for the poorest children.
body:
In 1394 Carthusian monks founded the monastery of Sint Andries ter Zaliger Haven here, outside the city. It was wrecked in 1566, and after Amsterdam turned Protestant in 1578 its ground served as a graveyard. In 1649 the city bought the plot for 5,087 guilders, and on 28 February 1650 the first stone was laid of the Huiszittenweduwenhof: a city charity run by the Huiszittenmeesters, overseers of the poor who still had a home. City architect Daniël Stalpaert set 104 small upper and lower homes in four wings round a big courtyard. Widows, some with children, and elderly unmarried women lived here rent free, with a yearly ration of peat.

The elderly residents left in 1973 and the empty court was squatted with the city's consent. Since a renovation in 1986 it holds 65 social rental homes. The courtyard is open daily from 10:00 to 20:00, but not to groups.

The graveyard across the street became the Karthuizersplantsoen in 1889. In 1899 H. Leguyt built a double school on it for about 1,200 of the poorest children, and in 1905 another school went up on its south side. Both are now flats.

Look for:
- the two 17th-century pumps in the courtyard, with spouts shaped as a fish head and a grotesque face
- the arms of Amsterdam and the old city seal, a cog ship, in the pediments
- the white drying racks under the street windows, which gave the street its nickname Droogstokkenstraatje

title: De Turksche Keizerspoort, a Turkish flag in the Hazenstraat
summary: Over a gateway in the Hazenstraat hangs a stone with a red flag, a white crescent and a star. It keeps the name of an older complex behind it, the Turksche Keizerspoort, and nobody is quite sure where the Turkish emperor came from.
body:
The Hazenstraat, nicknamed the tenth of the Nine Streets, has a double house with twin stepped gables. Between them a small gate leads into an alley. Above it is a stone with the words De Turksche Keizerspoort (the Turkish Emperor's gate), the year 1893 and a simple Turkish flag: a white crescent and star on red.

Behind the gate stood an older complex of that name, pulled down around 1892. J.H.A. Wescher then had the architect Gerrit van Arkel design shop-houses here, with three more houses on the yard behind. Van Arkel drew spout gables; stepped gables were built.

Where the name comes from is not settled. Jacob van Lennep and Jan ter Gouw, in their book on shop signs, linked it to coffee houses with a stone of a Turkish emperor. A text of 1628 mentions chamois-leather dressers and silk makers in this area, "where the Turkish Emperor then hung". A newer idea is that a warehouse here traded in goods from the eastern Mediterranean, which Amsterdammers simply called Turkish.

The shops are still shops, with homes above. The yard behind the gate is closed.

Look for:
- the name stone with the flag and 1893 over the gate
- the two wooden shop fronts and the patterned brickwork round the windows

title: Breitner's view on the Lauriergracht
summary: In the 1890s the painter George Hendrik Breitner lived at Lauriergracht 8 and photographed and painted the row of houses across the water. His 1895 canvas belongs to the Stedelijk Museum; most of the houses in it still stand, a few still slightly out of plumb.
body:
The painter George Hendrik Breitner (1857–1923) lived at Lauriergracht 8 in the 1890s with his wife and two children. A plaque on the front says so. He also worked with a camera, and from here he photographed the houses across the canal. His painting Lauriergracht, Amsterdam of 1895 is in the Stedelijk Museum.

Most of what he saw is still there. Numbers 3, 9 and 11 have hardly changed since his photographs; number 5 kept its front but lost its old doors. In 1953 numbers 3 and 5 leaned to the right and number 1 to the left. Number 1 was pulled down in the mid-1960s and rebuilt in old style around 1990; 3 and 5 were put on new foundations and listed in 1970, still a little crooked.

Further along, numbers 19, 21 and 23 go back to a mason, Jan Egbertsz, who built three houses here on plots he owned from 1619 and sold them straight away. The houses are private.

Look for:
- the Breitner plaque on no. 8
- on no. 5, a stone of two smiths at an anvil, which hung in the Koningsstraat until the houses there came down for the metro and was set here in 1970
- on no. 2, the stone In 't casteel van Malaga, a Moorish tower of Málaga, for centuries in the back wall and on the front since 1961
- lions in the scrolls of the neck gable of no. 23, dated 1658

title: De Voorzienigheid's hidden chapel and the ad agency inside
summary: Behind a plain front at Lauriergracht 39 hides a neo-Gothic convent chapel of 1882, the heart of a Catholic home for girls that filled the block. Neighbours saved it in 1992; from 1997 the ad agency KesselsKramer worked inside. Now the chapel is for sale.
body:
From the Lauriergracht you see only a three-bay house with tall windows. Behind it, on an enclosed yard, stands a chapel that A.C. Bleys built in 1882 for De Voorzienigheid (Providence), a Catholic institution for neglected girls founded here in the 1850s. Its buildings grew to fill most of this block, through to the Elandsstraat. Inside the chapel, very slender cast-iron columns with leaf capitals carry pointed arches.

The institution kept building. In 1901 Jac. Duncker squeezed an orphanage onto a plot shut in on all sides, lighting its playrooms from above; a girls' school followed in 1922 and a new motherhouse on the Elandsstraat in 1927.

The last sisters left in 1991. A developer then wanted 108 apartments on the site. Neighbours objected, and in 1992 the chapel became a national monument. In 1997 the young advertising agency KesselsKramer answered a newspaper ad for a church to let and moved in. After more than 28 years it is moving elsewhere in the city, and the chapel is for sale. It is private and can't be visited.

Look for:
- the stone in the porch of Lauriergracht 47 saying the school building was dedicated in 1923
- at no. 37, a sign for Last & Co, the coffee brokers of Multatuli's Max Havelaar
- round the block at Elandsstraat 24–44, De Voorzienigheid over the motherhouse door between a male and a female saint, and ST MARIA-SCHOOL on the lintel next door

title: Platanenhof, the Catholic boys' orphanage
summary: In a city where Catholics had to worship out of sight, they still raised the money for an orphanage of their own. From 1686 it took in Catholic boys between the Lauriergracht and the Elandsstraat. Since 1971 it has been called after the plane trees in its courtyard.
body:
Catholic girls in Amsterdam had a home at the Spui, the later Maagdenhuis, but Catholic orphan boys were boarded out with families. Around 1684 Catholics collected enough money, despite the hostility of the Protestant city, to build an orphanage for them. Steven Vennecool designed it in a strict style, and the first part opened in 1686. The main wing on the Elandsstraat followed in the early 1700s, with more building around 1790 and in 1883.

It stayed an orphanage until 1954, then took in children under guardianship, boys and girls, no longer only Catholics. From 1971 it housed a therapeutic centre, De Triangel, which left in 1992. The name Platanenhof dates from 1971, after the ten plane trees in the courtyard. After a restoration from 1992 to 1997 it holds 22 rental homes, a day nursery and a theatre: the youth theatre company De Toneelmakerij has its address at Lauriergracht 99c.

The homes are private; the complex is best seen from the Elandsstraat and the canal.

Look for:
- on the Elandsstraat, the long main wing with its stoop, door surround and three dormers, the middle one with a clock face
- the gateway of 1747 in the row of bell gables on the Elandsstraat
- a 17th-century gable stone in the separate house at Elandsstraat 152
- the closed middle part of the Lauriergracht wing, with three door surrounds

title: The Lutheran orphanage on the Lauriergracht
summary: The widest front on the Lauriergracht, nine windows across under a pediment with a swan, was built in 1784 for the Lutheran orphanage. Since then it has been a soldiers' lodging, a police station, a youth hostel and now offices, and it survived a fire in 1978.
body:
Lauriergracht 116 began as an ordinary three-window house with a gate to a yard, over which a print of the 1770s shows the words Het Lutherse Weeshuys. In 1784 the orphanage swallowed its neighbours and rebuilt the house three times as wide, with a classicist front of nine windows, one of the biggest buildings on the canal. In 1811 the city claimed it.

Later uses were many: around 1900 a lodging for soldiers passing through, then a police station, later the youth hostel De Laurier and youth care. In 1978 a fire destroyed the roof, but the pediment survived; for years the building stood without a roof. In 2010 a water cellar in good condition was found underneath. After new foundations in 2010–2012 it became an office building.

The orphanage's neighbours on the left, nos. 112 and 114, are near mirror images of each other, both dated 1720. The pediment of no. 112 went missing for decades; it had been stored in the basement and was put back in 2012.

Look for:
- the year 1784 among the garlands in the pediment, and the swan, symbol of the Lutheran church
- the carved door and the fanlight with radiating bars
- the twin neck gables of nos. 112 and 114, with ox-eye windows and acanthus scrolls

title: Birthplace of the Jesuit general Jan Roothaan
summary: A stone portrait on Laurierstraat 62 marks where Jan Roothaan was born in 1785. The surgeon's son from the Jordaan led the Jesuits worldwide from 1829 to 1853; his heart is kept in a reliquary in the Krijtberg church.
body:
Jan Philip Roothaan was born in this house on 23 November 1785, the youngest of three sons of a surgeon. He was an altar boy at the Krijtberg church, studied at the Athenaeum Illustre and in 1804 began his Jesuit novitiate at Dünaburg (now Daugavpils), then in the Russian empire. In 1829 he was elected Superior General of the Society of Jesus, the 21st, and led it until his death in Rome in 1853. He is sometimes called its second founder, because he steadied an order that had been banned by the pope from 1773 to 1814.

A process for his beatification began in 1927. It has stalled but was never closed. His heart, preserved in a bust in Rome from 1935, has been in a new reliquary in the Krijtberg since 2008.

The house itself is mostly from 1933. Six condemned dwellings were pulled down and replaced by a workshop with three homes, and the old 18th-century bell gable top was put back on the new front. The stone by Lou Asperslagh was placed in 1934; newspapers of the time disagree on the month.

Look for:
- the relief of Roothaan's head on the stone in the middle of the front
- the sandstone bell gable with its crest, older than the brick below it
- in the Krijtberg on the Singel, the reliquary with his heart

title: Laurierstraat's "fight unemployment" blocks of 1915
summary: Two plain blocks face each other in the Laurierstraat, each built on eight old plots in 1915–16. A stone over one door explains how: in these dear times, three fifths of the money came from the city, to fight unemployment in a war year.
body:
Halfway down the Laurierstraat two near-identical blocks face each other across the street, both set back a little from the old building line. Each took the place of eight narrow plots. They were built in 1915 and 1916 for P. Smitt, an architect active in social housing, with workshops and garages on the ground floor and twelve and sixteen homes above.

The north block carries a stone that says why: Bestrijding Werkeloosheid, in deze duren tijd is met 3/5 deel Gem. geld dit huizencomplex saamgesteld, Oorlogsjaar 1915/16. In plain English: fighting unemployment, in these dear times this housing block was put together with three fifths of its money from the city, war year 1915/16. The Netherlands stayed out of the First World War, but the stone still calls it a war year.

The design is sober: red-brown brick, small balconies with iron railings, and door surrounds of red granito with broken pediments. On the south block a small relief of a man in a toga, labelled St Chrispin, probably comes from a building that stood here before. The homes are private.

Look for:
- the unemployment stone in its arched niche over the paired doors of nos. 214–216
- St Chrispin in his niche over the paired doors of the south block
- the four-part wooden garage doors, original only at no. 167

title: Noorderkerk, where the February strike was called
summary: The Jordaan's own church, a Greek cross by Hendrick de Keyser, has a quieter claim: on the square in front of it, on the evening of 24 February 1941, banned communists called on Amsterdam to strike against the deportation of Jewish men. The city stopped work the next morning.
body:
The Noorderkerk was built in 1620–1623 for the fast-growing population of the Jordaan and the western canal belt, to a design by Hendrick de Keyser, who died before it was finished. The plan is a Greek cross with small service houses tucked into the corners between the arms, a model later copied in Groningen and Emden. It is still a Protestant parish church, with Sunday services, and there are concerts on Saturday afternoons.

The square has a sharper history. On Monday 24 February 1941, at six in the evening, members of the Communist Party, already banned by the occupier, spoke here to some 250 people and called for a strike against the rounding up of 400 Jewish Amsterdammers. The next morning the February strike broke out. A bronze plaque on the church records it, next to a memorial to local residents killed in the war.

By the church door stands a bronze for the Jordaan riot of July 1934, when cuts to unemployment benefit led to street fighting in which five people died.

Look for:
- the two bronze plaques on the low annexe on the south side
- the Jordaanoproer monument (Sofie Hupkens, 1987): three figures bound by one band
- behind the church, Noordermarkt 26, a police post of 1860 by city architect B. de Greef, built for the 5th police section
- the farmers' market on Saturdays and the market on Monday mornings

title: Raepenhofje and Bossche Hofje, two hofjes bought on one day
summary: In 1648 a city treasurer and a Mennonite merchant bought land on the Palmgracht on the same day and built two almshouses side by side. They now share one garden. The Raepenhofje is let to women students, who may stay after graduating but must leave if they move in with a partner.
body:
Pieter Adriaanszoon Raep was the city's extraordinary treasurer for 24 years. In 1648 he founded a hofje (almshouse round a courtyard) for Protestant women out of his father's inheritance, paid for by the rent of a house his father had built next to today's Krasnapolsky. Vondel wrote a four-line verse for it. For two centuries an L was painted on the door frames, to show that the women were members of the Reformed church. Descendants of the regents still run it. Its nine homes go to women students, who apply by letter; they may stay after their studies, but have to leave if they want to live with a partner.

Next door, the Mennonite merchant Arend Dirckszoon Bosch founded a smaller hofje for eight elderly Mennonite women. The land for both was bought on the same day. Declared unfit after the war and restored in 1952–1953, the Bossche Hofje has belonged to the Hendrick de Keyser society since 1997 and houses four women. A hedge once split the garden; now the residents keep it together. Both hofjes are private and their gate is locked at night.

Look for:
- over the Raepenhofje gate, a stone with a turnip (raap) and the letters P.A., with the founder's arms and 1648 above it
- a cross-window with bars in the street wing of the Raepenhofje
- the stepped gable of the Bossche Hofje with five lily-shaped wall anchors

title: Suyckerhoff-hofje, behind a deep passage
summary: A Reformed citizen left his estate in 1667 for a hofje for old Protestant women. It hides behind a long passage off the Lindengracht, its residents got their peat tax free from 1752, and a gable stone put up in a late restoration finally spells the founder's name right.
body:
Pieter Janszoon Suyckerhoff, a member of the Reformed church, founded this hofje (almshouse round a courtyard) by his will of 4 January 1667, for elderly Protestant women and widows. You reach it through a deep passage from the Lindengracht; behind it the houses stand in an L round a garden, two storeys high with paired windows upstairs. As a Protestant charity the hofje was exempt from 1752 from the state and city taxes on peat, the residents' fuel. Until the 1940s the women still received part of their allowance in kind, and they were expected to help each other when needed.

A series of restorations at the end of the 20th century left 19 homes, still let only to women. A new gable stone from that time gives the founder's name in its proper spelling. The hofje is owned by the Stichting De Drie Hofjes, which also runs Hofje Venetiae on the Elandsstraat. The courtyard is private.

Look for:
- the gable stone over the entrance to the passage
- at the end of the passage, the two wings of 1678 with paired windows upstairs

title: Lindenhofje, from Mennonite widows to young care workers
summary: Mennonites bought this plot on the Lindengracht in 1616 to house needy widows. In 1801 it passed to the Catholic poor office and became a home for elderly couples. From 2004 a children's hospice, it now houses young people who work in care for the elderly.
body:
In 1616 the Waterland Mennonites bought land here to give needy widows a home. The plan was a classic hofje (almshouse round a courtyard): two side wings of five small houses each with a bleaching field between them, and on the canal a gatehouse with four houses let out to pay the costs. The layout has hardly changed since; the buildings have.

When the hofje needed repair in 1801 it was sold to the Roman Catholic poor office for the old (R.C. Oude Armen Kantoor), and from then on it housed elderly Catholic couples. In 1885 the office added two plots and gave it the present front on the canal, by J.H. Coelewij, the architect of its other hofje on the Marnixstraat. In 1939 the two wings behind were rebuilt, so that 25 couples each had a living room, bedroom, kitchen and attic. From the 1970s students lived here.

In 2004 the hofje was rebuilt as a children's hospice, run by the Salvation Army on a lease from the poor office. The hospice has since left. The RCOAK, still the owner, rebuilt the hofje and reopened it in June 2024 with 21 affordable flats, mostly for young people working in elderly care. It is not open to visitors.

Look for:
- two gable stones under the gables: 1801, the year of the Catholic purchase, and 1885
- the sandstone cartouche with the name over the left-hand door, which leads to the courtyard

title: Hamer- en Bouwershofje, two old hofjes moved to the city's edge
summary: In 1877 the Catholic poor office merged two decaying hofjes from the old city, one of 1626 on the Herengracht and one of the 1630s in the Wijdesteeg, into a new building at the edge of town. It has no courtyard at all, just a corridor between two rows of rooms.
body:
The Roman Catholic poor office (R.C. Oude Armen Kantoor) ran two small almshouses in the old city: the Hamershofje on the Herengracht, from 1626, and the Bouwershuisjes in the Wijdesteeg, from the 1630s. When both fell into decay, the office decided to bring them together in one new building on the Marnixstraat, then the edge of the city. It opened in 1878, designed by J.H. Coelewij, who later rebuilt the office's Lindenhofje in the same plain brick style.

It is a hofje without a court. A broad corridor runs from the Marnixstraat to the Lijnbaansgracht, with 24 one-room homes along it, each facing a street, and a caretaker's flat. The rooms were for widows and unmarried women over 50, who also had to cook in them. In 1974, 25 women still lived here, with a washbasin and no kitchen. Interest then faded and the hofje emptied. Younger people lived here for a while; around 2018 it was owned by Hotel Okura and housed Japanese staff on temporary postings.

Look for:
- over the door, a stone with a marriage coat of arms and the initials of the founders of the Bouwershuisjes
- a second stone with the name of the hofje and its year
- the three stepped gables and the pointed niches round the windows; the back on the Lijnbaansgracht is almost the same

title: Concordia's hofje of workers' homes on the Lijnbaansgracht
summary: In 1858 the businessman C.P. van Eeghen bought up slum plots at the edge of the Jordaan and had P.J. Hamer build five blocks of workers' homes round a shared yard: one of the first such schemes in the Jordaan. His building company Concordia kept adding to it until 1897.
body:
In the mid-19th century the Jordaan was among the worst-housed parts of Amsterdam. The businessman and philanthropist C.P. van Eeghen bought plots here and between 1858 and 1860 had the architect P.J. Hamer, a name tied to the city's earliest social housing, build five blocks on the Elandsstraat, the Lijnbaansgracht and the Lijnbaansstraat. Three storeys of sober brick close round a yard, so that the whole works like a hofje (almshouse round a courtyard), though it was built for working families rather than the old. It is one of the first housing schemes in the Jordaan.

The homes later went to the building company Concordia, founded in 1864 from the holdings of Van Eeghen and H.S. van Lennep, both active in the Vereeniging ten behoeve der Arbeidersklasse (association for the working class). Concordia built on: in 1876 Hamer added a block of 18 back-to-back homes on the Lijnbaansgracht, and in 1897 A.P. Timmers a block on the Lijnbaansstraat. The city took the homes over in 1917, and they were renovated in the 1980s. They are rented homes; the yard is private.

Look for:
- the corner building at the Elandsstraat, with a cut-off corner that once held a shop, red brick bands and two dormers with hoisting beams
- on Lijnbaansgracht 182, two original dormers with curved tops
- Anno 1897 in the doorway of Lijnbaansstraat 27-29

title: Marnixstraat, workers' homes on the old ramparts
summary: When the city walls came down, the strip along the Singelgracht filled with housing for workers. A report on cellar dwellings led the city to lend money, land and its own architect for 774 homes; next door a Remonstrant foundation built flats with Remonstrants first in line.
body:
For two centuries the strip between the Lijnbaansgracht and the Singelgracht was the city's edge. In the mid-19th century the ramparts were levelled, and the plans of Van Niftrik (1867) and Kalff (1875) set this land aside for cheap housing along the new Marnixstraat.

Two schemes stand side by side here. In 1873 the Amsterdam health commission reported on the miserable state of the cellar dwellings, and in 1875 this led to the Amsterdamsche Vereeniging tot het bouwen van Arbeiderswoningen: the city lent money and gave land and its architect, B. de Greef, while the association ran the homes. Between 1876 and 1881 De Greef built 774 workers' homes for it, two long rows of them here, each house with eight two-room flats round one stair.

On the corner of the Marnixplein, a Remonstrant foundation built a block in 1875, designed by G.B. Salm, of 36 one- and two-room homes. Its rules let them to small families of good name, Remonstrants first, others only after. In 1891 the Reformed church added a district hall with flats above, a chalet-style roof among the plain blocks. All were rebuilt inside in the 1980s and are homes now; the hall is a shop.

Look for:
- the stones Remonstrantsche Stichting and Anno 1875 on Marnixplein 2-8
- the overhanging roof with carved wooden struts on Marnixplein 2
- the alternating spout and stepped gables over each stair on Marnixstraat 106-138
- at Marnixstraat 215-231 and Westerkade 1-9, a third block of the same scheme

title: Turnzaal of 1887, the gym hall with Rust Roest on its front
summary: A company set up to build gymnasiums opened this hall in 1887 for four gymnastics clubs, with flats and a beer cellar round it. High on the gable it says Rust Roest (rest is rust). From 1978 to 2020 it was the children's theatre De Krakeling; now it is restored as offices.
body:
In the 1880s, when a healthy mind in a healthy body was the slogan of the day, the newly founded Maatschappij voor Turngebouwen (company for gymnasium buildings) had this complex built at the corner of the Marnixstraat and the Leidsekade. Jonas Ingenohl and Karel Muller designed it in Dutch Renaissance revival style: a gym hall set back from the Nieuwe Passeerdersstraat, flanked by blocks of flats on both streets, with homes for a caretaker and an innkeeper and a beer cellar in the basement. Money was tight and building dragged on through a frosty winter, but it opened on 19 November 1887. Four clubs shared the hall, among them Olympia.

When gymnastics lost its pull, the youth theatre De Krakeling moved in in 1978 and split the hall into an auditorium, cloakroom and foyer. It is one of the few free-standing gym halls of its time left in the country, and the inside, with wooden floor, panelling and open roof trusses, was largely intact when it was listed. In 2020 the building was sinking and De Krakeling left for the Westergas site. By 2023 Kodde Architecten had given it new foundations and made it an office, keeping the hall open. It is not open to visitors.

Look for:
- TURNZAAL carved over the doors and Rust Roest high in the middle gable
- the tiled porch on the Marnixstraat side
- the bronze plaque of 1952 by Henk Dannenburg, Aan onze gevallen makkers 1940–1945 (to our fallen comrades)

title: The lost fruit market's last blocks, Marnixstraat 200–220
summary: From the 1890s to 1934 Amsterdam's vegetable and fruit market ran 400 metres along the Singelgracht, with seven little harbours dug into the canal and quays lettered Wal A to Wal W. Three blocks with low storerooms and slanted corners are all that is left.
body:
In 1890 and 1895 the city council decided to move the vegetable and fruit markets from the Prinsengracht and the Singel to the strip along the Marnixstraat. The new market was over 400 metres long. To get enough quay for unloading, seven narrow harbours were dug into the partly filled Singelgracht. The tongues of land between them had quays lettered from Wal A in the south to Wal W in the north; the Lijnbaansgracht served as the growers' market. Along the street stood short blocks of shop-houses, with gaps between them so that produce could be carried from the boats to the road.

The market soon proved to be in the wrong place: no room to grow, and traffic jams. In 1934 it moved to the new market halls in Amsterdam-West, and from then to the 1970s the site was rebuilt beyond recognition. Only between the passage to the Lauriergracht and the Groenmarktkade do three blocks survive.
