Their ground floors are unusually low, storerooms rather than shops, with large doors front and back, and the corner houses are bevelled towards the back to let the crates through. The blocks are homes now.

Look for:
- the low ground floors with wide doors and the bevelled corners of nos. 202, 210 and 214
- the surviving water passage, once between Wal P and Wal Q
- on the back of no. 200, a faint painted sign for a vegetable and fruit trader, sales round the corner

title: Europarking, the garage nicknamed Zanstra's buttocks
summary: A garage owner who had studied car parks in Paris built this concrete garage with two round ramps, sited for a metro station that never came. Months after the 1972 opening it was 2 percent full. Now a listed early public car park, its curves are known as de billen van Zanstra.
body:
In the early 1960s the Amsterdam garage owner Hendrik Tabak looked at car parks in Paris and asked the architect Piet Zanstra to design one for him. The plan was approved in 1964 and the garage went up in reinforced concrete between 1966 and 1971, on a spot chosen because the first metro plan put a Rozengracht station on a western line here. A block of homes was demolished for it, which met protest.

When it opened in July 1972 the city council stayed away, apparently because alderman Han Lammers disapproved of Tabak's practices as a landlord. Within months occupancy fell to 2 percent and the garage lost 2,000 guilders a day. Tabak said he wished he had broken his legs before starting on it. The metro line was never built.

The garage survived and was listed in 2018 as one of the oldest public car parks in the country, a modernist design that makes the flows of cars its main theme. The two spiral ramps earned it the nickname de billen van Zanstra (Zanstra's buttocks). In 2007 the artist Spencer Tunick photographed about 2,000 naked people in it, and in 2022 the ramps were painted in rainbow colours for Pride. It is still a car park, open to the public.

Look for:
- the two round ramps on the Singelgracht side
- the high ground floor, made tall enough to park buses
- the bus station next to it, opened in 1957

title: ATVA, the hotel for single working men
summary: Opened in 1918 to get single workers out of filthy lodging houses, this block had 350 rooms of 2.20 by 2.90 metres, a cheap restaurant, foot baths and a library. War prices pushed the rents up, so clerks, policemen and actors moved in instead.
body:
Single working men in Amsterdam often slept in dirty, crowded lodging houses. The Amsterdamsch Bouwfonds wanted something better on the English and German model of the lodging house and Ledigenheim, and the city gave it land on the site of the old Amstel sugar refinery. Architect Jan Ernst van der Pek designed the Amsterdamsch Tehuis voor Arbeiders (Amsterdam home for workers), ATVA for short; his wife Louise Went was for years the secretary of the Bouwfonds.

The First World War sent costs soaring, from a planned 410,000 guilders to 780,000. Mayor J.W. Tellegen opened the home on 1 September 1918. It had 350 rooms on four floors, each 2.20 by 2.90 metres, with an iron bed, table, chair, washstand and a rail for hanging pictures. Toilets, foot baths and bathrooms were along the corridors, and there was a reading room and a canteen. The higher costs meant rents the intended tenants could not pay, and office workers, policemen and skilled tradesmen moved in. By 1931 some 10,000 men had lived here, among them the actor Albert van Dalsum and the artist Erich Wichmann.

In 1970 the rooms were combined into 171 flats, and in 2016 the housing corporation Stadgenoot renovated the block again. It is lived in and not open to visitors.

Look for:
- the two arched entrances with stone stairs of ten steps
- the projecting eaves on brick and timber brackets

title: Bureau Raampoort, the police station with a castle tower
summary: Built in 1888 on the site of a demolished city gate, this police station with battlements and an octagonal tower was the home base of detectives in Baantjer novels and a TV series. The police left in 2014; a Japanese furniture maker now has its shop inside.
body:
A small gate in the city walls, the Raampoort, stood here until 1844. In 1888 assistant city architect Willem Springer built a police station on the spot, mixing a classical layout with medieval touches: battlements, corbelled turrets and a tall octagonal tower with a weather vane. The back stands on foundations in the Singelgracht, a storey below street level. At first the building housed both a police post and the district secretary's office; from 1898 it was all police, and in 1929 three neighbouring houses were added.

The station had a second life in fiction. In Appie Baantjer's crime novels the Raampoort appears more than once, and in the De Waal & Baantjer series it is where the detectives work. In 2014–2015 SBS6 ran a police series called Bureau Raampoort.

The police first closed the front desk and in early 2014 left the building altogether. In 2017 the Japanese furniture brand Time & Style opened a store here; its four floors and basement are open in shop hours.

Look for:
- the city arms on a stone between the two turrets in the middle
- the round, battlemented back on the Singelgracht, best seen from the Nassaukade
- across the water at Bloemgracht 300, a corner tower that mirrors the station's

title: The first Tooneelschool building, Marnixstraat 150
summary: In 1878 the drama school founded four years earlier moved into this low building on the old ramparts: three classrooms and a stage of 4.9 by 5.7 metres, built for under 19,000 guilders. It trained actors here for about a century and now houses artists' studios.
body:
The Tooneelschool (drama school), founded in 1874, needed a home, and found it on a narrow strip between the newly laid out Marnixstraat and the Singelgracht. Dolf van Gendt designed the building, which opened in November 1878. Upstairs were three classrooms and a small stage of 4.9 by 5.7 metres; movable walls could turn the four rooms into one. On the ground floor lived the caretaker. A newspaper wondered how it could be built for under 19,000 guilders, and regretted that it was not in the centre.

It stayed low, two storeys under a hipped roof, while the blocks around it rose higher. Carvings over the ground-floor windows refer to the theatre, and a panel over the door once read Tooneel school. Later the side towards the Singelgracht was rebuilt to a design by Lau Peters, and the school, by then part of the Theaterschool, had left by 1982 for Keizersgracht 418, judging the building too old-fashioned. Its pupils included Hella Haasse and Ramses Shaffy. The national register describes it as an eclectic building with Renaissance revival touches, listed for its architecture and its use as a drama school. In 2023 it was Het Witte Huis, a broedplaats (subsidised studio building) for artists.

Look for:
- the theatre carvings over the ground-floor windows
- the empty panel over the door where Tooneel school was written
- the small Gothic-pointed window in the stone dormer among round-arched windows

title: De Weichsel, from city foundry to flour mill to power station
summary: On the site of the city foundry of 1614–1821 a steam flour mill put up one of the first grain silos in the Netherlands in 1886. After the mill closed in 1901 the complex made electricity for its neighbours. Next door stands a timber-framed liquor store of 1850.
body:
From 1614 to 1821 the city's foundry, 't Giethuis, stood at the corner of the Lijnbaansgracht and the Gietersstraat, the street named after it. The Jordaan was where the trades kept out of the rest of the city ended up, and in the 19th century the steam flour mill De Weichsel took over the site. In 1886–1887 its owner J. Reynvaan replaced the millstones with roller mills and had the engineer J.F. Klinkhamer add a silo of eight shafts and a machine house. The city register calls it an early example of the silo in the Netherlands and a possible trial run for the huge Korthals Altes silo that Klinkhamer later built on the Westerdoksdijk.

The mill closed in 1901 and the complex became a private power station, with a wire-weaving works, a shoe factory and other firms using its power; supply probably ended during the First World War. Today the buildings are homes, with businesses on the ground floor along the canal.

Round the corner at Lijnbaansgracht 61, liqueur distillers built a storehouse in 1850, a wooden frame with low brick walls, put up by a local carpenter. Timber frames were unusual by then.

Look for:
- the stone VERBOUWD DOOR HELLINGMANS BOUWMAATSCHAPPIJ ANNO 1902 in the front on the canal
- the gateway in the Gietersstraat and the tall Oude Molen (old mill) beside it
- the shed's wide arched door and round window at Lijnbaansgracht 61

title: Tichelkerk, the Capuchins' church built without an architect
summary: In 1911 the Capuchin friars started a church for the Jordaan's 14,000 Catholics, and a newspaper found that they were building it themselves, with no architect or site supervisor. Since 2005 it has been an Orthodox church; its nave hides behind the old friary.
body:
Around 1900 the Catholic church in the Netherlands set out to 'go to the people': in the big cities it feared that workers would drift into unbelief and socialism. The parish of De Posthoorn on the Haarlemmerstraat had 14,000 Catholics in the Jordaan to care for, and in 1911 the Capuchin friars began a friary church here, dedicated to Saint Anthony of Padua. The Algemeen Handelsblad discovered that they were building it in their own hands, without an architect or supervisor. That may be why the story went round that a friar designed it, though the drawings are signed by A.A.M. Brüning.

From the Lijnbaansgracht you see little: a friary wing, a wall round a triangular forecourt, and the roof of the nave with a wooden bell turret. The side aisle runs along the Tichelstraat, named after the tile makers who once worked here. Inside, the columns and ribs are painted blue and red, the apse windows are by Jaap Min (1952) and the aisle windows by the Franciscan Lando van den Berg (1964). The Capuchins closed it in 2004 and in 2005 sold it to the Russian Orthodox parish of Saint Nicholas of Myra, which left the Moscow Patriarchate in 2022. Visitors are welcome at the Sunday liturgy, 10:00.

Look for:
- the bell turret over the nave, seen from the Lijnbaansgracht
- the round-arched windows and gated porches on the Tichelstraat

title: The colonial army advert on the Palmgracht
summary: Around 1920 the blind wall above a corner shop on the Palmgracht carried a painted call to join the Dutch East Indies army. In about 2015 a group that restores old wall adverts painted it back, and some neighbours objected.
body:
This corner house on the Palmgracht has an older core behind a 19th-century front. Above the shop windows a large stretch of wall has no windows at all, probably to save on the old tax on window glass, and it made a perfect advertising board. A photo of about May 1920 shows a painted advert there for the Indisch Leger, the Royal Netherlands East Indies Army (KNIL). Later adverts were painted over it, and by 1983 the wall was bare. The house was then renovated, and the blank wall was kept.

Around 2015 the Werkgroep Historische Gevelreclames Amsterdam, which restores old painted wall adverts, chose to bring back the army advert. The owner, the housing corporation Ymere, and the resident agreed. Reports differ on how much the neighbours objected: some papers spoke of protest, others of a single complaint. Ymere defended it as a way to start a conversation about the colonial past. Others pointed out that the advert had been aimed at poor boys from the neighbourhood, to give them army discipline and a future in the Indies. The restored sign was still there in a photo of October 2022. The house is private.

Look for:
- the advert on the blind wall above the shop
- the shop front of columns and glass, typical of an Amsterdam corner shop

title: Palmdwarsstraat, where urban renewal learned to mend the old streets
summary: Around 1980 Theo Bosch, then with Aldo van Eyck's office, slotted four clusters of council homes and shops into the old street lines of a run-down corner of the Jordaan. The scheme gave Dutch planners the term semi-public space, and was listed in 2025.
body:
By the 1970s the north of the Jordaan had become a backstreet area, its back yards cluttered and decaying. In 1979–1981 the city housing department had four clusters of new homes and business spaces built around the Palmdwarsstraat, designed by the architects' office Van Eyck en Bosch, with Theo Bosch in charge. It was one of the first urban renewal schemes in the Netherlands that set out to repair the historic street pattern instead of replacing it: the new blocks keep to the old building lines, narrow plots and individual roof shapes.

The scheme was labelled experimental. Its novelty lay behind the fronts: the doors to the homes open onto galleries round the inner yards, with roof terraces and balconies, so that the yards became shared, half-public places. The scheme gave rise to the Dutch term semi-openbaar (semi-public). Bosch based the design on Woningdak, his graduation project of 1973, and worked hard to get daylight into small social-rent homes, with split-level shops, glazed roofs and glass stairwells. A few shops have since become homes. The city listed the clusters in 2025.

Look for:
- the half-round roofs over the narrow fronts
- the glass stairwells
- shops with split levels on the ground floor

title: The city masons' house at the dead end of the Leidsegracht
summary: A low square house where the Leidsegracht stops short was for over a century the lodging of the city's master masons and architects, beside the city's stone yard. Now a student society meets in it, and next door stands a corner house Stadsherstel rebuilt as a bookend.
body:
The Leidsegracht was meant to cross a new Lijnbaansgracht here, but that canal was never dug at this point. On the leftover ground stood the city's masons' yard and stonemason's works. Old maps and the building itself suggest that this low, square house under a hipped roof went up around 1663–1664 as home and workshop for the city's master mason; until 1829 it belonged to the city and housed master masons, city architects and city master builders. Later it was a store for the Hollandsche Manege riding school next door, fell into decay and was boarded up. When the riding school's buildings came down, this one was kept and was later used by the vinegar makers J.F. Tack. The national register calls it a unique former garden house on the ramparts.

Its number is on the Leidsegracht but its door, up a flight of steps, is in the Raamdwarsstraat. Since at least 2010 it has been Sociëteit Pylades of the student society SSRA, which put the building in its emblem.

Next door, Leidsegracht 106 leaned so badly that Stadsherstel called it a bookend. Part of it collapsed when work began; it was rebuilt on new foundations with old material, including volutes saved from houses demolished in the Haarlemmer Houttuinen.

Look for:
- the entrance stoop with its wooden door on the Raamdwarsstraat side
- on no. 106, the flattened spout gable with re-used volutes

title: Palmgracht 12–16, three rescued tops on one block
summary: What look like three old houses on the Palmgracht are one block of flats of 1938, wearing three 18th-century stone tops from houses in the Sint Jorisstraat. The order came from Eelke van Houten, the inspector who saved the city's gable tops; two stones in the front give it away.
body:
At Palmgracht 12–16 you seem to see three old canal houses, each under its own 18th-century top: two bell gables and a neck gable. In fact it is one block of flats, built in 1938 on three old plots, and the three carved sandstone tops came from houses in the Sint Jorisstraat. The order for the building came from Eelke van Houten himself, the city's head building inspector, who spent decades saving stone tops from condemned houses and having them set on new fronts. Three columns of bay windows keep up the illusion of three houses. Two stones in the front give the game away: herbouwd (rebuilt) and 1938.

The northern Jordaan has more of his rescues. On the Lijnbaansgracht, nos. 93–95 are three equal fronts under bell tops, the last a sharp corner with the Nieuwe Leliestraat known as a taartpunt (slice of cake); the historicist architect J.H. Scheerboom worked on them. At Egelantiersgracht 191–195 the two tall canal houses of 1938 carry the crested bell gables of the houses that stood there before, a rebuild Van Houten watched over and photographed. The houses are private.

Look for:
- the stones reading herbouwd and 1938, left and right in the Palmgracht front
- the three different tops over one even run of bay windows
- the taartpunt corner of Lijnbaansgracht 95 and Nieuwe Leliestraat 196
- the crested bell gables of Egelantiersgracht 191–195, and the single rescued top on Anjeliersstraat 23 (1935)

title: Two schools on the old Leidse cemetery
summary: Until 1866 this corner of the Jordaan was a burial ground. On it the city built a commercial school, where the young Willem Drees took his exams, and a double free school for the poorest children, where Jac. P. Thijsse was head.
body:
Until 1866 this end of the Passeerdersgracht was the Leidsche Kerkhof, a burial ground at the city's edge. Once it closed, the city filled it with schools for two very different kinds of pupil.

On the Raamplein stands the Openbare Handelsschool (public commercial school), which moved here in 1901 from the Huis met de Hoofden on the Keizersgracht. Willem Drees, later prime minister, studied here from 1901 and took his final exams in 1903; a diamond worker's son in his class first got him interested in socialism. The school became the Hogeschool voor Economische Studies and left for Zuidoost in 2004. A television production company used the building from 2013 to about 2018.

Round the corner, H. Leguyt of the public works department built a double school for the city's free schools for the poorest: two schools of 600 children each, with an entrance apiece. From 1897 one of the two heads was Jac. P. Thijsse, who with Eli Heimans was writing the nature series Van vlinders, bloemen en vogels for schoolchildren. It still houses schools.

The walled former playground beside the Handelsschool, long a car park, is to get a block of flats.

Look for:
- the gilded eagle on the middle pediment of the Handelsschool
- the gym hall on the Raamstraat side, with bands of glazed tiles under the eaves
- the caretaker's house at Passeerdersgracht 27, between the two schools
- KONINGIN EMMA SCHOOL, still over the door of Passeerdersgracht 23

title: Arbeidsbeurs, the labour exchange that sorted you at the door
summary: In 1915–1917 the city built its labour exchange a home of its own, the first office designed for finding people work, in early Amsterdam School brick. Men and bakers came in at the side, employers and women on the canal, and each trade had its own waiting room.
body:
Looking for work in Amsterdam around 1920 meant coming here, and the building sorted you at the door. The Arbeidsbeurs (labour exchange) began in 1887 as an initiative of the Maatschappij voor den Werkenden Stand, a society for working people, and the city took it over in 1907. In 1915–1917 the city gave it this building, the earliest municipal office designed for the job. The public works department drew it; the expressive brickwork is usually credited to Piet Kramer, who worked there.

The plan was strict. Bakers and men came in through the low wing on the Tweede Passeerdersdwarsstraat, and the big men's waiting room was in the main block. Employers and women used the doors on the canal. Upstairs, women office workers, maids and cleaners each had their own rooms; one floor higher were male clerks and a waiting room for boys. Employers and job seekers were kept apart.

In the late 1950s the exchange moved to the Singel and the city's housing bureau took over, the office that handed out scarce homes, until 1973. From 1981 to 2012 the children's circus Elleboog played here. Now the Vinse School, a private school, uses it.

Look for:
- the bay window climbing three storeys over the canal door, with leaded glass
- the stepped stone surround of that door
- the tower-like corners and the three dormers on the side street

title: The refuge for the needy in the Walenhoek
summary: Around 1850 a charity pulled down the houses here to build a day refuge for the homeless, one that did not order its guests to mend their ways. Two old warehouses hide behind it in the Walenhoek alley, and Bordewijk made it the brothel of his novel Rood paleis.
body:
From 1844 the Toevlugt voor Behoeftigen (refuge for the needy) had a room in one of the houses here: a place where homeless people could rest from the day. There were other shelters in the city, but this one did not demand that its guests change their behaviour. Around 1850 it pulled down the houses on this spot and built the closed, blank-faced block you see now, with one door for the guests and one for the board. For its first years the west windows looked out over the Leidsche Kerkhof, the cemetery that closed in 1866.

The refuge closed around 1924. A wholesaler in glass, china and earthenware turned it into storerooms with a garage and knocked through to the warehouse behind. That warehouse (no. 17) and its neighbour (no. 15) stand inside the block on the Walenhoek, or Walengang: one of the narrow alleys that led to back yards where the poorest lived in ramshackle housing. In his novel Rood paleis, set just before the First World War, Ferdinand Bordewijk put an imaginary brothel in the building and called the Passeerdersgracht a short, lugubrious canal. It holds an office and flats today.

Look for:
- the pilasters, the attic and the double door of no. 19
- the street sign of the Walenhoek, and down the alley the spout gable of no. 15 ending in volutes
- the steel frame propping up the front of no. 17

title: The London Police on Prinsengracht 70, the mural the neighbours kept
summary: When the house on the corner came down in 1950, this canal house of 1741 was left with a blank wall that drew tags and rubbish. In 2009 the residents had The London Police paint it. The city's monuments office wanted it removed; the neighbourhood objected, and it stayed.
body:
Prinsengracht 70 stands where the Tuinstraat leaves the canal at a slant, so the corner plot is a wedge. Until 5 January 1950 an almost triangular house filled the point, with a pothuis (a small lean-to) at its tip. When it was pulled down, the listed house of 1741 was left with a grey wall without a window.

The wall gathered graffiti and rubbish. In 2009 the residents took matters into their own hands and asked the street-art duo The London Police to paint it. They covered it from pavement to roof with their cheerful little figures, added a painted cherry picker with its crew, and worked the house number 70 into the picture. In July 2010 the city's monuments office called it a serious blot on the protected streetscape, and the city wanted it removed. The neighbourhood fought back and the mural stayed. The graffiti writer Laser 3.14 counts it among the finest in Amsterdam and sees in it how murals went from outlawed to indispensable. In 2018 The London Police quoted this wall in a new one on the Zeeburgerdijk in Oost.

Look for:
- the number 70 in the painting
- the cherry picker and its painters
- the wooden ground floor front, partly from 1741, and the neck gable with its hoisting beam

title: Prinsengracht 206, the banker's stone and the black money
summary: When the bank chairman André Batenburg retired in 1985 he asked for gifts to Stadsherstel instead of presents, and they bought this corner house. Its stone shows silver thrown into a castle and gold pouring out. When the silver tarnished, the banker objected to the black money.
body:
In the early 17th century this corner was a garden of Reynier Cant, eleven years one of Amsterdam's four burgomasters after 1578 and a signer of the Union of Utrecht for Holland. His widow's heirs sold the land in 1623 and by 1625 a house stood here. For centuries it was a shop with homes above: a tobacconist rented the ground floor in 1742, a shoe and boot dealer advertised on the side wall around 1900, and in 1931 the second-floor homes were declared unfit to live in.

In 1985 André Batenburg stepped down as chairman of the Algemene Bank Nederland. He was also on the board of Stadsherstel, the company that buys and restores old buildings, and asked for gifts to its friends' society instead of presents. They came to 56,292 guilders, enough to buy this house. A stone in the side wall, designed by Jan Six and cut by the workshop of Snoep and Vermeer, puns on his name: silver thrown into the top of a castle (burg) comes out at the bottom as gold (baten, profits). Over the years the silver paint turned black, and the banker did not like being linked to black money. When he left the Stadsherstel board, he painted it silver again himself.

Look for:
- the Batenburg stone in the side wall on the Rozenstraat
- the carved wooden tree of life in the fanlight
- the basement windows and cellar door, put back in 1987

title: Gunters & Meuser, an ironmonger's name cut in stone
summary: In 1826 Johannes Gunters and his mother opened a shop for cobblers' tools on the Prinsengracht. As Gunters & Meuser it grew into a well-known Amsterdam ironmonger, and in 1883 it put up this corner block with the firm's name carved over the door.
body:
The firm began small. In 1826 Johannes Petrus Gunters and his mother opened a shop for shoemakers' tools and supplies at Prinsengracht 46, by the Prinsensluis. By about 1851 it had moved to Egelantiersgracht 2 and sold ironmongery. Gunters' son took a partner in 1870; after that partner died, Carel Meuser joined in 1875 and the firm became Gunters & Meuser.

In 1882 it bought this neighbouring house, where paper collars, cuffs and shirt fronts had been sold, and in 1883 built the present corner block. The ground floor, behind a broad round-arched doorway, was probably for packing and dispatch; the floors above were homes. Who designed it is not known. The front bends at the corner, so each floor has one window on the Egelantiersgracht and three on the Prinsengracht. In 1917–1918 the firm added a concrete shop and warehouse in Amsterdam School style next door, by P. Vorkink and Jac.Ph. Wormser. In 2016 Gunters & Meuser was taken over by the hardware chain Isero.

Look for:
- GUNTERS EN MEUSER carved in the stone band over the door
- the original double door with wrought-iron grilles and a fanlight with radiating bars
- next door on the Egelantiersgracht, the 1917 building with ANNO 1917 over the hoist

title: Saturn eating his child, a gable stone on the Prinsengracht
summary: Set in the front of this canal house is a painted stone labelled SATVRNVS: the Roman god of time, scythe in one hand and a child in the other. It follows a print by Jacob Matham after Hendrick Goltzius, with one change the carver may have got wrong.
body:
Most Amsterdam gable stones show a trade, a ship or a pun on a name. This one, between the first and second floors of Prinsengracht 394, shows a myth at its darkest. Under the label SATVRNVS stands Saturn, the Roman god of time and farming, counterpart of the Greek Kronos, who devoured his own children. He wears a red cloak and a loincloth, holds a scythe in his right hand and a child in his left, and stands on a mound with plants growing on one side and a two-faced Janus head on the other.

The society Gevelstenen van Amsterdam traced the picture to an etching by Jacob Matham after Hendrick Goltzius, in which Saturn stands on a pedestal. Where the stone has the Janus head, the print has a cloud, and the society thinks the carver misread it. It dates the stone to the second half of the 17th century, and had it cleaned and painted in 1996.

The house is a private home: an older house behind a front with a straight cornice from the 19th century, with a double door surround of the early 1800s.

Look for:
- the child in Saturn's hand and the scythe
- the Janus head at the foot of the mound
- the paired doors at the top of the stoop

title: J.J. van Noortschool, eyes shut and eyes open
summary: A Reformed church school of 1925 by Cornelis Kruyswijk, the only Amsterdam School building on this stretch of the canal. By its door, two carved heads by Theo van Reijn make the point of schooling: one has its eyes closed, the other open.
body:
In 1917 the Netherlands put church schools on an equal financial footing with public ones, and the Primary Education Act of 1920 released money for a wave of new school buildings. This is one of them. The Dutch Reformed congregation already had a school on this plot; it was pulled down, and on 21 March 1925 H.C. de Zwart, secretary of the congregation's schools, laid the first stone of a new one. It was named after J.J. van Noort, a Reformed minister and champion of Christian schooling who had died in 1922, and had ten classrooms for at most 426 pupils.

The architect, Cornelis Kruyswijk, came from a Reformed family himself, and the churches and schools he built were for Reformed clients. On a narrow canal front he fitted a corridor school with a rounded tower in the middle and curved brick corners. The sculpture is by Theo van Reijn, who often worked with him. By the door are two heads with features from the Dutch East Indies, a frequent source for Amsterdam School sculptors: one has its eyes shut, the other open, for the way schooling opens eyes and mind. At the outer corners a bird flies towards the sun. The school later became a mavo; a language school uses it now.

Look for:
- the two heads either side of the door
- the school's name in wrought-iron letters over the entrance
- the first stone at the far left

title: In de Buis, a silk trader's pun on the corner of the Leidsegracht
summary: High on this corner house sits a stone of a herring buss, a fishing boat. It has nothing to do with fish: the silk trader who bought the plot around 1664 was called Jan Adriaansz. Buys. In 1969 the barber's shop downstairs trained a pioneer woman barber.
body:
Before Amsterdam had house numbers, this corner was known by the stone In de Buis in its front. A buis (buss) was the broad boat of the Dutch herring fishery, and the stone, about 50 by 90 centimetres, shows one. The name is a pun. Around 1664 the silk trader Jan Adriaansz. Buys bought the plot here; he died in 1666. Two date stones in cartouches keep the stone company.

The front is far younger than its sign. In the second half of the 19th century the house was rebuilt around its 17th-century core, with a new front and roof, which is why an old stone looks down from a 19th-century gable on the Prinsengracht. Towards the Leidsegracht, where the neighbours are lower, the side is plain and plastered.

In 1969 and 1970 the papers took an interest in the barber's shop at Leidsegracht 70. The barber had trained his daughter there, and she became the first woman in Amsterdam to earn the men's barber diploma. A year later she told De Telegraaf that men still did not like being cut by a woman.

Look for:
- the herring buss over the middle window of the top floor, on the Prinsengracht side
- the two date stones in the gable
- the heavy wooden front of the ground and first floors

title: Fatih mosque, the new De Zaaier church the beauty committee lost to
summary: The city's architecture panel rejected this twin-towered Jesuit church; the parish priest went over its head and got it built anyway. It has been the Fatih mosque since 1981. Across the road stands the parish's own club house, named after a Jordaan-born Jesuit general.
body:
In 1928 the city's Schoonheidscommissie (the panel that vetted new fronts) turned down H.W. Valk's design for a new St Ignatius church on the Rozengracht. The parish priest asked the mayor and aldermen to approve it regardless, and they did. The architecture weekly Bouwkundig Weekblad printed a photo with a sour caption: an embellishment of the city "which the beauty committee opposed, in vain". The church took over the name De Zaaier (the sower) from the old Jesuit church on the Keizersgracht, and was consecrated on 19 March 1929.

Mass was said here until 1971. After some years as a carpet and music hall, the Islamic Foundation Netherlands bought it in 1981 and made it the Fatih mosque. Because Mecca lies the other way, the mihrab now stands in the old main doorway, shops sit in the former entrance and the faithful use a side door. Crescents replaced the crosses on the towers.

Opposite, at no. 133, the same parish had Valk build the Roothaanhuis, a parish and youth club house opened in December 1929 and named after the Jesuit general Jan Roothaan. Johnny Jordaan and Tante Leen won a talent contest there.

Look for:
- the two 40-metre towers with the round rose window between them
- the shops tucked under each tower
- across the road at no. 133, the tall brick bay window that rises through the roof

title: Bols on the Rozengracht, and the year 1575
summary: Bols says it began distilling in 1575 in a shed called 't Lootsje on this spot. Genealogists call that a myth; what is certain is a wine house bought here in 1649. Berlage gave the firm a front copied almost literally from a 17th-century shop.
body:
The liqueur house Bols tells a founding story: a Protestant family fled Antwerp and opened a distillery, 't Lootsje (the little shed), outside the city wall in 1575, on what became the Rozengracht. Genealogical research treats that as a myth. What is documented is that in 1649 Pieter Jacobsz Bultius bought a house here, called it Het Lootsje and sold wine. His son Lucas began distilling brandy and liqueur and by 1713 ran five stills. The "about 1575" claim was put into Bols advertising after 1868.

The firm leaned on that tradition in its buildings. In 1892 it asked H.P. Berlage to remodel its office and tasting room here in the spirit of the Renaissance, and he copied a 17th-century shop-house almost literally, down to the tall wooden shopfront with a canopy. From 1902 Ed. Cuypers extended the complex and mirrored Berlage's front, in simpler form, on the other end. In the 1970s Bols left, and the tasting room's interior was moved whole to its new offices in Nieuw-Vennep. The building now holds shops and offices.

Look for:
- Berlage's front on the left, with its twisted wall anchors and the date stone 1902
- across the road at no. 106, a 17th-century house behind the street, uncovered in 1957 and long known as the Bols Taveerne
- next to it at no. 110, the 1671 warehouse where Bols kept stock
- further on at no. 204, a wide gabled storehouse built for Bols in 1896

title: Rozentheater, a picture palace with Pierrots on the door
summary: Built in 1912–1913 as a neighbourhood cinema and variety hall, with a front like a small temple and four Pierrots playing the lute over the door. It was Ritsaert ten Cate's Mickery theatre for sixteen years and is now home to the English-language comedy troupe Boom Chicago.
body:
The Jordaan had no cinema or theatre when a merchant, H.D. Zwaluw, and his son had one built on the site of a row of workers' houses. The architects Z.D. Gulden and M. Geldmaker gave it a symmetrical front of two towers with a domed middle part over the stage, the kind of "temple of culture" front the national register says was typical for cultural buildings of the time. Opening night, on 22 March 1913, offered a singer, a pony and dogs, a male double quartet, a balancing act and a film, with a Rozenmarsch written for the occasion.

It showed films and from 1918 also variety. The name changed with the times: Asta from 1926, Capitol from 1948, then from 1972 to 1988 Mickery, the theatre with which Ritsaert ten Cate brought foreign experimental companies to Amsterdam. Since 1994 it has been the Rozentheater again, and since 2013 the home of Boom Chicago, an improv and sketch comedy group founded by Americans in 1993, which plays its shows here.

Look for:
- four reliefs of Pierrot with a lute over the three arched doors
- stained glass with flowers and wayang puppets in the windows above
- on the towers, a seated man holding his hands to his ears

title: Rozenhofje, an almshouse on an old pleasure maze
summary: A timber merchant's will of 1740 paid for a hofje for old women on the site of a 17th-century maze garden. It grew to 55 tiny homes, was cut back to 28 in 1990, and in 1935 its board rebuilt three houses down the street behind second-hand 18th-century gables.
body:
Jan de Jager, a timber merchant who died on 13 August 1740, left money for a hofje (almshouse round a courtyard) for elderly Protestant women. Around 1741 the fund of the Collegiants bought a plot on the Rozengracht where a pleasure garden with a maze, De Nieuwe Doolhof, had been. The first women moved in in 1744, and gifts and legacies let the hofje grow to some 55 homes. Around 1850 the residents received peat for fuel, three loaves a week and groceries at Christmas.

In 1884 the old sandstone gate gave way to the present front building by Gerlof and Abraham Salm. By the 1980s the homes no longer met modern standards; a renovation from 1987 to 1990 turned 55 homes into 28. The hofje still belongs to its founding foundation and takes women over 50, preferably Mennonites. The courtyard is private.

In 1935 the hofje had the houses at nos. 183–193 pulled down and rebuilt in old style. Under the eye of city inspector Eelke van Houten, their fronts got 18th-century stone tops saved from demolished houses; the one on no. 183 is said to come from the Boomstraat.

Look for:
- the oriel over the gate with "Rozenhofje", a rose in a medallion and the year 1884 above
- at nos. 183–193, three near-identical 1935 fronts under old tops
- on no. 191, a pediment with an otter, kept from the house that stood there

title: Rijpenhofje, where the date over the door is wrong
summary: The gate says 1747, but the hofje was founded in 1736 by the will of a man who seems to have fallen out with his wife. Rebuilt in 1913, it still belongs to the Mennonites and has taken men since 1968, with student caretakers living at the front.
body:
Gerard de Rijp, who was apparently not on good terms with his wife, made his nephews his heirs in 1733 on one condition: that they found a hofje (almshouse round a courtyard) for poor Mennonite or Protestant people. He died in 1736 and the nephews built it. The year 1747 over the gate is not the founding date: it is the year they handed the management, which they had had enough of, to the Mennonite congregation Lam en Toren. The regents' room once held at least eight old paintings, two of them by Govert Flinck; they went on loan to the Rijksmuseum in 1899.

In 1903 an old resident fell from her window and died; the minutes record that from then on a window cleaner would do the first floor. Around 1910 the decayed hofje was pulled down and the women were housed meanwhile in the empty Konijnenhofje. Abraham Salm designed the new building, opened on 10 June 1913: a sober front with a richly carved gate.

The United Mennonite Congregation still owns it. Since 1968 men may live here too, from age 55; three students living at the front help the residents in return. The courtyard is private.

Look for:
- the stone gate frame with RIJPENHOFJE on the lintel and 1747 in the pediment
- the wrought-iron gate in front of the original double door
- the brick balustrade along the roof

title: Hofje De Zeven Keurvorsten, a joke that became a name
summary: A gunpowder maker's son founded this Catholic hofje around 1645. Neighbours mocked its seven little houses as the palaces of the seven prince-electors, and the name stuck so well that a 1724 stone trying to rename it never caught on.
body:
In 1641 the gunpowder maker Cornelis Martsz Pronck bought a plot here, opposite the city's carpentry yard; the hofje (almshouse round a courtyard) was probably founded around 1645, perhaps by his son. Seven small houses along the street took in poor elderly Catholic women "of blameless conduct". Properly it was the Pronckhofje, and the story goes that Amsterdammers, who had little time for Catholics, sneered that its seven little houses looked like the palaces of the seven Keurvorsten, the prince-electors who chose the German emperor. A cash book of 1739 already writes "Pronckenhofje called the Seven Electors".

In 1724 seven more houses went up behind, forming the courtyard, and a stone on them tried to rename the place Alida's hofje. Its last lines are a chronogram: the capitals add up to 1724. Nobody adopted the name. A stone over the gate marks a new wing of 1775, when a small chapel was made upstairs; in 1862 a neo-Gothic chapel followed. A 15th-century panel of the death of the Virgin from the hofje was sold to the Rijksmuseum in 1940 for 80,000 guilders, which paid for repairs.

Renovated in 2012, it now has 12 homes, let as social housing through Ymere. The courtyard is private.

Look for:
- the framed gateway with the 1775 memorial stone
- the wall that closes off the courtyard from the street

title: Regenboogs Liefdehofje, from Catholic elderly to music students
summary: A banker's back-yard houses became a Catholic hofje in 1806. Its 1884 extension hides behind a showy front of two stepped gables and a carved gate stone. After the hofje wound down, a foundation bought it in 1985 and lets the rooms to music students.
body:
Around 1800 the banker Joannes Baptista van Aerde owned a group of small houses on an inner plot here. After his death they became a hofje (almshouse) on 1 May 1806, for elderly Catholic men and women, married without children or single, who lived rent free. The rent of a house on the Herengracht and one in the Kalverstraat paid for its upkeep, and a chapel was set up at no. 110. In 1850, 43 people lived here.

In 1884 the charity grew with a new block a little to the east, designed by L.W. Mulder and J.G. Sarlemijn: two long rows of homes facing each other across a narrow yard, closed off from the street by a high wall. The street side is the show front, in an old Dutch style, with two stepped gables and a wide double door under a richly carved sandstone stone bearing the hofje's name.

After the Second World War the hofje declined. From 1979 empty rooms went to young people; a residents' group that bought it in the 1980s could not keep it going, and in 1985 the Stichting Jan Pietersz. Huis took it over. It lets the restored homes to music students. The yard is private.

Look for:
- the carved name stone over the gate
- the brick stepped gables with their arched tops, resting on stone brackets
- the decorative wrought-iron wall anchors

title: Johanna ter Meulen's model flats in the Tuinstraat
summary: A sugar refiner paid, and a young woman trained by Octavia Hill in London ran the houses: three Tuinstraat blocks of 1895–1902 by a pioneer of social housing. One carries a stone to her memory, another two stones about hardship.
body:
Johanna ter Meulen (1867–1937), a businessman's daughter, escaped the life of an unmarried daughter at home when the sugar refiner W. Spakler agreed to put money into workers' housing with her as woningopzichteres (lady housing manager). With her parents' leave she went to London to learn from Octavia Hill, who managed tenements in poor districts. Back in Amsterdam she founded and ran the Woningmaatschappij Oud-Amsterdam, which built 94 new workers' homes in the Tuinstraat, Willemsstraat and Rozenstraat in place of condemned slums. She paired fundraising with strict rules of conduct for her tenants, as part of what she saw as educating them. In 1905 Oud-Amsterdam was the first to be recognised by the city as a housing association.

The architect P. Smitt drew the three blocks here. At nos. 166–172 (1895–1896) two H-shaped blocks are joined in the middle, so the homes at front and back each get windows on two sides. At nos. 137–141 (1897), run by her pupil E.A. Pijnappel, the top floor steps back behind a row of small roof terraces, an early example of the idea.

Look for:
- on nos. 166–172, the memorial stone to Johanna ter Meulen where the two halves meet, and the years 1895 and 1896 over the doors
- on nos. 99–101 (1902), two stones: DRUK VERLICHTEN IS IEDERS PLICHT ("easing hardship is everyone's duty") and an older one, DRUK IS IN D'WERELT VEEL
- the openwork brick balustrades on the roof terraces of nos. 137–141

title: Ons Huis, where the classes were meant to meet
summary: In 1892 Hélène Mercier's society opened a house where Jordaan workers could take classes, read, fence or play chess. The devout called it a socialist bulwark, socialists called it patronising charity. COC Amsterdam and a hotel named after her are in it now.
body:
The Vereniging Ons Huis (Our House) was founded in 1891 by Hélène Mercier, a campaigner for women and the poor, and the wealthy philanthropist Christian Wilhelm Janssen. Following the English Toynbee work, it wanted to bring the classes into contact and give working people a better chance, without politics or religion and without talking down to them. Both sides distrusted it: confessional critics called it a socialist bulwark, socialists called it a tool of capitalism.

C.B. Posthumus Meyjes designed the building, opened on 10 May 1892 and far taller than its neighbours. There was a reading room, gym and fencing, cooking and sewing classes, lectures, music and drama. A chess club started that same month, the first workers' chess club in Amsterdam, and in 1899 the first school for social work held its lessons here. In 1904 Berlage extended the house by one bay and, unusually for him, kept to its Renaissance style. Ons Huis grew to thirteen houses in the city and sold this one in 1979. COC Amsterdam has its address here, in the Hotel Mercier.

Look for:
- the cartouche ONS HUIS over the left-hand door
- round the corner at Rozengracht 19–21, a volkskoffiehuis (coffee house for working people) by the same architect, 1892
- further along at nos. 215–225, a 1912 block of the housing company Oud-Amsterdam with a stone of May 1913 in memory of Hélène Mercier
- at nos. 211–213, flats of 1891 by the same architect, dressed up as one grand house

title: A timber clinic for the poor and a fire station at the city's edge
summary: Where the Rozengracht meets the Singelgracht, the city put two services for the crowded Jordaan: a half-timbered wooden building of 1888 for medical care for the poor, rare in brick Amsterdam, and a fire station of 1893 placed to reach several directions fast.
body:
Once the Rozengracht had been filled in, in 1889, it became the main road to the new districts in the west, and its far end, on the old city edge, was a handy spot for city services. In 1888 the Public Works department put up a building here for Geneeskundige Armenverzorging, the city's medical care for the poor. It is built entirely of wood, in a half-timbered style with overhanging roofs, which the national register singles out as rare in type and material. In 1902 it got a consulting room for the municipal health service on the Singelgracht side, and in 1916 a bedroom was added to that. It sits back from the road and is best seen from the Singelgracht.

Next door, on a triangular plot squeezed between the street and the canal, the fire station went up from 1893, so the brigade could set out quickly in several directions. The pump wagon stood behind the big double doors with the horses' stable behind it, and the firemen's waiting room and bedroom were upstairs. It is now a house.

Look for:
- the timber framing with St Andrew's crosses and the boarded frieze under the eaves of no. 226
- on the fire station, the Amsterdam arms in a stone over the ground floor and the iron grilles in the double doors
- on the bridge parapet beside it, a fireman fighting a dragon by Frans Werner

title: Rozenstraat's 1934 row under borrowed gable tops
summary: Five houses of 1934 in a row, each crowned with an 18th-century stone top: two from the Konijnenstraat, one from the Laurierstraat, one from the Kattengat, one from the house that stood here. In 1970 the national register listed them for those tops alone.
body:
In the early 1930s this stretch of the Rozenstraat was in such a bad state that in 1934 the old houses at nos. 35–43 were replaced by one new row, and the Suikerhuizengang, an alley into the block, disappeared. To keep an old look, the city's head building inspector Eelke van Houten had the new fronts finished with sandstone gable tops he had saved from demolished houses. According to the Amsterdam Monumentenstad database, the tops of nos. 35 and 37 came from the Konijnenstraat, no. 39's from Laurierstraat 50, just pulled down, and no. 43's from Kattengat 7, demolished that year; no. 41 kept the top of the house that stood on its own plot. In 1970 all five were listed as national monuments "because of the sandstone parts" of their tops.

The street has more. At nos. 250–254 (1933–1934) the architect first drew two plain gables; under Van Houten's influence they became bell gables, one from the old building, one from Oudezijds Achterburgwal 16. No. 222 (1936) has no front door, because the Drie-Roemersgang alley once ran through here, and its two "bull's-eye windows" in the register are in fact blind cartouches reading A and 36. The houses are private.

Look for:
- the five different tops in a row over identical 1930s brickwork at nos. 35–43
- the near-twin bell gables of nos. 250–254, only the right one with a crest
- at Tweede Laurierdwarsstraat 45, two neck gables dated anno 1723 on a 1939 rebuild

title: Café Theo Ruiter, the resistance man's literary bar
summary: From 1940 this corner house held the café of Theo Ruiter, a resistance fighter who used his standing with the Germans to get people out of their custody. Writers such as Ed Hoornik and Jan Campert drank here, and until 1980 it drew artists, actors and journalists.
body:
Theo Ruiter (1911–1965) took over the café in this 18th-century corner house in 1940. Early in the war he saved a German officer, and the credit that earned him with the occupying authorities let him get people released from German custody; how many is not certain. He was also active in a knokploeg, an armed resistance squad. Writers and journalists who later joined the resistance, among them Ed Hoornik, Wim Schouten and the poet Jan Campert, came to his café.

After the war Café Theo Ruiter stayed a meeting place for former resistance people, artists, writers, actors, singers and journalists until 1980. In the early 1960s the entertainer Wim Ibo presented a cabaret-style television programme from here. Ruiter received the Resistance Memorial Cross, and in 2010 his grave at Zorgvlied cemetery was taken over by the cemetery as a permanent monument.

The house itself is a typical canal house from before the Rozengracht was filled in; a bridge once crossed the canal right at its door. The flat at the top has its entrance round the corner in the Akoleienstraat.

Look for:
- the bell gable with its crest, in Louis XV style
- the low step up to the old raised ground floor
- Ruiter's grave at Zorgvlied, plot 22, if you go further afield

title: Tweede Laurierdwarsstraat, what the clearances left standing
summary: A corner house on the vanished Vuile Weespad (Dirty Weesp Path), facing its old twin the Schone Weespad (Clean Weesp Path); a glazed warehouse probably built for a rag trade; a gable with a white lamb. A few survivors of the 1970s and 80s urban renewal in one short street.
body:
Within fifteen years of being laid out, these blocks were packed with back houses reached by narrow paths. Two faced each other here: the Vuile Weespad and, across the street, the Schone Weespad. The urban renewal of the 1970s and 1980s cleared most block interiors, and the paths went too; a gap in the frontage, the numbering and the name signs remain.

No. 42, on the corner of the Vuile Weespad, still has the frame of a house from the first quarter of the 17th century; its side wall along the old path is untouched, while the street front is from the late 19th century. No. 52, of 1884, was built by two carpenters as a warehouse but with ordinary glazed windows, rare for a store. From at least 1922 to 1954 it held a trade in rags and metal, and the city register thinks it was built for one: rags were sorted here for paper making. It has hardly changed. At no. 8 only the front of an older house survived the renewal, built into the new block behind it.

Look for:
- the break in the houses at nos. 40–42, with the Vuile Weespad name sign
- the wide central doors on every floor of no. 52, and its cast-iron door panels
- the lying lamb on top of the bell gable of no. 8, known as Het witte lam
- nos. 58 and 60, a pair that stood alone between cleared plots in 1974

title: Three gable stones on the Rozengracht
summary: Within a few doors of each other: a portrait of the brand-new Noorderkerk set in a house of 1636, three piggy banks that are said to mark a 17th-century bank, and two spies of Canaan carrying a giant bunch of grapes, worn almost smooth.
body:
Gable stones were the house signs of the 17th century, and three good ones survive on this stretch of the filled-in canal.

At no. 48, a house of 1636 with a front of stone and brick pilasters, the owner Jan van Cruijskerken set a stone showing the Noorderkerk, which had opened only in 1623 a few streets away. It has no inscription; it was painted red and white in the 21st century.

Across the road at no. 81, a stepped gable from the second quarter of the 17th century carries a stone with three piggy banks, flanked by two blank stones. According to the gable-stone society's database it points to a bank in the house, and the slot of the piggy banks is horizontal, a form that came up then. An alley, the Driespaarpottengang, once ran under the house through the basement.

At no. 80 an 18th-century bell gable holds an older stone, 't Land van Beloften (the Promised Land), from the first half of the 17th century: two of the spies Moses sent into Canaan carry a bunch of grapes on a pole, as in Numbers 13:23. Wear and dirty air have made it hard to read.

Look for:
- the Noorderkerk stone and the year stones "Anno 1636" at no. 48
- the three piggy banks between the first-floor windows of no. 81
- the two men and the grapes high in the gable of no. 80

title: An insurer's branch with its head office in tiles (Rozengracht 58)
summary: Above a 1907 shopfront on a plain 19th-century house hangs a tile picture of the Astoria building on the Keizersgracht: the life insurer that built it had the same architect, Gerrit van Arkel, give its branch office here a front to match.
body:
Rozengracht 58 is an ordinary house under a straight 19th-century cornice, with one exception. From 1907 its ground floor is a showy shopfront of carved stone, wood and stained glass, and above it hangs a tile picture of the Astoria, the head office of the Eerste Hollandsche Levensverzekeringsbank (First Dutch Life Insurance Bank) on the Keizersgracht. The insurer had hired Gerrit van Arkel for both: the new head office, and the front of a branch office in this shop building. His name is cut into the shopfront. The tiles came from the Amsterdam pottery De Distel.

The result is a house in two styles, a 20th-century advertisement for an insurance company stuck under a 19th-century front. The house itself is private.

Look for:
- the tile picture of the Astoria over the shopfront, with the De Distel mark at bottom left
- Van Arkel's name in the stonework of the shopfront
- the chequerboard tiles in the doorways and the stained glass above
- the Astoria itself at Keizersgracht 174–176, ten minutes' walk away

title: Club Mazzo, behind an upholsterer's granite front (gone)
summary: From 1980 to 2004 this 1922 furniture showroom held Mazzo, the members-only club of video projections, new wave and theme nights, and from 1989, with the RoXY, one of the first places in Amsterdam to play house. The club is gone; the granite front remains.
body:
In 1922 the upholsterer and furniture dealer J.Th. Drilling jr. had this house rebuilt as workshops, showrooms and a shop with three flats above. The architect, H.J. Zonsveld, gave it a ground floor entirely of grey granite with two odd iron grilles in angled granite frames over the doors. The firm stayed until the 1970s.

On 5 June 1980 a group of friends from a student house opened Club Mazzo on the ground floor. The name was a twist on Maso, a neighbour who complained about their noise every day. Mazzo became known at home and abroad for theme nights built with video and slide projections. In the 1980s it was the main Dutch club for new wave and punk, and from 1989, together with the RoXY, it was where house music first came in. The door was strict: only people who were "audiovisually active" could become members. A fire in 1995 and a police raid over drug use started its decline, and it left the building in September 2004.

An Italian restaurant borrowed the name from 2010 to 2017. The granite front survives.

Look for:
- the grey granite shopfront and cornice, unusual on the Rozengracht
- the angled granite frames over the two doors, their iron grilles now covered up
- the geometric stained glass in the upper windows

title: Willemsstraat, the slum canal the philanthropists filled
summary: The Goudsbloemgracht was a ditch without quay walls, lined with 57 alleys of the worst slums in town. In 1857 it was filled in and the first housing association in the country spent almost forty years rebuilding it house by house.
body:
The Goudsbloemgracht was never a proper canal: a ditch without quay walls. In 1775 it had 57 alleys running off it, and its banks held some of the most notorious slums in Amsterdam. The Vereeniging ten behoeve der Arbeidersklasse (association for the working class), founded in 1852 as the first housing association in the Netherlands, pressed for it to be filled in. That happened in 1857.

The association then rebuilt almost the whole block between the Willemsstraat, the Lijnbaansgracht, the Palmstraat and the Palmdwarsstraat, starting in 1860 at the corner here. Buying out the owners was slow, so it took until 1894, but the architect P.J. Hamer, and then his son W. Hamer, kept to the same plain brick throughout. Their last scheme, nos. 132–150 of 1899, dropped the back-to-back homes for flats with their own kitchen and bedroom. Other builders filled the gaps: Concordia in 1878, the company Oud Amsterdam in 1898 with flats so cramped they were criticised as substandard when new, and in 1926 the city health service, on the site of the Wijde Gang, an alley locals called the Rotten Alley. The blocks are rented homes.

Look for:
- the tiles naming the old alleys, by the houses between nos. 24 and 108
- the wrought-iron lantern over the former health service door at no. 24
- the arched gateway to the back homes at nos. 160–176
- at Palmstraat 87–97 (1867–72), a row set three metres back for light and air

title: Constantiahofje, free homes for loyal old workmen
summary: In 1863 the chairman of Amsterdam's first housing association built 36 homes round a green court, named after his wife. They were rent free, but only for workmen over sixty who had served one and the same master for at least twelve years.
body:
Old workmen who could no longer work fell outside the rules of the Vereeniging ten behoeve der Arbeidersklasse (association for the working class), which built homes for working families. So in 1863 its chairman, Josua van Eik, set up a separate foundation for them and named it after his wife, Constantia van Loon. P.J. Hamer designed 36 small homes round a square green court, with a pump and a bleaching field, and a tower over the back wing like an old hofje (almshouse round a courtyard). The homes were free of rent, for workmen over sixty who had worked at least twelve years for one and the same master in a trade.

Around 1870 the foundation added more homes next door, at nos. 143–147. After the Van Eiks died in 1878 it carried both their names. In 1921 the homes passed to the association; the old men still living there could stay rent free until they died. In the 1980s the one-room homes were merged into larger flats, and they are now ordinary social rented homes. The court lies behind the central gateway.

Look for:
- CONSTANTIA in the brickwork under the curved gable over the entrance
- the wings with blind windows set far apart, which make the front look closed
- next door, the cast-iron letters CONSTANTIA WONINGEN on nos. 143–147

title: Bewaarschool of Tot Heil des Volks, where a preacher came with peat and a Bible
summary: In 1849 a Mennonite preacher started Bible readings in a house on this stinking canal. His association Tot Heil des Volks built a school for toddlers here, and over a century and a half later it still feeds and showers homeless people in the same building.
body:
Jan de Liefde, a Mennonite preacher, moved to Amsterdam in 1849 and began his mission in the Jordaan, as the phrase goes, with a block of peat under one arm and a Bible under the other. His Bible readings in a house on the Goudsbloemgracht, now the Willemsstraat, soon drew hundreds. In 1855 he founded Tot Heil des Volks (for the salvation of the people), known locally as Het Heil.

Its bewaarschool (a day school for children of two to six, boys and girls apart) opened here in 1855. In 1909 the architect Adriaan Moen took in the houses on both sides and gave the whole a 22-metre front, keeping the old party walls in its rhythm. The two doors in the middle are dummies, put there for symmetry; the real doors are in the wings. Upstairs were two meeting halls, with homes for the head teacher and caretaker in the wings.

The association's schools had all closed by 1974. Today the building holds flats and De Tweede Mijl, a walk-in centre for homeless people at no. 39, open three days a week with meals, showers and clean clothes. It is not a place to visit; the front is the thing to see.

Look for:
- the yellow tile panels with the association's name in the wings and BEWAARSCHOOL under the middle window
- the peepholes behind iron grilles in the side doors

title: Pianola Museum in police station no. 21
summary: From 1905 to 1930 this was the Jordaan's police station, with four cells. Since 1994 it has been a museum of self-playing pianos, and the cells hold one of the world's largest collections of paper music rolls.
body:
The old police post by the Noorderkerk was too small for a market quarter, so in 1903 the city bought nos. 106–110, two of them with Anno 1663 stones, and pulled them down. Herman Misset painted them just in time. The city's public works office designed police station no. 21, which opened in 1905 and closed on 1 October 1930.

The upper floors were lived in, but the station itself stood empty for years. In the 1990s Kasper Janse needed a new home for his collection of pianolas, pianos that play themselves from punched paper rolls, built from about 1900 to 1935. After years of tugging with the city's land office, and squatters coming and going, the Pianola Museum opened on 30 October 1994. The four cells now hold part of more than 40,000 rolls. In 2018 the city planned to sell the building; after a campaign with tens of thousands of signatures a solution was found, but the museum still uses only part of the house and is petitioning for more.

It is open on Friday and Saturday afternoons and Sunday until 4, with a guided tour in which the instruments are played, and there are concerts most weeks, from classical to stride piano and tango.

Look for:
- the tiled panel over the door, where Politiebureau no. 21 once was
- the Jugendstil plant tiles in the oriel on the right

title: Westerstraat's 1930s rebuild, crooked houses out, old stones kept
summary: In the 1930s a family of Jordaan landlords and a few others replaced sagging old houses on the Westerstraat with sober new brick, renewal before the word existed. One had sunk into a parallelogram; its successors kept the old gable stones.
body:
By the early 1930s five houses on the north side of the Westerstraat were leaning ever further for want of foundations and upkeep. No. 184, one door and one window wide, had sunk into the shape of a parallelogram; under its stoop a passage, the Engelschmansteeg, led to homes behind. Between 1935 and 1939 they were replaced one by one. Jacob Dunnebier designed nos. 184–186 for a film hall, a consulting room, a shop and three flats; then came nos. 194–196 and no. 198, for members of the Reijnhoudt family, who owned several houses in the Jordaan and rebuilt a number of them in these years.

The style is the same everywhere: traditional shapes and red brick, with wide oriel windows that borrow from the Amsterdam School. The Reijnhoudts did the same further east: nos. 109 and 111–117 on the corner of the Eerste Anjeliersdwarsstraat, and no. 114 opposite, by A.J. Westerman. No. 109 has long been Café Nol, a home base of the Jordaan's own music. The buildings hold shops, a restaurant and flats.

Look for:
- in the oriel of no. 198, the stone ORANJE APPEL 1749 with an apple tree, brought from the old house
- on no. 184, a head in profile recorded here since 1740 as a Moor's head
- the former film-hall entrance with an old iron roller shutter at no. 184
- the blue glazed tiles of a De Gruyter grocery on the corner of no. 111

title: Burgerschool of 1867, the day school that flopped
summary: A national law of 1863 obliged every town of over 10,000 people to open a day and evening school for craftsmen. Amsterdam built this one, possibly its first school with classrooms off a corridor. The day school flopped; working families needed their children's wages.
body:
Thorbecke's secondary education act of 1863 required every town with more than 10,000 inhabitants to found a burgerdag- en avondschool, a two-year course of general education for future craftsmen: mathematics, physics, chemistry, mechanics, Dutch, history, geography and drawing. Amsterdam had its city architect Bastiaan de Greef design this one, finished in 1867. Its whole second floor was drawing rooms, because freehand, linear and model drawing each needed the furniture set up differently. As far as is known it was the first school building in Amsterdam with several classrooms off a corridor.

The day school did not work. Families had little use for general education when a child's earnings came first, and the evening classes drifted towards plain technical training. In 1883 the building became a trade school, probably gaining a storey; the newer brick shows where. By 2004 it stood empty, covered in graffiti and posters. In 2007 the designer Marcel Wanders and a property company bought it and turned it into offices and studios, among them Wanders's own, as the Westerhuis.

Look for:
- the line in the brickwork where the extra storey begins
- the two plain stucco panels under the second-floor windows, which on the drawings read Openbare Dag- and Dag- en Avondschool
- the curved pediment over the middle bay and the 1950s wing on the east side

title: Concordia on the Westerstraat, Peace be to this house
summary: Right after the Anjeliersgracht was filled in, a wealthy lawyer had 72 workers' homes built on its corner with the Lijnbaansgracht. A Bible text over the rounded corner wishes peace on the house; a lamp post in the courtyard quotes Proverbs.
body:
The Anjeliersgracht was filled in in 1861 because its water was so unhealthy, and became the Westerstraat. Straight after, the lawyer Henrick Samuel van Lennep, who wanted to do something about the dreadful housing and rack-renting in the Jordaan, had P.J. Hamer build 72 workers' homes on the corner of the Lijnbaansgracht. They were finished in 1862, partly back-to-back homes and partly two-room flats with windows front and back. In 1864 Van Lennep and the banker C.P. van Eeghen put their housing into the building company Concordia, which also owned two more courts nearby, Concordia Noord on this street and Concordia Zuid on the Elandsstraat.

The plain brick front turns the corner in a curve marked by blocked pilasters. A gateway on the Westerstraat leads to the courtyard, where the walls are fully plastered. The homes have been renovated several times and are rented out by the housing corporation Ymere.

Look for:
- over the corner door, the stone Vrede zij dezen Huize (Peace be to this house, Luke 10)
- the tile pictures in the passage to the courtyard, added in a renovation
- in the courtyard, a lamp post on a base reading De vreeze des Heeren is een springbron des levens (Proverbs 14:27)

title: Victoria Hotel and the two houses that would not sell
summary: The grand hotel opposite Centraal Station has two little old houses stuck in its side. Their owners asked too much, the builder ran out of time, and in 1890 the hotel simply went up around them.
body:
When the German architect J.F. Henkenhaf planned a modern hotel opposite the new Centraal Station, his company bought up five houses on the Damrak and three on the Prins Hendrikkade, among them a corner house of 1633 with a little tower. Two small houses on the Prins Hendrikkade could not be had: the price was too high. Time was running out, so Henkenhaf built around them. The Victoria Hotel opened on 19 August 1890, with electric light in every guest room, and the two old fronts are still wedged into its side wall today. Thomas Rosenboom turned the episode into his novel Publieke Werken (1999), filmed in 2015.

The hotel has a darker page too. At the end of the war an SS unit was quartered here, and on 7 May 1945 it opened fire on people in the street, at almost the same moment as the shooting on the Dam. A Dutch military policeman was killed. A plaque on the Prins Hendrikkade side remembers it.

It is still a hotel, part of the Park Plaza group since 1993.

Look for:
- the two small fronts tucked into the hotel on the Prins Hendrikkade side
- VICTORIA HOTEL VICTORIA painted in gold in the frieze of the corner tower
- the memorial plaque for 7 May 1945 on the Prins Hendrikkade front

title: De Utrecht, the insurance office with baboons on the roof
summary: An insurance company's office of 1905 on the Damrak that preaches its trade in stone: Vigilance, Thrift and the Wheel of Fortune with a bronze widow. Higher up, under the eaves, sit baboons.
body:
Around 1900 the Damrak changed from a street people lived on into a street of offices and shops, and the life insurer De Utrecht was one of the first to build big here. Alexander Kropholler and Jan Staal designed this office in 1904–1906, faced with polished Labrador granite below and green Swedish marble above (later painted over). At 35 metres it was taller than the rules then allowed; it got special permission.

The sculptor Joseph Mendes da Costa gave the front a sermon on insurance. Five figures at first-floor level stand for the things of life: Vigilance, the Fickleness of Time, Wisdom Restraining Evil, Thrift and Protecting Love. Over the left-hand door a Wheel of Fortune turns above a bronze widow, the person a life policy was meant to look after. The capitals are pairs of owls back to back, the brackets are stylised pelicans, and up under the gutter sit baboons and other animals. The shop on the corner was the household-goods firm Dake, whose name is still cut in the granite.

The building has apartments and shops now; it is seen from the street.

Look for:
- the bronze widow under the Wheel of Fortune over the left door
- DAKE carved over the corner entrance
- the owls on the capitals and the baboons under the eaves
- UTRECHT in the tile panel of the shop wing at Damrak 26

title: Damrak, the boulevard that never was
summary: After Centraal Station opened, shopkeepers and architects lobbied to turn the Damrak into a grand boulevard like those of Paris and Vienna. It never happened. What came instead was a jumble, and the jumble is full of jokes about fish, soap and Rembrandt.
body:
Once the station was built, entrepreneurs and architects pushed in the 1880s and 1890s to make the Damrak a boulevard on the model of Paris and Vienna, a grand way into the city. The plan never went through. Owners rebuilt one plot at a time, taller and showier than before, and the result is the mixed row you see now, with small old houses between offices and hotels.

Each newcomer advertised itself on its front. The widow A. van Laar's fish shop at no. 25 (A.L. van Gendt, 1888) carries heads in old fishing costume and, higher up, fish and crabs. The soap works De Vergulde Hand built a plain, almost industrial shop and office on the corner of the Haringpakkerssteeg in 1905. Café-restaurant Westrust at no. 60 (1889) has Rembrandt's self-portrait in its stained glass. At the Damraksteeg, H.P. Berlage built a bank office in 1901, and in 1908 Kropholler and Staal answered it at the Valkensteeg with a mirror image for a firm of stockbrokers. De Roode Leeuw (Foeke Kuipers, 1911) is still a hotel and restaurant.

All of it is seen from the pavement.

Look for:
- fisherfolk heads, fish and crabs on no. 25
- Rembrandt in the bay window glass of no. 60, first floor
- the Four Sons of Aymon on a stone of no. 47-48
- two angled mirrors by the first-floor balcony of no. 11, for daylight
- Berlage's corner (no. 95) and Kropholler's reply (no. 98), signed in a brick on the right wall

title: Cineac Damrak, the newsreel cinema
summary: In 1938 a cinema opened on the Damrak that showed only the news, round the clock, so you could pop in and out. Television killed the idea. The travertine front and the big neon arrow are still there, now pointing into a casino.
body:
The newsreel cinema was a 1930s idea, worked out in Paris around 1930 under the name Cineac (Ciné Actualités): a continuous programme of news films, a short visit, a quick flow of people in and out. Amsterdam got two. The first, by Jan Duiker on the Reguliersbreestraat, is the famous one. This second one, opened in 1938, was designed by the engineer H. van Vreeswijk, and he made it look grand rather than mechanical: a front of costly travertine that bulges forward, a canopy for the queue, and neon, red and white, with an arrow pointing in.

The format did not survive television. The Cineac Damrak switched to feature films in 1941, became a twin cinema in 1974 and closed in 1983. It is now an amusement arcade and casino. The neon lettering was changed to suit, but the signs still hang where the cinema put them.

You see it from the street.

Look for:
- the big neon arrow pointing into the building
- the travertine slabs, right down to the plinth
- the year and the architect's name on the right-hand pier

title: De Papegaai, the hidden church on the Kalverstraat
summary: Between the chain stores of the Kalverstraat a narrow passage leads into a church that began in 1672 as a hidden Catholic chapel in a house. It is open every day, and a sign invites shoppers in for a quarter of an hour.
body:
After 1578 Catholics in Amsterdam could only worship out of sight, in churches hidden inside ordinary houses. In 1672 the priest Willem Willemart started one in a house he rented on the Kalverstraat. The house had a compass on its front, after its owner Willem Compas, yet the hidden church became known as De Papegaai, the Parrot.

In 1846 the parish bought the property back from the Catholic poor relief fund, and in 1848–1849 Gerrit Moele built the present church: the first neo-Gothic church in Amsterdam, a hall church whose plaster vaults are pure decoration. It is the largest former hidden church in the city still in use. On its roof sits the little bell turret of the Heilige Stede, the medieval chapel of the Miracle of Amsterdam a few doors up the street, demolished in 1908. Since 2021 the church is officially dedicated to Saint Joseph again.

It is open Monday to Saturday 10.30 to 16.00 and Sunday 12.00 to 14.30, with a second entrance on the Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal. Masses are partly in Latin, and there are concerts in the series Muziek in de Papegaai.

Look for:
- the parrot mosaic
- the sign asking for "een kwartier voor God" (a quarter of an hour for God)
- the bell turret of the Heilige Stede on the roof

title: Nieuwezijds Kapel, the Holy Place inside a shopping block
summary: Pilgrims came to this spot for the Miracle of Amsterdam for five centuries. In 1908 the Protestant owners tore the medieval chapel down, despite Catholic protests, and hid a new church inside a block of shops. It has since been a mosque and the Amsterdam Dungeon.
body:
In 1345, Catholic tradition says, a consecrated host was found unharmed in a fire in a house on the Kalverstraat. A chapel, the Heilige Stede (Holy Place), went up on the spot in 1346–1347, and every year a procession and a market marked the miracle. After 1578 the city's new Protestant rulers took it, used it for a while as a stable and store, and renamed it the Nieuwezijds Kapel. Catholics revived the walk as a silent night procession, the Stille Omgang, in 1881.

In 1908 the Reformed congregation had the old chapel demolished, arguing that the valuable land was worth more sold. Catholics protested in vain. Christiaan Posthumus Meyjes built a smaller, octagonal church in its place, 1908–1912, and wrapped it in shops, among them the art dealer Van Wisselingh on the Rokin. Its walls are almost invisible from any street. Princess Beatrix made her confession of faith here on Palm Sunday 1956. The church left in 1970; a Turkish mosque followed (1972–1980), then a conference centre, and since 2005 the Amsterdam Dungeon.

The gates of the church are in the alleys; inside is the paid attraction.

Look for:
- the gatehouses with wrought-iron gates in the Enge and Wijde Kapelsteeg
- the old 16th-century gate of the Heilige Stede in the Kapelsteeg
- the corner turrets that frame the block on the Rokin and the Kalverstraat

title: Korenmetershuisje (the corn measurers' house)
summary: A small guild house of 1620 standing on its own in the middle of a square, where the men who measured out the city's grain met. Its predecessor on this spot may have saved Amsterdam for the Catholics in 1577: the rebels mistook it for the city hall.
body:
Grain was Amsterdam's mother trade, and before a load was sold on the corn exchange it had to be measured out in standard measures by sworn corn measurers and corn setters. The city decided in 1558 to give them a house on the Nieuwezijds Kolk; the present one was built in 1620. It is one of the few Amsterdam guild houses left, and one of the few buildings in the old centre that stands free on all sides. The guild met on the main floor, the porters worked in the basement, the bookkeepers in the attic.

On 23 November 1577 a force of about four hundred rebels tried to take Catholic Amsterdam. In Geert Mak's telling the raid failed because its leader took the corn measurers' house for the city hall.

In 1896 the architect H.G. Jansen restored the house to what he believed it had looked like in 1620, with cross windows, shutters and spired dormers. After the guild's successor was wound up in 1921, the house held the Press Museum (1924–1950) and the port association. The heritage society Heemschut has had its office here since 1967; Stadsherstel bought the building from the city in 2021.

It is an office; you see it from the square.

Look for:
- the measure, the barrel and the strickle carved over the main door
