- the stained glass with the tools of the two guilds in the upper lights
- the spired dormers of 1896

title: In de Wildeman, the liqueur distillery that became a beer café
summary: In 1908 a liqueur distiller built a shop on the Kolksteeg in 17th-century dress, the way old distilling firms liked to show off a long past. Since 1986 it has been one of the city's best-known beer cafés.
body:
The firm V.H. Levert & Co, liqueur distillery and wine merchant De Wildeman, had old houses on the corner of the Kolksteeg and the Nieuwezijds Kolk pulled down and in 1908 put up a distillery, shop and offices to a design by C.Th. Spaninga. He dressed it as a 17th-century building: step gable, wooden shopfront with small panes, bands of sandstone. Distillers liked that look; Bols had done the same on the Rozengracht in 1893. Such traditional firms wanted their buildings to point to their long history, and De Wildeman may have had the same in mind.

Two stones flank the shop: 1690 and 1908. The first may be the year the firm was founded. In the western part a red tile panel still advertises the distillery, and beside it sits an older gable stone, probably saved from one of the demolished houses: D'4 Gekroonde Evangelisten, four little men at a table under a crown.

The ground floor has been the beer café In de Wildeman since 1986, with a long list of draught and bottled beers.

Look for:
- "in de wildeman" on the wooden shop beam
- the stones with 1690 and 1908
- the red tiles reading LIKEURSTOKERIJ 'de WILDEMAN' vh LEVERT en Co
- the four crowned evangelists at their table

title: De Gouden en De Zilveren Spiegel, twin houses of 1614
summary: Two step-gabled houses on the Kattengat, built as a pair in 1614 and named the Golden and the Silver Mirror, with one date stone shared between them. Inside, a restaurant has taken the silver one's name.
body:
The Kattengat was once a narrow V-shaped canal between the Spuistraat and the Singel, filled in in the 19th century and widened by demolition in 1936. Its name is usually explained as a gap so tight not even a cat could get through. On it stands a pair: two houses of 1614, De Zilveren Spiegel (the Silver Mirror, no. 4) and De Gouden Spiegel (the Golden Mirror, no. 6). They are twins, with step gables in plain brick, and the stone with the year sits on the line between them.

Both are now the restaurant De Silveren Spiegel, which serves modern cooking built on Dutch produce in rooms with an open fire and old tiles. It is open in the evenings from Tuesday, with lunch on some days; check before you go.

Look for:
- the date stone on the dividing line between the two fronts
- the two plain stepped gables side by side
- the domed former Ronde Lutherse Kerk at the end of the street

title: The guardhouse at the Munttoren, where the coins were struck
summary: The Munttoren owes its name to the guardhouse at its foot, where Amsterdam struck its own coins in the disaster year 1672. The present guardhouse of 1887 was cut through in 1939 so that walkers could pass behind the tower, as Berlage had suggested half a century before.
body:
The Regulierspoort, built 1480–1487, had two towers and a guardhouse. After the gate burned in 1618, only the west tower was rebuilt, and Hendrick de Keyser gave it its lantern. In 1672, the year French troops overran much of the country, Amsterdam was allowed to mint its own money, and the coins were struck in the guardhouse beside the tower. Hence the Munt.

In 1885–1887 the old guardhouse made way for a neo-Renaissance one by Willem Springer. Berlage criticised the design and in 1886 published a lower alternative that would leave the tower more room. In the late 1930s the busy Vijzelstraat needed a wider bridge, and the city decided to send pedestrians from the Kalverstraat behind the tower. Springer's building, damaged by fire, was rebuilt in 1939 in a much plainer form, with a low new part and a passage through it, much as Berlage had proposed.

Below the guardhouse, reached by stairs along the Singel, was a public urinal that gay men used for decades as a meeting place; they nicknamed it "Delfts Blauw" after the souvenir shop above. The shop sells Delft Blue still.

Look for:
- the passage with its two small brick vaults
- Springer's sandstone doorway on the west end
- the stairs down to the water side, part of the 1915 bridge

title: Peek & Cloppenburg: from the Nieuwendijk to the Dam
summary: In 1885 the clothing chain was on the Nieuwendijk. In 1917 it moved into a limestone palace on the Dam, its fronts set with stones from the houses it replaced. After 110 years it leaves the Dam at the end of February 2027.
body:
In the 1880s the Nieuwendijk was where clothing stores grew into department stores. On the corner of the Dam, W. Langhout built a showy shop in 1886 for the clothier Kattenburg, possibly the first big clothing store in the city. Further up the street, Peek & Cloppenburg had a new front put on Nieuwendijk 168-170 in 1885, probably by Joseph Cuypers, then took over plot after plot on the corner of the Nieuwe Nieuwstraat in 1891, 1896 and 1900.

In 1914–1917 the firm made the jump to the Dam itself. A.J. Joling designed a store faced entirely in shell limestone, filling the block between the Dam, the Rokin and the Kalverstraat, with sculpture by Kees Smout. The gable stones on it recall the houses that were pulled down for it. Madame Tussauds has filled the upper floors since 1991.

In November 2026 the chain announced it will leave the Dam at the end of February 2027: few locals shopped there, a spokesman said, and the building no longer met technical standards. The store is to be split into two shops. The Cloppenburg family still owns it.

Look for:
- the gable stones on the Dam store
- the rams' heads over the two open corner galleries on the Dam side
- the carved swans under the corner bay of Nieuwendijk 164-170
- the cut corner entrance and big arched windows of Dam 4

title: De Bisschop, the corner that settled the Dam question
summary: For decades Amsterdam argued about what the Dam should look like. In 1933 a bank simply built on the key corner, and architects were furious. Over its door hangs a stone with Saint Nicholas, carved four centuries earlier.
body:
From the early 20th century the Dam question kept the city busy: how to fit traffic and new buildings around the square in one harmonious design. A prize-winning plan by Van der Mey (1908) and an approved Dam plan (1910) came to little, as the city sold plots one by one. In 1933 three buildings on the corner of the Dam and the Damrak were demolished, among them the café De Bisschop, and J. Gratama built a branch office for the Incassobank on the spot. That more or less closed the question.

The architects' society BNA protested to the council that the crucial corner was given away without a word about the square's final form. Critics also mocked the design as fake Renaissance: brick fronts hiding a steel frame, and one office dressed up as two unequal old houses with tiled roofs and gables. Gratama said it gave the corner the picturesque look of historic Amsterdam. He later turned into a nationalist who wanted architecture to express the national past.

It is seen from the Dam.

Look for:
- the 16th-century stone with Saint Nicholas over the door to the upper offices on the Dam side
- a stone with a hand grabbing a rooster on the lower part along the Damrak
- the two "houses" that are really one building

title: Look up in the Kalverstraat
summary: Amsterdam's busiest shopping street has lost almost all its old shopfronts. Look one floor up and the shops of 1890 are still talking: painted children playing with fish for a fish restaurant, elephants for a jeweller, a chamois for a Mr Gems.
body:
The Kalverstraat has been a shopping street for centuries, and its ground floors have been rebuilt in wave after wave, most thoroughly in the late 20th century when nearly every shop got an open walk-in front. Above the plate glass, the 19th-century owners' advertising survives.

At no. 3-5 the fish restaurant of J.C. van Laar opened in 1889, designed by Schill and Haverkamp. Over the first-floor windows are lava panels, fired by F. Gillet in Paris and painted by Ernst Witkamp and Nicolaas van der Waay, with children playing with sea creatures. The restaurant lasted about ten years. During a refit in 2024, paintings hidden for decades behind panelling came to light inside, and were covered up again. Next door, the jeweller Citroen had H.Th. Wijdeveld build no. 1 in 1915–1917, with a frieze of crowns, festoons and elephants.

Walking south: at no. 28 heads carved by Lambertus Zijl, who later worked on Berlage's Beurs; at no. 37 and no. 73 two of the very few old shopfronts left in the street (1909 and 1886); at no. 174 a little seated dragon on the gable top; at no. 182 a chamois, in Dutch a gems, over the name D. GEMS.

Look for:
- the painted panels over the windows of no. 3-5
- the elephants in the corners of the frieze of no. 1
- the chamois and D. GEMS on no. 182
- the dragon on top of no. 174

title: Henri Julien, the watchmaker's house on the Rokin
summary: A tall, narrow shop of 1905 built for a watch wholesaler, and every ornament is about time: Christiaan Huygens, inventor of the pendulum clock, in profile, the sun and the moon, a tile panel with swinging pendulums. Even the gable is a bell gable.
body:
In 1905 the watchmaker and wholesaler Henri Julien, in business since 1843, had the brothers Van Gendt build him a shop with a house above on the corner of the Rokin and the Gapersteeg. It is five storeys high but only two windows wide, and the architects ran the shopfront up over two floors to make the proportions work.

The front tells you what was sold. Between the third-floor windows is a relief portrait of Christiaan Huygens, who invented the pendulum clock. Higher up are the sun and the moon, as on clock dials. In the alley, a Jugendstil tile panel advertises Henri Julien Horlogerie en Gros, founded 1843, with two pendulums. Merchants' houses with a picture programme were common enough then; the city register knows of no other one about watches. The bell-shaped gable, a klokgevel (klok also means clock), may well be part of the joke. Even the almost invisible back wall has one.

The ground floor is a shop; the rest is seen from the street and the Gapersteeg.

Look for:
- Huygens in profile between the third-floor windows
- the sun and the moon above the fourth-floor window
- the tile panel with the pendulums in the Gapersteeg
- the years 1843 and 1905 in cartouches on the corner piers

title: NACO-huisje and the boat offices of the IJ jetties
summary: A wooden ticket office of 1919 whose roof leans forward like a house on Sumatra. It sold passages to Zuiderzee towns, was floated off to Zaandam in 2004 to make way for a bus station, and came back seventeen years later.
body:
From the 1880s some fifteen jetties stuck out into the IJ behind Centraal Station, and dozens of boat services left from them every day with passengers and freight. On jetty 7, in 1919, the shipping agency J.G. Koppe had Guillaume la Croix build a light wooden office. He mixed the Amsterdam School with the houses of the Minangkabau on Sumatra: the roof leans forward at the land end, with a flagpole slanting out of the gable. Tickets were sold here for boats to Zuiderzee ports such as Lemmer. From the mid-1960s the shipping department of the coach company NACO used it, hence the name.

In 2004 the new bus station needed the space. The listed building could not be demolished, so it was lifted onto a pontoon and towed to Zaandam, where it stood far longer than planned. Stadsherstel bought it, raised money from its friends and restored it, and on 13 December 2021 it came back by water to a new spot about 150 metres east, beside the ferry to the Meeuwenlaan. Stadsherstel lets it to the Scheepvaartmuseum, the Plantage museums and Stromma, who mean to use it as a boarding point.

Farther west, at the end of jetty 10, J. de Meijer built a white concrete office in 1932–1933 for a freight service to West Friesland, with a rounded glass end facing the water. It is now a pancake house you can go into.

Look for:
- the forward-leaning gable and the slanting flagpole
- the saw-tooth trim on the corners

title: Molsteeg 4, the first stone laid by an eleven-year-old
summary: A small shop front of 1886 in an alley off the Spuistraat, with two caryatids holding up its cornice and, low in the plinth, a line telling you that the first stone was laid by a boy of eleven.
body:
In 1886 the owners of this house in the Molsteeg, the Schogt family, had the architect W. Hamer give it a new front in a busy eclectic style: a neck gable with scrolls, stone frames round the windows, bands studded with diamond-cut blocks. The shop entrance is the showpiece, with Corinthian colonnettes either side of the door and two caryatids beside the transom that seem to carry the cornice above the shopfront. Doors and windows are still the originals.

The best detail is at knee height. In the plinth to the right a line records that the first stone was laid on 25 May 1886 by a member of the family who was eleven years old. Such stones usually name an alderman or the owner; here a child got the honour, and the date, the boy's name and his age are cut for everyone to read.

It is still a shop with a house above, seen from the alley.

Look for:
- the first-stone inscription in the plinth on the right
- the two caryatids by the shop door
- the neck gable with scrolls and the curved pediment on the dormer

title: Rasphuispoort, the gate of the house of correction
summary: Over a side entrance to a shopping centre on the Heiligeweg, a woman with a whip looks down on two chained men, and wild beasts haul a cart of wood. This was the gate of the Rasphuis, where young offenders rasped Brazilian wood into dye.
body:
Above a shop entrance on the Heiligeweg sits a sculpture that leaves no doubt about what once lay behind it. A seated woman holds the city arms on her knee and a whip in her hand; the word CASTIGATIO (punishment) names her. Two naked men kneel beside her in chains. In the relief over the arch, lions, bears, wild boar and tigers pull a cart of logs while a driver whips them on. The Latin line says it is a virtue to tame what everyone fears.

This was the gate of the Rasphuis, the house of correction the city opened in 1596 in a former convent of the Poor Clares. The idea was new: young male offenders were not only to be punished but set right by work. Their work was rasping brazilwood into powder for textile dye, a trade the house long held as a monopoly in Holland. Within years the inmates had become cheap labour. Families could pay to have unruly relatives locked up, and visitors paid to look around.

The gate dates from about 1603 and is attributed to Hendrick de Keyser; the figures on top were added later in the century. The Rasphuis was pulled down in 1892 for a swimming bath. The gate stayed.

Look for:
- Castigatio with her whip and the two chained men on top
- the animals pulling the cart of wood over the arch
- the motto VIRTUTIS EST DOMARE QUAE CUNCTI PAVENT

title: Maagdenhuis, the girls' orphanage the students occupied
summary: For almost 170 years Catholic orphan girls lived behind this sober front on the Spui. Since 1962 it has housed the university's board, which is why students have occupied it again and again, first in May 1969 and for six weeks in 2015.
body:
The Maagdenhuis (maidens' house) was built in 1783–1787 by city architect Abraham van der Hart as an orphanage for Catholic girls of about eight to fourteen. The care had begun in 1570 with two Amsterdam women taking in a few orphan girls, and from 1628 the home stood on this spot. It was paid for by Catholic citizens, not the city, at a time when Catholics still worshipped in hidden churches. In its first decades nearly four hundred children lived here, with a bakery and a sewing room where the girls were trained.

The orphanage closed in 1953. A bank moved in and built vaults in the courtyard, and in 1962 the university bought the building for its administration. That made it a target. In May 1969 students held it for five days, demanding a say in how the university was run. Occupations followed in 1978, 1980, 1986, 1990, 1993, 1996 and 2005. In 2015 some 300 students took it on 25 February and held it until riot police cleared it on 11 April.

It is still the university's administrative centre; the outside is seen from the Spui.

Look for:
- the pediment with two orphan girls around a medallion of Christ blessing the children
- the anchor, heart and cross for hope, love and faith
- the name MAAGDENHUIS on the edge of the front steps

title: Oude Lutherse Kerk, the church behind the warehouse name
summary: Amsterdam's Lutherans first met in a warehouse called De Vergulden Pot. In 1633 they built a church on its spot at the corner of the Spui, and since 1961 the university has used it as its hall for ceremonies.
body:
From 1600 the Lutherans of Amsterdam, many of them immigrants, held their services in a warehouse on this corner called De Vergulden Pot (the gilded pot). They bought the houses around it one by one, and in 1631 the city allowed them to replace the seven buildings with a real church. It opened in 1633. Because the plot was made of so many old ones, the church stands on a crooked ground plan; inside, the rectangle is ringed by galleries on columns, and the pulpit dates from 1640.

In 1790 the Maatschappij tot Nut van 't Algemeen, the society for the public good, held its first general meeting here. Within forty years of opening the church was too small, and the Lutherans built a second one on the Singel, the domed Ronde Lutherse Kerk.

Since 1961 the church council has let the building to the University of Amsterdam, which uses it as its aula, the hall for doctoral ceremonies and other occasions. It is still used for services too. From the Singel and the Spui you see the forecourt with its fence and the plain brick church behind.

Look for:
- the forecourt and railings on the Singel side
- the two raised side parts on the Spuistraat side
- the crooked line of the walls, following the old plots

title: Militiegebouw, the city arsenal where Euwe played for the world title
summary: Built in 1606 to store the city's cannon, this building on the Singel later housed girls winding silk, French conscription boards and, in 1935, games of the world chess championship that Max Euwe won.
body:
In 1606 the city finished a new bushuis (gun house) on the Singel to store its weapons and ammunition, replacing an older one on the Kloveniersburgwal that the East India Company had taken over. The two tall doors in the front were made to roll the heavy guns in and out; muskets, swords and other light arms went on the upper floors. A date stone records the year. The front, with its scrolls and decorated window arches, may be by Hendrick de Keyser.

From 1682 the upper floors held the Zijdewindhuis, a workhouse where girls wound raw silk into skeins, while the ground floor kept its guns until 1787 and then became a stable. Under French rule from 1810 the first floor became the Militiezaal (militia hall), where young men were examined for conscription, and it kept that role for Dutch military service afterwards. The hall also served for auctions and exhibitions, as the city council chamber in 1926–1928, and in 1935 for some of the games between Max Euwe and Alexander Alekhine, the match that made Euwe world chess champion.

Since 1972 the building has been part of the University Library; you see it from the Singel.

Look for:
- the two tall doors made for the cannon
- the date stone of 1606
- the scrolls on the cut-off top of the front

title: Ronde Lutherse Kerk, the dome that was not allowed to be a tower
summary: The Lutherans were not allowed a church tower, so in 1671 they built a dome instead. It burned out in 1822 and again in 1993, lost its congregation in 1935 and is now a hotel's event hall, reached by a tunnel under the street.
body:
By the 1660s the Lutheran church on the Spui was too small for the many Lutheran immigrants in the city, and in 1668–1671 Adriaan Dortsman built a second one on the Singel. Lutherans were forbidden to build a church tower, so they built a round church with a copper dome. On the small lantern on top they put their emblem, the Lutheran swan.

On 18 September 1822 a fire left only the walls standing. The church was rebuilt in 1823–1826 much as before, but with a higher dome, and got a new organ by Johan Bätz. The Lutherans left in 1935. The church was used for concerts and for a while held a tent and sail maker's business.

In 1975 the hotel opposite took it over and dug a tunnel under the street so guests could walk to it. On 3 February 1993 the dome caught fire again and the interior was lost; after sixteen months of work it reopened in June 1994, with a roof that was copper-coloured instead of green. The Renaissance hotel runs it as the Koepelkerk (dome church), a hall for meetings, weddings, galas and concerts, so the only way in is a booked event or a ticket.

Look for:
- the swan on the lantern at the top of the dome
- the lower side aisle built against the back half of the round
- the dome seen from the Kattengat and the Singel bridge

title: Passage Central, the shopping arcade that blew shut
summary: Built for the visitors of the 1883 colonial exhibition, this covered arcade between the Nieuwendijk and the Prins Hendrikkade was too draughty and lasted barely four years. A century later an Albert Heijn heir sank his inheritance into a New Age centre here.
body:
The International Colonial and Export Exhibition of 1883 was expected to bring wealthy visitors, and the Brix brothers' company had four plots between the Nieuwendijk and the Prins Hendrikkade cleared for a covered shopping arcade. Y.G. Bijvoets designed Passage Central in 1882–1883: some twenty shops along an inner street under a roof of glass and iron, with a hotel above on the waterfront side and flats above on the Nieuwendijk side.

The passage door on the Prins Hendrikkade was closed soon after opening because of the wind. In 1886–1887 A.L. van Gendt rebuilt the inside, the passage disappeared and the central entrances were walled up; from 1896 it was an office building. On top of the front stand zinc figures of Mercury, god of trade, between the Amstel and the IJ, which gave the building its later name, Gebouw Mercurius.

In 1992 Ronald Jan Heijn, a great-grandson of the founder of Albert Heijn, bought it to open Oibibio, a spiritual centre, in 1994, paid largely from his inheritance. It went under and left in 2001. Since 2009 an Albert Heijn supermarket has filled the ground floor, so the founder's name came back after all.

Look for:
- Mercury with the river gods of the Amstel and the IJ on top of the waterfront front
- the slightly projecting middle bay that marks the old arcade entrance on both fronts
- the word MERCURIUS in metal letters

title: Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal 282, where Tina Strobos hid more than a hundred people
summary: A burgomasters' house of about 1725 that became a girls' school, a hiding place, a cabaret and a theatre. In the war Tina Strobos and her mother sheltered more than a hundred people here, never more than five at a time; eight searches found no one.
body:
Two older houses were joined under one cornice around 1725, and members of the Bicker family, burgomaster Hendrick Bicker among them, lived here until 1835. From about 1910 to 1957 it housed the Prinsenschool, a well-known primary school.

During the German occupation Tina Strobos and her mother Marie Schotte lived here and turned their big house into a hiding place. There were never more than five people hidden at once, but over the war more than a hundred passed through: Jews, resistance workers and political refugees, among them the socialist Henri Polak, the resistance fighter Johan Brouwer and the painter Martin Monnickendam. The house was searched eight times and no one was ever found. Tina, a medical student, also forged ration cards and identity papers, carried weapons and radios as a courier, and hid stolen weapons in the house.

After the war the stage took over: the cabaret Tingel Tangel of Sieto Hoving, then from 1989 the Betty Asfalt Complex of Paul Haenen and Dammie van Geest. Stadsherstel bought the house from the city in 2019 and, while restoring the foundations, found an 18th-century rainwater cellar. Today it is Theater De Richel (formerly the Betty Asfalt Complex), so the way in is a ticket to a show.

Look for:
- the narrow left-hand house still readable in the wide front
- the carved doorcase and the stoop with fourteen bottle balusters
- the stamp garden in front, once the Postzegelmarkt

title: Politieposthuisje, the police post that became a public toilet and a café
summary: A wooden chalet of 1896 on its own little island in the Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal. It was a police post, a public toilet for almost seventy years and now a café, standing in the garden where stamp dealers traded for nearly a century.
body:
When the canal was filled in around 1884, the new street left a little triangle of land here. In 1896 the city's Public Works department put police post no. 7 on it: a cross-shaped wooden building on a brick base, with deep overhanging roofs and carved boards in the gables, in a chalet style. Four were built that year, here, on the Nieuwmarkt, in the Plantage and in the Czaar Peterstraat. The spot was not ideal: in 1897 it was noted that the officers were getting on too well with the brothel Maison Weinthal across the street, which closed in 1902.

From 1915 to 1984 the post served as a public toilet for men and women. Similar police houses disappeared from the streets; this one stayed and was listed for its rarity. It has been a café since, now Het Stadspaleis.

For almost a century stamp collectors met in front of it on Wednesdays and Saturdays, at the Postzegelmarkt. When the street was redone in 2022 the square became a small park with a fountain, and two statues went up: Argus, the newspaper reporter from the Tom Poes comics, for the street's newspaper past, and a gnome recalling the Kabouter movement of fifty years earlier.

Look for:
- the carved boards under the eaves on the west and east sides
- the open round and cross-shaped braces under the overhangs
- Argus and the gnome in the garden

title: Die Port van Cleve, Heineken's first beer house
summary: On the spot where a widow set up the Hooiberg brewery in 1592, Gerard Heineken had a beer house opened in 1870 that poured only his beer. Its restaurant began numbering its steaks in 1874, and a 26-metre parade of Delft tiles still runs through the bar.
body:
In 1592 the widow Weyntgen Elberts moved her late husband's brewery De Hooiberg (the haystack) here, because goods could come in by water. In 1863 Gerard Adriaan Heineken bought it. When the city decided to fill in the canal, he moved his brewing to the Stadhouderskade and had the old beer stores on the Nieuwezijds converted into a beer house. During the works the Hulscher brothers, who ran it, found a stone inscribed Die Port van Cleve (the gate of Kleve), and that became the name. It opened on 5 September 1870, serving only Heineken.

In 1874 a restaurant was added, De Poort, known for its numbered steaks. Waiters shouted the orders, and a man at the buffet, the echo, shouted them on to the kitchen word for word. In 1888 Isaac Gosschalk gave the building its present front, a free mix of Gothic and Renaissance. That July the bodega De Blauwe Parade opened, lined with a Delft blue tile panel of about 26 metres made by De Porceleyne Fles: a parade of children in honour of Emperor Maximilian.

It is still a hotel, with the restaurant and bar open to passers-by.

Look for:
- the lobed window arches and the central gable on the main front
- the bay window and Baroque bell gable on the left-hand extension
- the tile parade inside De Blauwe Parade
- at the back, Spuistraat 129, a step-gabled pair dated 1662

title: Makelaers Comptoir, the brokers' guild house
summary: One of the few guild houses left in Amsterdam, built in 1633–1634 for the city's sworn brokers. What was said inside stayed sub rosa, and a gilded rose still hangs from a ceiling beam. The guild sold it in 2002 for one euro.
body:
The brokers' guild was founded in 1612. Its members, appointed by the burgomasters, acted as middlemen in the trade of coffee, tobacco, grain and the other goods that reached Amsterdam from all over the world, and secrecy was the heart of the job: what was said in the guild house stayed sub rosa, under the rose. The first pile for this house went in on 5 March 1633 and it was finished on 1 November 1634, in the red brick and stone bands of the Dutch Renaissance.

In 1836 the stepped gable was swapped for a bell gable and the brick was oiled dark brown. Architect Jan de Meyer put the old look back in 1937, but changed the motto over the door: Soli Deo Gloria (to God alone the glory) made way for Vrijheid is voor geen geld te koop (freedom cannot be bought for money).

Because the guild never sold it, the inside survived: the front hall with its black and white marble floor, a mantelpiece of 1760 with a painting of the Exchange by Philips Vingboons, and a gilded rose carved in a beam. In 2002 the guild sold the house for a symbolic euro to the Vereniging Hendrick de Keyser, which restored it. It is let for small meetings and dinners; otherwise you see it from the street.

Look for:
- the doorway with Ionic half-columns and the cartouche dated 1633
- the motto over the door
- the scrolls and vases on the stepped gable

title: 't Kasteel van Aemstel, the newspaper's castle that became INK Hotel
summary: In 1904 the daily De Tijd built its printing works and newsroom here and named it after the castle of Gijsbrecht van Aemstel, said to have stood nearby. It wraps around the old brokers' guild house. Since the 1980s it is a hotel, now called INK.
body:
In 1904 P.J.F. Vermeulen of the daily De Tijd had six old houses on the Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal and the Nieuwe Nieuwstraat pulled down. A.J. Joling designed a building in a sober Art Nouveau for the presses, the typesetters, the newsroom and the offices, plus a separate printing shop for outside work. The floors are reinforced concrete on the Monier system, strong enough to carry the machines. The new building wraps around the Makelaers Comptoir of 1633 on the corner, which stayed.

The name refers to a castle of Gijsbrecht van Aemstel, the medieval lord of Amstel, which tradition places near the Dirk van Hasseltssteeg a few doors away. Theo Molkenboer designed the tile panels. His first idea, Chronos as an old man with great wings, was soon dropped for a panel with the name of the building guarded by the river gods of the Amstel and the IJ.

After the paper left, the complex, together with the early 19th-century house next door at no. 67, became a hotel in the 1980s; the entrance moved into no. 67. The paper held its last reception here in 1990. After several names the hotel is now INK, after the printer's ink.

Look for:
- the tile panel with the name high in the gable
- Ao Di 1904 cut in stone beside it
- A.J. JOLING ARCHITEKT between the basement windows
- the loggia with its open stone parapet on the second floor

title: The newspaper street, from Handelsblad to De Standaard
summary: For most of the 20th century the Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal was Amsterdam's Fleet Street. Three buildings still wear their papers' names: the Handelsblad with a gilded dawn and two cockerels, De Standaard of Abraham Kuyper, and Concordia, a club house turned printing works.
body:
Printers worked here from the 17th century; in the 19th the newspapers followed. In 1902–1903 the Algemeen Handelsblad, published since 1831 from across the street, built new offices and a printing works to a design by Eduard Cuypers, faced in French Pouillenay limestone. High on the narrow right bay a gilded rising sun between two cockerels probably refers to the morning edition the paper had added to its evening one.

De Standaard took over no. 56 in 1917. The building had gone up in 1912–1913 for the Elberfelder trading company, which the embargoes of the First World War ruined. De Standaard was the paper of the Anti-Revolutionaries, led by Abraham Kuyper from 1872 until his death in 1920. After the liberation it never returned as a daily, and the resistance paper Trouw moved in.

Concordia, at the tip of the block by the Sint Luciënsteeg, was built in 1859 as a gentlemen's club and hosted the first international chess tournament in 1899. That year the Nieuwsblad voor Nederland bought it and kept only the shell; De Telegraaf's newsroom followed in 1913, de Volkskrant in 1948–1965.

Between 1967 and 1976 the papers moved out to the Wibautstraat, the Basisweg and Rotterdam. A statue of Argus, the comic-strip reporter, in the stamp garden recalls them.

Look for:
- the gilded dawn with two cockerels and ALGEMEEN HANDELSBLAD (nos. 232-240)
- DE STANDAARD and four nude figures high on no. 56
- the white marble arched doorway of Concordia (nos. 327-333)

title: Hajenius, the cigar shop with its 1915 interior
summary: The cigar seller Hajenius started in 1826 in a hotel on the Dam called De Rijnstroom. In 1915 the firm moved into this stone shop on the Rokin, put the old hotel's name on the front, and kept the marble, mahogany and Delft tobacco jars to this day.
body:
Pantaleon Hajenius opened a cigar shop in 1826 in the hotel De Rijnstroom, on the corner of the Warmoesstraat and the Dam. The firm became a purveyor to the court in 1851, and from 1856 members of the Nyman family were partners. In 1914–1915 A.J.N. Nyman had three houses on the Rokin pulled down and the brothers Van Gendt built a shop with a warehouse, offices and a caretaker's flat, faced in Obernkirchen sandstone in the restrained Um 1800 style. The name De Rijnstroom on the front recalls the long-demolished hotel where it all began.

Inside, much of the shop is as it was: walls and counters clad in several kinds of marble, mahogany cabinets with bronze fittings, a ceiling painted gold and bronze with two brass chandeliers, specks of mother-of-pearl in the panelling and Delftware tobacco jars painted with Chinese scenes. The room once used for tasting cigars is now the humidor.

Hajenius has been owned by the Scandinavian Tobacco Group since 2010, and the shop on the Rokin is still open, Monday from noon and Tuesday to Sunday through the day.

Look for:
- DE RIJNSTROOM on the front
- the gable top shaped like a trefoil, with a round window and a hoisting bracket
- the carved oak door in the right-hand bay

title: Arti et Amicitiae, the artists' club on the corner of the Spui
summary: Since 1840 Amsterdam's artists have had their own club and exhibition rooms here, from Breitner and the Maris brothers to today. In 1941 it expelled its fifteen Jewish members on German orders, and in 2022 it apologised.
body:
The society Arti et Amicitiae (for art and friendship) was founded in 1839 by artists and art lovers. In 1840 it bought the Grand Salon Duport on the Rokin, and around 1854 added the inn Het Wapen van Utrecht on the corner of the Spui, then still water. In 1856 J.H. Leliman pulled the houses together behind one richly decorated plaster front. Behind it are exhibition halls, board rooms and a private members' club, with much of the interior by Berlage; a board in the stairwell lists members such as Breitner, Israëls, Mesdag, Toorop, Lizzy Ansingh and Jan Sluijters.

In 1941 Arti joined the Kultuurkamer, the Nazi-controlled chamber for the arts, and on the occupier's orders expelled fifteen Jewish members. Only three of them survived the war; most were murdered in the camps. In September 2022 an exhibition looked at those choices, and the chairman apologised on behalf of the society.

Arti has shown work by Van Gogh and Chagall, displayed the wreck of Rob Scholte's car after the bomb attack on the artist, and from 1974 to 1997 the VPRO radio programme Welingelichte Kringen was broadcast from the club. The exhibition halls are open to everyone, Tuesday to Sunday from 12.00 to 17.00.

Look for:
- the plaster front that ties the old houses together on the Rokin
- the name ARTI ET AMICITIAE on the front
- the former lifesaving society's house next door at no. 114, now part of Arti

title: Athenaeum, the bookshop in the iron-fronted corner of the Spui
summary: In 1966 two publishers opened a bookshop in a former art dealer's shop of 1904 on the corner of the Spui. Its cast-iron front stayed; inside they built a maze of narrow passages and wooden stairs that is still selling books and newspapers.
body:
In 1904 the contractor-architect L.G. Mohrmann built this corner house with a shop for an art dealer on the ground floor, offices above and a flat on the second floor. Its most striking part is the shop front: cast iron, made by the Amsterdam firm T. Rincker, with the flowing lines of Art Nouveau and big curved windows.

In 1966 the Athenaeum bookshop opened here, co-founded by the publisher Rob van Gennep. The Spui was then, in Van Gennep's words, a miserable square full of cars. The architects Wiek Röling and Patrice Girod rebuilt the inside into a labyrinth of narrow passages and wooden staircases leading to small cellar rooms and attics, once compared to a drawing by Escher. A place in its shop window came to matter to Dutch writers, and the shop, with its news centre for papers and magazines, made the Spui a bookish meeting point.

Athenaeum Boekhandel and its Nieuwscentrum are still here at Spui 14-16; you can walk in and wander the little rooms.

Look for:
- the cast-iron shop front with its curved lines
- the window displays on the Spui
- the narrow side front on the Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal

title: Het Leesmuseum, the reading club that would not have Aletta Jacobs
summary: From 1800 to 1930 Amsterdam gentlemen read the world's newspapers in the Leesmuseum on the Rokin. When the physician Aletta Jacobs applied to join around 1880, the members panicked. The 1904 building later became an art auction house.
body:
The Leesmuseum (reading museum) was founded in 1800 to make foreign and Dutch journals available to many readers at once. It was a success, with 210 members by 1805, and from 1820 it had its own building on this spot on the Rokin. Like most reading societies, it was for men. When Aletta Jacobs, who had been a member of the reading society in Groningen, wanted to join around 1880, she was told no woman had ever thought of it, that she would probably be blackballed, and that if she were not, many men would resign to avoid trouble at home, since their wives would read something else into their visits.

In 1902–1904 C.B. Posthumus Meyjes built the present club house in a Berlage-like Art Nouveau, with a lofty reading room on the first floor, club chairs and electric light, and a smaller room for ladies and non-smokers. The society closed in 1930. In 1933 the auctioneer S.J. Mak van Waay held his first sale in the old reading room; Sotheby's took over the firm in 1974 and stayed until 1998.

It is seen from the street.

Look for:
- the stone Gebouw Leesmuseum between the balcony brackets
- the long wrought-iron balcony across the front
- the corner entrance of 1938 on the Watersteeg side

title: The six lanterns of the Royal Palace, lit for a king who never saw them
address: Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal, behind the Royal Palace (two) and Dam (four)
summary: King Willem I wanted his palace on the Dam lit by gas at night. The six cast-iron lanterns, with winged lions at their feet and a crown on top, went up in 1844, a year after he died. Most people walk right past them.
body:
Willem I wanted the front and back of his palace on the Dam lit by gas at night, and asked M.G. Tétar van Elven, who headed the architecture department of the Royal Academy, for a design. Tétar van Elven drew a three-sided base with curved sides, plant ornament and winged lions, rising into a six-sided lantern under an openwork crown. The machine works Dixon & Co cast them at their factory De Atlas on the Zoutkeetsgracht.

The king did not see them: he died in 1843, and the lanterns were placed in May 1844 under his son Willem II. Four stand on the Dam side of the palace and two at the back on the Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal, where hardly anyone looks. They were listed in 2001, as a set, for their design and for the way they belong to the palace.

You see them from the street; the two at the back are the easiest to study up close.

Look for:
- the three winged lions on each base
- the cartouches naming the designer, the foundry and the year of casting
- the crown on top of each lantern

title: Candida, the office tower that was the last straw
summary: In 1931–1932 a ten-storey office block of steel windows and concrete rose among the old fronts of the Nieuwezijds. The outcry was so loud that, a few years later, a new building down the street was dressed up as a canal house.
body:
In the early 20th century the Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal became the office street of Amsterdam. New buildings ran through the shallow blocks from the Nieuwezijds to the Spuistraat and grew ever bigger, though architects still masked the scale with brick and stone, as at the Neptunus building of 1915 next door. Candida ended that. F.A. Warners designed it in 1931–1932 for a company that built flats: ten storeys of brick hung in a concrete frame, with steel window bands across the whole front and a three-sided steel bay holding the lift. At the back, on the Spuistraat, round balconies stick out on every floor.

The criticism was loud, from the public and from the architects' association, which attacked it in its weekly in 1932. The city register calls it the drop that made the bucket overflow. After it, the climate turned cautious. When Anton Hamaker built a shop and offices for the NV Centrale Warenmagazijnen at no. 314 in 1935–1940, he deliberately did not follow the modern buildings next door but gave it the shape of an Amsterdam canal house, though in modern materials.

All three are seen from the street.

Look for:
- the glass column of bays over the canopy at Candida's entrance
- the round balconies on the Spuistraat side
- the canal house front of no. 314, further south

title: Think before you act: the tile sermon at Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal 112-114
summary: Over the two doors of a rose-glazed Jugendstil shop house of 1908, tile panels deliver a little sermon: DENKT ALEER GIJ DOENDE ZIJT, EN DOENDE DENKT DAN NOG (think before you act, and while acting, think some more).
body:
In 1908 one B. van der Pol had this shop with flats above built to a design by Th. Diks Rzn., an architect of whom nothing else is known. It is a full-blooded piece of Jugendstil: a front of pink glazed brick, a curved bay, granite lintels and leaded glass with waving lines.

The surprise is over the doors. In the arched fields above the two entrances, colourful tile panels with stylised flowers carry a two-part motto: DENKT ALEER GIJ DOENDE ZIJT over one door and EN DOENDE DENKT DAN NOG over the other, roughly "think before you act, and while acting, think some more". A signature on one of the panels shows they came from the Utrecht pottery Holland (1893–1917), which from 1906 made mainly tiles; the flowers are in the manner of the Amsterdam designer Jac. van den Bosch. Why a shop would preach at its customers is not known; the city register suggests it may have had to do with the first shop here.

There is still a shop downstairs and flats above; the panels are seen from the street.

Look for:
- the two tile mottos over the doors
- the pottery's signature on one of the panels
- the leaded glass in the transoms

title: Noord-Zuid-Hollands Koffiehuis, the tram station taken apart for the metro
summary: The wooden coffee house in front of Centraal Station was a tram station: boats left here for the steam tram to Purmerend and Volendam. In 1972 it was taken apart for the metro, its numbered parts stored, and in 1980 it was put back up.
body:
The little wooden building with towers in front of Centraal Station was built in 1911 as a station for the Noord-Hollandsche tram company, whose steam trams ran from Amsterdam-Noord to Purmerend and Volendam. The journey officially began here: a boat took passengers across the IJ to the tram. Architect J.H.W. Leliman was asked to echo the old buildings of Waterland; he drew on the North Holland farmhouse and on a painting of the Paalhuis, a toll house that once stood on the Nieuwe Brug. The city also demanded that it not block the view of the station. Mayor Röell opened it on 29 April 1912. In 1932 the NZH took over the line, and the building got its present name.

When the metro was dug in 1972, the koffiehuis was dismantled and its numbered parts stored in a warehouse. It was rebuilt in 1980, at a slightly different spot, partly on top of the metro station box. Smits ran the café from 1919 to 2014; since 2016 it has been a Loetje restaurant, open daily.

Look for:
- the gallery of columns on the water side
- the NZH name on the front
- the later towers, added in the same style for the transport and tourist offices

title: Pakketpostgebouw, the parcel machine beside Centraal Station
summary: The plain brick block east of the station entrance was the city's parcel post office, built in 1924–1925 by Jos Cuypers where his father's station had a baggage wing. Mail came up from the platforms through a tunnel.
body:
Most people pass this sober brick building on their way to the station without a glance. Jos Cuypers, son of the man who designed Centraal Station, built it in 1924–1925 and made no attempt to outshine his father's palace next door.

Post had first been handled inside the station itself. As the volume grew, a separate building was needed. A plan of 1912 for a site on the north side fell through when a second train shed was built there, so the post office went up on the site of the station's eastern baggage wing, which was pulled down; it stands partly on the old foundations. Inside it was a machine for parcels: a large open hall on the ground floor, letters on the floor above and offices on top. Mail trains unloaded on platform 2 and the parcels came up through a tunnel with a ramp. On the city side, vans and trams loaded under a canopy that has since gone. The public got only a small counter.

In 1968 the post moved to a new office on the Oosterdokskade, and the railways took over the building.

Look for:
- the heavy corner tower on the east side, almost a castle keep
- the stone portal of the main entrance on the west
- the zinc and lead work on the roofs of the corner pavilions

title: Dominicuskerk, the church that broadcast the first mass on Dutch radio
summary: Cuypers' church on the Spuistraat replaced a hidden church called the Stadhuis van Hoorn, never got its tower, put the first Dutch radio mass on air and later left the Catholic Church altogether. It is still a church, and you can go in.
body:
The Dominicans had a hidden church here from the 1620s, known by a house name: Het Stadhuys van Hoorn (the Town Hall of Hoorn). The name stuck to the large church that Pierre Cuypers built in its place from 1884. It was consecrated in 1893. The parish asked for a church with a lot of light, and Cuypers gave it a very broad nave with a flat ceiling carried on iron beams and arches.

Cuypers designed a tower about as high as the Westertoren. It stopped at roughly a third, just below the roof of the nave; accounts differ on whether the city refused the permit or the parish ran out of money. The stump still sits on the corner of two narrow alleys.

In 1925 the parish priest, Lambertus Perquin, founded the Catholic broadcaster KRO, and this became the first church in the Netherlands to have its mass broadcast on the radio. In the 1960s and 1970s it was a centre of liturgical experiment, which led to a break with the bishop. Since 1990 it has been run by an independent ecumenical congregation.

The Dominicus holds services on Sunday at 11:00 and rents the church out for concerts and events.

Look for:
- the unfinished tower on the alley side
- the balustrades and pinnacles along the roof
- inside, Cuypers' own furnishings, paintwork and glass

title: Keuken van 1870, the soup kitchen of the Spuistraat
summary: In 1870 a society for the public good opened a kitchen in an old livery stable here, where working people could get a hot meal for 10 or 15 cents. Rebuilt in 1901 with Jugendstil touches, it fed the city for over a century as the Keuken van 1870.
body:
On 13 September 1870 the Maatschappij tot Nut van 't Algemeen, a national society for the public good, opened a gaarkeuken (public kitchen) in a former livery stable on this spot. For 10 to 15 cents you got a meal. The society rented the building for six years and then bought it. It also ran kitchens in the Utrechtsedwarsstraat and the Pijlsteeg, later moved to the Nes; those closed in 1937, but this one carried on.

In 1901 the old building was replaced by the present one, designed by A.L. van Gendt, who had worked on the Concertgebouw and Centraal Station in historical styles. Here he tried the new Jugendstil: plant motifs in the stone around the windows and door, green glazed bricks among the red, decorative iron anchors and a gable top with a touch of Swiss chalet. The front is unchanged, with the door to the upstairs flats on the left and the kitchen door on the right.

For its last decades the kitchen went by the name Keuken van 1870. Since late 2012 an ordinary restaurant has been here.

Look for:
- the stained glass with plant motifs over the big ground-floor window
- the green glazed bricks in the brickwork
- the overhanging chalet-style top with its hoist beam

title: Spuistraat 34, where Berlage got his first job
summary: Architect Theodor Sanders lived and worked in this tall house from 1879. In 1881 a young H.P. Berlage joined his office here, and in 1888 Sanders founded the tram company whose line ran from Amsterdam-Noord to Edam.
body:
This narrow, tall house with a balcony on big brackets looks like many others on the Spuistraat. Its story is in who worked behind it.

Architect Theodor Sanders (1847–1927) rebuilt an older house here in 1875 as three homes, and from 1879 lived in it himself. He also ran his architecture office from here, and in 1881 he took on H.P. Berlage, who would later design the Beurs on the Damrak. Sanders was more than an architect. From this address he ran his other businesses, and in 1888 he founded the Noord-Hollandsche Tramweg-Maatschappij and became its director. Its steam tram ran from Amsterdam-Noord to Monnickendam and Edam; the wooden koffiehuis on the Stationsplein was later built as the station of its successor. Sanders married in 1887, a son was born here a year later, and in 1894 the family moved to the Roemer Visscherstraat.

Later the house became offices. From 1922 to 1926 the Christian daily De Amsterdammer had its editorial offices here. Since 1997 it has been flats again; you see it from the street.

Look for:
- the cast-iron balcony on four large brackets
- the row of six round-arched windows at the top
- the original arched doorway with its panel door

title: Spuistraat 53, the Flying Calf that is a horse
summary: A step-gabled house of 1633 carries a stone called Int Vlygende Kalf (the Flying Calf), but the gilded animal on it is a winged horse. In 1940–1941 the whole front was taken down and rebuilt with the old stones put back.
body:
The stone in the frieze of this step-gabled house says Int Vlygende Kalf: in the flying calf. The gilded animal above the words, though, is a winged horse, surrounded by tied bales of cloth. In the 17th century the house belonged to a family called Kalf, who sold it early in the 18th century, which may explain the name if not the horse.

Year stones with garlands give the date 1633. The house stood on the east quay of the Nieuwezijds Achterburgwal, the canal that became the Spuistraat when it was filled in. It was built as a home below with a warehouse above. Before house numbers it was known as the second building south of the Korte Lijnbaanssteeg, which it still is.

By 1939 the front was in such a poor state that it had to be held up with props, and the owner could not pay for repairs. In 1940–1941, during the occupation, the whole front was taken down and built up again, with the old stones set back in. It had been on the national list of buildings to keep since 1933, which probably saved it from demolition.

Look for:
- the gilded winged horse and the bales of cloth
- the year stones of 1633 with garlands
- the step gable with its large arch blocks

title: Justus van Maurik's cigar factory
summary: This tall red-brick factory of 1895–1896 made cigars for the firm of Justus van Maurik, better known as a writer of farces and Amsterdam stories. Later it was the first head office of HEMA, a press agency and a block printer's works.
body:
When this building rose in 1895–1896 it towered over its neighbours, and big letters on the front soon told the street what it was: the cigar factory of Justus van Maurik Jr. Van Maurik (1846–1904) had inherited the business from his father, who had it from his own father, all three called Justus. Today he is remembered mainly as a writer of farces, plays and hundreds of stories full of Amsterdam characters, and as one of the editors of the weekly, founded in 1877, that is now De Groene Amsterdammer.

The factory moved here from the Damrak, where it had run out of room. Architect H. Moen designed workshops, offices, stores and drying rooms for about 170 workers, sorting, stripping and rolling tobacco and packing cigars in boxes. A newspaper reporter given a tour in 1896 was struck by the hydraulic lifts, fireproof concrete stairs and toilets with running water on every floor.

Around 1926 the factory left for Zaandam, where wages were lower. HEMA had its first head office here in 1926–1927, the Vaz Dias press agency moved in in 1928, and a block-making works followed. Since 1987 it has been flats; you see it from the street.

Look for:
- the small step gable crowning the middle bay
- the yellow, orange and grey bricks in bands and arches
- the bricked-up factory doors, still readable in the front

title: De Vorstenlanden, Eduard Huf's cigar shop in the Zoutsteeg
summary: A small Art Nouveau shop front in the Zoutsteeg, signed by its architect in the stone, still carries the name of the cigar chain De Vorstenlanden, named after the princely lands of colonial Java. In the side wall sit stones of 1669 with a glass seller.
body:
The Zoutsteeg is a short alley between the Damrak and the Nieuwendijk. Stop at nos. 9–11. This shallow, wide shop was built in the 1890s for Eduard Huf, a tobacco dealer whose chain of cigar shops was called De Vorstenlanden. The Vorstenlanden (princely lands) were the parts of the Dutch East Indies on Java where a native ruler still reigned, in name at least. Huf already had a shop across the alley, and others on the Leidsestraat and in London, Ghent and Aachen. The interior had tile pictures after paintings by Van Ostade, Teniers and Jan Steen, made by the De Distel pottery; they are gone. In 1915 the address book listed a Turkish cigarette factory, Stelios, here too.

The architect was Gerrit van Arkel, who worked in a light Art Nouveau in those years, and he signed the building in the stone plinth. On the iron beam over the shop window the words IMPORT, DE VORSTENLANDEN, EDUARD HUF, EXPORT can still be made out. The ground floor is a café now; the front is seen from the alley.

Look for:
- the shop name on the iron beam over the window
- G. VAN ARKEL ARCHITECT cut into the plinth
- in the side wall, ANNO 1669 and a man with glassware, DE JONGE GLASCRAMER

title: De Gouden Bril, the optician with a monkey on the roof
summary: High on the corner of the Rokin and the Wijde Kapelsteeg a stone monkey peers down through binoculars. Below it, behind an oak shop front of 1918, the oldest optician in the Netherlands still sells glasses, partly from its original mahogany cabinets.
body:
Look up at the corner of Rokin 72. A carved monkey sits there with a pair of binoculars, staring out over the Rokin. Around the corner in the Wijde Kapelsteeg a second figure, a striding man in hat and cloak, stands on a bracket: Zacharias Jansen, the spectacle maker. Both came from the workshop of sculptor Dirk Polet.

They belong to De Gouden Bril (the golden spectacles), the optician's business that Johan Michaël Schmidt began in 1866. In 1872 he moved to Wijde Kapelsteeg 1, where a gable stone with a lorgnette still recalls the shop. His descendants bought this corner and its neighbours in 1917, had them pulled down, and asked P. van Dijk, helped by the young Co Franswa, for a new shop with workshop and offices. It opened on 9 November 1918. The city's building-aesthetics committee had wanted the old buildings kept, but they proved past saving. Two gable stones from them, a crowned calf and a view of IJsselstein, were set into the new front.

The register calls it the oldest optician still trading in the Netherlands. It is still an optician, now under the name Schmidt Akkerman, and much of the 1918 interior by J.B. Hillen survives.

Look for:
- the monkey with binoculars at the top of the corner
- the name De Gouden Bril in the oak shop front, and the spectacles sign on its iron arm
- the crowned calf, IJsselstein and the year 1917 in the alley front

title: Magna Plaza, the post office nicknamed Perenburg
summary: Behind the Royal Palace stands the city's old main post office of 1895–1899. Its pear-shaped tower tops were meant to receive telephone lines, which went underground before they were needed. A Swedish developer turned it into a shopping centre and named it with a wink at himself.
body:
Rijksbouwmeester C.H. Peters, the state architect, built this main post office in 1895–1899 to replace the Royal Post Office of 1854 a little further along. It is a lavish mix of Gothic and Renaissance revival in brick and stone, with dormers each under their own step gable. The three towers end in openwork pear-shaped tops. They were meant to carry the telephone lines into the building, but the lines were laid underground before they were ever used, and Amsterdammers soon called the building Perenburg (pear castle).

Inside, a central hall rose through two floors of arcaded galleries under a glass roof, though the public only ever got to see the ground floor. The PTT announced in 1987 that it would leave. A year later the Swedish developer Lars-Erik Magnusson bought it for 7.5 million guilders. Stripping the interior turned up surprises: the foundations had to be replaced, and some columns proved to be hollow. On 27 August 1992 it reopened as a shopping centre, Magna Plaza, a name that winks at its owner. He had to sell it in 1999.

The hall is open daily: 10:00 to 19:00, Sundays from 11:00 and Thursdays until 21:00.

Look for:
- the pear-shaped tops of the three towers
- the stepped dormers along the roof
- inside, the galleries around the hall and the glass roof

title: P.C. Hoofthuis, the faculty built to look like a street of houses
summary: On the site of a demolished bank, Theo Bosch built the university's arts faculty in 1976–1984 as a reply to the bank palaces of the time: broken into towers the width of canal houses, with corridors meant as streets. Lovers call it open, others the ugliest building in the street.
body:
In the 1960s and 1970s Amsterdam fought over its centre. Banks and offices were pushing out homes, and in 1966 the protest against these big closed blocks boiled over at the new bank on the Vijzelstraat. This building is an answer to that. The university bought the site of the Twentsche Bank complex between the Spuistraat and the Singel, and the office of Aldo van Eyck and Theo Bosch got the job. The two fell out over it in 1982, and Bosch finished it under his own name; it counts as his main work.

Instead of one block, Bosch broke the faculty into tower-like parts with three bays each, four on the Spuistraat and five on the Singel, so that it reads as a row of buildings. Inside, every floor has a long internal street with glass-walled seminar rooms along it. The plan included shops, a café and a public passage from the Spuistraat to the Singel; the passage was later closed for safety. Students call it the house of the goblins.

The name comes from the poet and historian P.C. Hooft, whose family house In den Huypot stood here. Students occupied the building in 2018. It is still a university building; you see it from both sides.

Look for:
- the rounded corners and bay windows, three to each tower
- the yellow hoist beside the Spuistraat entrance
- the sloping glass-block entrance steps

title: Bungehuis, from grain traders' office to occupied faculty to Soho House
summary: Twenty houses came down for this sleek stone office of a grain and colonial-goods firm in 1932–1934. The university later filled it with language students, who occupied it for eleven days in 2015, the month it was sold to become a private members' club.
body:
Bunge began in Amsterdam in 1818 as a trading house for colonial goods, timber and grain, and its founder's sons and grandsons spread it to Belgium, the Congo and South America. For its Dutch branch it built this office in 1932–1934 on a free-standing block between the Spuistraat, the Paleisstraat and the Singel. Twenty older houses were demolished. A.D.N. van Gendt drew it but died in 1932, and W.J. Klok finished it: a clean, symmetrical block faced in shell limestone, with bronze-framed bay windows and hardly any ornament. A newspaper of the day saw it as one more step in turning the old centre into a business district.

Bunge moved to Rotterdam in 1969–1970 (the firm is now one of the world's largest grain traders). From 1971 the university used the building for its arts faculty, first renting and from 1974 owning it. On 13 February 2015 students occupied it in protest against cuts and university policy; police cleared it eleven days later. That same month it was sold to an investor, who let it to Soho House. The club opened on 30 July 2018 with 79 hotel rooms and a pool on the roof. Members only, apart from the restaurant.

Look for:
- BUNGE-HUIS over the entrance on the Spuistraat
- the bay windows with angled side lights
- the meander pattern under the first-floor windows

title: The Tabakspanden, Amsterdam's longest-running squat
summary: A slum landlord's empire of houses and car parks on the Spuistraat and the Wijdesteeg was squatted in 1983 and only evicted in 2015, by then the oldest squat in the city. The 1901 office on the corner and a 1930s garage in the alley are listed.
body:
Hendrik Tabak started out selling vegetables from a cart. After the war he bought property, and at his peak owned 118 buildings with some 800 homes in Amsterdam. Here, around the Wijdesteeg, he knocked houses together into car parks. He was convicted of charging key money for neglected homes, and in 1974, at 73, he died after being robbed in one of his own buildings on the Spuistraat. His properties kept his name: the Tabakspanden.

The corner office at Spuistraat 219–221, built in 1900–1901 with a round corner bay and a little tower, was let floor by floor; in the 1960s it housed editors of the Haagse Post, and in 1966 the young broadcaster TROS. Across the corner, Wijdesteeg 3–7 is a garage with offices and flats above, built in the 1930s on the site of a row of old houses; one gable stone survived, with a sledge and the words Lang gewagt.

Squatters took no. 199 in March 1983, while police were busy with Ajax against PSV, and the corner building in April; it went by the name Langgewagt. Artists lived and worked here alongside them. The eviction on 25 March 2015 turned into a battle between police and squatters. The buildings were then turned into flats; you see them from the street.

Look for:
- the round corner bay and tower of no. 219
- the open concrete ground floor of the garage
- the Lang gewagt stone over the alley door

title: Gerzon's fashion works, where a thousand seamstresses sewed
summary: In 1923 the Jewish-owned fashion house Gerzon built its head office between the Singel and the Spuistraat, with three floors of workshops where about a thousand women made clothes. In 1941 a German administrator marched in. It is a hotel now.
body:
The brothers Eduard and Lion Gerzon opened a fashion shop on the Nieuwendijk in 1889 and grew it into a national chain. From 1913 they made much of their own clothing, and in 1923 they built this head office, designed by Adriaan Moen. The top three floors were workshops. About a thousand women worked there, turning out some 1,200 women's and children's raincoats a week. The firm also held fashion shows here, and from 1927 members of the royal family visited Gerzon every year.

Figures at the corners show women from the Indies with crowned pigeons and peacocks, carriers at the Spuistraat door hold bales of cotton, and over the stairwell window sits the firm's trademark, a lead globe with the letters GG. An extension of 1926 added the corner tower in the Amsterdam School style.

On 12 February 1941 a German administrator and his men walked into the building to take over the firm. The Jewish directors were removed, Jewish staff were dismissed one by one, and about 300 of them did not survive the war. Gerzon left in 1971. Since 1994 the building has been a hotel, today an NH hotel. The register calls the building De Kaatsheuvel van 1713, after the ball game kaatsen that was once played on this spot.

Look for:
- the women with peacocks at the corners
- the GG globe over the tall stained-glass window
- the hammered lead panels where the stone base meets the yellow brick

title: Spuistraat 289, the listed gable that came from the Rozengracht
summary: This house is a national monument for the stone edges of its bell gable, yet the gable is a transplant: it came from a Rozengracht house demolished in 1926 and was fitted here in 1928, when an old warehouse was rebuilt for the restaurant next door.
body:
Until 1928 a plain warehouse stood here on the Nieuwezijds Achterburgwal, the canal that became the Spuistraat. From 1919 it belonged to the café-restaurant Dorrius, which wanted to rebuild it in a historic style. It got help from Eelke van Houten of the city's building inspection, who made a habit of saving old building parts and reusing them where they fitted.

The bell gable with its sandstone edges came from Rozengracht 150, which was pulled down in 1926 for the church De Zaaier, now the Fatih mosque. The old top had been in storage since then. To fit the new front it had to be stretched a little at both ends. Below it, the front got modern rectangular windows, so the house looks like a smart canal house from the outside rather than a warehouse.

In 1970 the state listed the house, for the natural stone edges of its bell-shaped top, dated to the first half of the 18th century. That is, for the very part that had been brought in from elsewhere. It counts as one of the Van Houten monuments.

Look for:
- the sandstone edges of the bell gable
- the small hatch and hoist beam in the top
- the gable stone 't Schaep (the sheep) between the ground and first floor

title: West-Indisch Pakhuis (the West India Company warehouse)
summary: From 1647 to 1674 the men who ran New Amsterdam, today's New York, worked from this warehouse where the Oudeschans meets the harbour. Their company traded in hides, sugar, gold and enslaved Africans, and its initials are still on the front.
body:
The Dutch West India Company (WIC) built this warehouse in 1641–1642 at the mouth of the Oudeschans, then the edge of the harbour. On the ground floor it stored and pressed hides shipped in from trading posts such as New Amsterdam, the settlement that became New York.

From 1647 to 1674 the building was also the company's headquarters. From here the directors ran all of its trade, including gold, sugar and enslaved people, and from 1647 they were formally in charge of New Amsterdam, until the English took the town in 1664 and renamed it. The letters GWC on the front stand for Geoctroyeerde West-Indische Compagnie, the company's official name.

The complex is L-shaped. The front on the 's-Gravenhekje has stone bands, two trapezium-shaped tops cut through by a pediment, round windows and year stones; the Prins Hendrikkade and Peperstraat sides end in pointed gables. On the corner of the Prins Hendrikkade and the Peperstraat stands a small office for the company's clerks, built around 1690, on a closed little courtyard.

Today the warehouse holds offices and rooms that are hired out for events. It is not open to visitors; the outside is best seen from the quay across the Oudeschans.

Look for:
- the letters GWC on the front
- the pediment between the two tops and the year stones
- the clerks' house with its tent roof on the Peperstraat corner

title: Kikkerbilssluis, Piet Kramer's lift bridge
summary: Lift bridges with towers are rare in the old city. Piet Kramer built this one in 1940–1941 to close the Oudeschans off from the harbour, and had its name cut in granite. Where that name comes from, nobody has proved.
body:
The bridge and water barrier between the Oudeschans and the Oosterdok were rebuilt between June 1940 and September 1941 to a design by Piet Kramer of the city's public works department. He used a design for the lifting towers from a drawing of 1930. A lift bridge in the historic centre was a bold choice, since towers like these were thought to spoil old streets; it is one of the few Kramer lift bridges still working.

The quays were widened for it. A tram line was planned and then dropped, few tall ships were expected, and the bridge was worked from a distance, from the Kortjewantsbrug, from the start. It was one of the first bridges with barrier arms instead of gates. Trams and buses crossed it until 22 July 2018.

The name may come from De Kikkerbil, a 17th-century timber yard nearby, or from a piece of wood used in shipbuilding; neither has been proved. It has also been called the Kalkmarktsluis, the West-Indische sluis, after the warehouse beside it, and the Ken-U-Zelvesluis (Know-Thyself lock), after the inscription on a nearby house.

Look for:
- the two lifting towers over the Prins Hendrikkade
- the name cut into granite rather than on an iron plate
- Kramer's plain wrought-iron railings

title: Scharrebiersluis, the cheap-beer bridge
summary: This iron drawbridge is named after scharrebier, a cheap beer of poor quality that waiting skippers bought here. On hot days it has to be cooled to keep moving, and its little bridge-keeper's house is now a hotel suite.
body:
Brug 278 crosses the lock between the Nieuwe Herengracht and the Schippersgracht, on the Kadijksplein. Skippers waiting for the lock bought scharrebier here, a cheap beer of poor quality, and the name stuck.

The bridge is younger than it looks. In 1876 a double bascule bridge came here for the route of ships with standing masts. When a tram to the Czaar Peterstraat was planned, that bridge was thought too unstable, and in 1906 the city's public works department put in this iron drawbridge, in a style that already looked old-fashioned. Who designed it is not entirely clear. It was worked by hand until 1913, when the electric tram brought power. A mistake during building left the span slightly twisted; that was only put right in a renovation in 1986–1987. From October 2022 to August 2023 it was taken away for repairs and lifted back onto its piers by a crane on a pontoon. In warm weather it has to be cooled so that it keeps opening.

The brick bridge-keeper's house beside it, with shutters, dates from about 1906. Its job ended long ago; since 2021 it can be booked for the night as one of the city's bridge-house suites.

Look for:
- the riveted gate frame and the counterweight above the deck
- the cast-iron railings on the fixed parts, in an 18th-century style
- the bridge-keeper's house at Rapenburgerplein 100

title: Scheepvaarthuis (the Shipping House)
summary: Six shipping lines built one office here in 1913–1916, on the spot where the first Dutch fleet left for the East Indies in 1595. Shaped like a ship, it is seen as the first building wholly in the Amsterdam School style, and is now a hotel.
body:
Six Amsterdam shipping companies, among them the KNSM, the Stoomvaart Maatschappij Nederland and the Royal Packet Company, set up a joint company to build an office together. Thirteen houses on the Prins Hendrikkade and the Binnenkant were pulled down for it, at the western tip of the Waalseiland, where Cornelis Houtman's first voyage to the East Indies had set out in 1595.

The Van Gendt brothers engineered the concrete frame; the design went to the then little-known Jo van der Mey, who brought in Michel de Klerk and Piet Kramer. It is generally seen as the first building wholly in the Amsterdam School style. The plan has the shape of a ship, with the directors' offices in the bow on the corner. Bricks for the 1926–1928 extension were baked at the same time as those for the first phase, so the colours would match. In 1942 the building was requisitioned for a German administration; the last shipping line left in 1981, and the city transport company GVB had its head office here from 1983 to 2004.

Since 2007 it has been the Grand Hotel Amrâth. The restaurant and bar are open to non-guests, and Museum Het Schip runs Sunday guided tours of the building.

Look for:
- the stepped tower over the corner entrance, clad in copper-coloured slate
- the lead roof edge shaped as ropes, waves and little fish heads
- inside, the stairwell under its stained-glass roof by Willem Bogtman

title: Van der Mey's heavy bridges (Brug 283 and the Bantammerbrug)
address: Waalseilandsgracht, between Binnen Bantammerstraat and Buiten Bantammerstraat
summary: In 1914 the architect of the Scheepvaarthuis gave the Waalseilandsgracht a bridge of solid brick walls, and critics called it far too heavy for the old city. He replied that he saw the water as a harbour basin. Iron seahorses sit in its lamps.
body:
Brug 283 crosses the wide Waalseilandsgracht between the Lastage and the Waalseiland. Jo van der Mey designed it in 1913 for the city's public works department, at the same time as the Scheepvaarthuis next to it. Instead of arches he gave it five angular openings between massive brick walls. People found it far too heavy and out of place in the historic centre. Van der Mey answered in the city's technical journal that new bridges had to carry heavier loads, and that he saw this water as a harbour basin rather than a canal. The seahorses in the lamps are thought to be the work of his assistant Piet Kramer, but that has never been settled. Metro building in the 1970s damaged the bridge; it was repaired after 1977 and listed in 2001.

Its sister crosses the Geldersekade between the Stormsteeg and the Binnen Bantammerstraat. The Bantammerbrug was probably designed by Van der Mey around 1914 but only built in 1921; Kramer is credited with its lamps and ironwork. It first came with a transformer house and a urinal. The name goes back via the street to Bantam on Java: the ships of the first voyage to the East were unloaded opposite the new street in 1597.

Look for:
- the seahorses in the four lamps of Brug 283
- the bridge number 283 in wrought iron
- the stone columns and Kramer's lamps on the Bantammerbrug

title: Binnen Bantammerstraat, Amsterdam's first Chinatown
summary: Chinese stokers who fired Dutch steamships lodged in this short street between contracts, from around 1911. For half a century it was the heart of Amsterdam's Chinese community, long before the Zeedijk. Since 2005 its street sign has been in two scripts.
body:
From around 1900 Chinese seamen, mostly stokers, worked on the steamships of Dutch lines such as the KNSM and the SMN. Between contracts they stayed in boarding houses, and in Amsterdam the community lived in and around the Binnen Bantammerstraat. They were cheap to hire; in the big seamen's strike of 1911 they were held in reserve as strike-breakers. They earned about 70 per cent of a Dutch sailor's pay, and most of that went to the boarding-house keeper who found them work.

In the crisis of the 1930s, with steam giving way to diesel, many were stranded without work. From 1931 laid-off seamen sold peanut biscuits in the streets, and the Dutch government is believed to have sent about a thousand back to China against their will. For the first half century the community centred on about ten restaurants in this street; only in 1959 did the first Chinese business open on the Zeedijk, where Chinatown is now.

The street itself is far older: it was laid out across the Lastage in the 1590s and named after Bantam, the Javanese port of the first Dutch voyage. Its listed fronts are mostly shop-houses of 1875–1900, unusually shallow because their backs stand on a former alley, the Kollegat.

Look for:
- the street sign in Dutch and Chinese, put up in 2005
- the 1916 Jugendstil shopfront of number 8
- the carved wooden shopfront running across numbers 16 and 18
- the stepped gable of 1892 on number 27

title: Staalmeestersbrug and Monet's view of the Zuiderkerk
summary: Claude Monet painted the Groenburgwal from here in 1874, wooden drawbridge and Zuiderkerk tower included. In the 1920s the city wanted a wide fixed bridge instead; the beauty committee fought for the view, and the drawbridge stayed.
body:
The wooden drawbridge in the Staalstraat is named after the staalmeesters, the cloth inspectors of the nearby Saaihal who judged samples of cloth; Rembrandt painted a group of them in The Syndics. Looking north from the bridge, the Groenburgwal runs straight up to the tower of the Zuiderkerk. Claude Monet painted that view in 1874, bridge and all; the canvas is now in the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

In the mid-1920s the mayor and aldermen proposed a wider, fixed bridge for the growing traffic. The city's beauty committee, with the Oud-Amsterdam society, fought back: the view from the Amstel to the Zuiderkerk would be lost, and the narrow Staalstraat led nowhere anyway. After two years the city chose a new bridge that looked just like the old one, built in 1928. It was nearly rebuilt again in 1964, which kept one of the few wooden drawbridges left in the city at that time. Couples hang love locks on its cables; the city cuts them off regularly because the bridge cannot carry the weight.

At the other end of the Groenburgwal, where it meets the Raamgracht, Brug 226 has an oddly flattened arch. In 1937 a Van Gend & Loos horse and cart came off it into the basement of the corner house.

Look for:
- Monet's view: stand on the bridge and look north to the Zuiderkerk
- the name board, which says Staalmeesterbrug, without the s
- the flattened arch of Brug 226 at the far end

title: Christ Church, the English church in a cloth hall
summary: Amsterdam's Anglicans have worshipped since 1771 in a cloth hall of 1626, where the cloth inspectors once met under their group portraits. Around 1829 it got one of the very first neo-Gothic fronts in the Netherlands, in smooth ground brick.
body:
The building began in 1626 as a cloth hall, part of the Staalhof, a group of halls between the Groenburgwal and the Staalstraat where cloth was inspected. The English Episcopal congregation, founded in 1698, met in an upstairs room on the Oudezijds Achterburgwal and later in the Agnietenkapel before it moved in here in 1771.
