It could use the meeting room of the staalmeesters, the cloth inspectors, where their group portraits still hung; Rembrandt's had already gone to the town hall and is now in the Rijksmuseum. Under French rule, from 1806 to 1821, the congregation lost the building.

In 1827–1829 the hall was turned into a proper church under J.J. Janssen, probably also the designer of the front: soft red ground brick with hair-thin joints, pointed arches and crockets, one of the first neo-Gothic fronts in the country. Behind it is not the church but the chaplain's house and the vestry. The stained-glass windows of 1929–1931 show William III and Mary Stuart, the arms of two English regiments that served under William, a window given by an American society and one given by the City of London.

It is still an English-speaking Anglican church, with a Sunday service and a lunchtime gathering on Wednesdays.

Look for:
- the smooth pink brick and pointed windows of the front
- the four little turrets where pinnacles used to stand
- the pointed lancet windows in the side wall

title: Van 't Hoff's laboratory, where the first chemistry Nobel was earned
summary: Built around 1650 as the silk weavers' inspection hall, this house became the university's chemistry lab in 1857. Here Jacobus van 't Hoff did the work that won him the very first Nobel Prize in Chemistry, in 1901.
body:
Groenburgwal 44 was built around 1650 by the silk weavers' guild as a hall where silk was inspected. In 1857 the University of Amsterdam turned it into its chemistry laboratory, and it stayed one until 1891.

Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff was appointed professor in 1877 and was not impressed by the facilities. Even so, his years here were his most productive. He wrote Études de dynamique chimique (1884), which laid the foundations of physical chemistry, and did the research on chemical dynamics and the osmotic pressure of solutions that brought him the first Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1901. In 1887 the University of Leipzig tried to lure him away; to keep him, Amsterdam built him a new laboratory on the Roeterseiland, which he moved into in 1891. In 1895 he left for Berlin after all. The Roeterseiland lab burned down in 1987.

On 17 November 2021 the Royal Netherlands Chemical Society named the building a national chemical heritage site and put up a plaque. At the time the ground floor held a café and exhibition space. The outside, a plastered front of seven bays with a slightly projecting middle, is seen from the quay.

Look for:
- the plaque of the chemical society on the front
- the projecting middle part of the plastered front

title: Workers' hall on the site of the Blauw Jan menagerie
summary: Here Amsterdammers once paid four stuivers to see lions, tigers and a cassowary at the inn of Blauw Jan. In 1883 a society for the uplift of working men built its hall on the spot, with carved craftsmen at work over the windows.
body:
From about 1675 the inn De Hoop at Kloveniersburgwal 87 kept a menagerie. Everyone called the place Blauw Jan, after innkeeper Jan Westerhof, who was also a blue dyer. It began with parrots, a king vulture and a cassowary; later came lions, tigers, panthers and apes brought in on East India Company ships. People were shown too, such as a Frisian dwarf in 1767 and 1774. The menagerie closed in 1784 and is seen as a forerunner of Artis.

In 1883 the old building made way for the hall of the Maatschappij voor den Werkenden Stand (Society for the Working Class), founded in 1854 by a carpenter, a metal caster and four painters to improve the lot of craftsmen. It set up the first trade school in the Netherlands in 1861 and the country's first labour exchange in 1886; its industrial school moved in here. The design, by L. Beirer and J.J. Bekker, won a competition. After 1946 the big lecture hall became a theatre, the Doelenzaal, later home to the International Dance Theatre. Since 2016 it has held offices and flats.

Look for:
- the medallions with scenes of people at work in the first-floor windows
- the bands of carved diamond points around the arches
- round the back at Groenburgwal 24, "Mij voor den WERKENDEN STAND" carved in stone

title: Poppenhuis and De Kloof, from Catholic palace to shelter
summary: Philips Vingboons built this palace in 1642 for a rich merchant shut out of high office after turning Catholic. Since 1903 it has belonged to the Catholic Vincentius society, and its basement is De Kloof, the city's oldest walk-in shelter for the homeless.
body:
In 1601 Jan Poppen built a house here called De Gulden Steur. In 1642 his grandson Joan Poppen replaced it with this one. Joan had become a Catholic, which barred him from the important offices, and the house had a chapel of its own. His architect, Philips Vingboons, was a Catholic too. It is Vingboons' first front in the Palladian manner: five bays, the middle three set forward between Corinthian pilasters that rise through the floors to a pediment, their proportions following the Italian Vignola almost to the letter. The family arms in the pediment were removed in the 18th century. Until 1904 the main door was in the middle, up a high double stoop.

In 1903 the Sint-Vincentiusvereniging, a Catholic charity, bought the house for a school, meeting rooms and offices, and it became known as the Vincentiushuis. The same year the society opened its St. Vincentius Tusschenschool round the corner at Groenburgwal 30, now six flats. In 1975, the heroin years, the new De Regenboog foundation ran a coffee bar for young drifters in the basement, and the house became its base. The basement is now De Kloof, a walk-in centre for the homeless, open Monday to Saturday from 9 to 15. Look from the street.

Look for:
- the pilasters, pediment and festoons of the front
- at Groenburgwal 30, the tile panel ST. VINCENTIUS TUSSCHENSCHOOL, a stone cross and the letters S and V

title: Trippenhuis, the arms dealers' palace
summary: Two brothers who traded in cannon built the widest canal-house front in Amsterdam in 1660–1662, with chimneys shaped like mortars. Later the Rijksmuseum started here, with the Night Watch on the wall, and the Academy of Sciences still uses it.
body:
Louys and Hendrick Trip traded in copper, tar, iron, weapons and ammunition, and owned mines, furnaces and cannon foundries in Sweden. They meant to outshine the Huis met de Hoofden of their rival and uncle Louis de Geer, and had Justus Vingboons design two complete houses behind one front: seven bays and eight Corinthian pilasters, at a cost of 250,000 guilders. It is now the widest canal-house front in the city. Behind the middle row of windows runs the thick wall between the two homes, and those windows were at first blind. The brothers chose the Kloveniersburgwal over the new canal ring, and over the low houses of the time the town hall on the Dam could be seen. A cupola like the town hall's was planned; its timber base is still in the attic.

The brothers called themselves arms dealers of peace, and the front says so: olive and palm branches in the middle, cannon barrels and cannonballs around the Trip arms in the pediment. From 1812 the Royal Institute, forerunner of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences (KNAW), was based here, and from 1817 to 1885 the house was also the Rijksmuseum, with the Night Watch, until Cuypers' new museum opened. The Academy still uses it; it is not open to visitors.

Look for:
- the two chimneys shaped like mortars
- cannon, cannonballs and the Trip arms in the pediment
- the windows over the dividing wall in the middle

title: De Engelbewaarder, the first literary café
summary: Opened in 1971 as the first literary café in the Netherlands, named after a novel by W.F. Hermans, with a reading table, book auctions and pinball world championships. Since the 1980s it is the place for Sunday afternoon jazz sessions.
body:
Two school friends, Bas Lubberhuizen and Jan in 't Hout, opened Het Amsterdamsch litterair café De Engelbewaarder on 1 September 1971, on the raised ground floor of this 18th-century canal house. The name comes from Herinneringen van een engelbewaarder (Memories of a Guardian Angel), a novel by W.F. Hermans. There was a well-stocked reading table, there were book auctions, lectures, chess matches and world championships in pinball, and for more than ten years writers, poets and musicians such as Hans Verhagen, Johnny van Doorn and Wim T. Schippers found a stage and an audience here. From 1975 friends of the café published a quarterly of the same name.

In 1982 a new owner started Sunday jam sessions, led by the American drummer King L. Mock, where Woody Shaw, Archie Shepp and David Murray played. The sessions still run on Sunday afternoons, with free entry, except in summer.

Part of the interior came from De oude Postbar in the Gravenstraat, including the antique mirror over the Spiegeltafel in the covered courtyard. Above the bar hangs the only photograph of the writer Joseph Roth in Amsterdam, taken on the day he left the city.

Look for:
- the hanging sign on the front, designed by Joep Paulussen
- the house's raised top cornice
- inside, the Roth photograph above the bar

title: Goslerhuisje, the last house of the Joden Houttuinen
summary: A crooked lock-keeper's house of 1695 is all that is left of the Joden Houttuinen, a street of the old Jewish quarter pulled down in the late 1960s. It is named after the Jewish metal dealers A. Gosler & Zonen, and is now the café De Sluyswacht.
body:
The little house leans slightly beside the Sint Antoniessluis, the lock at the head of the Oudeschans built in 1602. It went up in 1695 for the lock-keeper, who worked and kept the lock for the city; the national register puts it in the 18th century.

Its later name comes from A. Gosler & Zonen, dealers in machinery and metals and contractors for demolition work, who used it as their office and store. The owner, born in 1874, ran the firm with two of his sons. He was murdered in Auschwitz in 1942; his wife and four of their six children were also killed. The two sons who survived kept the business going for a while after the war. Then the house stood empty and boarded up for years, until it was restored in 1979.

By then its street had gone. The Joden Houttuinen was demolished at the end of the 1960s, all but this house, for the Maupoleum, an office block of 1971 that many called one of the ugliest buildings in the city. That too was pulled down in the mid-1990s; the building that replaced it houses the Amsterdam University of the Arts. The lock-keeper's house is now the brown café De Sluyswacht, with a terrace over the Oudeschans.

Look for:
- how the house leans
- the year 1695 painted on it, added in this century
- the lock beside it and the view down the Oudeschans

title: Huis Wilhelmina, a house in an alley
summary: A front just one window wide, slotted in 1898 into the passage between Geldersekade 59 and 63 that once led to a house behind. It carries the name Wilhelmina and the year the eighteen-year-old queen was inaugurated.
body:
Geldersekade 61 is strikingly narrow, a single, three-part window wide. That is because it stands on what used to be a passage, a gang, between numbers 59 and 63, which led to a house at the back. The 1830 land registry map still shows it.

The house was built in 1898, the date given in the front, with natural stone details and a cornice broken in the middle. It also carries the name Wilhelmina; in 1898 the young queen came of age and was inaugurated. Who chose the name is not known.

It is a private home: look from the quay.

Look for:
- the name Wilhelmina in the front
- how the house fits between its wider neighbours
- the broken cornice at the top

title: De Ruijterkade's last shipping offices
summary: Most of the offices built along the IJ behind Centraal Station were pulled down for the station's second train shed. At the east end a row survives, including the office of the Royal West India Mail with a half-timbered staff canteen in English cottage style.
body:
The De Ruijterkade was laid out on the new station island and named in 1880, and was lined with offices and company buildings one plot deep between about 1890 and 1910. Most were demolished before 1920 to make room for a second train shed at Centraal Station; only the eastern stretch survives.

Number 125 was built in 1892 by A.L. van Gendt for the Koninklijke West-Indische Maildienst (KWIM), whose ships sailed from this quay to Suriname, the Caribbean and New York. A stone frieze once carried its name, and a sun with a face crowns the gable. Five years later the line bought the plot next door and added a staff canteen at number 126: a little half-timbered building with black beams and green-painted infill, in English cottage style, attributed to A.D.N. van Gendt. The KWIM was taken over by the KNSM in 1912, run from the Scheepvaarthuis, and dissolved in 1927.

Number 139 was built in 1914 by H.G. Jansen for the ship brokers Vereenigd Cargadoorskantoor. Number 140 is a company building of 1912 with a tiled date panel by the Amsterdam firm Distel.

All are offices: look from the quay.

Look for:
- the half-timbered canteen at number 126
- the sun with a face in the gable of number 125
- the stone with a three-master and ANNO 1914 in the bay window of number 139
- the Distel tile panel "Anno 1912" on number 140
- the frieze of children on De Zeevaart, nos. 105–106 (1884–85)

title: Boas diamond factory, once the largest in Europe
summary: In 1879 three Jewish brothers opened a steam-driven diamond factory here with 357 cutting mills, the biggest in Europe. The war ended it; in 1990 diamonds came back, and today you can walk in on a free tour.
body:
The brothers Israël, Marcus and Hartog Boas started cutting diamonds in 1870 on the Nieuwe Keizersgracht, with mills turned by horses. Their way of working was new for the time: they paid their cutters wages instead of renting them a mill. When the South African mines flooded the trade with rough stones, they built this factory on Uilenburg, then one of the poorest Jewish neighbourhoods of the city. It opened on 29 June 1879: 357 mills driven by steam, with 357 cutters, 122 setters, 142 apprentices and 52 errand boys. A wing of 1887 raised the number of mills to 600. Hartog Boas died in 1894 of tuberculosis, a common illness among cutters who breathed diamond dust.

The crisis of the 1930s stopped the cutting. In the war the factory was seized, run for the occupier from 1942 and wound up in 1944, after which the remaining Jewish workers were deported.

Samuel Gassan had trained here as a cutter before the war. His firm bought the complex in 1989; plans to pull down the gatehouses, boiler house and chimney were dropped when it was listed. Gassan Diamonds has been here since 1990 and gives free tours.

Look for:
- the 33-metre chimney beside the boiler house
- the twin gatehouses (office and porter's lodge) and the carved stone gate piers
- ANNO and 1879 over the side entrances of the main building

title: Uilenburgersjoel, the synagogue behind the wall
summary: Poor Ashkenazi Jews of Uilenburg prayed upstairs and held their weddings downstairs in this synagogue of 1766, reached only through an alley. After 1943 it stored old building parts for decades; now it hosts a congregation and concerts again.
body:
From the late 17th century poor Jews from Eastern Europe settled on Uilenburg, one of the islands laid out in 1593. A house synagogue opened on this plot in 1724; in 1766 it was replaced by the present building. The prayer hall was upstairs, the two rooms below were let for wedding parties, and in the cellars were a kitchen and a place for the ritual slaughter of poultry. For a long time it could only be reached through an alley, the Koning Davidgang.

It served as a synagogue until 1943. Its congregation was largely murdered in the Holocaust and the building was plundered. In 1954 the city bought it for 75,000 guilders and used it to store salvaged building parts and as a restoration workshop; it was restored in 1996 and 2015.

When the old streets were merged into the wide Nieuwe Uilenburgerstraat, the synagogue ended up behind a high wall. A foundation leases it from the city and hires it out, and the progressive Jewish congregation Beit Ha'Chidush has met here a few times a month since 1997.

Look for:
- the bell-shaped gable over the middle bay, seen through the gate
- Amsterdam's arms in the wall, a stone from the old Haarlemmersluis set here in 1957
- the 1974 stone of the restoration workshop

title: Splendor, the bathhouse of the Jewish island
summary: This 1923 public bathhouse opened Sunday to Friday, not on the Sabbath, for its Jewish neighbours. In the war it was a Jews-only bathhouse and its bath master was arrested for hiding a Jewish couple. Musicians now play in the old bathrooms.
body:
Many homes on Uilenburg had no bath, so the city built its tenth public bathhouse here, with a yard for the street-cleaning service next to it. It opened on 13 December 1923. Unlike the other municipal baths it was open from Sunday to Friday, for the many Jewish residents, and it had Jewish staff. Men came in from the Houtkopersburgwal to 14 showers and 2 tubs; women from the Nieuwe Uilenburgerstraat to 6 showers and 3 tubs. Gable stones from houses demolished in the slum clearance were set in its walls.

In 1941 the occupier made it one of only two bathhouses Jews were still allowed to use. The bath master, who lived on site with his wife, was arrested in February 1944, probably for hiding a Jewish couple, and died in Neuengamme in January 1945. The bathhouse closed in August 1943, after its Jewish neighbours had been deported.

After the war it held a chemical works, a meat-products factory and a bicycle factory. Since 2013 it has been Splendor, a music club founded and run by around fifty musicians, with concerts, open rehearsals and workshops; the men's and women's bathrooms are now its two halls.

Look for:
- the timber corner with three windows under a widening eave
- the black glazed brick plinth
- gable stones D' Turcksche slaeff, D' koffibaal and D' vogelstruis 1742

title: The bridge yard and the last of the Jewish nursery school
summary: Behind the fence of a 1920s city works yard stands the house of a nursery school for poor Jewish children that once took 600 pupils and had a royal visit. The school is gone; the house may have to move for a new power station.
body:
In 1887 the banker George Rosenthal and his wife Sophie Rosenthal-May paid for a nursery school on Uilenburg, for children of the poorest Jewish families. Two boys of twelve and thirteen laid its first stone on 15 June 1887. It was well run and much wanted: in April 1893 the thirteen-year-old Queen Wilhelmina and her mother came to see it, and after an extra storey in 1895 it took 600 children. After the slum clearance the city took it over. The school was pulled down in 1956 for a power substation; only the house of its head teacher, by Constantijn Muysken, survived.

It stands in the yard that the city's public works department built in 1925–1926 for its sewer and bridge-maintenance sections, a strict Amsterdam School building with a tower-like corner. On 1 November 1940 the yard took over the house, and in 1941 it was gutted to store carts and ladders.

The substation now has to be renewed. In the plan shown in 2024 the house is moved to make room, while the works office is kept and may become housing for older people.

Look for:
- PUBLIEKE WERKEN, AFDEELING RIOLEERING EN BRUGGEN in gilt bronze letters over the door
- the 17th-century stone Het Wape va Portugal at the foot of the corner tower
- the stepped gable of the school house behind the gate

title: Uilenburg rebuilt, the workers' block and the Witte Olifant school
summary: Uilenburg was the city's first slum clearance. A Jewish workers' association made sure some residents could come back to this new block of 1927; across the street a school served warm kosher meals for 5 cents and in 1941 became Jewish school no. 2.
body:
In 1910, 368 of Uilenburg's 861 homes were declared unfit to live in, and the island became Amsterdam's first slum clearance. The two narrow main streets were knocked into one wide street, and the city filled it with Amsterdam School buildings.

The block on the even side, 72 homes designed by Jo Mulder of the city housing department and finished in 1927, was handed to the building fund of the Handwerkers Vriendenkring, a Jewish workers' association of 1869, so that people from the old slums could return. Its stairwells sit on the joins between the units, so neighbours from different houses share a door. A sculpture on the corner with the Oostersekade is dated 1927, the year the clearance was finished. In 1942 the occupier banned the association and the city took the homes over.

The double school of 1920 at the other end, by Nico Lansdorp of public works, served warm meals for 5 cents in the 1930s crisis, ritually prepared for Jewish children. From September 1941 until the last big deportation in May 1943 it was Jewish school no. 2. Since about 1985 it has been called De Witte Olifant.

Look for:
- the female figure on the corner of the block at the Oostersekade
- the old gable stones in the school walls: an owl with UYLENBURGH, King David with his harp, an axe and adze of 1734, and a white elephant
- the stepped round corner window of the school on the Oudeschans

title: Armenian church in a warehouse (Surp Hoki)
summary: Armenian merchants turned a warehouse into their church in 1714. For more than a century it was a Catholic girls' school, until Armenians bought it back in 1985. The Sunday liturgy is sung here again, and the bridge outside is named after it.
body:
From the early 17th century Armenian merchants settled in the Lastage, the old shipyard district east of the Nieuwmarkt. They met for worship in the homes of their priests, and in 1666 the first printed Armenian Bible came off a press in Amsterdam. In 1714 the city allowed them to buy a warehouse on what was then the Dwarsboomssloot and fit it out as a church. In 1749 it got a marble door surround, iron stoop railings and a gable stone with a lamb and an Armenian inscription, paid for by the priest Johannes de Minas.

After 1800 the community dwindled. From 1835 the church was let to other congregations, and in 1874 it was sold at auction and became a Catholic primary school for girls. When the school left in 1984, members of a new Armenian community, many from Turkey, bought it back in 1985; the Armenian archbishop of Paris consecrated it in 1989. A restoration from 2009 gave it its yellow and white front, and it was consecrated again in 2014.

The Holy Liturgy is held every Sunday from 10:00, and visitors are welcome.

Look for:
- the lamb stone and stoop railings of 1749 at the door
- the name board of the Armeensebrug, official since 2013
- the 2018 memorial stone for the Armenian genocide on the Keizersstraat corner
- the priest's house stone of 1765 with a chalice at Koningsstraat 27

title: Schottenburch, the warehouse older than its date stone
summary: Its stone says 1636, but this double warehouse already stands on a map of 1597 and may be older than the Lastage's inclusion in the city. Next door a coffee roaster built a Jugendstil roastery; both were later saved by artists and squatters.
body:
Schottenburch, a double warehouse with two spout gables and a full set of shutters, is often called the oldest warehouse still standing in Amsterdam. Its date stone reads 1636, but the building is already on Pieter Bast's map of 1597. It may even predate the 1580s, when the Lastage, the shipbuilding ground along the Krom Boomssloot, was taken inside the city; its plot runs at an angle to the later buildings. In the 20th century it housed a fuel dealer, a cart hire and a coffee roaster. From 1979 to 1988 it was an artists' space run by the artist Wim Vonk; it was then converted into homes without enlarging a single window.

Next door at number 16, the tea and coffee firm Alex Meijer & Co built its roastery in 1902, to a design by E.M. Rood with a curved, Jugendstil top floor. The rival Simon Lévelt took the firm over in 1971. The empty building was squatted in 1976; at the squatters' urging the city bought it, and in 1980 it became ten homes with a workshop.

Further south, at numbers 59 to 63, two warehouses of 1723 share a gable stone pieced together from parts of different ages: a tiger and DE TEYGER.

Look for:
- SCHOTTENBVRCH and the year stone on the party wall with number 20
- "Alex Meijer & Co" carved over the roastery door
- the tiger stone at numbers 61 and 63

title: The first stone of a five-year-old (Korte Koningsstraat 14)
summary: On 21 April 1896 the youngest son of a carpenter, aged five, laid the first stone of this narrow house. His father hardly got to live in it. The front plays a game too: children's heads over the lower windows, lions' heads above.
body:
The carpenter Willem Knuijt had this tall, narrow house built in 1896 to a design by H.H. Baanders, whose name his architect sons carried on in the family firm. The first stone, set between the cellar windows, says it was laid on 21 April 1896 by his youngest child, aged five. The father did not enjoy his new house for long: he died in 1897. A second stone names the architect.

The front is a careful classical stack: a stone base and cellar, then a tall main floor reached up a few steps in a porch, with each storey lower than the one below. Over the windows of the main floor the keystones are little children's heads; on the floor above they are lions' heads, and the arches are filled with diamond-patterned tile mosaics. The two front doors in the porch, one to the main floor and one to the upper homes, are framed like small temples.

Beside the house a passage leads to the Bremertuin, an inner garden. It is a private home; everything described here is seen from the street.

Look for:
- the first stone between the cellar windows, and the architect's stone
- the children's heads and lions' heads over the windows
- the tile mosaics in the window arches

title: Premsela & Hamburger, the jewellers of the Nieuwe Hoogstraat
summary: A stone over a corner shop still reads Premsela en Hamburger anno 1823. The Jewish firm of jewellers and antique dealers had two shops in this street; the occupier closed it in 1943, and the survivors started again in the emptied shop.
body:
The Nieuwe Hoogstraat was part of the old main road from the Dam to the east of the city, and a shopping street in the Jewish quarter. The firm of Premsela & Hamburger, jewellers founded in 1823, had a shop at numbers 27 and 29, whose front was rebuilt for them in 1893 by E.M. Rood in a Dutch Renaissance style, with bands of stone and five coupled windows on the first floor.

In 1921 the firm moved to the corner of the Kloveniersburgwal, a shop-house of 1892 with a wooden bay window running up two floors over the cut-off corner. The Jewish weekly was full of praise: it felt like a palace of gold and silver jewellery, old and new. In 1943 the occupier closed the shop. After the war surviving relatives tried to rebuild the business in the plundered premises, and in 1952 it moved to the Rokin, where more dealers were based.

The corner building is still a shop with homes above.

Look for:
- the stone "Premsela en Hamburger anno 1823" just above the shopfront on the Nieuwe Hoogstraat side of the corner
- the timber bay window over the corner door
- the striped stone bands of numbers 27 and 29

title: Sophia Adriana Stichting, the Stedelijk founder's almshouse
summary: The widow whose art collection founded the Stedelijk Museum also turned this canal house into an almshouse for eight women over fifty, in memory of her husband's family. A long stone under a window tells you so, in one breath.
body:
Sophia Adriana de Bruijn (1816–1890) married August Pieter Lopez Suasso, of a banking family, in 1860. The couple travelled widely and collected all kinds of art objects. After her death she left the collection and their house on the Kloveniersburgwal to the city, on condition that it be shown to the public; that bequest became the basis of the Stedelijk Museum.

This house on the Nieuwe Herengracht had long been in the family. In 1882, as a widow, she had it rebuilt as an almshouse for eight women over fifty. Women of any church were welcome, though no more than one Catholic could live there at a time. It was only used as an almshouse after her death; until then it stood empty and held large pieces of furniture. Until 1943 it was called "Gesticht door Augustus Pieter Lopez Suasso"; why the name changed is not known.

The front is a neat 1882 piece of neo-Renaissance: a black-painted brick wall under a richly decorated neck gable, with all the original sash windows. The inscription runs across the parapet of the middle first-floor window.

Look for:
- the stone: rebuilt in 1882 by S.A. de Bruijn, dowager of A.P. Lopez Suasso, at his wish, in memory of Diego Lopez Suasso
- the neck gable with claw pieces and pediment

title: Huize Avondrood, a merchant's house with nine lives (Nieuwe Herengracht 143)
summary: Built in 1720 for a Sephardic merchant whose son-in-law gambled away 100,000 guilders in one night, this house later saw the first talks on the Free University, sheltered Boer War exiles, was an old people's home, and in 1980 was squatted.
body:
In 1720 the merchant Jacob Abrabanel built this broad house with a sandstone front opposite the Plantage, with two narrow houses beside it, probably for his daughters. Both married sons of his brother. One son-in-law soon ran through his wife's dowry and once ran up a gambling debt of 100,000 guilders in a single evening. Abrabanel sold the three houses in 1735.

From 1818 to 1826 the big house was the orphanage and old people's home of the Restored Lutheran church. Between 1877 and 1900 it belonged to Willem Hovy, owner of the brewery De Gekroonde Valk; in his house, in December 1877, a group of orthodox Protestants first talked about founding a Reformed university, which opened in 1880 as the Vrije Universiteit. From 1900 to 1902 it sheltered exiles from the Boer War as Die Afrikaansch Tehuis, and from 1902 to 1978 it was a Reformed home for the elderly.

After standing empty, it was squatted in 1980. The squatters called it Huize Avondrood, "evening glow", and it still goes by that name. The city bought it and in 1985–1986 turned it into twenty small homes for young people, now let by a housing association.

Look for:
- the carved middle bay of the sandstone front
- the raised cornice on consoles
- the eight stoop posts and the Empire-style door

title: Arsenaal, the poor relief's peat stores
summary: Around 1610 the city's poor relief built these warehouses to store the peat, grain and butter it handed out. Later an arsenal, they were nearly sold for demolition to the diamond dealers in 1909. Architects are trained here now.
body:
Amsterdam's huiszittenmeesters looked after the poor who still had a home of their own, and handed out food and peat for the stove. Around 1610–1613 those of the old side of the city built this complex of warehouses on the grounds of the leper house: a double warehouse with a flat trapezium gable between two single ones with pointed gables, at front and back, decorated with big blocks of stone over the arches and lintels. Next to it they built their office in 1655, the Oudezijds Huiszittenhuis, where the poor came in through a gate on the Nieuwe Amstelstraat.

In 1776 the city architect Jacob Eduard de Witte closed off that poor people's courtyard with a low building of two shallow houses under one hipped roof, with tall corner chimneys; it still stands at the start of the Nieuwe Amstelstraat.

In 1808 the state took over the warehouses as an arsenal, which gave them their name. In 1909 the government proposed selling them to the diamond dealers' association, which wanted to pull them down for new premises; after protests by the antiquarian society, parliament voted it down. Since 1946 the Academie van Bouwkunst, a school of architecture, has used them.

Look for:
- the stone blocks over the openings on the Waterlooplein side
- the low 1776 houses with their tall chimneys on the Nieuwe Amstelstraat
- next door at Waterlooplein 211, the gate of the Oudezijds Huiszittenhuis, which ran these stores

title: Cotton Club, the Nieuwmarkt's Surinamese jazz café
summary: A plain 19th-century front on the Nieuwmarkt hides a café that became the first haunt of Amsterdam's small Surinamese community and of Black American soldiers after the war. It took its name from a Surinamese trumpeter, Teddy Cotton.
body:
Until 1951 this was simply café Smit. After the war it became the place where the still very small Surinamese community of Amsterdam met, along with Black American soldiers on leave. The soldiers brought stacks of American jazz records, which were played to death on the jukebox; in 1955 the paper Het Vrije Volk wrote that the hits were often heard in the Cotton Club before they reached the radio. Jazz musicians who had played in the dance halls on the Zeedijk came on here afterwards.

In 1949 the owner's daughter fell for a Surinamese regular, the trumpeter Theodorus Gustaaf Kantoor, who played as Teddy Cotton. They moved in together and the café was renamed the Cotton Club, after him and after the famous club in New York. Teddy left the scene around 1960, but the name stayed. Of all the Surinamese meeting places of the 1950s to 1970s on the Nieuwendijk and the Zeedijk, this is the only one left. Jazz is still played, now alongside salsa.

The house itself got its cornice in 1876; the wooden shopfront is from 1924.

Look for:
- Cotton Club over the wooden shopfront of 1924
- the three-light window under a continuous brick arch on the top floor

title: Huis De Pinto, the house that stopped a motorway
summary: A VOC director's house of about 1606, later the home of a Portuguese Jewish banking family. In 1968 the city bought it to pull it down for a four-lane road; squatters and campaigners held on, and in 1972 the council dropped the road by one vote.
body:
The house was built around 1606 for Jan Jansz. Carel, one of the first directors of the Dutch East India Company (VOC), on a street rather than a canal, which is rare for a house this grand. In 1651 it was bought by Isaack de Pinto, a banker and merchant from Antwerp whose Portuguese Jewish family stayed for a century. In the later 17th century it got its sandstone front, a type of facade the national register calls unique in Amsterdam. In 1696, during the undertakers' riot, the house was plundered.

After the war it stood almost alone on a cleared plain: most people of the Jewish quarter had not come back, empty houses had been stripped for firewood in the Hunger Winter, and the neighbours were demolished. The city bought it in 1968 to make way for a wide road through the Nieuwmarkt area. Campaigners squatted it, and on 5 January 1972 the council decided by one vote not to build the road and to rebuild along the old street lines. Restored in 1974–1975, it was a public library until 2012.

Today it is Huis De Pinto, a cultural centre with a reading room, open on weekdays and Saturday afternoons. The painted ceilings downstairs date from the 1975 restoration, not the 17th century.

Look for:
- the sandstone front with marble panels under the windows
- the coach-house doors of the Pintos' stables, Snoekjesgracht 32–46
- the narrow side wing and back, seen from the alley

title: Pentagon and the rebuilt Nieuwmarkt, building for the neighbourhood
summary: Where the wide Jodenbreestraat suddenly narrows, the planned motorway stopped. In its place Theo Bosch built the Pentagon over the new metro tube, on rubber blocks, with homes planned together with the residents who had fought the demolitions.
body:
Stand on the bridge over the Sint Antoniessluis. To the south the Jodenbreestraat is 40 metres wide, cleared in the 1960s for a through road; to the north the Sint Antoniesbreestraat is narrow again. The road never got past this bridge: in 1972 the council voted to rebuild along the old street lines, and after the metro riots of 1975 the city turned to small-scale building for the people who lived there.

The Pentagon (designed from 1975, finished around 1983) by Theo Bosch, with Aldo van Eyck's office, is the key building of that turn. It follows the old frontages of the Sint Antoniesbreestraat, Raamgracht and Moddermolenstraat, with gates, alleys and an inner square, and mixes social housing with shops and workshops under an arcade. Residents and action groups had a say in the plan. Because it sits on top of the metro tunnel, the foundation includes rubber blocks that cut the vibration of the trains.

Paul de Ley, who had studied with Bosch, did the same nearby: his rounded, plastered corner block at the Zwanenburgwal and Staalstraat (1984–1986) holds eleven social homes. On the Oudeschans, Herman Zeinstra slotted a glass and steel canal house into the old row in 1977–1978 as his own home and studio.

Look for:
- the exposed concrete columns and coloured panels of the Pentagon
- the bridge at the Sint Antoniessluis, as wide as the road was meant to be
- De Ley's corner at Zwanenburgwal 218–230
- Zeinstra's front at Oudeschans 3

title: Zuiderkerk, the first church built for Protestants
summary: Amsterdam's first church designed for Protestant worship, by Hendrick de Keyser, who is buried in it. Rembrandt's children were baptised and buried here, and in 1945 the dead of the Hunger Winter lay here waiting for their funerals.
body:
Building began in 1603 and the church opened at Whitsun 1611, the first in Amsterdam designed for Protestant services rather than taken over from the Catholics. The designer was the city architect Hendrick de Keyser; the tower, with its sandstone octagon and wooden lantern, was finished in 1614, and De Keyser was buried inside in 1621. Rembrandt and Saskia buried their first son here in 1636 and had Titus baptised here in 1641. Claude Monet painted the tower from the Groenburgwal in 1874.

Services ended in 1929. From February to August 1945 the bodies of Amsterdammers who died in the Hunger Winter were kept in the church until they could be buried. In the 1960s the city showed its plans for the future here with scale models, and from 1979 to 2010 the church was the city's planning information centre.

Today it is hired out for events, concerts and meetings; a church congregation also holds services, and since 2025 the Amsterdam Book Fair has been held here every year. The churchyard is now a small square, the Zuiderkerkhof.

Look for:
- the gate on the Sint Antoniesbreestraat with skulls and bones on a shroud
- the tower's top, repainted dark grey in 2017, its original colour
- Hendrick de Keyser's tombstone, if the church is open

title: Uylenburgh's corner, where Rembrandt lived first
summary: Next door to the Rembrandthuis, on this corner, stood the house of the art dealer Hendrick Uylenburgh, where Rembrandt lodged from 1631 and met his wife Saskia. The building there now was rebuilt in 1889 for a Jewish iron dealer, with the Hebrew year on its front.
body:
Most people queue at the Rembrandthuis and never look at its corner neighbour. Around 1625 the art dealer Hendrick Uylenburgh settled in the corner house here, on the Zwanenburgwal. In 1631 Rembrandt put a thousand guilders into Uylenburgh's business and moved in. Through the dealer he probably met Saskia Uylenburgh, Hendrick's cousin. After their wedding in 1634 the couple lived here until May 1635. In 1639 Rembrandt bought the house next door, now the museum.

Nothing of Uylenburgh's house is visible today. In 1889 the iron dealer K.S. van Raap had the corner rebuilt, and a stone with the year 5649, 1889 in the Jewish calendar, was set into the front. A drawing of about 1900 shows a sukkah, the leafy booth for the feast of Tabernacles, in front of the door. Before the German occupation the Jodenbreestraat, from number 1 to 105, was lived in entirely by Jewish families. This corner is one of the few older buildings left in what was the heart of the Jewish quarter. Since the late 1990s it has held four homes and a café-restaurant.

Look for:
- the stone with the Jewish year 5649
- the corner itself, seen from the bridge over the Zwanenburgwal

title: Mozes en Aäronkerk, the church named after two houses
summary: This temple-fronted church grew out of a hidden Catholic church in two houses called Moses and Aaron. A relief recalls Franz Liszt, Saint-Saëns and Widor came to play the organ, and in 1978 asylum seekers went on hunger strike inside.
body:
From 1641 Franciscan friars ran a hidden church at the back of this site, in a house on the Jodenbreestraat called Moyses, with a statue of Moses on its front. In 1682 the neighbouring house, Aäron, was bought as well, and the names stuck. The present church was built in 1837–1841 to a design by Tieleman Franciscus Suys, borrowed from an unbuilt plan for a cathedral on the Nieuwmarkt: that is why it is the only neoclassical church in the Netherlands with a front of two towers. The baroque high altar of about 1700 came from the hidden church.

The French romantic organ of 1871 drew Charles-Marie Widor and Camille Saint-Saëns. A relief on the Waterlooplein side recalls a concert visit by Franz Liszt. In 1978 a group of Moroccan workers threatened with deportation went on hunger strike in the church. It closed for worship in 1980 and became a venue for cultural events; since 2014 the Community of Sant'Egidio holds services here again.

Beside it, on the Jodenbreestraat, stands the Mozeshuis (1962–1969) by Sier van Rhijn: a low parish house built with a new idea of what a parish house was for; in those years young travellers were taken in at the church. A jury of leading architects praised it in 1970; the Franciscans still live there.

Look for:
- the statue of Melchizedek halfway up the blank back wall
- the Liszt relief on the Waterlooplein front
- the 8 December monument on the Mr. Visserplein side

title: Oudezijds Huiszittenhuis, where the poor queued for food and peat
summary: From 1655 the city's poor of the old side came to this back gate to be registered and to collect food and peat. The regents met at the front under paintings of themselves handing out charity. Architecture students have worked here since 1946.
body:
The huiszittenmeesters were city officials who looked after the 'house-sitting' poor: people with a home of their own who were not in an almshouse. For the old side of the city, food had been handed out from the Oude Kerk until 1654, when the church asked them to move. They built this house in 1654–1655 on part of the garden of the lepers' house, next to their own peat warehouses.

The regents used the stately front building for their office and meetings. The poor came in at the back, through the gate on the Nieuwe Amstelstraat, onto a covered gallery with windows where they signed up and where food and peat were handed out. The front hall still has its 17th-century wall and ceiling paintings; in the regents' room hang a regents' portrait by Bartholomeus van der Helst and paintings of the officials distributing peat and food. Poor relief here ended in 1870. The building later served as a royal printing works and an arsenal.

Since 1946 it has housed the Academie van Bouwkunst, the city's architecture school, which also uses the warehouses next door. The interior is not open to visitors; the outside and the gate are seen from the street.

Look for:
- the gate on the Nieuwe Amstelstraat with the city arms in its pediment
- the decorated stoop of the front building
- the arched windows of the back galleries, seen through the gate
- next door, the Arsenaal, where the poor relief kept its peat

title: Saaihal, the serge inspection hall with no front door
summary: In 1641 Pieter de Keyser gave the hall where serge cloth was inspected a stone front with a cornice carved as draped fabric. The hall has no door of its own: you enter through the little house next door, now a café and event space.
body:
In the 17th century Amsterdam was Europe's main wool market, and the streets around here, Raamgracht, Verversstraat, Staalstraat, are named after the cloth trade. The Saaihal was part of the Staalhof, the group of halls where the city checked the quality of cloth; some of the cloth inspectors are the men in Rembrandt's Syndics. In this hall saai, or serge, a light twilled woollen cloth, was inspected.

Pieter de Keyser, a son of Hendrick de Keyser, designed its front in 1641. It is a trapezium-shaped gable decorated with draperies, balls and the arms of Amsterdam with the imperial crown, and its cornice is carved to look like folded cloth. The front was restored in 1919–1920, when the oval stained-glass panels were put in the windows.

The hall is now part of the larger building at number 7 and has no front door of its own. Since 2005 it has been the home of the design company Droog, today @droog: a café, a shop and event spaces with a garden, which anyone can visit through the entrance next door.

Look for:
- the cornice carved as a draped cloth
- the Amsterdam arms with the imperial crown
- the oval stained-glass panels of 1919–1920

title: Jesuit house church behind a canal front (Raamgracht 6–8)
summary: Behind this sober 17th-century front, two houses hide a square galleried church that Jesuits served from 1672 to 1705. After it closed the church was split into two homes, but its columns and galleries are still inside.
body:
In 1672 Maria Theresia Tensini bought a house here, then called De Blauwe Bock, on what was still the dyers' canal. On the first and second floors of the new plot she had a house church built, a place where Catholics could worship out of sight, and it was served by Jesuits until 1705. In 1709 the prayer house was closed and turned into two separate homes behind one shared front.

The church never quite left. Inside, four wooden Doric columns still mark out the square prayer room, and a gallery with a balustrade on four more columns runs above it; a 17th-century spiral stair survives on the second floor of number 6. Number 8 is the most complete. In 1962 the building was refitted under the restoration architect P. Pals for the AVSV, a women's student society of the University of Amsterdam, and the front was restored in 1967.

From the street you see a plain cornice front with an attic storey on top, in the restrained classical style of the late 17th century, its windows and cornice altered in the 18th and 19th centuries. The interior is private and not open to visitors.

Look for:
- the one front shared by two houses
- the attic storey above the cornice
- the 19th-century changes to number 6 beside the plainer number 8

title: Montelbaanstoren, the tower that had to be pulled straight
summary: A defence tower of 1516 that lost its purpose, got a fancy top by Hendrick de Keyser in 1606, and promptly began to lean. It was pulled upright again. Its bells once rang at odd moments of their own accord, which earned it the nickname Malle Jaap.
body:
After troops from Guelders burned the shipyards of the Lastage in 1512, the city dug a new moat on its east side, today's Oudeschans, and in 1516 built this round tower beside it as a lookout towards the IJ. By the 17th century the threat had gone. In 1606 the city architect Hendrick de Keyser gave the tower an ornamental Renaissance top, bringing it to 48 metres, with a clock and bells. Around 1610 the tower, which stood on a foundation of sods, sank out of true; it had to be pulled straight and given a new stone foundation.

The name is said to come from Monte Albano, the castle the Duke of Alba wanted to build here. The nickname Malle Jaap (Silly Jaap) comes from its bells, which at times started ringing at irregular hours on their own. Rembrandt, who lived nearby, drew it in 1644; Claude Monet painted it in 1874.

The tower was threatened with demolition in 1852. From 1878 to 2006 it housed the city's water office, after which it was thoroughly restored. It is now an office and not open to visitors; the best view is from the bridge over the Waalseilandsgracht or from across the Oudeschans.

Look for:
- the wooden top with two open storeys above the octagon
- the round brick base of 1516 under De Keyser's top

title: Joodsche School nr. 1 (Van Alphenschool) and its restored neighbour
summary: In September 1941 the occupiers turned this city school into Jewish School No. 1, for Jewish children and teachers shut out of all other schools. By May 1943 so few pupils were left that it closed. Next door, a 17th-century house was being restored in the same year.
body:
The city architect A.W. Weissman designed this school in 1892, in red brick and sandstone in the neo-Dutch Renaissance style; it opened for the school year 1893–1894 on the Uilenburg side of the Oudeschans, where slums had been cleared for it. It was called the Van Alphenschool.

In September 1941 the German occupiers ordered it to become Joodsche School nr. 1, a school only for Jewish children and Jewish teachers, who were no longer allowed in other schools. The neighbourhood had many Jewish residents. As the deportations went on, the classes emptied; in May 1943 there were so few pupils left that the school was closed. A plaque on the front has recalled this since 2018. After the war it became a school again.

Next door, number 39 is one of the few old buildings on this side of the canal to survive the slum clearances. Neglected and damaged by vandals, it was restored by the city in 1941, the same year the school was turned over, with new ground-floor parts taken from elsewhere and a reconstructed stepped gable. Stones on the front say Hersteld 1941, restored 1941.

Look for:
- the 2018 plaque for Joodsche School nr. 1
- the carved owl at the top of the stepped gable, a symbol of wisdom
- the Amsterdam arms held by two lions over the entrance, with the year 1893
- the Hersteld 1941 stones on number 39

title: Second-hand gables of the 1930s
summary: In the 1930s several new houses around the Rechtboomssloot were given real 18th-century gable tops and cornices, rescued from demolished houses elsewhere. One top on the Rechtboomssloot came from a house in the Slijkstraat.
body:
At first glance these look like old canal houses. Look again: below the tops the fronts are plainly 1930s, with even rows of windows. In those years builders here reused real 18th-century tops and cornices on new fronts, so that the newcomers would sit quietly in the old rows.

At Rechtboomssloot 35 the architect J.H. Scheerboom built a house in 1937–1938 for G.W. van Lochem. Its neck gable, with crest and scroll pieces, is 18th-century and came from a house that stood at Slijkstraat 11. For the same client Scheerboom put a new front on Oudeschans 48 in 1939, because the old one had subsided, and put the probably 18th-century cornice back on top. Further along, Rechtboomssloot 97 was built in 1932 by P.J. Vloeybergh Jr. for a building company and crowned with a heavily decorated 18th-century bell gable brought from elsewhere. And on the Prins Hendrikkade, at number 103, C. de Geus designed a new front in 1938 under an old cornice of about 1800.

The houses are private homes; all four tops are easy to see from the quays.

Look for:
- the neck gable from the Slijkstraat at Rechtboomssloot 35
- the bell gable with semicircular pediment at Rechtboomssloot 97
- the reused cornice on brackets at Oudeschans 48

title: Van Kollem's clothing factory dressed as canal houses
summary: In 1934 a menswear firm built offices, stockrooms and a workshop here, and gave the building the cornice, windows and dormer of the two 18th-century houses next door, to hide what it was. Tile pictures in the basement are said to show the houses it replaced.
body:
The firm J. van Kollem, with Soesan & Przerowsky, made menswear and made-to-measure clothes and had earlier been on the Amstel. In 1934 it replaced two old houses on the Oudeschans with a building for offices, stockrooms, a workshop and dispatch: a clothing factory on a canal in the old Jewish quarter.

The architect, Simon Vieyra, made it look anything but industrial. The front is five windows wide and much bigger than its neighbours, but its height, storeys, cornice with small windows in the frieze and arched central dormer are copied from the two 18th-century houses directly to the south. The brick is a hand-made look-alike laid with deep joints, and the base is rough granite. A double stoop with an iron balustrade leads to the old main door, still with its iron grille and original lantern. According to the city register, two tile pictures in the basement show the houses that stood here before and the new building.

The building now holds apartments and is not open to visitors.

Look for:
- the cornice and dormer, matched to the two houses next door
- the granite door surround and the original lantern
- the double stoop with its iron balustrade

title: D'Oude Werf, Company warehouses on Rapenburg
summary: Two double warehouses of about 1600, built for the East India trade when the Company's yard and stores were still on Rapenburg, before they moved out to the eastern islands. Their stepped, trapezium-shaped fronts still face the harbour.
body:
Around 1600 Rapenburg was a new harbour island at the edge of the city. The East India Company (VOC) and the Admiralty had their shipyards here, with timber merchants supplying them; the street names Peperstraat and Foeliestraat (pepper and mace) recall the spice trade. In the second half of the 17th century, short of space, the Company moved its yards and warehouses to the new eastern islands, and the land along today's Prins Hendrikkade was sold for houses.

This complex, called D'Oude Werf (the old yard), is one of the things left from the first period. The national register describes it as a former East India Company warehouse complex of about 1600, later altered: two double warehouses with trapezium-shaped fronts, rows of paired windows, and on the first floor windows under arches built of large blocks. There are four wind boxes, the little roofs that protected the hoisting gear. To the right of the complex stands a small mid-17th-century gateway with pilasters and a pediment.

The warehouses are not open to visitors; the fronts are seen from the Prins Hendrikkade.

Look for:
- the four wind boxes on the fronts
- the arches of big blocks over the first-floor windows
- the little gateway with pediment beside the complex

title: Café De Druif and the corner that outlived the IJ tunnel
summary: When the approach to the IJ tunnel was cut through here in the 1960s, a photo of 1968 shows everything around this corner house gone, except the distillery café De Druif. It still pours under the old liqueur-distillery lettering.
body:
Rapenburgerplein is a small square by the lock between the Nieuwe Herengracht and the Schippersgracht. A lock and a drawbridge meant waiting, for boats and carts alike, and waiting meant customers: the city register points out that several old cafés still stand around it.

The corner house at numbers 81–83 is 18th-century, with a 19th-century roof and cornice and a wooden lean-to running round it. It stands at right angles to the rest of the square. The start of the Rapenburgerstraat was given up in the 1960s for the roads of the IJ tunnel; a photo of 1968 shows all the buildings around it gone and only this house, then numbered Rapenburgerplein 10, still standing. Café De Druif has been here for many years. The cornice reads Likeurstokerij De Druif, the door frame Distilleerderij 2e klasse P1585, and a bunch of grapes hangs outside.

Across the square, number 1 was built in 1909 as an apartment block, probably with a café on the ground floor from the start, and has a stone recording the laying of the first stone. Number 6, tall and narrow, carries a gable stone of 1726 showing Oost Beveren; it was once taken out and stored at the Rijksmuseum, then put back with new paint.

Look for:
- the distillery lettering and the grapes on De Druif
- the gable stone of Oost Beveren at number 6
- the 1909 foundation stone at number 1

title: Jewish girls' orphanage of the Rapenburgerstraat
summary: From 1861 until 1943 Jewish orphan girls grew up behind these two 18th-century fronts. The Hebrew texts in the cornices, naming the charities and the year of the extension, were restored by the residents in 2003, in memory of the girls who were deported and murdered.
body:
Jewish orphan girls in Amsterdam were at first placed with families, supported by charitable societies. In 1861 the orphanage moved into its own building here at number 171, later extended with number 169. The girls wore a uniform that made them recognisable everywhere, but they were washed, fed and clothed and had a bed of their own. Until 1930 they were trained to be maids or seamstresses; later nursing, secretarial work and teaching were added. In the 1930s the house had to grow to take in Jewish girls from abroad, some sent ahead by their parents.

In February 1943 the German occupiers cleared the orphanage. The girls who lived there were taken away and murdered.

The houses are now apartments. In 2003 the residents, with the society of friends of Amsterdam gable stones, had the gable stones and the Hebrew texts in the cornices restored. Over 171 the text names the charities Megadle Jetomot and Ma'asim Tovim and the year 1861; over 169 it reads 'and they added house to house' with the Jewish year of the extension, 1889. The cornices carry a line meaning: among good works is the upbringing of orphan girls.

Look for:
- the Hebrew lettering in both cornices
- the stone Vergroot 5649-1889 (enlarged) on number 169

title: Beth Hamidrasj Ets Haim, house of learning with a synagogue at the back
summary: In 1883 a Jewish college of learning moved into this building, with lecture rooms and a library at the front and a square synagogue behind. The front still carries the year 5643 in Arabic and Hebrew numerals; two doors down stands the Jewish infant school of 1862.
body:
Beth Hamidrasj Ets Haim, the House of Learning Tree of Life, had a study room above a synagogue in the Amstelstraat before it moved into this building in 1883. Designed by G.B. Salm and his son A. Salm, it combined a Jewish study house, a theological seminary and a synagogue. The front held a lecture hall, study rooms, a board room, classrooms, a library across the whole second floor and a caretaker's flat. Behind it lay an almost square synagogue with galleries on cast-iron columns on three sides; its ark stood in a niche framed in an oriental style and was modelled on that of the Portuguese Synagogue.

The house of learning did not survive the Second World War. After the war the building became factory space, and in 1973 it was thoroughly rebuilt, when the glass and iron bays between the old pilasters were put in. The Nieuw Israëlietisch Weekblad later had its office here until 2004. It is now offices and not open to visitors.

Two doors along, number 105 (registered as 103) was built in 1862 to a design by W.J.J. Offenberg as an infant school for poor Jewish children and turned into a religious school for girls by G.B. Salm in 1890. Its richly decorated entrance is still there.

Look for:
- the year 5643 in Arabic and Hebrew numerals on the front
- the round window over the middle bay, which once held a Star of David
- the ornate doorway of the infant school at number 105

title: Artists' studio houses in the gaps of the Jewish quarter
summary: After the deportations and the Hunger Winter, the Rapenburgerstraat was full of holes where stripped houses had been pulled down. In 1958 the city filled two of them with homes and double-height studios for artists, an experiment found nowhere else in the old centre.
body:
The two plots here became empty after the houses on them, left vacant when their Jewish residents were deported, were stripped for wood in the Hunger Winter and then demolished. After the war the old Jewish quarter was full of such gaps.

The city housing department filled two of them in 1958 with buildings by Joh. Brouwer and C.W. Schaling: homes on the upper floors and, behind a double-height front of decorative concrete, two tall artists' studios on the ground floor, with two more studios in each roof under big skylights. Studio homes were an ideal of post-war housing that was hardly ever built; as far as is known this was a unique experiment in the old inner city. The beauty committee called it very successful building in a street that had fallen into such decay. The architects said that whoever builds in an old setting should keep to the old plot sizes and materials.

In fact the buildings look like slices of a 1950s block of flats; only the tall concrete fronts nod to the old street. More studios were built in the back gardens, to the annoyance of the planner Cornelis van Eesteren.

Look for:
- the double-height concrete fronts of the ground-floor studios
- the large skylights in the roofs
- the narrower building at 77–81 and the wider one at 93–97

title: Valkenburgerstraat 202–210, the street's last old building
summary: The Valkenburgerstraat was a crowded Jewish street of slums and alleys until clearances in the 1920s and the IJ tunnel in the 1960s swept it away. This one housing block of 1877, built for a Jewish owner, is all that is left of the old street.
body:
The Valkenburgerstraat ran down the middle of the island of Marken, in the heart of the Jewish quarter. In 1926 the city called it a disgrace and planned to declare 532 dwellings unfit; at house number 195 more than 300 people had lived in 39 one-room homes in a single alley, without running water or sewers. Clearance came first. Then, from the 1950s, the street was sacrificed for an 18-metre-wide approach road to the IJ tunnel, and in 1968 the Markengracht behind it was filled in.

This block of 1877 survived both. It was built for a Jewish owner, with shops on the ground floor and homes above: three in the middle bay and six in each side wing, each with a front and back room, box beds, a wall of cupboards and a kitchen at the back, good for the standards of 1877. After the war the homes were made habitable again with few changes to the layout. The city register calls it the last surviving monument in the street.

The fronts show rich brickwork in the revival styles of the time. Tall pilasters that once rose high above the cornice were removed in the later 20th century, and the shopfronts have been heavily altered. The flats are private.

Look for:
- the symmetrical brick front with its slightly projecting side wings
- the wide passage on the south side that led to the back yard

title: Stadsbank van Lening (the city pawnshop)
summary: Amsterdam has run its own pawnshop here since 1614, and it still takes in gold and watches. The poet Vondel worked at the counter for ten years, and a rhyme of 1740 over the gate tells you not to bother coming in without a pledge.
body:
The city's pawnshop opened in 1614 to put a stop to the usury that was spreading in the city. It moved into two buildings between the Oudezijds Voorburgwal and the Nes: a peat warehouse of 1550 and the north wing of the former Maria Magdalena convent, emptied after the city turned Protestant in 1578. A third block followed in 1669. In 1658 the poet Joost van den Vondel was given a job here as a clerk; he stayed more than ten years.

It is still a municipal bank and still lends money against a pledge, now only jewellery, gold, silver, diamonds and watches. Pledges have nine months; what is not redeemed is auctioned, since 2021 online. The office is open to the public.

Over the gate on the canal side is a rhyme written by Balthazar Huydecoper in 1740. It opens: "Hebt gy noch geld, noch goed: gaa deze deur voorby" (if you have neither money nor goods, walk past this door), and ends by calling the bank the grave of usury.

The footbridge in front of it is the Lommertbrug, named after the bank (a lommerd is a pawnshop). Piet Kramer rebuilt it in 1926.

Look for:
- the rhyme on the board over the gate at Oudezijds Voorburgwal 300
- the memorial stone of 1614 and the carved little gate in the side wall on the Enge Lombardsteeg
- Kramer's granite steps and the wrought-iron ends of the railings on the Lommertbrug

title: Makelaarsbruggetje (the tobacco brokers' bridge)
summary: A footbridge a tobacco broker built for himself in 1893, so he and his colleagues could get from their offices to the tobacco auction in Frascati without a detour. They paid for it, kept it clear and even paid the city rent for the water under it.
body:
In 1893 the tobacco broker Frederik Olie had a bridge built over the Oudezijds Voorburgwal at his own initiative. The tobacco traders had their offices on the odd-numbered side of the canal; the auction was held in Frascati on the Nes, at the end of the Sint Barberenstraat. The bridge gave them a straight line. Olie and his colleagues had to pay for it, maintain it and keep it free for people on foot, and they paid the city a yearly rent for the ground and the water its piers stood in. In 1907 the city took it over.

It sits high above the water, because boats still had to pass under it, while the quays here are low: hence the steps at both ends. Unusually, even the piers were cast iron, poured by the Hilversumsche IJzergieterij. When the bridge was worn out in 1991 the span and railings were redone in steel, and the rest was kept. Amsterdammers also called it the Tabaksbruggetje and the brug der Tabakieten (bridge of the tobacco men).

It is a public footbridge between the Sint Barberenstraat and the east quay.

Look for:
- the name MAKELAARSBRUGGETJE in cast-iron capitals on the parapet at the east end
- the decorated cast-iron uprights on the piers, just above the waterline
- the steps up from both quays

title: The Nes, Amsterdam's tobacco street
summary: Around 1900 the dance halls of the Nes made way for tobacco: brokers' offices with sample rooms under saw-tooth roofs, and an auction in Frascati. The trade has gone, the theatres came back, and the fronts still talk tobacco, one of them in 18th-century spelling.
body:
In the 19th century the Nes was a street for a night out, with singing cafés and variety halls. Around 1900 most of them had closed and tobacco offices had taken their place. The leaf came from the colonies, first through the VOC and later through the Nederlandsche Handel-Maatschappij and plantation companies in Deli, on Sumatra. From 1879 it was auctioned in Frascati. The first-hand brokers sat in sample rooms, where buyers judged the leaf in even light from above, under saw-tooth roofs.

Nes 73-87, now the Tobacco Theater, was built in 1906–1907 as a tobacco office and works, with a smart Jugendstil front on the Nes and a plain working side on the alley Gebed zonder End. After the tobacco left, the auctioneers Mak van Waay held sales here into the 1960s. On Rokin 111 the Internationale Tabaksplantmaatschappij put up a stone office in 1920–1923, crowned with a barrel of tobacco plants; the company went bankrupt in 1922. The Nes is a theatre street again.

The street is public; Frascati and the Tobacco Theater can be visited on performance nights.

Look for:
- on Nes 39: "Hier doet men in gedrooghde blaedjes" (dried leaves sold here) and "1710 Van ouds d'Vogelkooy 1910"
- on Nes 112-114: a sandstone door frame carved with tobacco leaves
- on Grimburgwal 1-5: stained glass with men carrying bales of tobacco
- the barrel of tobacco plants on top of Rokin 111, seen from the Rokin

title: Oudemanhuispoort and its book stalls
summary: A covered passage through a former old people's home, lined since 1757 with little shop cupboards behind wooden shutters. Booksellers have traded from them since 1879; until 1941 most were Jewish, and only two came back after the war.
body:
Around 1601 the city built a home for elderly men and women here, where old Amsterdammers could buy a place for life. When it was rebuilt in 1754–1757, eighteen shop cupboards (winkelkasten) were set into the wall of the passage between the Oudezijds Achterburgwal and the Kloveniersburgwal, let out to dealers in gold, silver, books and trinkets. In 1879 the book market on the Botermarkt (now Rembrandtplein) was closed down and its booksellers moved into the passage. They are still there: fourteen cupboards are in use, since number 6 was knocked through in 1979 to make a doorway.

Until 1941 the trade was mainly in the hands of Jewish booksellers. Under the occupation they were driven out, deported and murdered. Only Betsy and Jacques van Kollem survived and came back to the passage for some years. From 1877 to the early 1970s Italian knife grinders also worked here, sharpening scissors, knives and skates.

The university has used the buildings since 1880. In 1925–1927 P.L. Marnette of the city's public works department added a wing in Amsterdam School style on the Kloveniersburgwal, called De Schaats (the skate) after the shape of its big ground-floor window.

The passage is public; the courtyard opens off it during university hours.

Look for:
- the numbered cupboards with their hinged shutters
- the gate of 1786 on the Kloveniersburgwal, with sculpture by Anthonie Ziesenis
- the skate-shaped window in the Kloveniersburgwal front of De Schaats

title: Binnengasthuis, from dreaded hospital to university library
summary: For three centuries this was the city hospital, and in the 19th century a notorious one: 600 patients and two doctors, and childbed fever that quadrupled once surgeons and midwives shared hands. Its surgical clinic became the university library in 2025.
body:
After the Reformation of 1578 the city moved its hospitals into empty convents here, and from 1635 the whole was called the Binnengasthuis (inner hospital). In the 19th century it had a bad name. After a surgery department opened in 1828, deaths from childbed fever on the maternity ward went up fourfold: students cut corpses and then delivered babies without washing their hands. Antiseptic medicine only got its chance after 1880.

The buildings that stand now came with the rebuilding of 1868–1913, starting with a new maternity clinic on the Turfdraagsterpad. F.W.M. Poggenbeek's Second Surgical Clinic dates from 1897–1900, with a nurses' home. J.M. van der Mey's administration building of 1912–1914, in early Amsterdam School style, had a children's clinic as its southern half; that was demolished in 1991.

The hospital merged into the AMC in 1981 and the university took over. On 1 September 2025 the surgical clinic opened as the new University Library, with a glass roof over its courtyard.

Look for:
- a carved baby under the letters SPQA at the top of Van der Mey's front on the Grimburgwal
- the gate with T GASTHVISHOF (1732) in the front of the former St Bernardus home, Oude Turfmarkt 139
- the long brick front of the clinic and nurses' home on the Kloveniersburgwal
- 1875 on the clock turret of the old waiting rooms, Oudezijds Achterburgwal 235–237, and MANNENKLINIEK and VROUWENKLINIEK on the clinic beside it, plus GASTHUIS-APOTHEEK in the frieze of Kloveniersburgwal 80

title: Barndesteeg, the penitents' convent and the mission hostel
summary: In an alley of the red-light district stands the last wing of a 15th-century convent founded for 'fallen' women, later a hidden church. Across the alley, a Christian charity that also helps people leave prostitution runs a youth hostel in its old school.
body:
The Bethaniënklooster, the convent of Mary Magdalene of Bethany, came inside the city walls by 1425. It was a house of Augustinian nuns where women who had lived a "loose life" could do penance, but it became fashionable with the well-off, and by 1462 some 220 women lived here. The nuns also fattened cattle for the banquets of the civic guards, which is how the nearby Koestraat (cow street) got its name.

After the city turned Protestant in 1578 the convent was seized and in 1585 the order was dissolved. From 1705 the wing on the Barndesteeg was an Old Catholic hidden church, De Ooievaar (the stork): the floor between refectory and dormitory was taken out to make one tall space. In the 1970s the derelict building was restored and used for concerts; since 2017 it has been a bed and breakfast, open to its guests. Under it lies a vaulted Gothic cellar from about 1450.

Opposite, at Barndesteeg 21-25, the society Tot Heil des Volks (for the salvation of the people), founded in 1855 by the Mennonite preacher Jan de Liefde, built a nursery school in 1915. Since 1972 the society has run it as a youth hostel. Since 1985 its project Scharlaken Koord has helped people working in prostitution.

Look for:
- the entrance gate of the convent at Barndesteeg 6
- the plastered fronts of the convent wing at numbers 4 to 12
- the three separate doors of the 1915 school, for school, board and caretaker

title: Wijnkopersgildehuis (wine merchants' guild house)
summary: One of the few guild houses left in Amsterdam, with what are said to be the oldest neck gables in the city. Its rescue in 1917, when thirteen families lived inside, led to the founding of the Vereniging Hendrick de Keyser.
body:
Three houses of about 1551 were pulled together behind one new front in 1611 by a speculator, Claes Jansz Geus, and from 1613 the building was an inn. In 1630 the wine merchants' guild bought it and had the city architect Pieter de Keyser rebuild it. From 1633 the right-hand half, Koestraat 10, was the guild house, with a meeting room at the front, a guild hall at the back and big cellars; the left half became a home.

The guilds were abolished in 1798, and the house went downhill: theatre hall, workshop, cheap lodgings. When the wine merchant Jacobus Boelen bought number 10 in 1917, thirteen families lived in it. He bought number 12 as well and restored both, and the purchase led in 1918 to the founding of the Vereniging Hendrick de Keyser, the society that buys and restores historic houses; Boelen was its first chairman. The society bought the building in 1947. From 1952 it housed a museum of medical history and from 1961 a wine museum; now it is let as a home with a studio and is not open.

Look for:
- the three neck gables, rebuilt in the 20th-century restoration, over a front with little sandstone blocks
- Pieter de Keyser's gate of 1633: its pediment shows Pope Urban I, patron saint of winegrowing, who replaced an earlier Bacchus on a barrel

title: Klein Trippenhuis (the little Trip house)
summary: Opposite the 22-metre-wide Trippenhuis stands a house of about two and a half metres, dated 1696. The story says the Trips' servant wished for a house as wide as his masters' front door and got one. The dates say otherwise.
body:
Across the canal stands the Trippenhuis, built in 1662 for the arms dealers Louys and Hendrick Trip, 22 metres wide. Kloveniersburgwal 26 is roughly two and a half metres wide and for years was listed as the narrowest front in Amsterdam, until Singel 166 turned out to be 70 centimetres narrower.

The best-known tale: a servant of the Trips sighed that he would be happy with a house as wide as his masters' door, a Trip overheard him, and built it with the leftover stone. Other versions involve a bet or a mistress. None of it fits. The little house is dated 1696, 34 years after the big one, and both brothers were dead by then. The narrow front is usually put down to tax, which was charged on the width of the front: the house is twelve metres deep and almost seven metres wide at the back, where it wraps around its neighbour, numbers 22-24. Its design is attributed to Justus Vingboons, the architect of the Trippenhuis.

Number 22-24 next door is two 18th-century houses that a clothing dealer, Izaak Levison, joined under one cornice and roof in 1900. Both have shops below and homes above; look from the quay.

Look for:
- the sandstone front with its carved curved top, and the year 1696
- sphinxes with women's heads, grapes, sunflowers and an hourglass, attributed to the sculptor Jan Gijselingh the younger
- next door, the different window patterns of 22 and 24 under one cornice

title: Kleinste huis (the smallest house), Oude Hoogstraat 22
summary: A complete canal house in miniature, two metres wide and five deep, half built onto the gate of the Walloon Church. The city squeezed it onto a ten-square-metre leftover plot in the 1730s; today it is a tea shop.
body:
When a house called Koning David was pulled down in 1733 to make room for the present number 20, the city kept the scrap of ground that was left over: about ten square metres. By 1738 a house stood on it, because that year the city first paid tax for the spot. In 1742 it was let for 150 guilders a year to a clockmaker, Jan Tenking. At first it had only a ground floor; the upper floor and the little attic were added between 1768 and 1787.

It is 2.02 metres wide and 5 metres deep, with a bell-shaped top of the 19th century, and part of its front rests on the gate beside it. That gate, of 1616 and attributed to Hendrick de Keyser, leads to the Walloon Church and was the way funerals came in. Some call the house the smallest in Europe; it is not even the narrowest in Amsterdam, a title held by Generaal Vetterstraat 18b at 1.80 metres.

It is now a tea shop, Het Kleinste Huis, open Wednesday to Saturday from 11.00 to 17.30, so you can step inside.

Look for:
- the bell-shaped top, a canal house shrunk to fit
- the gate to the Walloon Church to its left, and where the house leans onto it
- the Oost-Indisch Huis next door, for scale

title: Oost-Indisch Huis (East India House)
summary: The first building put up for the Dutch East India Company, where its directors, the Heren XVII, usually met, crews were signed on and the company's maps were kept. A gate on the Oude Hoogstraat leads through a tunnel into its courtyard.
body:
The Amsterdam chamber of the VOC, the company that held the Dutch monopoly on trade with Asia, first used part of the city's arsenal on the Kloveniersburgwal as a warehouse. For offices and meetings it built this house next door in 1606, on the old orchard of the Sint-Paulusbroeders monastery: the first building made for the company. The twenty directors of the Amsterdam chamber met here, and usually also the Heren XVII, the company's central board. Crews were recruited here and the archives and maps were kept here.

After the VOC was wound up in 1798, the house served until 1808 as the seat of colonial administration of the Batavian Republic, and later it was a tax office, until 1958. Since the 1960s it has belonged to the university. In 1998 the lost 17th-century directors' room was reconstructed inside.

Behind it, on the Korte Spinhuissteeg, is the Sint-Jorishof: what is left of the monastery garden, which after 1578 became a home for old men given lifelong care. Its west wing is dated 1747.

The courtyard is reached through the gate on the Oude Hoogstraat; the building is in university use.

Look for:
- the gate with Tuscan half-columns on the Oude Hoogstraat and the vaulted tunnel behind it
- the gables around the courtyard, among them a trapezium-shaped one of 1606, with bands and small blocks of light stone
- the square turret with its curved spire over the Sint-Jorishof wing on the Dwars Spinhuissteeg

title: Compagnietheater (former Restored Lutheran Church)
summary: A church built in 1793 for Lutherans who broke away to keep 'the old light', on the site of the city's madhouse. When they reunited, the pulpit went to Elst and the organ to Arnhem; the empty church became a theatre, and is now offices.
body:
