In the late 18th century the Lutherans of Amsterdam split. The breakaway Hersteld Evangelisch-Lutherse gemeente (Restored Evangelical Lutheran congregation), the people "of the old light", had this church built in 1792–1793 to a design by the city architect Abraham van der Hart. It went up on the site of the former dolhuis, the city's madhouse. Anthonie Ziesenis carved the group of figures on the front, standing for steadfast faith; under the pediment it once said "Zij bleven volstandig in de leere der Apostelen" (they continued steadfastly in the apostles' doctrine).

The two Lutheran churches reunited in 1952 and services here stopped in 1956. For some years De Nederlandsche Bank kept its archive inside. The fittings left: the pulpit went to the Grote Kerk in Elst, and the organ by Johannes Stephanus Strümphler (1794–1796), his most important instrument, went in 1961 to the Eusebiuskerk in Arnhem, which had lost its own in the Battle of Arnhem. It is still played there.

In 1995–1996 Francine Houben of Mecanoo turned the church into a theatre, the home of Theu Boermans's company De Trust and later De Theatercompagnie. The theatre left and the building was sold in 2021. In 2024–2025 it became offices, called Venue, with new floors standing free in the old church hall. You see the front from the canal.

Look for:
- the pilasters and pediment on the canal front, and Ziesenis's sculpture group
- the three doorways with their stone frames

title: Allard Pierson, in the old Nederlandsche Bank
summary: For a hundred years the Dutch central bank ran the country's money from this sandstone palace on the Rokin. Since 1976 it has held the university's antiquities, a collection that began with a professor's plaster casts.
body:
De Nederlandsche Bank had long been on the Oude Turfmarkt, spread over nine small houses side by side. In 1865–1869 six of them made way for a proper head office, designed by W.A. Froger, though the builders reused their foundations and parts of their walls. The new front was all sandstone, with side wings and a central block under a pediment. The register counts it among the most important and monumental early office buildings in the Netherlands.

The bank stayed until 1968, when it moved to the Frederiksplein. The university, which already owned much of the neighbourhood, bought the building and gave it to its archaeological museum. After a conversion overseen by the designer Dick Elffers, Princess Beatrix opened it in October 1976. The museum is named after Allard Pierson (1831–1896), a preacher who left the church, became the university's first professor of art history and built up a collection of plaster casts of classical sculpture.

The museum, now simply called Allard Pierson, is open Tuesday to Sunday from 10.00 to 17.00.

Look for:
- the sandstone front with its pediment and projecting wings
- the canal side of the Rokin opposite, from where the whole front is in view

title: Rederij Kooij ticket booth
summary: A one-room ticket office for canal tours, built in 1937 in travertine, bronze and copper, when the filling-in of the Rokin pushed the boat company to this corner. The shopkeepers of the Rokin were so pleased they gave it a barometer.
body:
Piet Kooij started his canal-tour company in 1922, on the stretch of the Rokin that was filled in in 1936–1937. Forced to move, he set up at the open water on this corner, and had a ticket booth and landing stage built as one piece. Nobody skimped: the little building and the flood wall are clad in travertine, the column under the rounded canopy is sheathed in bronze, the roof edge is copper and the window bars are steel. The city register reads it as a sign of how much the canal tour already counted for, or of Kooij's enterprising spirit.

The neighbours agreed. The shopkeepers' association of the Rokin, already dealers in art and antiques, gave a bronze plaque with a barometer, presumably glad of the customers the boats brought. Visitors still buy their tickets at the window and go straight down the steps under the canopy to the boats; Rederij Kooij still sails from here, still owned by the Kooij family.

Look for:
- the bronze plaque and barometer: "Aangeboden door de vereeniging Rokin 1938"
- the lamp over the window with "kassa" (till) on the milk glass and an arrow below
- the bronze open letters and the sign under the canopy: "Rondvaart IJ-havens en grachten"
- the round windows with crossed bars, one in the wall that runs down into the water

title: Doelen Hotel, where the Night Watch used to hang
summary: This hotel stands on the site of the civic guards' headquarters where Rembrandt's Night Watch hung until 1715. Empress Sisi came here for massage cures, the Beatles took the whole first floor, and the city's first tour boat left from its door.
body:
A tower of the medieval city wall, Swych Utrecht, stood here, built against the bishops of Utrecht. From 1522 it belonged to the Kloveniersdoelen, the headquarters and shooting range of the kloveniers, the civic guard armed with arquebuses. In 1638 the doelen got a smart new wing, and in its great hall hung the guard's group portraits, among them Rembrandt's company of captain Frans Banning Cocq, the Night Watch, until 1715.

In 1815 the doelen became a hotel. Its owner J.F. Hahn had it pulled down in 1882 and replaced by the present building by J.F. van Hamersveld, ready for the colonial exhibition of 1883; the old tower went too, though parts of the old walls and foundations were built into the new hotel. The Empress Elisabeth of Austria, Sisi, stayed here in 1884 and 1885 while she was treated by the Dutch masseur Johann Georg Mezger. In 1909 the first tour boat of Amsterdam, De Tourist, started sailing from the hotel. On 5 and 6 June 1964 the Beatles had the whole first floor.

It is still a hotel, since 2023 the Tivoli Doelen.

Look for:
- the gable stone by J.H. Teixeira de Mattos showing the tower Swych Utrecht
- the domed turret on the Amstel side, a nod to the tower, with civic guards on its clock face
- the conservatory of 1889 over the Binnen-Amstel

title: Aluminiumbrug (the aluminium bridge)
address: Kloveniersburgwal, between Nieuwe Doelenstraat and Staalstraat
summary: In 1955 this drawbridge over the Kloveniersburgwal got the first aluminium bridge deck in the Netherlands: barely heavier than the old one, five times as strong, and 130,000 guilders cheaper. Today the danger is padlocks.
body:
A bridge has crossed here since at least 1599. It used to be called the Dwingerbrug, after the tower Swych Utrecht that stood at its western end, where the Doelen Hotel is now. The present drawbridge with three openings was built in 1896 by the city's public works department.

By 1955 it had rusted so badly that heavy traffic was a risk, and the city chose to replace the moving part with aluminium, a first in the Netherlands. Work began on 29 August 1955. The bridge was widened from 7.40 to 8.60 metres, and the new deck of 13.5 tonnes weighed hardly more than the old one of 13 tonnes but was reckoned five times as strong. The choice saved about 130,000 guilders. By the time it was finished six bridges like it already existed elsewhere in the world, but the name stuck to this one.

The bridge no longer opens. In recent years tourists have hung love padlocks on it, a real load on such a light structure.

Look for:
- the riveted steel portal and the lattice counterweight over the middle opening
- the quadrant gear that once lifted the deck
- railings in three patterns, of steel and wrought iron

title: De L'Europe and its answering corner
summary: The grand hotel on the Amstel follows the curve of the Rondeel, a round gun tower of the city wall that stood here until 1633. Hitchcock used it as a film location just before the war, and the architect gave the corner opposite a spire to answer his own round bay.
body:
Around 1480 the city wall got a half-round tower here on the east bank of the Amstel, the Rondeel, whose guns covered the way into the city by river. It was pulled down in 1633, and five years later an inn named after it took its place. In 1895 the inn, by then Hotel Rondeel, was demolished for the Hotel de l'Europe, opened in 1896 to a design by W. Hamer, the architect of the Vondelpark pavilion. The curve of the Rondeel still shapes the hotel's front along the Amstel.

Alfred Hitchcock used the hotel as a location for Foreign Correspondent (1940), shot just before the war; during the occupation it was used by German officers. Its bar is named after Freddy Heineken. It is still a five-star hotel, now called De L'Europe Amsterdam, with a terrace on the river.

Hamer also designed the corner house opposite, Oude Turfmarkt 153, in 1898. On the hotel he stressed the corner with a round bay; across the street he drew the eye away from the corner to a dormer on the Oude Turfmarkt side worked up into a little spire.

Look for:
- the curved front on the Amstel side, best seen from the Muntplein or the Rokin
- the round corner bay of the hotel, and opposite, the spire-topped dormer of Oude Turfmarkt 153
- the former Labouchère Oyens bank of 1889–90 at Nieuwe Doelenstraat 12–14, part of the hotel since 2010

title: Café De Jaren, in the old securities bank
summary: A big, light café on the Amstel in a bank building of 1906, whose business was keeping other people's bonds and bills safe. The bank's initials still sit high over the door and its vaults are still in the cellar.
body:
The building belonged to the brokers Mendes Gans until 1906, when the architect Willem Hamer jr. rebuilt it for the Ontvang- en Betaalkas (receiving and paying office), an institution that kept securities such as bills and bonds for a fee. The Kas-Vereeniging took it over in 1929. Behind it, the listed part on the river is an 18th-century wing under a hipped roof.

On 4 July 1990 Joseph Jansen opened café De Jaren here, with fresh food, no deep fryer so the place would not smell of chips, a reading table with good magazines and foreign papers, and at first an unlimited salad buffet. In 1999 a trade jury named it the best café in the Netherlands. It serves as the festival café of IDFA, the documentary film festival.

It is open as a café and restaurant. At the back, a terrace on a pontoon lies right on the Amstel, and upstairs there is a balcony terrace.

Look for:
- the initials O & B high above the entrance
- the 18th-century rear wing with its curved dormer, seen from the water side
- the low terrace on the pontoon, where boats can moor

title: Beursplein 5, the stock exchange that left Berlage
summary: Ten years after Berlage's Beurs opened, the stock traders moved out to their own building across the square: Beursplein 5, opened in 1913, with a direct line to New York from 1922. Berlage's lanterns and fountains stand between the two.
body:
Berlage's exchange on the Damrak opened in 1903, but share trading grew too fast for it. The Vereeniging voor den Effectenhandel, the stock dealers' association, borrowed three million guilders and had Jos Cuypers design a building of its own on the east side of the square, where the Bible Hotel had stood until 1911. It opened on 22 December 1913 and trading started on 2 January 1914. The trading floor of 1,350 square metres was upstairs, with state telephone and telegraph offices beside it; from 1922 there was a direct line to the New York exchange. In 1930 the post office in the building became a men's barber's.

From 1988 orders could be entered by computer, and in time screen trading made the floor redundant. Options traders took it over in 1998 and left within four years. The address lived on as shorthand for the market: a book on fifty years of Dutch share trading is called Het geheim van Beursplein 5.

On the square stand six cast-iron lanterns and two granite fountains that Berlage designed with his exchange. He wanted them lit by electric arc lamps; until the city's first power station was ready in 1904, the exchange had its own generator.

Look for:
- C.A. Stout's sculpture group of 1924 in the pediment, an allegory of the exchange
- the bronze bull in front of the entrance
- the ring of rosettes halfway up each lantern, once fitted with little bulbs and now empty

title: Accijnshuis (the excise house)
summary: The only city board that did not sit in the town hall collected its taxes on beer, grain, wine, peat and spices here, at the old harbour on the Damrak. After 1800 it became a pub, for decades the haunt of barge skippers.
body:
The Accijnshuis was built in 1637–1638 in classical style, at the end of the Oude Brug over the Damrak, the medieval harbour of the city. It is attributed to Jacob van Campen, the architect of the town hall on the Dam, and also to Pieter de Keyser. Here a board of five excise masters collected the duties due on ship cargoes of grain, beer, wine, peat, coal and spices. It was the only city board that did not sit in the town hall.

Around 1800, in the French period, a national tax system came in and the house lost its job. It became a café, from 1924 called Het Wapen van Amsterdam and popular with inland skippers. When the skippers' exchange moved to the Houthaven at the end of the 1980s, the customers went with it and the café had to close; another café opened here in 1997. The building originally had two storeys; the floor above the cornice is a later addition.

Look for:
- the sandstone Ionic pilasters running up the brick fronts
- over the left door the city seal, a cog ship, and over the right door the city arms with three St Andrew's crosses, each with two carved lions
- the ground-floor windows on the west side, with triangular and curved pediments in turn

title: Industria and the Beurspoortje
summary: A gentlemen's club for industry built in 1913–1916 on the corner of the Dam, with a public passage through its belly. Digging its foundations, the builders hit a medieval lock in the old dam across the Amstel.
body:
De Industrieele Club was founded in 1913 as a national meeting place for the growing Dutch industry and trade, and at once asked Foeke Kuipers, a pupil of Berlage, for a clubhouse. He designed both the building and its interior. Shops went on the ground floor, among them a cigar store called Industria; upstairs were a club restaurant, a reading room and meeting rooms.

The site was that of the old Beurspoortje, the narrow passage from the Dam to Hendrick de Keyser's exchange on the Rokin. Kuipers kept the route and widened it: the Beurspoortje now runs through the building. While the foundations were dug in 1913, the builders found remains of a medieval lock, part of the dam in the Amstel that once separated the Rokin from the Damrak. The new block also settled a long argument about how to close off the Rokin side of the Dam.

The club merged in 1976 with De Groote Club and has been royal since 2013. Since a restoration in 2017 the upper floors also hold a separate hotel, TwentySeven, and the ground floor a jeweller. The club rooms are private; the passage is public.

Look for:
- INDUSTRIA in black letters over the round-arched entrance on the Dam
- the barrel-vaulted porch of light brown brick with glazed tiles set in, and the ornate iron doors
- the Beurspoortje passage running through the building

title: Ship Chandlers Warehouse (Het Tabaksvat)
summary: A house by the Schreierstoren with a tobacco barrel carved over the door, from its days as a tobacco shop. In 1804 a grocer from Overijssel turned it into a ship's chandlery, and his family built a shipping line from here.
body:
The house at Geldersekade 8 was known as Het Tabaksvat (the tobacco barrel), and around 1775 it got a new front with a rococo ornament of a tobacco pot and tobacco leaves over the door. Downstairs was a tobacco shop.

In 1804 Jan Vinke from Overijssel bought it, opened a grocery and sold everything ships needed for long voyages; the name Ship Chandlers Warehouse went up on the front. The business made a fortune. In 1860 Albertus Vinke founded the shipping and cargo-broking firm Vinke & Co. here, which bought the neighbouring houses and opened offices in Rotterdam, Antwerp and South Africa. In the 1930s it became one of the main Dutch tramp shipping firms, and from 1946 to 1966 it also managed a whaling company. In 1985 all activity stopped and the ships were sold.

The building is now a private dining venue, so the inside is open only to guests; the front is best seen from the quay.

Look for:
- the carved tobacco pot and leaves over the door
- the carved cornice at the top and the carved shop cornice and door frame below
- the name Ship Chandlers Warehouse on the front

title: Spinhuis, the women's prison and its whipping gate
summary: From 1597 Amsterdam locked up beggar girls, drunk women and prostitutes here to spin and sew, paid for by a levy on every tavern in town. The gate in the alley still shows two women being whipped, with a verse by Hooft that says it is all for their own good.
body:
In 1597 the city turned part of the former Saint Ursula convent into a spinhuis, a house of correction for women. Girls found begging in the streets were brought in at once and set to spin flax and wool; women caught drunk, in a brothel or in adultery followed. Those convicted of theft were kept apart and made to read the Bible aloud. The bill was partly paid by anyone in the city who sold drink or tobacco: they needed a licence and owed the Spinhuis a fee every three months.

The building burned down in 1643 through the carelessness of inmates. The front of its 1645 replacement still stands on the Oudezijds Achterburgwal. The prison moved out in 1782, and the house later served as police headquarters and as a university faculty. Part of it was squatted in 2014; since 2016 it has housed research institutes of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences.

The gate in the Spinhuissteeg carries a relief attributed to Hendrick de Keyser of two women being flogged, and two lines by the poet P.C. Hooft: "Don't be afraid, I don't avenge evil but force you to good; my hand is strict but my heart is kind." It left with the prison in 1782 and came back in 1911.

Look for:
- the relief and Hooft's verse over the gate in the Spinhuissteeg
- the lions, shield and crown on the gate, copies and a reconstruction from 2010
- the 1645 front with festoons and a pediment on the canal

title: Hildo Krop's shouting urinal (Oudezijds Voorburgwal)
summary: A brick urinal of 1926 rising out of the canal wall, opposite what was then the city hall. On its roof Hildo Krop carved a street orator with a clenched fist and open mouth, and on the back a row of heads, all shouting.
body:
When the city's Public Works department was building a new Amsterdam School wing for the city hall on the Oudezijds Voorburgwal, it gave the quay opposite a matching urinal. Allard Remco Hulshoff, who designed the wing, drew it in 1926 as a stone version of the iron plaskrul (the curled street urinal) of Jo van der Mey: an oval stone base, a lattice of brick above it and a flat round roof. It stands on a steel footplate and rises out of the water's edge.

The new city hall wing has galleries of sculpture, and the urinal got some too. Over the entrance Hildo Krop, the city sculptor, put a grey stone figure of a volksredenaar, a soapbox orator, with a clenched right fist and his mouth wide open: a nod to the council chamber across the water. On the other side are several heads, mouths open as well.

It was listed as a national monument in 2001 as a rare piece of Amsterdam School street furniture. It is still a public urinal, for men only. The city hall moved out in 1988; the building opposite is now the Sofitel The Grand hotel.

Look for:
- the orator with the clenched fist over the entrance
- the open-mouthed heads on the back
- the small arched frieze on the wall beside the entrance

title: Prinsenhof, convent, admiralty and city hall (now The Grand)
summary: A convent became a lodging for princes in 1578, then the Admiralty's offices, and from 1808 to 1988 Amsterdam's city hall, after Louis Napoleon took the one on the Dam as his palace. Since then it has been a hotel, still with Neptune in the pediment.
body:
After the city turned Protestant in 1578, the convent of Saint Cecilia was made a lodging for high guests, and from about 1581 it was called the Prinsenhof, possibly after a stay by William of Orange. Leicester, Maurice and Frederick Henry slept here, and so did Marie de' Medici in 1638. The Admiralty of Amsterdam moved in, and in 1661 it rebuilt the main wing with a tall pilaster front. Jan Gijseling carved the pediment, with Neptune and a lion holding the Admiralty's arms.

When the city hall on the Dam burned in 1652 the burgomasters camped here for a few years. They came back for good in 1808, when Louis Napoleon took the Dam building as his royal palace. It remained the city hall until the Stopera opened in 1988. A new wing on the Oudezijds Voorburgwal was added in 1924–1926 in Amsterdam School style, with rows of carved heads. The roof turret over the Prinsenhofsteeg wing still recalls the convent chapel.

Today it is the Sofitel The Grand hotel; the courtyard is reached through the gate on the canal.

Look for:
- Neptune and the Admiralty lion in the pediment of the main wing, seen from the courtyard
- the little roof turret of the old convent chapel, with a clock face on the courtyard side
- the 1926 wing on the canal with its sculpted galleries

title: Agnietenkapel, where the university began, and the Purperhoedenveem
summary: A convent chapel of 1470 where Amsterdam's first professors lectured in Latin from 1632, with the city library in the attic and the Admiralty's arsenal downstairs. Next door, a 1909 office still wears the name of a warehouse company named after purple hats.
body:
The double chapel of 1470 belonged to a convent of Franciscan sisters of Saint Agnes. It was one of the few Catholic buildings in the city that survived the takeover of 1578 with a new use. In 1631 it became the Athenaeum Illustre, the forerunner of the University of Amsterdam; Vossius and Barlaeus gave their opening lectures here in January 1632. The lectures in the hall upstairs, the oldest lecture room in Amsterdam, were in Latin and open to anyone. The ground floor was the Admiralty's arsenal until 1656, and the city library sat in the attic.

The school moved out in 1864. The chapel was a primary school, then from 1921 the university museum, and since its restoration of 2004–2007 the UvA uses it for PhD ceremonies, farewell lectures and conferences.

The neighbour at no. 229 was built in 1909 to a design by P. Heyn for the Purperhoedenveem. The Amsterdam veem companies, warehouse firms with late-medieval roots, were named after hats: blue, fur, purple. Today the building carries the chapel's lift.

Look for:
- the richly carved gate of 1571, moved here in 1921 from the city carpenters' yard
- the tile panel "naaml. venn. Purperhoedenveem" and the carved PV on the doors of no. 229
- the back of the chapel on the Oudezijds Achterburgwal

title: Huis aan de Drie Grachten and its wartime bookshop
summary: A double house of about 1610 with a stepped gable on each of three canals. During the war the bookseller Balkema printed banned poetry here, and a hiding space found above a fireplace in 2005 still held a box of papers from those years.
body:
The house stands on the point where the Grimburgwal meets both the Oudezijds Voorburgwal and the Oudezijds Achterburgwal, so it shows a stepped gable to each of the three canals. The present building dates from about 1610, with parts from the second quarter of the 16th century. In the 18th century the gables were cut down; in 1909 the architect Jan de Meijer put them back, working from a painting by Gerrit Berckheyde, along with cross windows and a sandstone gateway.

From 1936 the bookshop of August Aimé Balkema was here. During the German occupation it was the base of his Vijf Ponden Pers, which printed poetry and other literature clandestinely. During the restoration of 2005 a hidden room was found above one of the fireplaces, possibly used by people in hiding, with a box of papers from the war years inside.

The house stayed a bookshop until 2002 and also housed a publisher of language and literature studies and the magazine Over Multatuli. It is now a private home; see it from the bridges around it.

Look for:
- the three stepped gables, best seen from the corners of the Grimburgwal with both canals
- the 1909 sandstone gateway and cross windows
- the view over the "three canals" from the Grimburgwal bridges

title: Vleeshal and the Brakke Grond gate, theatre and anatomy over the meat market
summary: Under one roof here the butchers sold meat downstairs while Vondel's rhetoricians acted and Dr Tulp dissected bodies in the attic. Three cow heads on a 1779 gable and a cobbled-together gate marked 1624 are what is left to see.
body:
Before 1578 this block held the convent of Saint Margaret and the Saint Peter's chapel. After the Reformation the city gave the buildings public uses. The ground floor of the convent church became a meat hall, and from 1598 the church attic was used by two chambers of rhetoric, amateur theatre clubs: the Brabant refugees of 't Wit Lavendel, whose best-known member was Joost van den Vondel, and the older Egelantier. It was also a fencing school and, until 1691, an anatomy theatre where surgeons such as Nicolaes Tulp gave their lessons.

In 1779 the church and the chapel were pulled down and the little square on the Nes appeared. The meat hall got a new front on the Sint Pietershalsteeg, crowned with three cows' heads; behind it is a building of 1932. The old convent became an inn called De Brakke Grond (the brackish ground, after the mix of river and sea water here), later an auction house, and since 1981 the Flemish cultural centre with a theatre and café.

Its back gate between Oudezijds Voorburgwal 290 and 298 says "De Brakke Grond" and 1624, but it was put together in the 19th century from old and new pieces.

Look for:
- the three cow heads on the gable of the meat hall front
- the gate with the name and 1624 on the Oudezijds Voorburgwal
- the square on the Nes where the church stood

title: Walloon Church and its gate of skulls
summary: A 15th-century friary chapel given to French-speaking Protestant refugees in 1586. Funerals came in through a gate of 1616 by Hendrick de Keyser, decorated with skulls, and in 1755 a lovesick baker's boy fired a gun at the minister in the pulpit.
body:
The Waalse Kerk was the chapel of the Saint Paul friary, built in the 1490s. After 1578 it was used for storage until 1586, when it was handed to Walloon refugees: French-speaking Protestants from the Southern Netherlands and France. When Huguenots poured in after 1685 galleries were added, and in 1719 a second Walloon church opened on the Prinsengracht. The painter Bartholomeus van der Helst and the naturalist Jan Swammerdam are buried here.

In 1616 the church got a second entrance from the Oude Hoogstraat. Hendrick de Keyser designed the gate, decorated with skulls because funeral processions came through it. On 12 October 1755 a French baker's boy walked in during the service and shot at the minister, who had helped end his romance with a rich merchant's daughter. The bullet only grazed him, but he fell backwards down the pulpit stairs. He recovered; the bullet holes were made invisible in the 1990s.

There is a service in French every second Sunday at 11 am, and the church, known for its acoustics, hosts concerts. Its Christian Müller organ of 1734 is one of the best preserved.

Look for:
- the skull gate of 1616 at Oude Hoogstraat, opposite the East India House
- the classical entrance of 1647 on the Walenpleintje
- the church front of 1885 on the Oudezijds Achterburgwal

title: De Gecroonde Raep (the crowned turnip)
summary: Hendrick de Keyser's showpiece stepped gable of 1615, with a crowned turnip on the back house. A neighbour across the canal copied its gable, a cigar factory and a sculptor later moved in, and KLM made it a Delft blue miniature.
body:
Hendrick de Keyser built this house in 1615 for Eduard Emtinck, and its stepped gable, with scrolls, paired pilasters, ogee arches over the windows, masks and two date stones, is counted as the best example of its kind in Amsterdam. A 17th-century book on De Keyser printed his design drawing of half of it. Diagonally across the canal, at Oudezijds Voorburgwal 18, a front of around the same date has a fragment that looks very much like it, probably a builder copying.

Unusually, the back house does not stand across the plot but runs through to the next canal: it faces the Oudezijds Achterburgwal at no. 46, and was enlarged in the 1630s. That back front carries the gable stone De Gecroonde Raep (the crowned turnip), date stones and a frieze with two lions.

In the 19th century a small cigar factory worked here, and in the 20th the sculptor Cephas Stauthamer had his studio in the old tobacco attic. The Vereniging Hendrick de Keyser has owned it since 1946. In 1959 it was the model for the 10th KLM Delft blue house. It is lived in; see both fronts from the street.

Look for:
- the masks, heads and scrolls on the gable at Oudezijds Voorburgwal 57
- the crowned turnip stone, the lions and the date stones at Oudezijds Achterburgwal 46
- the look-alike fragment at Oudezijds Voorburgwal 18

title: Het Wapen van Riga, a timber house in a brick coat
summary: A corner house of the early 1600s built for a merchant from Riga, with the Baltic city's crossed keys in its gable stone. Behind the brick it is a wooden house: the walls hang from the timber frame and the front leans out over the street.
body:
The house on the corner of the Oudezijds Voorburgwal and the Oudezijds Armsteeg was built in the first quarter of the 17th century for a merchant who had come from Riga. His gable stone shows two crossed keys, the arms of Riga, which look a lot like those of Leiden; so the house has also been called De Burcht van Leiden and De Leeuwenburg as well as Het Wapen van Riga.

It is a timber house turned to stone. It has a wooden frame and a wooden ground-floor front, and the brick walls hang from the frame by iron anchors. The front leans forward, as many old Amsterdam fronts were built to do (op vlucht), and the side wall in the alley sticks out over the ends of the floor beams.

By 1942 it was close to collapse, and the Vereniging Hendrick de Keyser bought it; what stands now is largely a reconstruction. It is a private house, seen from the street.

Look for:
- the gable stone with the crossed keys of Riga
- the side wall in the Oudezijds Armsteeg, overhanging on its beam ends
- the forward lean of the stepped gable

title: Vredenburgh, from old women's home to squat
summary: A rambling block on the tip of the Oudezijds island that a Catholic priest tried to turn into a church in 1725, that housed poor old Catholic women from 1836 to 1976, and that young squatters saved in 1979. In the empty niche meant for the Virgin there now stands a little punk.
body:
Vredenburgh stands on the northern point of the Oudezijds island with water on three sides; its oldest parts go back to the 15th century. In 1725 the priest of the hidden church Het Hert (now Ons' Lieve Heer op Solder) bought the house to pull it down and build a bigger hidden church. The Reformed church council heard of it, and the city council blocked the plan within days.

In 1829 Theresia Spijker took four poor Catholic old women into her home here, and in 1836 the Roomsch-Catholyk Burger Oudevrouwenhuis Vredenburgh opened officially. By 1861 it housed forty women. The Catholic architect Adrianus Bleys, who built the Nicolaas church nearby, reworked it, and in 1890 the corner house and the neo-gothic front in the alley were renewed.

The home closed on the last day of 1976. A property speculator bought it, his companies ran into trouble, and on 15 September 1979 it was squatted, at a time when the Zeedijk was overrun by hard drugs. The city bought it in 1987 and renovated it with the squatters; it now holds three group households and studios for dance, theatre and music.

The niche in the front was meant for a statue of the Virgin that never came. Since 2011 it holds a small figure by Joris Baudoin, a cheerful man with a mohawk, chosen by the residents.

Look for:
- the figure in the niche of the 1890 front in the Vredenburgersteeg
- the three parallel back wings with gables on the water
- the VB stone with the year of the 1883 rebuilding on the back

title: Sint-Olofskapel, the sailors' chapel that became a hotel's meeting hall
summary: A chapel of the 1440s built against a city gate and dedicated to Saint Olaf, patron of seafarers. Merchants used it as their exchange, Protestants as a church, cheese traders as a market. It burned in 1966, was sold for one guilder in 1991 and now hosts conferences.
body:
The first Saint Olaf's chapel was built between 1440 and 1450 against a large city gate, the Sint Olofspoort; the gate went in 1618 but the alley beside it still carries its name. Olaf, the Norwegian king who brought Christianity to his country, was the patron saint of sailors, a fitting choice in a port city, and Vondel still mentioned him in a poem of 1655.

After 1578 the chapel stood empty for a while. From 1586 merchants were allowed to hold their exchange in it, and from 1602 it was a Reformed church, the Oudezijds Kapel. It was enlarged in 1644 into the present three-aisled hall, gothic in spirit but with renaissance doorways. The last service was in 1912. In the 1950s a weekly cheese exchange was held here.

In 1964 the city closed it as unsafe, and in 1966 it largely burned down. For years the boarded-up ruin stood on the Zeedijk. In 1991 the city bought it for a symbolic guilder, and after restoration it became the conference centre of the Barbizon hotel next door. One of the restoration architects died during the work; a stone remembers him.

Look for:
- the doorway on the Zeedijk, moved here in 1644
- the two doorways in the Nieuwebrugsteeg, dated 1620 and 1671
- the memorial stone for architect Boudewijn de Court Onderwater

title: 't Aepgen, one of the city's two wooden houses
summary: A mid-16th-century timber house on the Zeedijk, one of only two wooden-fronted houses left in Amsterdam. Legend says sailors paid their bills here with monkeys whose fleas plagued the guests; there is no evidence it was ever an inn.
body:
Most houses in medieval Amsterdam were built of wood, because the soft ground could not carry much weight. Zeedijk 1 is one of the two wooden houses that survive, with the Houten Huys in the Begijnhof. Its timber frame has renaissance details, so it dates from the mid-16th century at the earliest. Each floor juts out further over the street, which gave more room upstairs. The side walls are now brick, but the structure is still all wood, with its original oak spiral stair.

The name goes back to Jan Claesz 'int Aepgen (in the little monkey), who lived here in the 16th century. Later it was a paper shop and a grocer's. Around 1800 the front got new boarding and windows, and the shopfront dates from 1878. The Vereniging Hendrick de Keyser has owned it since 1920 and restored it in 1986–1987.

The Dutch saying "in de aap gelogeerd zijn" (to be lodged in the monkey, meaning to be in a fix) is often tied to this house: sailors were said to pay with monkeys, whose fleas bothered the other guests. No source shows it was ever an inn, and there were inns named after monkeys elsewhere too. Since 1987 the ground floor has been a café, In 't Aepjen.

Look for:
- the overhanging wooden front, wider at every floor
- the 1878 wooden shopfront

title: Schreierstoren, the weepers' tower that probably wasn't
summary: The only defence tower left of Amsterdam's town wall, from the 1480s. Legend says sailors' wives wept here as the ships left; the name more likely comes from the sharp corner the wall made. Henry Hudson sailed from here in 1609, and New Yorkers put up the plaque.
body:
The tower was built around 1487 where the town wall along the IJ made a sharp turn south-east along the city moat, now the Geldersekade. It is the only defence tower of Amsterdam that survives. Big sandstone blocks of the wall can still be seen in the quay of the Geldersekade.

It was first called the Schrayershoucktoren, from schray (sharp) and houck (corner). The later story that the women of the town said tearful goodbyes to their seafaring men here is probably made up, but it stuck: a stone of 1569 shows a weeping woman pointing at a departing ship.

When it lost its military use the tower became a harbour office; the harbour master only moved out in 1960. In 1927 the Greenwich Village Historical Society of New York had a plaque put up recalling that Henry Hudson left from here on 4 April 1609 to look for a western passage to the Indies for the VOC, a voyage that led him to the river now named after him. A stone over the door on the Prins Hendrikkade, unveiled soon after the war, marks the departure of the first Dutch fleet to the East Indies in 1595. Since the restoration of 1966 the tower has had a café.

Look for:
- the weeping-woman stone and the old name Scrayer-Houck above the street sign
- the Hudson plaques of 1927 and 1959
- the 1595 stone with four ships and "navigare necesse est" over the door

title: Sint-Nicolaasbasiliek, the Catholics' answer opposite the station
summary: Built in 1884–1887 as the Catholics' third church of Saint Nicholas, after losing the Oude Kerk in 1578 and worshipping in an attic. Neo-baroque on purpose, a basilica since 2012 and a co-cathedral since 2025, with Saturday evensong in English.
body:
Amsterdam's first church of Saint Nicholas, patron of the city and of sailors, is the Oude Kerk; it went Protestant in 1578. The second was the attic church at Oudezijds Voorburgwal 40, now Ons' Lieve Heer op Solder. The third, built in 1884–1887 to a design by Adrianus Bleys, stands right opposite the Centraal Station and runs back to the Oudezijds Kolk.

Bleys chose neo-renaissance and neo-baroque rather than the neo-gothic most Catholic churches got at the time. The two front towers stand at different distances from the façade, so that both line up with the street, which runs at a slant; over the crossing rises an octagonal tower with a dome and lantern. Inside are wall paintings and Stations of the Cross by Jan Dunselman, a Sauer organ of 1889 and windows by Jan Dibbets from the 1999 restoration.

It was made a minor basilica in 2012. In March 2025, as a gift from Pope Francis for the city's 750th anniversary, it became co-cathedral of the diocese of Haarlem-Amsterdam, with the chair of the first bishop of 1853 as its bishop's seat. Since 2021 it keeps a relic of Saint Nicholas. Besides Mass in Dutch, English and Spanish there is an Anglican-style evensong in English on Saturdays and Gregorian vespers on Sunday afternoons from September to June; organ concerts are held in summer.

Look for:
- the two towers that are not quite level with the street
- the dome and lantern seen from the Oudezijds Kolk
- Jan Dibbets's windows in the nave

title: Gebouw Batavia, an arak company's office with monkeys and elephants
summary: A dark brick Amsterdam School office of 1918–1920 for a company that distilled arak in the Dutch East Indies. Carved groups of monkeys and elephant heads decorate the front; the name GEBOUW BATAVIA still runs across both façades, and the ground floor is a bar.
body:
The N.V. Batavia-Arak Maatschappij made arak, a strong spirit distilled from sugar cane, in the Dutch East Indies. In 1918 it commissioned J.H. Slot to design an office with storerooms and a caretaker's flat here, on a concrete frame, running from the Prins Hendrikkade through to the Oudezijds Kolk. The company moved in in March 1920. Slot used the Amsterdam School style, and with its dark brick the building looks like a small cousin of the Scheepvaarthuis around the corner.

The front on the Prins Hendrikkade is asymmetric: a closed section with a narrow half-round bay running up all floors, and a row of tall windows. The sculpture over the entrance shows groups of monkeys and elephant heads, a nod to the company's colonial trade. Iron letters spell GEBOUW BATAVIA on both fronts; on the canal side the first three floors keep their leaded-glass top lights.

The arak company was taken over in 1968. A shopping arcade with a sauna came first; in 1973 the ground floor became a café, and since 2008 it is the bar Batavia 1920, which held a yearly chess tournament between 2009 and 2020.

Look for:
- the monkey groups and elephant heads on the front
- the iron GEBOUW BATAVIA lettering
- the back on the Oudezijds Kolk with its leaded glass

title: Vettewinkel's paint factory, a façade that survived the fire
summary: A paint and varnish works of 1889 that caught fire four times in the 19th century and burned out completely in 1973. Only the front standing in the water of the Oudezijds Kolk was saved, still with mooring rings and the tiled name of H. Vettewinkel en Zonen.
body:
In 1889 H. Vettewinkel had a paint and varnish factory built on the Oudezijds Kolk, the little harbour behind the Prins Hendrikkade, to a design by W. Hamer in Dutch neo-renaissance style. Paint and varnish burn well: the building was hit by four big fires in the 19th century alone. On 3 July 1973 it burned out completely, and everything was demolished except the front that rises straight out of the water of the Kolk. That front alone is the listed monument.

It is in two parts, a low symmetrical left half and a tall right half, each under a stepped gable crowned by a lion holding a shield. The base is rough-cut stone coming up out of the water, with iron rings in the wall for mooring ships, and the shuttered cross windows still have their red-and-white painted shutters. Between the first and second floor two tiled friezes spell out the firm: "H. Vettewinkel en Zonen" on the left and "Verf- en Vernis Fabriek" on the right.

Look at it from the water's edge on the Oudezijds Kolk, between the Nicolaas church and the Zeedijk.

Look for:
- the tile friezes with the firm's name
- the lions with shields on the stepped gables
- the mooring rings in the stone base just above the water

title: Krasnapolsky's Winter Garden and the power station behind it
summary: A trained tailor built the grand hotel on the Dam. Its Winter Garden of 1879–1880 has one of the oldest wrought-iron roofs in the country, and the warehouse behind it held, in 1883, what the national register calls Amsterdam's first electricity plant.
body:
A.W. Krasnapolsky came to Amsterdam in 1856 trained as a tailor; by the 1880s his name stood on a complex of hotel, café and restaurant between the Dam and the Warmoesstraat. Its heart is the Winter Garden, built in 1879–1880 to a design by G.B. Salm: a glass-roofed hall nearly 14 metres high, carried by wrought-iron trusses with cast-iron ornaments and the arms of the Dutch provinces. The national register counts it among the oldest and rarest wrought-iron roof structures in the Netherlands. Paintings by Tetar van Elven, father and son, fill the end walls.

Behind it, on the Warmoesstraat side, stands a plain brick warehouse of 1879 with a tall round chimney. In 1883 it was enlarged for an electricity plant which, according to the register, was the first in Amsterdam and lit both the hotel and the area around the Dam. Inside the warehouse still has its cast-iron frame.

The hotel's Warmoesstraat front of 1883, by J.F. Henkenhaf and F. Ebert, copies Salm's entrance arch to the Winter Garden. The hotel is now the Anantara Grand Hotel Krasnapolsky; the Winter Garden is its breakfast room.

Look for:
- the round brick chimney of the power station on the Warmoesstraat side
- the faded crimson lettering "Maatsch. tot Expl. v/d Ondern. Krasnapolsky" by the entrance passage on the Warmoesstraat
- the lion-head keystones and granite columns of the arches

title: Max Beckmann's exile studio in a tobacco attic (Rokin 85)
summary: The German painter Max Beckmann fled Nazi Germany in 1937 and spent ten years in the attic of this former tobacco office, through the whole occupation. About a third of his life's work, some 280 paintings, was made here, under the glass roof meant for judging tobacco leaf.
body:
In 1894 the architect J. van Looy rebuilt an older house here as an office for a tobacco firm. Like many on this strip between the Rokin and the Nes, it got a sample attic under a glass roof, where buyers judged the leaf in good daylight. The front on the Rokin is exuberant neo-renaissance, with putti among flowers over the windows and a shell on top; the back on the Nes is plain.

In 1937 Max Beckmann left Germany, where the Nazis had branded his work degenerate, and settled in Amsterdam. From that autumn he and his wife Mathilde, called Quappi, lived at Rokin 85, and the former tobacco attic became his studio. He stayed until 1947, through the German occupation, with little recognition in the city. Yet he was productive: about 280 paintings, roughly a third of his whole work, were made in Amsterdam, among them the triptychs Acrobats (1939), Perseus (1941), Actors (1942) and Carnival (1943). His Double Portrait of Max Beckmann and Quappi (1941) is in the Stedelijk Museum. In 1947 he left for the United States.

The building has a bar or restaurant on the ground floor; the rest is private. See the front from the Rokin.

Look for:
- the glass roof of the old sample attic, visible behind the gable from the Rokin
- the putti among flowers in the arches beside the first-floor windows
- the plain back of the same house at Nes 98

title: Tobacco offices dressed as canal houses
summary: Around 1900 the tobacco brokers between the Rokin and the Nes built offices that look like gentlemen's houses from the front. Behind them were sample attics, sample halls and stores; one still has its ventilation arcade on the Nes and griffins holding the brokers' initials.
body:
From 1879 Sumatra tobacco was auctioned in Frascati on the Nes, and the brokers clustered around it. Their new offices along the quiet east side of the Rokin and the Oudezijds Voorburgwal mostly kept the width, height and look of the canal house, while behind the front lay offices, sample attics under glass and stores. The city register notes it again and again: a front that suggests a house, with only work behind it.

The fullest example is Rokin 93, built in 1896 by Schill and Haverkamp for the tobacco brokers Brusse & Gransberg. The Rokin side has a Mercury head and two griffins holding a shield with the partners' initials. On the Nes side, where the real work happened, the wall is almost blind, and an arcade along the top hid and ventilated the tobacco attic. The firm, later merged with Nienhuys & Hesterman, stayed until 1985.

Next door, Rokin 101 (1915, J.W. Hanrath) was the office of Scheltema & Co., whose sample hall was behind it on the Nes; its three window bays are bent slightly towards each other. On the corner of the Nes and the Sint Barberenstraat the Van Gendt brothers gave G. Harkema's tobacco office new fronts in 1923, and the Pappenheim brothers' office with sample room of 1906 stands at Oudezijds Voorburgwal 266, next to the meat-hall front.

Look for:
- the griffins, initials and Mercury head on Rokin 93, and the ventilation arcade on its back at Nes 104
- the gently bent window wall of Rokin 101
- the firm's name in wrought iron on the Nes front of Nes 67
- the house-number stone and 1906 date stone on Oudezijds Voorburgwal 266

title: Rokin 99, the postmodern front critics hated
summary: A blue mirrored bay window, pink granite and blue aluminium squeezed between old canal fronts in 1990. The critics were openly hostile; in 2016, at 26 years old, the city listed it as a monument. It is the only building in Amsterdam by Mart van Schijndel.
body:
In 1990 the stockbrokers Oudhof had a new office built here by Mart van Schijndel (1943–1999), in the 1980s the most outspoken postmodern architect in the Netherlands. Experts count it as his most radical building in the style, and it is his only one in Amsterdam.

The front keeps the old canal-house order of base, middle and crown, but in new materials: a plinth of long grey granite blocks, pink granite laid in a diagonal pattern, bands of polished sand-coloured granite and blue anodised aluminium, a blue aluminium pediment and, in the middle, a curved bay of blue-tinted mirrored glass. The door is burgundy aluminium, framed in granite carved with the name Oudhof, and three round windows sit in square granite frames. Behind the front, split levels fit four floors into the depth of the plot.

When it was finished the reviews were downright hostile, the sharpest in NRC Handelsblad on 20 July 1990. The city's 2016 listing argues that postmodernism can now be judged calmly as a period of architecture, and that real postmodern buildings are rare in the Netherlands. The interior was largely lost in a 2004 rebuilding. The row it stands in, between the Langebrugsteeg and the Kalfsvelsteeg, is otherwise a near-complete sample of Amsterdam architecture since a Vingboons house of 1646 at no. 95.

Look for:
- the curved blue mirror bay
- the name Oudhof cut in the granite by the door
- the round windows in square granite frames

title: The Marine Insurance building and its mosaic ship (Rokin 69)
summary: A 1901 office for a British marine insurer, with a sailing ship in mosaic under the company's name and a turret with an onion-like roof. In 1989 a newspaper called it kitsch that would never make the monument list; it was listed in 2001.
body:
Around 1900 the Rokin, then still open water, became something of a financial street, and several insurers settled here. The British firm The Marine Insurance Company Limited took the corner of the Wijde Lombardsteeg, and its Dutch agent Emanuel Orobio de Castro hired Gerrit van Arkel. The plan was filed as a rebuilding of a warehouse; in practice it was demolished and replaced. Van Arkel, who liked a turret on a corner, gave it a flat sandstone front in a sober art nouveau with touches of Berlage, and a corner tower capped with curved roof faces and little spires. The company had already left by 1919.

High on the front a mosaic spells out THE MARINE INSURANCE COMPANY LIMITED over a fully rigged sailing ship. In 1989 de Volkskrant dismissed the building as tasteless kitsch "that you won't find on the monument list", while Het Parool admired the slender turret. The older part was listed as a national monument in 2001. For years a little ferry crossed the Rokin opposite the Lombardsteeg.

It is an office; see it from the Rokin.

Look for:
- the mosaic with the company name and the ship
- the corner turret with its curved roof and spires
- the architect's name worked into a corner stone

title: Hildo Krop's insured blessings (Rokin 115)
summary: An Amsterdam School office of 1928 for the insurer De Algemeene Friesche. Hildo Krop carved four figures into its window posts: Prosperity, Work, Care and Rest, the blessings of life, as the city register drily puts it, provided you are well insured.
body:
Between about 1900 and 1930 many insurers built new head and branch offices in Amsterdam, often in a modern and showy style. This one was built in 1928 for De Algemeene Friesche by the office of the Baanders brothers, in their own variant of the Amsterdam School. It keeps the plot width of its neighbours but stands taller, softened by a set-back top floor.

The ground floor is shaped like a triumphal arch on four octagonal pillars, open to the street, with stone shields of Amsterdam and North Holland over the side openings. The big first-floor window is split by carved figures by Hildo Krop, woman and man in turn, each labelled: WELVAART (prosperity) with fruit, ARBEID (work) with tools, ZORG (care) with a little bird, and RUST (rest). The register reads them as the blessings of life, if you are well insured. Brackets for two flagpoles still sit around the second-floor windows.

It is an office building; see it from the Rokin.

Look for:
- Krop's four labelled figures in the first-floor window
- the arms of Amsterdam and North Holland over the side arches
- the round arch of tapered bricks over the entrance

title: De Roos, an art auction house with a carved menagerie (Rokin 9-15)
summary: A Jugendstil auction house and art shop of 1909–1915 for C.F. Roos & Co., built over five old houses. Its sandstone is carved with chameleons, monkeys and elephants by a sculptor nobody can name, and DE ROOS is still cut into the side wall.
body:
From the late 19th century the art and antiques trade gathered on the Rokin. C.F. Roos & Co. was one of the bigger dealers, with its own shop and auction room, and in 1909–1915 it replaced five houses on the corner of the Hermietenstraat with this building. Offices faced the Rokin; at the back an exhibition hall rose through two floors. The building was meant to run through to the Nes.

It has a concrete frame clad in brick, granite and sandstone, with an irregular skyline of two sandstone gables. Big shop windows sit between granite pilasters, and the deep entrance porch has a mosaic floor. The sculpture is the point: little elephants beside the double doors, oak leaves on the corners, and on the bases of the sandstone pilasters chameleons, monkeys and elephants in a stylised, expressionist manner. The register calls it high-quality work, by an unknown sculptor. Nothing is known of the architect, F.A. Bodde.

The shop floor is now split between several businesses. See it from the Rokin and the Hermietenstraat.

Look for:
- the little elephants beside the entrance doors
- the animal figures at the foot of the sandstone pilasters
- DE ROOS in the arch on the third floor of the Hermietenstraat side
- the six-pointed star in the arch at the top of the left gable

title: The nuns of the Warmoesstraat
summary: A draper's warehouse of 1917 and a printing works next door became, for over half a century, the home of the Augustinian Sisters of Saint Monica, who ran a shelter for women and the homeless in the middle of the red-light district. The last five sisters left in 2010.
body:
The block between the Warmoesstraat, the Sint Jansstraat and the Leidekkerssteeg was built for trade. In 1917 P. Schenk rebuilt no. 159 for E.A. Joachimsthal, a wholesaler in fabrics, with offices, a workshop and stores; a sandstone frieze above the shopfront once carried the firm's name. Next door the printer A. Adler had a building of 1915 by A.D.N. van Gendt, with its presses at the back on the Sint Jansstraat.

From 1952 the Augustinian Sisters of Saint Monica, a congregation founded to take in young women in trouble, ran a shelter here, a few steps from the windows of the red-light district. They took in women in crisis and gave permanent shelter to homeless people. In 1983 the buildings were joined and rebuilt as their convent. Short of money, they stopped the shelter work in 2009, and on 1 February 2010 the last five sisters moved away.

Since 2016 a supermarket fills the ground floor, with rental flats called d'Augustijn above it.

Look for:
- the sandstone frieze above the shopfront, where the Joachimsthal name once was
- the colossal brick pilasters with small saw-tooth edges
- the slanted glazing bars in the top lights of the shopfront

title: The infant school for Princess Juliana (Warmoesstraat 71)
summary: A 1911 'keeping place' for little children, built when four-to-six-year-olds of working families were looked after in bewaarscholen rather than kindergartens. Its stone still carries the name Kleine-kinderen Bewaarplaats Prinses Juliana.
body:
Before people spoke of kleuters (toddlers), from around 1920, children of four to six were simply called "small children". In the Netherlands the first bewaarscholen, keeping schools, were set up in the early 19th century to take in and bring up the begging, wandering children of working families while their parents worked.

This one was built in 1911 for the Vereeniging tot Verbetering van Kleine Kinderen Bewaarplaatsen, a society to improve such schools, to a design by F.W.M. Poggenbeek, and named after Princess Juliana, born two years before. In 1939 three houses on the Oude Kerksplein behind it were added. Later it lost its school use and became business space, but the front is remarkably intact.

The tall brick front fits neatly into the street wall. Black-tarred bands and stones run through the brick, the school entrance on the left keeps its original panelled door, and the third floor sits in a frame of brick strips under a row of small arches, topped by a wide wooden eave on carved brackets.

Look for:
- the stone with the school's name above the ground floor
- the original school door on the left
- the arch frieze and the wide eave at the top

title: The shop window that follows the old dike (Warmoesstraat 101)
summary: A neo-renaissance corner shop of 1893 by the Oude Kerk. Its stone window sill steps down along the street: the Warmoesstraat was once the dike along the Amstel, and the shopfront still follows the slope of the old dike body.
body:
The Warmoesstraat is one of the oldest streets of Amsterdam and began as a dike along the Amstel. On the corner of the Wijde Kerksteeg, where the view opens from the Oude Kerk square to the Warmoesstraat, a builder named D. van Oort put up a shop with flats above in 1893, in the Dutch neo-renaissance that suited the old quarter.

The detail to look for is low down. The stone sill of the shop windows does not run level but drops in steps, following the slope down the side of the old dike. It is one of the few places where you can still read the dike in a building.

Above the shop the front is almost overloaded with stone decoration: bands, cartouches, odd triangular colonnettes, and a little stone bay window over the corner door, on an iron bracket, with leaded glass in its top lights. An openwork balustrade with ball finials crowns it all. The shop entrance sits on the cut-off corner, as was usual in the 19th century.

Look for:
- the stepped shop-window sill along the Wijde Kerksteeg
- the stone bay window over the corner door
- the balustrade with quatrefoils and ball finials

title: The stone laid by a fifteen-year-old (Oudezijds Voorburgwal 131)
summary: An over-the-top eclectic front of 1892 with two caryatids, painted white against dark brick. Low on the façade an inscription records who laid the first stone: A.D. Hamburger, aged fifteen, on 15 July 1892.
body:
In the late 19th century Amsterdam fronts grew ever more lavish, and builders such as R.R. de Bruyn helped themselves freely from every historical style. This shop-and-flats building of 1892 on the Oudezijds Voorburgwal is a fine show of it: a stone ground floor for the business, dark brown brick above, and a wider middle bay pushed forward with balconies, framed by two caryatids and pilasters. Every window has a heavy frame topped by a pediment with grotesque faces, all picked out in white. The double door in the middle led to a storeroom; the doors at the sides go up to the flats.

Most first-stone inscriptions name a builder, an owner or a dignitary. This one names a boy: "A.D. HAMBURGER, 15 JAAR, 15 JULI 1892".

The big dormer lost its crown with scrolls and a shell after 1955. The building is private; see it from the canal side.

Look for:
- the first-stone inscription with the boy's name and age
- the two caryatids flanking the middle bay
- the grotesque faces in the window pediments

title: The monkey holding up the corner (Damstraat 20)
summary: A shop and flats of 1900 on the corner of the busy Damstraat, with a curved glass corner made possible by new industrial glass. The curve rests on a carved monkey, and a tile panel below the second-floor windows shows the year 1900.
body:
The narrow Damstraat has been a busy shopping street for a long time. On the deep corner plot with the Pieter Jacobszdwarsstraat the builder W. Schimmel put up a shop with flats in 1900, in a style that was new for its day: instead of the usual three windows and renaissance borrowings, broad windows nearly the full width of the front, natural ornament rather than historical quotes, red machine-pressed brick with tiles and stone accents.

The corner turns in a curve, glazed with large bent panes, which industry could only just make. Originally this curve ran from the shop door to the third floor. It is carried by the detail everyone walks past: a carved monkey that props up the corner above it. Lower down, the tiles under the second-floor windows spell out "1900".

The open shopfront dates from the late 20th century, but the floors above, and most of the window frames, are original. Look up from the corner.

Look for:
- the carved monkey supporting the corner
- the tile panel with 1900
- the bay window over the full width of the first floor

title: De Burcht (diamond workers' union building)
summary: The oldest trade union building in the Netherlands looks like an Italian town hall with battlements. Berlage built it in 1899–1900 for the diamond workers, at the same time as his Exchange, in the garden of a theatre.
body:
A brick fortress with battlements and a tower at its side, in a street of polite houses with front gardens: this is where the Dutch trade union movement set up house. The Algemene Nederlandse Diamantbewerkersbond (ANDB, the general diamond workers' union) grew under its chairman Henri Polak into the first modern union in the country, and Polak wanted a monument for the labour movement. In 1899 he gave the job to H.P. Berlage, who was building his Exchange on the Damrak at the same moment. The site was the garden of the Plantage Schouwburg, a theatre.

Berlage took his cue from medieval Italian town halls. Inside, the painter Richard Roland Holst covered the walls: in the boardroom a triptych shows the working man's ideal day, divided into hours of labour, hours of leisure and hours of sleep. The lamps in the stairwell are by Jan Eisenloeffel (1919).

From 1991 the building housed the trade union museum. Since 2011 it has been a research and documentation centre of the union movement, and its rooms are let for meetings and weddings. The interior can be seen on guided tours (see deburcht.nl). The street, once Plantage Franschelaan, has carried Polak's name since 1945.

Look for:
- the battlements along the roof line and the tower standing to one side
- the bare brick front, with almost no ornament
- through the door, if it is open: the stairwell in unplastered brick

title: Portuguese Jewish hospital (Henri Polaklaan)
summary: A hospital of forty beds, built in 1914–1916 for the Portuguese Jewish community by Harry Elte. In the war its patients, residents and nurses were deported. The architect's name is still cut into the front.
body:
Between the houses of the Henri Polaklaan stands a small hospital that few passers-by recognise as one. The Portuguese Jewish community had cared for its sick and its old women since 1834 in a worn-out house in the Rapenburgerstraat. In 1913 the church council decided to buy plots here, and in May 1916 the new Portugees-Israëlitisch Ziekenhuis was inaugurated, with room for forty patients.

The architect was Harry Elte, who had worked for Berlage for ten years, and it shows: purple-red brick, with stone only where it carries something. The men's ward lay on the first floor at the front and the women's ward at the back; the operating rooms were on the top floor, and the lift machinery sat in the little tower. The older house at no. 10 became the nurses' home.

During the occupation the residents and the nursing staff were deported, and most of them were murdered. Elte himself died in Theresienstadt in 1944. In 1951 the building became a home for the elderly, losing its glass canopy, its doors and the tile panel with its name. Since 1977 it has been housing. It is private; the front is seen from the street.

Look for:
- to the right of the entrance, the signature "Harry Elte PHzn Architect"
- the brick bay on three stone brackets (its balcony was closed in later)
- three Flemish gables hiding the top floor
- the small tower of the lift, with a later tent roof

title: The sculptor's house (Henri Polaklaan 25)
summary: Henri Teixeira de Mattos carved the figures on his own house in 1883 rough and unfinished on purpose. His designs for the Rijksmuseum had just been turned down as too coarse.
body:
Two old men in stone hold up the balcony of this house, and they look as if the sculptor walked away halfway through. He did it on purpose. Henri Teixeira de Mattos (1856–1908) was thought so radical that his fierce, realistic designs for Pierre Cuypers's Rijksmuseum were rejected as coarse and ignoble. On his own house, built in 1883 with the architect Jonas Ingenohl, nobody could stop him: the herms and caryatids are deliberately rough-hewn, at a time when fashion asked for calm, polished figures.

It was a house to work in. The studio lay at the back of the ground floor, with a showroom at the front, and under it a cellar for making plaster casts, reached by a small lift. A separate door led to painters' studios in the attic. Artis is around the corner, and in these years Teixeira made the animal figures he is best known for there.

The middle entrance has been bricked up and the roof was replaced by an extra storey, which spoils the balance of the front. The house is private; everything worth seeing is on the street side.

Look for:
- the two herms on the ground floor: strong men well on in years
- the figures higher up: the lighter the load, the slimmer they are
- four window bays instead of the usual three
- the round windows with a carved garland above the old side doors

title: Jac. Baars's own house (Henri Polaklaan 11)
summary: In 1930 the architect Jac. S. Baars gave himself a house that ignores its neighbours: yellow brick, flat canopies after Frank Lloyd Wright, and an outside staircase tiled in black and white.
body:
Every other house in this row dates from the 1880s and wears the ornament of its time. Then comes this one: flat yellow brick with deeply raked joints, a jutting bay, a canopy over the door and a broad overhanging gutter. It is the house the architect Jac. S. Baars (1886–1956) made for himself in 1930. On paper it was a conversion of an older house, of which little can be left.

The horizontal lines come from Frank Lloyd Wright, much admired in the Netherlands in the 1920s; the leaded glass and the tiled roof slope are still Amsterdam School. Baars came from a family of demolition contractors and became an architect all the same. He worked mostly for the Jewish community and designed several synagogues; the one he rated highest, on the Polderweg (1928), was pulled down in 1962. When their exemption from deportation lapsed during the occupation, he and his family went into hiding in Friesland.

The house is private and is seen from the pavement.

Look for:
- the straight outside stair, tiled black on the treads and white on the risers
- light blue and yellow mosaic on the posts between the ground-floor windows
- the leaded glass in the bay on the first floor
- the low ground floor in red-brown brick under all that yellow

title: Apostolic church in the street wall (Henri Polaklaan 36–40)
summary: A church of 1912 squeezed between the houses: two square towers, a door on the first floor at the top of a stair, and tiles by the ceramist Willem Brouwer. Since 1994 there are flats in the nave.
body:
A church with no churchyard, no spire and no room: the Hersteld Apostolische Zendingsgemeente (a small Apostolic congregation) had to fit its building of 1912 into an ordinary row of house plots. The architect H.F. Sijmons took two plots for the church and one for a service building, and made the front do all the work. Two square corner towers with pyramid roofs rise above the neighbours, and the entrance is not at street level but on the first floor, in a round-arched porch at the top of a straight flight of steps.

Where the houses around it pile on plaster ornament, Sijmons followed Berlage: flat walls of bare red brick, with decoration only in a few places. The best of it is the terracotta by Willem Brouwer (1877–1933), a well-known ceramist. The sandstone of the keystones came from the Elbe region.

In 1994 flats were built into the nave. The building is private and is seen from the street.

Look for:
- Brouwer's terracotta above the row of windows on the second floor of the church
- the leaded glass in the round-arched porch
- the service building on the right, with a loggia set into the wall on the first floor
- the open brick balustrades that tie the two buildings together

title: Wertheim fountain (Wertheimpark)
summary: The only park inside the old city got its name and its fountain in 1898, a year after the banker A.C. Wertheim died. From 1942 to 1945 the park had to be called Parktuin again, because Wertheim was a Jew.
body:
Abraham Carel Wertheim (1832–1897), banker, politician and benefactor, had been dead only a few days when a committee set out to give him a street. The trouble was that new streets lay in new districts where nobody would notice. Samuel Sarphati had been given a park with a monument, so Wertheim should have one too. The old pleasure garden opposite the Hortus, a park since 1812, was tidied from wilderness into lawns and broad paths, the council agreed to the name in May 1898, and on 3 October the fountain was unveiled.

The architect Jonas Ingenohl stacked two basins: an octagonal one of ten metres at ground level and a round one of four metres, carried on eight short granite columns. From the upper basin rises a column of polished granite with Wertheim's portrait.

On 14 August 1942 the mayor installed by the occupier scrapped all street and park names that honoured Jews or living members of the royal family. Until May 1945 this was the Parktuin again. Jan Wolkers's Auschwitz monument of broken mirrors lies in the same park, a few steps away.

The park is freely accessible.

Look for:
- the pelicans on the capital at the top of the column, a symbol of charity
- four bronze dolphins spouting into the upper basin
- the portrait medallion halfway up the column
- at the gate on the Plantage Parklaan: two marble sphinxes, remade in 1982 after the zinc originals were removed in 1949

title: Theo Thijssen's school on the paupers' graveyard (Hortusplantsoen)
summary: A double school for about a thousand children, built in the 1890s on a burial ground closed in 1866. The writer Theo Thijssen taught here, and from 1928 no. 2 was a school for deaf children, with Rinus Michels as gym teacher.
body:
Under this school lies the Sint Antonieskerkhof, where from 1640 the city buried people who could not pay for a gravestone. It was closed in 1866 with all the other old churchyards. The eastern half became a trial garden of the Hortus, and in the 1890s the city put a double school on the rest: 26 classrooms for some 1,020 children, designed by H. Leguyt of the public works department. The left half was a school "of the first class", meaning for the poor; the right half was one step up.

The writer and politician Theo Thijssen worked at no. 1 as a teacher from 1899 to 1905, and met his future wife here. From 1928 to 1976 no. 2 housed the J.C. Ammanschool for deaf and hard-of-hearing children; the football coach Rinus Michels taught gymnastics there from 1956 to 1965. A plaque, unveiled in 2007, remembers the school's Jewish pupils who were deported, and since 2010 a monument for Jewish deaf victims of the war has stood in the gardens opposite.

Since 2015 the Reinwardt Academie, the heritage school of the Amsterdam University of the Arts, has used the building. It is not open to visitors.

Look for:
- the two halves: one front, two schools with separate entrances
- Dutch Renaissance gables mixed with chalet-style woodwork
- the plaque for the pupils of the Ammanschool
- the monument in the gardens across the street

title: Johan van Hulstbrug and its twin
summary: Two little bridges of 1877 over the Hortus pond. In 2016 the city named the wrong one after Johan van Hulst, who helped save hundreds of Jewish children; in 2018 the name moved to its neighbour, while he was still alive.
body:
The city has a rule that nothing is named after a person until five years after their death. For Johan van Hulst it made an exception. As head of the Protestant teacher training college on the Plantage Middenlaan he had, with others, saved some six hundred Jewish babies and young children who were held at the Hollandsche Schouwburg. He was over a hundred when the name was chosen.

It went wrong the first time. In 2016 the name was given to bridge 232, the iron bridge that leads from the gardens to the Hortus and is shut off by a gate, so that nobody can cross it. In January 2018 the name was moved to bridge 233, forty metres west, which carries a public footpath, the Dr. D.M. Sluyspad.

Both date from 1877. Bridge 233 used to be called the Victoria regia bridge, after the giant water lily the Hortus has kept since 1859: until 2002 it grew in a hothouse the bridge led to. The ironwork of bridge 232 was made by H. Dalhuizen in Kampen.

Look for:
- on 233: heavy cast-iron balusters between square posts topped with balls
- on 232: the arched iron ribs with S-shaped scrolls and the plank deck
- the vases on the round brick ends of bridge 232
- the gate on 232, bristling with spikes against climbers

title: Hidden synagogue of the Nieuwe Keizersgracht (nos. 33 and 37)
summary: From mid-1944 until liberation the sexton of the Portuguese Synagogue held services in his flat at no. 33, with a ritual bath in a garden cellar. Two doors along, a firm at no. 37 had invented a doorbell you were allowed to ring on the Sabbath.
body:
Before the war this canal was nicknamed the Joodsche Keizersgracht, the Jewish Keizersgracht. In February 1944 the occupier dissolved the Portuguese Jewish congregation, and services in the Portuguese Synagogue stopped. From the middle of that year until 5 May 1945 the synagogue's sexton (sjammes), who had been allowed back from the Westerbork camp, kept a hidden synagogue in his flat on the second floor of no. 33. Up to thirty men came on a Sabbath, and a cellar in the garden was fitted out as a mikveh, a ritual bath. The painter Anton Witsel, who lived on the first floor, drew the services; his drawings have helped to identify some of the men who prayed here.

No. 37, two doors along, is one of three nearly identical houses built in 1730. In 1934 a small firm based here applied for a patent on an electric doorbell that made no spark, so that the rabbinate allowed it on the Sabbath. Of the twenty people living in the house before the war, three survived.

Both houses are private. Since 2013 small plaques along the quay edge, the Schaduwkade (shadow quay), have named the murdered residents of this stretch.

Look for:
- at no. 33, the Art Nouveau porch and balconies (1909)
- at no. 37, the gable stone of 1996 with a radiant sun and the words "Eens in de vier jaar" (once every four years), made for a leap year
- the Schaduwkade plaques on the quay, each opposite a house

title: Washing house and nurses' home of the Jewish hospital
summary: 'In at the Nieuwe Keizersgracht, out at the Nieuwe Kerkstraat', Amsterdammers said before the war. The Jewish hospital between the two streets is gone, but the house at its back door where the dead were washed survives, and so does the nurses' home.
body:
Before the war, when things had ended badly for someone, people said: "op de Nieuwe Keizersgracht erin, op de Nieuwe Kerkstraat eruit", in at the Nieuwe Keizersgracht, out at the Nieuwe Kerkstraat. The Nederlandsch Israëlietisch Ziekenhuis (Dutch Jewish hospital) of 1881–1884 had its front on the canal, and at the back a door led into Nieuwe Kerkstraat 127: the metaheirhuis, where the dead were washed according to Jewish rite. Harry Elte designed it in 1926 and it opened on 27 March 1927. Coffins were made in workshops on the upper floors. The front shows how much Elte admired Frank Lloyd Wright.

On the canal side Elte had already built the nurses' home in 1914, on land given by the philanthropist Sophie Rosenthal-May. It had no door of its own: the nurses came and went through the hospital. During the occupation the people in the hospital and the nurses' home were deported, and few returned. After the war the home took in survivors, and from 1953 it held small flats, mainly for older Jewish residents. The hospital was pulled down in the 1970s.

Both buildings are housing now and are seen from the street.

Look for:
- at Nieuwe Kerkstraat 127, the three tall window bays under the jutting canopy; the ground floor was broken out in the 1960s
- at Nieuwe Keizersgracht 500–568, the tile panel with the name Rosenthal-May Zusterhuis above the ground-floor windows

title: Harry Elte's first synagogue (Nieuwe Kerkstraat 10–14)
summary: Only the front survives: plain brown-red brick of 1913, with a row of windows on the first floor drawn with odd care. Behind it was the women's gallery of a synagogue for 192 men and 26 women. After the war it became a warehouse, then flats.
body:
Most people walk past this front without a second look. It reads as a house with flats above, but the first floor gives it away: a wide arched window divided into six lights, flanked by small arched windows, all set between projecting brick bands that rest on sandstone springers. Behind that row of windows lay the women's gallery of a synagogue.

The congregation Neir Mitswoh Wetouro Our ("the commandment is like a light, the teaching like a fire") had met in this street since 1841, at no. 26. On 28 October 1913 it moved into this new building, with seats for 192 men and 26 women. It was the first synagogue by Harry Elte, who had spent ten years in Berlage's office, and it shows: flat walls of brown-red brick, stone only where it carries something. The men came in through the middle door under the round arch. The two doors against the side walls led to the women's gallery and to four flats on the floors above.

Before the war a large part of Amsterdam's Jewish population lived in this corner of the canal belt. In 1953 the synagogue was turned into a warehouse and its interior was stripped; later the warehouse became housing, and only the front is left. It is private.

Look for:
- the six-part arched window of the women's gallery
- the very narrow arched windows of the two stairwells at first-floor level
- the round-arched men's entrance in the middle

title: Palacheschool (Lepelkruisstraat)
summary: A city school for poor boys of 1890 became one of Amsterdam's three Jewish primary schools in 1929. By 1943 its classrooms were empty. Squatters later stopped its demolition, and the old name Brugsmaschool can still be made out over the door.
body:
Stepped gables in red brick with yellow accents, pointed arches beneath them, and over the entrance a faded name: Brugsmaschool. The city opened the building in 1890 as a public school "of the third class" for boys, in a neighbourhood that was filling up fast on the site of the old cattle market.

In 1929 it got a second life. Since 1895 the association Kennis en Godsvrucht (Knowledge and Piety) had been setting up Jewish schools again, worried that children in the public schools would lose their faith. It took over this building, and the architect Jac. S. Baars was given four weeks to fit it with bigger windows, a wider entrance and granite floors.
