On 2 September 1929 it opened as the Palacheschool, named after Isaac Juda Palache, chief rabbi of the Portuguese Jewish congregation, who had died in 1926. It was one of the city's three Jewish primary schools before the war.

During the occupation the classes emptied with every raid, and by 1943 no pupils were left; most had been deported and murdered. Other schools used the building until 1985. Squatters prevented its demolition, and the housing association Lieven de Key had it converted into fifteen flats, designed by Rudy Uytenhaak. It is private.

Look for:
- the name Brugsmaschool, faint above the entrance
- the stepped gables at both ends on the Lepelkruisstraat, and one on the side of the former Lepelstraat
- glass entrances where there used to be windows

title: Diamond factories of the Nieuwe Achtergracht
summary: In 1846 Amsterdam's jewellers opened the city's first purpose-built steam diamond works here, with 168 polishing mills. Its oldest buildings survived the clearance of Roeterseiland and now house a student culture centre; two later factories stand along the same canal.
body:
For centuries diamonds were polished at home, on mills turned by women, later by horses. In 1845 Amsterdam's jewellers pooled their works into the Diamantslijperij Maatschappij and built, on the Roeterseiland, the first steam polishing works designed as such in the city. It opened in August 1846 with 168 mills; a year later the complex had 280, at a time when the whole city counted about 600. For three decades the company held a near monopoly. After 1870, with rough stones pouring in from South Africa, dozens of rival factories opened, many around this canal.

In the 1960s everything on the island was demolished for the university, except Berlage's housing block and, by some luck, part of this factory. Since 2012 its oldest buildings have housed CREA, the University of Amsterdam's cultural centre for students.

Further west stand two later works. Benjamin Soep's factory at no. 17 (1906, by Gerrit van Arkel) ran on electricity; from 1963 the diamond firm Gassan polished here for coach tourists until the traffic on the narrow canal drove it out in the early 1990s. Van Weerden and Slijper's works at nos. 134–138 (1887) still has its chimney inside.

Look for:
- the long, narrow factory blocks of CREA, built for daylight on both sides
- at no. 17, the initials of Samuel Gassan in the railings before the basement windows
- the cast-iron Diamantbewerkersbrug (diamond workers' bridge) of 1900 at the end of the Onbekendegracht, named in 2016

title: Bridges with wartime names (Roetersstraat and Plantage Middenlaan)
summary: Walk from the Muiderpoort past the Hollandsche Schouwburg and down the Roetersstraat and you cross five bridges named, between 1982 and 2021, after people who saved lives in the war or survived it. One has hippos and crocodiles carved into its quay walls.
body:
Amsterdam names bridges after people, and around the Plantage those names tell one story. The Hollandsche Schouwburg on the Plantage Middenlaan was where the occupier assembled Jews for deportation, and the bridges on either side of it now carry the names of rescuers and survivors.

At the Muiderpoort, the bridge over the Singelgracht (1902) was named in 2021 after Henriëtte Pimentel, who ran the crèche opposite the Schouwburg; the name was moved here from a bridge in Nieuw-West to be closer to the theatre. The bridge over the Muidergracht towards Artis (1907), long called the Artisbrug, became the Jules Schelvisbrug in 2016, after a survivor of Sobibor and six other camps and later wrote about them. In the Roetersstraat, the Lau Mazirelbrug (named in 1982) remembers a lawyer in the resistance, the Ben Polakbrug a doctor in the resistance and later alderman, and the Halverstadbrug Felix Halverstad, who registered the Jews brought into the Schouwburg and wiped the names of children who were smuggled out, through the garden of the teachers' college next door.

Look for:
- on the Lau Mazirelbrug, quay stones shaped as hippos and crocodiles, and frogs and fish on the piers
- the plaque for Ben Polak on a railing of his bridge
- the plaques and name boards on the Henriëtte Pimentelbrug
- the stone balustrades on the Jules Schelvisbrug

title: Hogesluis
summary: The 'high sluice' was never a sluice: in Amsterdam a stone bridge was called one, and this one stood as high as the city ramparts. In 1883 Willem Springer rebuilt it on its 17th-century piers after the Pont Neuf in Paris, with lantern posts shaped like ships' bows.
body:
When the city wall was extended across the Amstel in 1662, a bridge 220 metres long joined the ramparts on both banks. It was as high as the wall, about six metres, so it was soon called the Hooge Sluis. "Sluis" is an old Amsterdam word for a stone bridge without a moving part, not a lock; think of the Torensluis. Two bastions guarded it, and at night the narrow passage was closed with beams.

The bridge has been cut down to size ever since. In 1823 King Willem I had the middle arches replaced by an opening with two lifting leaves for bigger barges. In 1875 the deck was lowered by more than a metre, because the slopes were too steep for the city's first horse tram. In 1882–1883 the architect Willem Springer built a new bridge on the old brick piers, taking the Pont Neuf in Paris as his model, to match the grand new Sarphatistraat with the Amstel Hotel and the Paleis voor Volksvlijt.

Trams still cross it, and it opens for boats. Carré is just north, the Amstel Hotel just south.

Look for:
- eight lantern posts shaped like ships' bows
- painted city arms and masks on the cast-iron ornaments along the sides
- the stone obelisks on the piers and the vase balustrade
- at the south-west end, a stone stair down to the Sarphatikade

title: Corvershof and the couples' homes behind H'ART
summary: A young widower and his second wife, both dead before thirty-two, left their fortune for a home where elderly married couples could live together. Their punning arms, three baskets and three pattens, are on the front. Next door stand two more charity houses of the same church.
body:
Joan Corver, grandson of a burgomaster who held the office nineteen times, died in 1719 at the age of 31. His first wife had died in childbirth; his second, Sara Maria Trip, died in 1721, aged 27. They had no children, and by their will the deacons of the Reformed church got the money for a hofje. It went up in 1721–1723 on the deacons' land behind their old people's home on the Amstel, now the H'ART Museum, and it was meant for elderly Reformed married couples: 28 homes for couples and 6 for single people. The founders' arms are a pun on their names: three baskets (korven) for Corver and three pattens (trippen) for Trip.

Couples lived here until 1928. Later came students and refugees, and since 2006 the Protestant Diaconie of Amsterdam has had its office here. Two neighbours belong to the same story. At no. 20 stands a small poorhouse given in 1789 by Johanna Bontekoning; a poem of nine lines over the door says her widower laid the first stone. At no. 14 the deacons added a wing of homes for married couples in 1872, paid for by donors who wished to stay unknown.

The buildings are offices and are seen from the canal.

Look for:
- the huge carved curved pediment over the middle of the Corvershof
- the original door with side lights
- the nine-line poem over the door of no. 20

title: Van Brants Rus Hofje
summary: A grain trader who befriended Peter the Great was made a Russian nobleman and the tsar's man in Amsterdam. Half a year before he died he laid the first stone of this almshouse for Lutheran women, dressed up as a patrician canal house. Students live here now.
body:
Christoffel Brants, son of a cooper from Wittmund in East Frisia, went to Archangelsk as a young trader and met Tsar Peter the Great there in 1693; the two became friends. Brants shipped grain from Russia to Amsterdam and grew rich. In 1717 the tsar raised him to the Russian nobility, so that he could call himself Van Brants, and made him Russia's representative in Amsterdam. That is where the "Rus" in the name comes from.

On 20 May 1732 he laid the first stone of this hofje, for childless Lutheran women over fifty who had lived in Amsterdam for at least ten years. He died that November; in 1733 the finished house was handed to the Lutheran church. The design is attributed to Daniël Marot: from the canal it looks like a grand double house, with three wings round a courtyard behind it.

In the 1970s, when rooms stood empty, nurses of the nearby Wittenberg nursing home lived here, and since 1984 the hofje has housed students. It is not open to the public; the front is seen from the quay.

Look for:
- the double stoop with Louis XIV balusters
- the relief symbolising charity, with Brants's noble arms beneath it
- the name of the hofje and a poem over the door
- the carved crest on top of the cornice

title: Occo Hofje
summary: Cornelia Occo, an unmarried businesswoman from a banking family, left orders in 1752 for a 'Building of Mercy' for poor Catholic women over fifty. It went up in 1774 and still houses older women of Catholic background, with Mass in its own chapel.
body:
Cornelia Elisabeth Occo (1692–1758) came from the family of the banker Pompeius Occo, traded and invested on her own account, and never married. In her will of 1752 she ordered that a large part of her fortune be spent on a hofje, to be called "Het Gebouw van Barmhertigheijd" (the Building of Mercy) and built within fifteen years of her death. It was for 33 poor childless widows or spinsters over fifty, of the Roman Catholic faith, Amsterdam citizens first; the regents were also to pay for doctors and medicine. Her youngest brother carried it out: building began in 1774 and the first women moved in in 1776.

The hofje has kept changing inside its 18th-century front. In 1816 a chapel to Saint Elizabeth, patron saint of the sick, was given at the cost of three homes. Around 1893 the back wing came down and longer side wings went up, and the clock turret moved to the inside of the gate. In 1990–1991 the homes were joined into 25 two-room flats. The original foundation still runs it, for older women of Catholic background, and services are still held in the chapel.

The hofje is private and closed to visitors; the front is seen from the quay.

Look for:
- the stoop with rococo railings ending in eagles' heads
- the sandstone pilasters and the pediment over the middle bay
- the frieze of triglyphs under the roof

title: Wittenberg (Luther Museum)
summary: A Lutheran home for 300 old people, built in 1769–1772 on land the city gave for nothing. It doubled as an orphanage, and the orphans had their own front door. Today it is a short-stay hotel with the Luther Museum in the old regents' rooms.
body:
One long front, two front doors, as far apart as they could be: the left one led to the old people, the right one to the orphans, which is why it is still sometimes called the Wezenpoort (orphans' gate). The Lutheran diaconate, the church's charity board, could build it thanks to a large bequest from Abraham Kromhuijsen and his sister. The city gave the plot along the Muidergracht, now the Nieuwe Keizersgracht, free of charge and asked no excise, so the house could grow bigger than planned. Jan Gildemeester laid the first stone on 6 September 1769, for a home of three storeys and 300 residents, designed by Coenraad Hoeneker. For much of the 19th century it was also the Lutheran orphanage.

The old people moved to a new building in Osdorp in 1967. The house was renamed Wittenberg, after Luther's town, and served as a nursing home until 2015. Since December 2017 it has been a short-stay hotel with 115 apartments, and the Luther Museum Amsterdam fills the former regents' rooms. The museum entrance is at no. 570, open Wednesday to Sunday, 11:00 to 17:00.

Look for:
- the two wide doors at either end of the front, each with two lanterns
- the clock in the pediment over the middle bay
- round the corner on the Nieuwe Kerkstraat, the hospital wing of 1856 and the nursing wing of 1876 with its corner turret

title: Amsterdam chess house (Henri Polaklaan 14)
summary: A merchant's mansion of the 1870s that became the home of Amsterdam chess: from 1936 to 1967 the clubs played here every night of the week, and national championships were held in its rooms. Before that it was a meeting place for the Jewish neighbourhood.
body:
Behind this mansion front with a rounded bay, the chess clocks ticked for thirty years. The house was built in the 1870s for Pieter Goedkoop, a merchant and shipowner, to a design by A.L. van Gendt. From 1917 the leisure association Samenwerking used it for meetings and courses, and it became a gathering place for the Jewish community of the Plantage.

In 1936 two Amsterdam chess clubs bought the house to give the game a home of its own. On 30 December 1936 the Amsterdamsche Schaakhuis was opened by the alderman for education, Emanuel Boekman, with Max Euwe, then world champion, in the room. Club after club moved in, each with its own night: in July 1939 there was one for nearly every evening of the week, and draughts players came too. The Schaakhuis hosted several Dutch chess championships and international tournaments.

Money ran out in 1967 and the house closed. Youth organisations used it for a while; now it is housing again, and it is seen from the street.

Look for:
- the semicircular bay on the left with a balcony of cast-iron tendrils
- the fluted pilasters marking the wider left-hand bay
- the mansard roof and the dormer with a broken pediment

title: The city's teacher-training school (Nieuwe Prinsengracht 89)
summary: A walled block holds three school buildings of 1861–1877: a free school for the poorest children, a practice school, and the municipal college where future teachers learned their trade on them. The college now houses the National 4 and 5 May Committee.
body:
After the Education Act of 1857 the Netherlands suddenly needed teachers: in twenty years the number in public schools grew by about 150 percent. Amsterdam set up its own training college, with a practice school where students could try out what they learned. Together with an older pauper school they fill a block between the Nieuwe Kerkstraat and the Nieuwe Prinsengracht, tied together by one wall.

The pauper school at Nieuwe Kerkstraat 122–124 (1861, by the city architect Bastiaan de Greef) was for children whose parents could not pay school fees; lessons there rarely went beyond reading, writing and arithmetic. An 18th-century garden wall of the Nieuwe Werkhuis next door is built into it. The practice school at no. 126 and the college on the canal (both 1877) are thought to be by De Greef's assistant Willem Springer, in a richer Dutch Renaissance manner. In the college the library and the director's office lay in the wide centre behind the front, with the classrooms at the sides.

The college building now houses the Nationaal Comité 4 en 5 mei, the national committee for Remembrance Day and Liberation Day, together with the Dutch Foundation for Literature and Amsterdam University Press. The buildings are offices and are seen from the street.

Look for:
- the lions' head masks on the college front
- the curled-over cornices against the side walls of the college
- the plain stepped gables of the pauper school in the Nieuwe Kerkstraat

title: Bombach's wall on the old cattle market (Nieuwe Prinsengracht)
summary: This block was the cattle market. In 1888 the city sold the ground, and within two years one little-known architect had designed almost a whole canal front of rented flats, in the only 19th-century enclave of the canal belt. It escaped urban renewal intact.
body:
Inside the canal belt this block is a rarity: built in one go, around 1890. The ground between the Nieuwe Prinsengracht, the Roetersstraat, the Nieuwe Achtergracht and the Lepelkruisstraat had been the cattle market (veemarkt). In 1888 the council agreed to sell the ground, the plots were auctioned in 1889 and 1890, and the whole block was built up around 1890: houses of rented flats for the middle class, put up by speculators.

Almost the entire canal front was designed by C.A. Bombach, an architect of whom little is known except that he died in 1917, aged sixty. It was the largest job of his life. Each block is a row of three-bay houses in the Dutch neo-Renaissance style, mostly with four small alcove flats per house; one drawing of 1890 shows rich gables that were dropped when it came to building. On the Roetersstraat and the Korte Lepelstraat H.H. Baanders, in one of his first works, did the same for shops with homes above, with gables set off-centre and bays on the corners.

The register's verdict on the canal front: it escaped "as by a miracle" the damage that urban renewal did elsewhere. The houses are private and seen from the quay.

Look for:
- at no. 64, the corner shop front with slender half-columns under the cornice
- lion heads on the keystones of nos. 64–78
- at nos. 80–84, a woman's head over the middle window of the third floor
- Baanders's corner bays at the Roetersstraat

title: Hildo Krop's carvings on the old geology institute (Roeterseiland)
summary: Around 1930 the city built a geological and mineralogical institute and a chemistry laboratory at the tip of Roeterseiland, and Hildo Krop carved its walls with scenes from palaeontology and geography. The university still uses the building.
body:
The long brick building at the tip of Roeterseiland looks severe from a distance: hard edges, deep eaves, upright window strips. Walk along it and the stone starts telling stories. The city architect's office, probably under A.R. Hulshoff, built it in 1930–1931 around a courtyard: a geological and mineralogical institute on the Nieuwe Prinsengracht side and a laboratory for organic chemistry and thermodynamics on the Nieuwe Achtergracht side. The wings bend with the canal, and at the eastern end they step back to leave a small square at the head of the island.

The sculpture, mostly in French limestone, is by Hildo Krop, who made it in 1930–1932 as part of the design. It shows subjects from palaeontology and geography. This is late Krop: unusually anecdotal, and distantly related to Berlin expressionism. A separate relief of 1934 on the Nieuwe Prinsengracht side, made for the social geography department, is called "Moeder Aarde" (Mother Earth).

The building is part of the University of Amsterdam's Roeterseiland campus. The carvings are on the outside and can be seen from the quay.

Look for:
- carved corbels and panels around the entrances on both canals
- the jutting stair tower in glass beside the entrance on the Nieuwe Achtergracht
- the tower-like crown over the entrance on the Nieuwe Prinsengracht

title: Postwar flats on the Amstel (Amstel 135–141)
summary: In 1954 even the director of Public Works, the office everyone blamed for demolitions, wrote in to save the old houses on this corner. He lost. The flats that replaced them were drawn by a young Bart van Kasteel and fit the Amstel front better than anyone expected.
body:
Three old houses stood on this corner of the Amstel and the Korte Amstelstraat until the 1950s. On 18 October 1954 A. van Walraven, director of the Dienst der Publieke Werken, wrote a letter with photographs attached objecting to their demolition: they dated from the end of the 17th century, he argued, and gave the river its proper scale. Coming from the feared city works department it was an unusual plea, and it changed nothing.

The city's committee for the old town, the Commissie voor de Oude Stad, then said it had little faith in the architect J.A. Landman. He sensibly called in Bart van Kasteel, who had just left the office of F.A. Eschauzier, and on 6 August 1955 the redesign was approved at once. The plan to face the closed parts in prefab concrete with artificial granite proved too ambitious and became plaster. The result is a concrete-frame block of 23 small flats above business space, reached by galleries on the courtyard side: an early postwar design in the old city, kept to the height and rhythm of its 19th-century neighbours. Van Kasteel later made his name with his conversions of the Stedelijk Museum and the Amsterdam Historical Museum.

The building is private and seen from the street.

Look for:
- balconies alternating with big living-room windows
- beige strip tiles under the windows and black ones under the steel shop fronts
- the closed, slightly taller end bays that clamp the front in place

title: Gateway to the city carpentry yards (Amstel 161–163)
summary: The long, even front of the Amstel has one hole in it: a passage under no. 161 that once led to the city's carpentry and timber yards. When the yards left, A.J. Tijmensen built this double house over it in bright orange brick.
body:
Along this side of the Amstel the house fronts run on without a break, except at no. 161, where a passage cuts under the house. Behind the block lay the stadstimmertuinen, the city's carpentry and timber yards, an industrial site since the city extension of the 17th century, and the passage was their way in from the river. It also had to stay open so that the fire brigade could get through.

When the yards left around 1900, the space opened up for housing, which is why this stretch was built so late. In 1910–1912 A.J. Tijmensen put up this double house over the passage. Most of his many housing blocks in the 19th-century ring are run of the mill, but here he clearly had a larger budget: a Dutch take on Jugendstil, with lopsided lines, new ornament and striking orange machine-pressed brick. Because the old yards are now open ground, the back of the house can be seen from the street as well. The name lives on in the street behind, the Stadstimmertuin.

The house is private.

Look for:
- the passage under no. 161, the only opening in this stretch of the Amstel front
- the bright orange brick among the darker neighbours
- the back of the house from the Stadstimmertuin side

title: Plancius, the choir's clubhouse (Verzetsmuseum)
summary: The Resistance Museum sits in a clubhouse built in 1876 for a Jewish men's choir. The Star of David is still in the pediment. In between, the building was a taxi garage, a horse stable and a police office.
body:
Look up at the pediment of the Resistance Museum and you see a Star of David above the word PLANCIUS. The building was not made for a museum. In 1874–1876 the Jewish men's choir Oefening Baart Kunst (practice makes art) built itself a clubhouse here, with a concert hall of a thousand seats. A house called Plancius, after the preacher and map maker Petrus Plancius, had to be pulled down for it, and the new building kept the name. It opened on 24 May 1876 and was also used for meetings of the labour movement.

The choir left in 1894. In 1913 a taxi company bought the building and turned it into a taxi depot, with a garage behind it by Harry Elte. When horses came back into use in the Second World War it served for a while as a stable, and in 1944–1945 German vehicles were parked here. Later came a lingerie workshop and, from 1970, the accident unit of the Amsterdam traffic police.

The Verzetsmuseum (Dutch Resistance Museum) moved in and opened on 1 May 1999. The museum can be visited with a ticket, bought online or at the door.

Look for:
- the Star of David and the name PLANCIUS in the pediment
- the Amsterdam arms in the plaster around the small middle door
- the two wide carriage doors under basket arches on either side

title: Desmet, the theatre of many names (Plantage Middenlaan 4)
summary: Frascati, Rika Hopper, Beatrix, Theater van de Lach, Hortus, Desmet: one building, six names. From autumn 1941 only Jews were allowed in. Today it is a TV and radio studio behind a 1927 front.
body:
Most people know this as Desmet, the cinema, and before that it had a whole string of lives. In 1879 Gustave Prot, a theatre man from the old Frascati in the Nes, opened his own small theatre here and called it Frascati too. Everyone called it Prot. The new Artis Schouwburg next door nearly finished him in the 1890s, but it was Prot that survived.

In 1926 Jacques van Hoven bought the run-down house and named it after his wife, the actress Rika Hopper. The front you see now is from that rebuild, by Jan Boterenbrood: Art Deco with a touch of Amsterdam School. In 1938 the theatre became the Beatrixtheater, until the occupier banned names of the royal family in 1941. From September 1941 only Jews were allowed in, and it was called the Theater van de Lach (theatre of laughter). It closed in spring 1942.

After the war it became cinema Desmet, named after the film pioneer Jean Desmet, and until 1997 it was one of the city's best loved art-house screens. Since 2001 it has been Desmet Studio's, where radio and TV programmes are recorded; it is also hired out for events.

Look for:
- above the 1927 front, the top of the older theatre wall with its corner blocks
- the square pillars topped with white globe lamps
- the fan-shaped glazing in the round-arched corner doors

title: Café Eik en Linde (Plantage Middenlaan 22)
summary: A café named after the oak and the linden of Ovid's tale. It began as a pleasure-garden inn that Artis swallowed (the old inn is now the wolves' house), and its present home was the coffee room of the Hollandsche Schouwburg.
body:
In Ovid's story an old couple who took in two gods in disguise were turned, at their death, into an oak and a linden, their trunks grown together. Eik en Linde (oak and linden) was the name of an inn in the pleasure gardens of the Plantage, at the corner of what are now the Plantage Badlaan and the Henri Polaklaan. From 1834 it advertised concerts. When the gardens were sold for building and Artis grew, the zoo took over the inn. Its building still stands inside Artis as the wolves' house, with a plaque on the wall.

The café moved to the Plantage Middenlaan and, after two other addresses, came to no. 22 in 1967. The house was built in 1872 by Jean Servais. In 1912 the Hollandsche Schouwburg next door bought it and turned the ground floor into a café, the first floor into the theatre's coffee room and the top floor into offices. The theatre became the memorial to the Jews who were held there for deportation, and the city listed the café building for that bond.

It is an ordinary neighbourhood café, open to all, with a billiard table in the middle.

Look for:
- the ground floor of 1913, a middle door between two big sash windows
- the billiard table, and through the back the garden
- in Artis, the plaque on the wolves' house

title: Aldo van Eyck's Mothers' House (Hubertushuis)
summary: A building in every colour for single parents and their children, opened in 1980 by Aldo van Eyck. It stands where the Jewish crèche was, from which children were smuggled into hiding during the war. Now a hotel.
body:
Among the white stucco villas of the Plantage Middenlaan stands a front that steps forward and back, up and down, in glass and colour. It is the Hubertushuis, better known as the Moederhuis (mothers' house). Aldo van Eyck designed it from 1973 with Theo Bosch for the Hubertus Vereniging, a society that gave temporary shelter to single parents and their children. It opened in 1980. Van Eyck meant it as a small town of its own, with passages, roof terraces and courtyards, and corners and changes of level inside to make it a place for children to play. Two houses of 1885 on the right were taken into the scheme.

The site has an older story. Here stood the school and meeting halls of the Talmoed Thora society, by Isaac Gosschalk, which later housed the Jewish crèche opposite the Hollandsche Schouwburg. During the deportations children were taken from it to hiding places outside the city by student resistance groups and others. A few round elements in the front recall the old building.

The Mothers' House was listed as a national monument in 2026, with the garden behind. It is now a hotel, the Quentin Zoo, so the building has guests again rather than families.

Look for:
- the staggered, see-through façade in many colours
- the concrete base faced with coloured tiles in mirror frames
- the two white houses of 1885 on the right, one with a stone stair and balcony

title: Sint Jacob, the old people's home where Artis began
summary: A baron's legacy of 250,000 guilders built a Catholic home for the poor old here in 1863–1866, on the site of the inn where Artis had shown its first animals. Only the cross-shaped chapel wing is left, hidden in the block.
body:
In 1838 the new zoological society Natura Artis Magistra showed its first collection in a room of the Nieuwe Stadsherberg, an inn on this spot. The zoo soon found land across the street. The inn's plot went another way. Jacob baron van Brienen, who died in 1858, left 250,000 guilders to the Catholic poor relief, and with it the Sint Jacobsgesticht was built for poor old men and women, named after its benefactor's saint. A design competition produced only plans that were too expensive, so the jury member W.J.J. Offenberg drew it himself. It opened in 1866.

Offenberg's front wing on the street and the later Barbarahofje for married couples (1911) were pulled down in the 1970s and 1980s for a new care home. That one went in turn: by 2022 De Nieuwe Sint Jacob stood here, 305 flats for older people round a garden. Of Offenberg's building only the middle wing survives, shaped like a Latin cross, with the chapel on the first floor and its original stained glass showing the life of Saint James. Amstelring now runs it as a home for people with dementia, so it is not open to the public. The stone Saint Barbara from the hofje ended up on the forecourt of the Sint Barbara cemetery.

Look for:
- above the entrance of the new building, Saint James standing between two old people

title: Hugo de Vries's house and laboratory
summary: The botanist Hugo de Vries lived at Plantage Parklaan 9 until 1916. Later it was a Jewish youth club and, after the war, offices of the Jewish community. Round the corner stands the laboratory the city built for him.
body:
Hugo de Vries, one of the scientists who rediscovered Mendel's laws of heredity and the author of the mutation theory, was among the first to live in this house of 1880 and stayed until 1916. He was director of the Hortus across the road. In 1915 the city opened a laboratory for him on the Plantage Middenlaan, at the Hortus, as a mark of recognition: the first building that J.M. van der Mey, later of the Scheepvaarthuis, ever saw built, designed with De Vries and his assistant Theo Stomps.

The house went on to other lives. In 1918 a blouse factory worked in the attic. In 1930 the Jewish youth association Beisjisraeil made it its clubhouse. In 1941 two Jewish families lived upstairs; five of them were murdered in 1942 and 1943. From 1948 to 1976 it housed offices of the Dutch Jewish community. A gable stone with Hebrew letters recalls those years, though a company sign has hidden it.

The house is private. The laboratory, called De Groene Plantage since 2014, is a centre for nature education and meetings.

Look for:
- two small owls in the plaster pediments over the first-floor windows of the house
- at the laboratory, the wrought-iron gate with "D'ARTZENIJHOFF" and the city arms
- the stone above the laboratory door with a relief of the building itself

title: Zeeman laboratory, built without iron
summary: A physics lab of 1923 for the Nobel laureate Pieter Zeeman, put up without steel or iron so nothing would disturb his magnetic experiments. Under the floor sits a separate concrete block of 250 tonnes. Einstein came to visit.
body:
Pieter Zeeman won the Nobel Prize in 1902 for the effect that bears his name: in a magnetic field, the lines in the spectrum of glowing atoms split. To measure such things you need a building that does not shake and does not bend a magnetic field, and Zeeman pushed the city hard for one. The Laboratorium Physica, designed by A.A. Kok of the city's Public Works, opened on 18 June 1923. No steel or iron was used in its construction. Massive concrete tables, each on its own foundation and free of the rest of the building, kept vibrations out. The largest weighs 250 tonnes and was made to carry the great grating set-ups, among them a grating that the American physicist H.A. Rowland had engraved for Zeeman in 1900.

Meetings, demonstrations and visits by famous physicists, Albert Einstein among them, made it a meeting point of Dutch physics. It took Zeeman's name in 1940. The university left in 2007 and the building was turned into flats; it is private.

Look for:
- the window above the entrance, a grating that shows a beam of light breaking into rays
- the tile panel ZEEMAN LABORATORIUM above it
- on the side facing the little park, a fountain by John Rädecker with the city arms

title: Boarding school for steam engineers (Plantage Muidergracht 14)
summary: From 1887 boys learned to drive the steam engines of ships, trains and factories here, at home and in the Dutch East Indies. Most of them slept on the top floor, above a smithy and a turnery.
body:
Sailing ships were giving way to steam, and someone had to run the engines. The Kweekschool voor Machinisten (training school for engine drivers) started on 19 October 1878 on the Oostenburg island and in 1887 moved into this building by Abraham Salm, put at its disposal by the city. It was a three-year course: first classroom theory, then a placement, learning the steam engines of ships and trains, for work in the Netherlands and in the Dutch East Indies, in shipping, trade and industry. In its first six years it trained 306 boys, 33 of them from the Indies. The fee was 300 guilders, and pupils paid for their own books, instruments and uniform.

School and boarding house were under one roof. The classrooms lay along a corridor, with room for a smithy, a turnery, an engine room and labs; the pupils slept on the top floor behind the small windows. The director lived in the right wing, the engineer in the left. One former pupil, Henri Gorter, went on to found the Hercules steam skate factory in Zwolle. The building now holds offices of the University of Amsterdam.

Look for:
- two stones in the front with the founding year 1878 and the year of this building
- the small top-floor windows of the old dormitories
- the stone balcony on the director's wing, with men's heads on the brackets and beside the doors

title: The city workhouse (Dr. Sarphatihuis)
summary: A vast block of 1779–1782 built to put beggars and vagrants to work. Later it was the city poorhouse, with up to a thousand people inside. Since 1978 it has been a nursing home named after Samuel Sarphati.
body:
Walk along the Nieuwe Kerkstraat side and the wall seems to go on for ever. Behind it lie four courtyards. Abraham van der Hart, director of the city works, designed this Stadswerkhuis (city workhouse) for mayor Joachim Rendorp; building began in 1779 and it opened in 1782. The plan was to move the Spinhuis and the Rasphuis, the city's houses of correction, here. King Louis Napoleon wanted to turn it into a Palace of the Arts in 1809, but let the idea drop.

From 1822 it was the Werkhuis again: beggars and vagrants were set to work here for pay, until about 1870. Then it became the city poorhouse, taking in old people with incurable illnesses and people then called "idiots". Residents had to work, and in times of much sickness up to a thousand people lived inside. Until 1911 the Jewish old and disabled were cared for here as well. In 1933 it became a municipal home for the elderly, and after a rebuilding of 1971–1978 it took the name Dr. Sarphatihuis. It is still a nursing home; the singer Ramses Shaffy was one of its residents.

Look for:
- the front on the Roetersstraat stepping forward in three stages to a carved pediment
- the long wall on the Nieuwe Kerkstraat, with buttresses and small gates

title: Sarphati's Amstel Hotel and the masseur who saved it
summary: Samuel Sarphati wanted a first-class hotel for Amsterdam and work for the jobless; he died before it opened in 1867. Guests were slow to come until a pioneer of physiotherapy set up practice inside and drew royalty from all over.
body:
The doctor and city planner Samuel Sarphati (1813–1866) told the city it needed a grand hotel of international standard, and saw the building work as a way to fight unemployment. Cornelis Outshoorn, also the architect of Sarphati's Palace of Industry, gave it the outline of a French château. The main front was first planned on the new boulevard, now the Sarphatistraat, and was turned a quarter before building to face the Amstel. The site had been one of the bastions of the old city wall. Sarphati died before the company was founded in 1866; the first stone was laid on 26 April 1866 and the hotel opened in the summer of 1867. Four wings were planned and only one was built.

At first visitors stayed away, and it looked as if the money would never come back. Rescue came from Dr Johann Georg Mezger, a founder of physiotherapy, who treated patients in the hotel from 1870 to 1888. His aristocratic clients made it a spa for royal and noble guests from all over the world.

It is still a five-star hotel. The rooms are for guests, but the bar and restaurant let anyone see the inside.

Look for:
- the château silhouette, best seen from across the Amstel
- the long front facing the river, not the Sarphatistraat it was first drawn for

title: Kriterion, the cinema the resistance students built
summary: Students who had smuggled Jewish children into hiding opened a cinema here in November 1945, so students could pay for their studies by working. It is still run by students, in a building taken from a Jewish workers' club.
body:
During the war the Amsterdamse Studenten Groep around Piet Meerburg, working with other resistance groups, took Jewish children from the crèche opposite the Hollandsche Schouwburg to hiding places outside the city. Long before liberation Meerburg had a plan: a cinema where students could earn their way through university without depending on their parents or the state. The foundation was set up on 1 June 1945. With money they had collected, the students bought the clubhouse of the Handwerkers Vriendenkring, a Jewish workers' association whose building the Dutch Nazi party had seized in the war, and turned it into a cinema. They chose the name Kriterion, Greek for a standard or touchstone. It opened on 6 November 1945.

The building at the Roetersstraat was added in 1924 by Kleinhout and Van der Steur to the older club on the Nieuwe Achtergracht. In 1982 the foundation wanted to close the cinema; the staff occupied it and have run it themselves as an association ever since, still without bosses. Every year opens with Citizen Kane, and every academic year with Once Upon a Time in the West.

Look for:
- the jutting bay of contrasting brick on the first floor, once the meeting hall
- the flagpoles fixed against the side walls at the top
- the café inside, the club's old coffee room

title: Cavalry barracks turned art academy (Rijksakademie)
summary: Horses and troopers lived around this square courtyard from 1865. Since 1992 artists do: the Rijksakademie moved in, and once a year it opens its studios to everyone.
body:
Over the gate a stone still reads KAVALLERIE-KAZERNE, in the old spelling. The Ministry of War built this cavalry barracks in 1864–1865, in the square type named after Vauban: four wings around a courtyard, with rooms for the men and stables for the horses, and a gate in the middle of each wing. In 1874 a riding hall was added on the east side. German troops were quartered here in the war. As tanks replaced horses the stables emptied, and in the 1950s part of the complex stored medicines for the state. The army left for good in 1988.

Then the Rijksakademie van beeldende kunsten, the national academy of fine arts, came from the Stadhouderskade. Koen van Velsen rebuilt the complex in 1991–1992: a new building with exhibition space and library in the courtyard, a canteen on the Singelgracht, and steel-and-glass skybridges between them. The old wings became studios for artists in residence.

The academy is not open every day, but each year it holds Open Studios over a few days (in 2026, 19 to 22 November).

Look for:
- the arched gate with the year 1864 on its keystone and the KAVALLERIE-KAZERNE plaque
- the iron fence along the street
- the riding hall's gables, with cast-iron rose windows in yellow brick frames

title: Muiderpoort, the gate Napoleon rode through
summary: Amsterdam's only surviving gate from its 17th and 18th-century walls. The first one slid off its foundations one January night in 1769; its successor saw Napoleon ride in behind eight white horses. Tax collectors work in it again.
body:
On the night of 29 to 30 January 1769 the old Muiderpoort of 1663 slid off its foundations and sank sixteen feet. Within days it was being pulled down. The city architect Cornelis Rauws designed the new gate, finished in 1770, with sculpture by Anthonie Ziesenis. Of all the gates in the 17th and 18th-century city walls, it is the only one left.

On 9 October 1811 Emperor Napoleon entered Amsterdam through it, in a coach drawn by eight white horses, under a triumphal arch put up for the day. In 1898 the outer gate on the bridge was removed because the passage was too narrow; it was rebuilt in 1938 at the entrance of the Flevopark. From 1903 a new bridge carried traffic past the gate, and it lost its use.

Toll and salt duty were once collected here. Since 2002 the Dutch association of tax advisers has had its office in the gate, so it still deals in taxes. The city sold it to the restoration company Stadsherstel in 2019.

Look for:
- on the city side, the old Amsterdam arms with a medieval ship (a hulk, not a cog)
- on the outer side, the newer arms with the three Saint Andrew's crosses
- the octagonal domed tower, whose bell was cast by the Hemony brothers in 1664

title: The Jewish schools of the Stadstimmertuin (Joods Lyceum)
summary: Two schools of 1901 face each other on the old city timber yard. From 1941 Jewish children were forced into them: Anne and Margot Frank went to the Joods Lyceum at no. 1. A twisted Star of David over the door marks 1941–1943.
body:
From 1 September 1941 the occupier banned Jewish children from all other schools. A month later the Joods Lyceum opened at Voormalige Stadstimmertuin 1 with 350 pupils. It was not a religious school but a public one with only Jewish pupils and teachers; the historian Jacques Presser taught history there, the scholar Sem Dresden French. Anne Frank and her sister Margot were pupils until the family went into hiding in July 1942. When the deportations began, the classes emptied: first the children whose surnames began with A stopped coming, then those with B. The school stopped in 1943 because there was nobody left to teach or be taught. Of the 489 children who went there, 45 per cent were murdered.

Across the street, at no. 2, the Jewish HBS (secondary school) had moved in on 21 September 1938, in a building refitted by Jac. S. Baars and opened by the minister of education. It closed at the end of May 1943; its furniture was shipped to Germany. After the war it returned and grew into Maimonides, which left for Buitenveldert from 1972. No. 2 has been flats since 2017. No. 1 now houses after-school care.

Look for:
- over the door of no. 1, the twisted three-dimensional Star of David with a tile panel, and the plaque beside it
- the panel "Ao 1901" high in its front
- at no. 2, the decoration over the school entrance and the plaque on its history

title: The Glass Palace of the Joodsche Invalide
summary: In 1937 the Jewish home for the disabled and elderly moved into a modern building of glass and grey tiles, nicknamed the Glass Palace. On 1 March 1943 its 256 residents and staff were taken away; most were murdered at Sobibor.
body:
Until 1911 Jewish elderly and disabled people who needed care were put in the city poorhouse. After rabbi Meijer de Hond wrote a pamphlet called "A Jewish heart knocks at your door", the society De Joodsche Invalide was founded that year. It grew fast, paid for new buildings with lotteries, and on 19 September 1937 opened this one by J.F. Staal, built round an earlier wing by Harry Elte. Amsterdammers called it the Glazen Paleis, the Glass Palace. Inside were a synagogue along the Weesperplein with a festive hall above it, whose floor could be tilted for a better view of the stage, kitchens run to Jewish dietary law, and a place in the garden for the sukkah.

On 1 March 1943, 256 residents and staff were deported. Only a few managed to escape. Most were murdered at Sobibor on 13 March 1943. After the war the shrunken Jewish community could not keep the building and handed it to the city, which used it as a hospital and, since 1979, for the municipal health service.

Look for:
- the corner of glass on slender columns, crowned by a boardroom under a curved roof
- the walls clad in grey glazed tiles and the curved canopy over the entrance
- by the entrance on the Weesperplein, the 1950 plaque by Cephas Stauthamer with three kneeling men

title: Diamond Exchange on the Weesperplein (Diamantbeurs)
summary: Built in 1910–1911 to get the diamond trade out of the cafés. It housed Belgian refugees in the First World War, lost two-thirds of its trade in the Second, and burned in 1956 without losing a stone. Now a creative hub with a grand café.
body:
Diamonds used to change hands in cafés. To bring the trade under one roof, dealers founded the Vereeniging Beurs voor den Diamanthandel in 1898 and rented a hall at the Waterlooplein. When the lease ran out in 1911 they built their own exchange here, designed by Gerrit van Arkel in Art Nouveau style. The mayor laid the first stone on 12 December 1910 and trading began in May 1911. The big trading floor was on the raised ground floor; in the basement were a barber, a vault and a restaurant.

In the First World War trade nearly stopped and Belgian refugees were lodged in the building. The Second World War was far worse: two-thirds of the city's diamond workers and dealers did not survive. On the afternoon of 12 February 1956 a big fire broke out; thanks to the fireproof vaults no diamonds were lost. The dealers sold the building in 1987. It is the only one left of Amsterdam's three diamond exchange buildings.

Since a conversion finished in 2022 it has been Capital C, with offices and studios for creative firms and a grand café open to the public.

Look for:
- the two tile panels by the door: Mercury's winged staff, and a polishing mill holding two diamonds
- the octagonal tower with a copper dome and four clock faces
- in the hall, the marble foundation stone of 1910

title: Hertzberger's student house with a street in the air (Weesperflat)
summary: Herman Hertzberger's first big building, finished in 1966: 250 student rooms on concrete legs, with an open gallery and terrace halfway up, set exactly at the ridge height of the old canal houses next door.
body:
In the early 1960s Amsterdam was short of student rooms, and Herman Hertzberger (born 1932) got his first big commission. Built 1963–1966, the Weesperflat holds some 250 rooms in two long concrete blocks on pillars. Halfway up, on the fourth floor, he left a covered street with a big terrace: homes for student couples, where their children could play safely, and a hall for parties and meetings whose glass doors open onto the terrace. He put it at the ridge height of the old canal houses of the Nieuwe Keizersgracht, so that old and new would meet at that level. The ideas came from the magazine Forum, which he edited with Aldo van Eyck and others: a building that mixes with the life of the street. It won the Amsterdam architecture prize in 1968.

Architects came from all over to see it; Amsterdammers were less impressed. On 24 April 1999 a night-time party got out of hand and students threw glasses, bottles and even fridges at passers-by. The flat is still student housing, owned by the housing association De Key, and is not open to visitors.

Look for:
- the fourth-floor terrace at the height of the canal-house roofs
- concrete benches between the pillars, lit by lamps under the seats
- the mural El Salvador (1980) on the north stair tower, by the Februari collective after a design by Kees Romeyn

title: Sarphatistraat 66, the diamond mansion where dolls watch the street
summary: A rich black-and-stone mansion built for two diamond merchants, later a diamond-tool firm's office and then a 28-room hotel. It has been for sale for years, and the dolls staring down from the first floor have neighbours calling it a haunted house.
body:
The Sarphatistraat filled up with grand houses for well-off Amsterdammers in the last quarter of the 19th century, and this is one of the showiest. The diamond merchants Beer and Raap of the Huddestraat had J.H. Schmitz design it: the drawings are from 1873, but the front says Anno 1878. Stone dressings run all over the black-painted brick: window frames with pediments and masks, pilasters, festoons and lion heads on the consoles, with a pediment and attic on top.

The first residents were a diamond merchant's family from Brussels. In 1921 the firm J.K. Smit & Zonen, which dealt in diamonds for industry and later made diamond tools, took the house as its office, and stayed until the 1970s. After that it was a hotel for a long time, probably until 2022.

Since then it has stood on the market, first for about seven million euros, in 2026 for nearly six. Passers-by told AT5 in July 2026 that they would bet it was haunted: from the first-floor windows, a row of dolls stares at the street. The house is private.

Look for:
- the dolls in the first-floor windows
- Anno 1878 on the front
- lion heads on the consoles and masks over the windows

title: The calendar warehouses of the Achtergracht
summary: Thirteen identical warehouses of about 1723 in a row: one called Zon (sun), the other twelve named after the months of the year, running backwards from December to January. Nobody knows why; a folk tale blames an elf.
body:
On the south side of the Achtergracht stands a row of thirteen narrow warehouses with spout gables, all built around 1723 to the same design. The corner one, by the Frederiksplein, is called Zon (sun). The twelve after it carry the names of the months, but in reverse: December comes first, and the row ends with Februari and Januari towards the Amstel. Several fronts are still entirely in their original state.

The names are an old puzzle, and a folk tale fills the gap. A skipper whose boats kept coming loose at night lay in wait and caught the culprits: elves playing on the moorings. The one he grabbed bought its freedom with twenty gold pieces. The skipper built the warehouses with the gold, named twelve after the months and the thirteenth after the elf, whose name was Zon. It is a story, not history; no source gives the real reason.

The Achtergracht itself is a stump. Dug around 1660 to link the Reguliersgracht with the Amstel, most of it was filled in 1870 and became the Falckstraat and the north side of the Frederiksplein. The warehouses have long been converted into offices and homes; the whole row can be read from the quay.

Look for:
- the month names painted on the loading doors, starting with December at no. 4
- the hoist beams and loading doors in the spout gables
- across the water, the little wooden police post at no. 11

title: Het witte huisje, a wooden police post
summary: A little wooden chalet on the Achtergracht that was once a neighbourhood police post, built when Amsterdam abolished its night watch and put constables on duty round the clock. It was moved here in 1913 and is one of the very few left.
body:
In 1878 Amsterdam abolished the old night watch and the police went on permanent duty. To save the constables long walks, the city put up small police posts in the neighbourhoods, and many were wooden chalets like this one. Inside, officers could rest between rounds.

This one, later nicknamed Het witte huisje (the little white house), has walls of vertically grooved boards in a frame of posts and rails, a zinc roof with ribs, a gutter on wooden brackets and a stylised palmette over the door and over the window on the south end. According to an article in Ons Amsterdam it first stood on the Hemonylaan and was moved here in 1913, to a spot opposite Achtergracht 9 by the Frederiksplein.

The city listed it in 1995 because it had become so rare: almost all the others were cleared away. One more stands on the Nieuwezijds Voorburgwal, opposite the stamp market, and a third, from 1915, on the Buiksloterweg across the IJ.

It is small enough to take in at a glance from the quay; the inside is not open.

Look for:
- the palmette crowns over the door and the south window, both missing a few pieces
- the triangular braces closing the gable overhangs
- the narrow lean-to on the east side, finished in the same boarding

title: Harry Elte's two Edwardian fronts, Achtergracht 17-19 and 33
summary: Two small 1916 designs by Harry Elte, the architect of Amsterdam's Jewish community, both signed on the front. One is a business building posing as a double house; the other has a foundation stone laid by a thirteen-year-old boy.
body:
Harry Elte trained under Berlage, worked for him for ten years, and became the architect of Amsterdam's Jewish congregations: his synagogue on the Jacob Obrechtplein is his best-known work. From 1915 to 1920 he worked with Gerard Mastenbroek, and these two fronts on the Achtergracht are from that short partnership, both in a style the city register calls Edwardian, rare in the old centre.

No. 17-19 was a business building for a client named Speijer. It is too big for this row of small houses, so the architects disguised it: what looks like a double house under one cross roof is only a roof slope, with a whole extra floor hidden behind it. The sandstone ground floor carries fine reliefs and a tile panel by the Amsterdam firm De Distel.

No. 33 is a narrow house with a copper-domed bay window. A stone low on the front records that it was laid in 1916 by Hartog Philip, aged thirteen; the client was M. Philip.

In 1942 Elte was taken to Westerbork; he died in Theresienstadt in April 1944. Both houses are private and are seen from the street.

Look for:
- the architects' signatures, at chest height beside the left door of 17-19 and on the low wall in front of 33
- the foundation stone of Hartog Philip on the left of the plinth of no. 33
- the green-lacquered wrought-iron cellar grilles of 17-19

title: Amstelsluizen, Hudde's locks of 1673
address: Amstel, between Prinsengracht and Singelgracht (opposite the Utrechtsedwarsstraat)
summary: Three lock chambers across the Amstel, designed in 1673 by the mathematician and later mayor Johannes Hudde to flush the stinking canals with river water. The old capstans still stand by the gates, and two little stone houses once collected the city's excise.
body:
When the canal belt was extended across the Amstel in the 1660s, this stretch of the river came inside the city. In 1673 a set of locks went in at the line of the Utrechtsedwarsstraat, designed by Johannes Hudde, mathematician, alderman and later mayor, with Gerard Hasselaer and Cornelis van Oudshoorn. Hudde also oversaw the building. Letting boats through was only part of the job: the locks were mainly there to refresh the water of the tidal Amstel and the old canals, which had become badly polluted.

The plan grew from two locks to three: a big one in the middle and a smaller one on each side, with a sluice between each and the quay. In the 19th century the locks were rebuilt, the western sluice was replaced by a fixed crossing, and in 1872 the new Oranjesluizen took over most of the work of keeping the water fresh. The gates usually stand open.

On the island in the middle is the lock keeper's brick office with its square plan and zinc roof. The two stone-clad houses on the other islands are thought to have served for collecting the city's excise duties, hence the nickname douanehuisjes (customs houses).

Best seen from the Amstel quays near Carré.

Look for:
- the capstans with horizontal windlasses and wooden bars beside the mitre gates
- the toll door in the remaining sluice on the east side
- the cast-iron balusters of the railings and the old bollards

title: De Balie, the courthouse beside the old remand prison
summary: A district court of 1891, built in front of the remand prison where Anne Frank was held after her arrest. Saved from a hotel plan in the late 1970s, it became De Balie in 1982, and debates now run in the old courtroom.
body:
In 1891 the state moved its prison from the Weteringschans to the Havenstraat and turned the old building here, on the former bastion De Schinkel, into a remand prison. On its forecourt the government architect for justice buildings, W.C. Metzelaar, put up a new kantongerecht (district court), finished in 1892.

Behind the court lay the cells. After their arrest in 1944, Anne Frank and the others from the hiding place on the Prinsengracht were locked up in this remand prison. That same year resistance groups raided it twice to free captured comrades: a group led by Gerrit van der Veen on 1 May, and one led by Johannes Post in the night of 14 to 15 July.

In the late 1970s court and prison were to make way for an eight-storey Bouwes hotel. The campaign "Bouw es wat anders" (build something else, a pun on the hotel's name) stopped it. After a spell as a stopgap theatre, in 1982 it became De Balie, a centre for culture and politics. The cell block was demolished in 1988 for the Max Euweplein.

De Balie is open for debates, theatre and films, and has a café-restaurant on the square; its main hall is the old courtroom.

Look for:
- the royal arms with lion and crown in the pediment over the entrance
- the reliefs about justice over the windows of the end bays, and the lion-head keystones
- the years 1891 and 1892 in the round blind windows of the two gables

title: Politiebureau No. 14, now The Bulldog
summary: The city built police station no. 14 on the Leidseplein in 1900 and spelled it out in tiles on the front. Since April Fools' Day 1985 it has held The Bulldog's grand café, with a coffeeshop next door in the same building.
body:
There had long been a police station on this square, close to the old Leidsepoort city gate. In 1900 the city's public works department, possibly the architect Jost van Genet, built a new one: police station no. 14, with two separate flats above it. It towers over its neighbours with a symmetrical front in red brick and plenty of hard stone, in a mix of sober rationalism and art nouveau, and the builders had its name and number laid in tiles in the middle of the first floor.

The police left, and on 1 April 1985 Henk de Vries, founder of The Bulldog, opened a bar here in the old station. The ground floor and basement now hold the grand café The Bulldog Palace, which turns into a nightclub after dark, and the coffeeshop The Bulldog Ex-Police Station at no. 17. The upper floors are still flats.

A wide glass extension now hides much of the ground floor, but above it the front is untouched.

Look for:
- the tile panel reading "Politiebureau No.14" in the middle of the first floor
- "ANNO" and "1900" in tiles at the foot of the two bell gables
- the art nouveau tile panels with house numbers over the side doors to the flats

title: Hirschgebouw, the fashion palace opened for men only
summary: Hirsch & Cie's domed fashion house of 1912, opened to an audience made up entirely of men so they could tell their wives about it. Its top floor held Merkelbach's portrait studio, where Mata Hari sat; since 2012 it has been Apple's first Dutch store.
body:
The fashion house Hirsch & Cie had a branch on this corner from 1882 and kept outgrowing it. In 1911–1913 the architect A. Jacot, with J.G. Snuif, gave it a new department store: a reinforced-concrete frame clad in grey sandstone from Arzviller, colossal Ionic half-columns, and a round corner crowned by a copper dome. More than 1,600 wooden piles went into the ground.

On 14 November 1912 alderman Delprat opened it for an audience made up entirely of men. The idea was that they would pass on their amazement to their wives and daughters, who would then come and shop.

From 1913 the photographer Jacob Merkelbach had his studio high up in the building, at Leidseplein 29. It became one of the city's best-known portrait studios, visited by Mata Hari, the conductor Willem Mengelberg and the actress Fien de la Mar among many others; his daughter Mies kept it going until 1969. The Stadsarchief holds its negatives.

Hirsch used the building until 1976. Since 2012 it has housed Apple's first store in the Netherlands, open during shop hours. Of the four original chandeliers, three went to the Stadsschouwburg across the square.

Look for:
- HIRSCH & Cie at the foot of the corner tower
- the balustrades with little candelabra columns on the first floor
- the dormer windows in the mansard roof, where Merkelbach's studio was

title: City Theater, a picture palace built in a year
summary: Jan Wils's 1,800-seat cinema of 1935, put up on a steel frame in under a year. A minister opened it only because its building had put 600 unemployed workers back to work. Hidden behind 1960s cladding for forty years, its front came back in 2010.
body:
In 1934 a company led by the Wilton family bought fifteen old houses on the Kleine-Gartmanplantsoen and the Korte Leidsedwarsstraat and pulled them down. The architect Jan Wils designed a cinema and theatre for 1,800 people, with a balcony, an orchestra pit and a 40-metre stage tower. Thanks to a steel frame it went up in record time: Huib Wilton laid the first stone on 25 July 1935, and it opened on 29 October.

The opening was done by the minister of social affairs, Marcus Slingenberg. He had doubts about a minister opening a place of entertainment, but in the middle of the Depression the building had given work to 600 unemployed builders.

In 1967–1968 the brick front disappeared behind panels of marble and anodised aluminium, and the big hall was later split into smaller screens. A restoration of 2008–2010 brought back the 1935 front, the lit strips that had been removed in the wartime blackout and the crown on the glass stair tower. It reopened on 2 December 2010 as Pathé City, with a grand café and a casino in the basement.

Look for:
- the slim glass tower with the spiral stair, lit from inside at night
- the black stone plaque by the entrance: "op 25 juli van 1935 werd de eerste steen van dit gebouw gelegd door HUIB WILTON"
- on the Korte Leidsedwarsstraat side, the plain yellow brick and black glazed plinth that were never covered

title: Leidsebrug, Kramer's bridge with hippos and benches
address: Leidseplein, over the Singelgracht to the Stadhouderskade
summary: Piet Kramer's Amsterdam School bridge between the Leidseplein and the Stadhouderskade, finished in 1925. Granite hippos guard its corners, and it was the first bridge designed with seats built into its parapets.
body:
The bridge over the Singelgracht at the Leidseplein is named after the Leidsepoort, the city gate that once stood here. Its predecessor was a stone arch bridge known as the Leidse Barrière. Traffic outgrew it, and Piet Kramer, the bridge architect of the city's public works department, designed a replacement in the Amsterdam School style. It was built in 1923–1925, ten metres wider than the old one and with two openings for boats.

The sculptor Johan Polet carved the heavy granite blocks on the corners of the abutments: two hippos and two lion heads, plus smaller carving that runs on into the low walls along the quays. Those walls have wooden benches built into them. According to the national register this was the first bridge whose design included seating. The walls end in round and pointed knobs, and wrought-iron railings run along the top.

The bridge was fully renovated from 2015. Trams cross it all day, and the benches look out over the Singelgracht and the Leidsebosje.

Look for:
- the granite hippos on the corners of the abutments
- the wooden benches set into the parapets along the quays
- the round and pointed knobs at the ends of the parapets

title: Dikker & Thijs, the oyster salon on the Leidsestraat corner
summary: An insurance office of 1915 with a stone bird on its corner that became the home of Dikker & Thijs: a delicatessen and a restaurant for oysters, lobster and caviar that won a Michelin star in the first Dutch guide of 1957. The name lives on as a hotel.
body:
The corner building was put up in 1914–1915 for the life insurance company De Nederlanden, to a design by B.J. Ouëndag: a concrete frame, black stone pillars around big shop windows below, dark brick with curved bays above. When the company became De Nederlanden van 1870, a large light sign with "1870" went on the roof. The shops were first let to a hat and cap firm.

Frederik Dikker had opened a delicatessen in 1895. In 1915 he went into partnership with Henri Thijs, who had worked for years under the French master chef Auguste Escoffier. In the early 1920s Dikker & Thijs moved into this corner, with the shop downstairs and, on the first floor, a restaurant for oysters, lobster and caviar. When Michelin first handed out stars in the Netherlands in 1957, it got one, and kept it until 1962. Delicacies sold in the shop were cooked in the restaurant kitchen upstairs.

The restaurant and brasserie closed in 1994. The hotel that carries the name is still here, with its entrance on the Prinsengracht.

Look for:
- the carved stone bird (perhaps a phoenix) above the cornice on the cut corner
- the black stone pillars and the leaded upper lights of the shop floor
- the curved bays on the third and fourth floors

title: Aalmoezeniersbrug, Kramer's bridge where traffic keeps left
summary: The Leidsestraat bridge over the Prinsengracht, by Piet Kramer, with four granite fabulous beasts designed by Hildo Krop. The First World War nearly doubled its cost. Cars on it drive on the left, so they can turn back along the canal.
body:
The bridge carrying the Leidsestraat over the Prinsengracht is bridge 68, named after the almoners' house (aalmoezeniershuis) that stood on the Prinsengracht, a shelter for poor orphans and widows. Around 1860 the city architect Bastiaan de Greef built a bridge here, but traffic and above all the trams made the Leidsestraat bridges too narrow.

In 1916 the city set aside 150,000 guilders for three new bridges on this route. Then the First World War pushed up the price of materials, and by 1920–1921 the budget had nearly doubled. That did leave room for decoration: Piet Kramer's plain-looking slab bridge, with three openings and stepped brick wings, got wrought-iron railings and four granite fabulous beasts, designed by Hildo Krop as early as 1916 and carved by the firm of Johan Polet. It was finished in 1921.

The Leidsestraat has been closed to cars since 1971. On the bridge, the few cars that come by drive on the left, which lets them turn back along the other side of the canal, while the trams keep to the right.

Look for:
- Krop's four fabulous beasts on the granite slabs low on the wings, best seen from the quays
- the stepped brick wings with their pattern in the brickwork
- the wrought-iron railings

title: The Concertgebouw architect's bakery, Leidsestraat 81
summary: A.L. van Gendt, who designed the Concertgebouw, also drew this corner bakery of 1896, with a slim zinc spire and a stone of two lions holding a crowned pretzel. More than a century on, the corner is still a bakery.
body:
In 1896 the widow E.A. Peters had a bakery with flats built on the corner of the Leidsestraat and the Prinsengracht. Her architect was A.L. van Gendt, one of the best-known Dutch architects of his day, whose Concertgebouw had opened ten years earlier.

He gave the shop richly carved wooden fronts with Mannerist pilasters and dressed the floors above in Dutch Renaissance style, red brick with plastered bands and diamond-point blocks. On the cut corner a wooden bay runs up from the first floor past the roof and ends in a slim eight-sided spire covered in zinc, which catches the eye from every direction. On the Prinsengracht side are a stone with the year 1896, a stone with the bakers' sign of two lions holding a crowned pretzel, and a blind window filled with a black stone plate carrying an old advertisement.

When the city listed it in 2006 the corner shop was still a bakery, which the register counted as part of its value, and it still is: Bakkerij Kwakman sells bread, pastries and sandwiches here every day from early morning until late. The old shop doors and windows have been replaced by glass doors; the rest of the fronts is largely original.

Look for:
- the crowned pretzel held by two lions on the Prinsengracht front
- the black stone advertising plate in the blind window on the first floor
- the zinc spire on the corner bay

title: Three almshouses of the Weteringbuurt
summary: Within two short streets: Grill's Hofje of the 1720s, founded by a Swedish-born silversmith and his German wife; the Hodshon-Dedelhofje of 1842 with a pump lantern held up by four iron dolphins; and a 'hofje' of 1898 that is really one house for six old women.
body:
Within a few steps of each other in the Weteringbuurt, between the Prinsengracht and the Weteringschans, three charities built almshouses (hofjes).

Grill's Hofje, at Eerste Weteringdwarsstraat 11-43, dates from the 1720s: the national register gives 1721, a study of Dutch hofjes 1727 and names the founders as a Swedish silversmith and his German wife, the Grill family. Eight houses with nine bell gables line the street around a gatehouse; through its passage a second row of small houses faces the courtyard. In the courtyard is a Louis XVI clock case.

Further down at nos. 83-105 is the Hodshon-Dedelhofje of 1842: three wings of two-storey houses around a courtyard, closed off from the street by a wall with a carved entrance gate. The wing facing the gate has a pediment with a clock dial, and in the courtyard stands a pump crowned by a lantern resting on four iron dolphins.

Round the corner, Derde Weteringdwarsstraat 25 is the Heemskerkhofje of 1898, built for a foundation in memory of Aletta Johanna van Heemskerk and her husband Willem Hendrik van Schuylenburg. It is not really a hofje but a single house with a back garden, with six one-room homes for elderly women, preferably Reformed.

All three are homes; look from the street.

Look for:
- the gate passage in the middle of Grill's nine bell gables
- the carved gate in the wall of the Hodshon-Dedelhofje
- the stepped Flemish-style gable over the door of the Heemskerkhofje

title: Jacob Olie's house, Huidekoperstraat 19
summary: The amateur photographer Jacob Olie, whose glass plates are now among the best-known images of 19th-century Amsterdam, lived here from 1878, with two makeshift studios in the garden. His plates were found in his daughter's attic in 1959.
body:
Jacob Olie (1834–1905) grew up among the timber rafters of the Western Islands, trained as a carpenter and draughtsman and became director of the Ambachtsschool, the trade school, which moved to the Weteringschans in 1868. Photography was a hobby. He built his own camera and made around 5,000 pictures on glass plates of Amsterdam and its surroundings, preferably from a high window or a tower.

After marrying Carolina Blössmann in 1878 he moved to the ground floor of Huidekoperstraat 19. In the garden behind the house he set up two primitive studios. His wife died in 1886, leaving him with four small children. His plates survived almost undamaged in his daughter's attic, where they were found in 1959; they are now in the Stadsarchief.

The house is part of one 1870 project on this corner, built in the wake of Samuel Sarphati's plans for the area: three stately houses on the Weteringschans for well-off families, and around the corner this lower house, meant for two middle-class households. In 1932 the Weteringschans ground floor became a car showroom with a quick service station, and the 1930s shopfront largely survives.

The house is private; look from the street.

Look for:
- the modest two-storey front of no. 19 beside the taller Weteringschans houses
- the 1932 showroom front on the Weteringschans side
- the matching corner block across the Weteringschans

title: Frederiksplein, the houses that faced a glass palace
summary: The stately fronts on the west and east sides of the Frederiksplein went up around 1870 as the setting for the Paleis voor Volksvlijt, Amsterdam's crystal palace. The palace burned down in 1929; the houses still frame the square, now facing De Nederlandsche Bank.
body:
This was once the Drilveld, a drill ground with cattle and pig markets and a barracks. The doctor and city planner Samuel Sarphati wanted to give Amsterdam a square to rival those of London and Paris. In the middle he built the Paleis voor Volksvlijt (palace of national industry), a vast hall of iron and glass inspired by London's Crystal Palace, opened in 1864 by Prince Frederik; the square was named after him in 1870.

Sarphati's building company, the Nederlandsche Bouwmaatschappij, got the land around it. Sarphati died in 1866, and from 1867 the company sold off plots to various builders. That is why the west and east sides, put up around 1869–1870 after the barracks came down, match in scale but not in detail. The corner houses at nos. 34 and 54, apparently both by the little-known G.R. Soum, are twins. The east side is a separate strip of houses set in front of a smaller block, to make the square look regular.

In the night of 18 to 19 April 1929 the palace burned down. De Nederlandsche Bank built its headquarters on the site in 1968.

The square is public; the houses are offices and homes.

Look for:
- the twin corner houses at nos. 34 and 54, with the big chimneys worked into the side front on the Falckstraat
- the Amsterdam School shopfronts of 1927 on no. 54, from its days as a café-restaurant
- the glass bays of no. 52 between heavy brick piers

title: St. Antoniusschool, a Catholic school for poor boys
summary: A 1907 Catholic school for poor boys, with a club hall for those who had left school, by Cuypers's pupil P.J. Bekkers. Jugendstil tile panels of three saints still name both on the front, though it is now homes.
body:
The Fokke Simonszstraat only exists since 1872, when the Nieuwe Looierssloot was filled in. In 1907 a large plot here, where six or seven houses had stood, became the home of the St. Antonius school and St. Willibrordus patronaat: a school for poor Catholic boys, and a patronage hall where boys who had left school could still meet. The building reaches through the block to the Nieuwe Looiersstraat and was extended in 1912 and 1915.

The architect was P.J. Bekkers (1859–1918), a pupil of Pierre Cuypers, who built many churches and other buildings for Catholic clients; much of his Amsterdam work has been demolished. Here he worked in a sober style with a nod to Berlage: red-brown brick on a heavy granite plinth, big windows under segmental arches, and brick pilaster strips with pinnacles on the right half of the top floor.

The building now holds flats, but the front still says what it was.

Look for:
- the tile panel naming the St. Antonius school and St. Willibrordus patronaat
- the Jugendstil tile panels above it with St. Francis Xavier, St. Anthony and St. Willibrord
- the pinnacles poking through the brick cornice

title: Hotel American and Café Américain
summary: Willem Kromhout's hotel of 1900–1902 on the Leidseplein, with an odd corner tower and a Jugendstil café that keeps what is called the oldest reading table in Amsterdam. Mata Hari spent her wedding night in the hotel that stood here before.
body:
The first American Hotel opened on this corner in 1882, designed by Cornelis Steinigeweg, with the young Eduard Cuypers as draughtsman and site supervisor. It shared its block with a police station and a fire station. In July 1895 the dancer Mata Hari, then still Margaretha Zelle, spent her wedding night there.

Around 1900 the whole block came down. Willem Kromhout and H.G. Jansen built the present hotel in 1900–1902, close to Berlage in its brickwork but far livelier, with galleries, bays, balconies and dormers. The national register singles out its curious corner tower: a round bell storey on a square base. Kromhout built only three buildings in Amsterdam. In 1927–1928 G.J. Rutgers and K. Bakker added a wing on the Leidsekade, now listed too, where a row of carved figures holds up the upper floors.

The ground-floor Café Américain, with its Jugendstil interior, is open to everyone; Amsterdammers call the whole place simply the Americain. The hotel has changed hands and names often: since 2023 it is the Clayton Hotel Amsterdam American.

Look for:
- the corner tower with its round top storey on a square base
- the carved figures under the concave front of the 1928 wing on the Leidsekade
- the reading table in the café

title: Maison Stroucken, the party hall inside DeLaMar
summary: Eduard Cuypers's party hall of 1881 for the Bellevue societies, where Domela Nieuwenhuis addressed voters and a winged dog guards the door. Its front now stands inside the glass skin of the DeLaMar theatre, next to Hildo Krop's memorial to a wartime reprisal.
body:
Around 1840 a building on the Leidsekade housed two societies: Concordia, for men only, and Bellevue, which also let in women and children. Its owner, a Mr Stroucken, expanded it towards the Marnixstraat. In 1881 a party hall with flats above went up here, attributed to Eduard Cuypers and perhaps his first work as an independent architect, linked by a gallery to the old hall. In 1884–1885 the ground between them got a glass roof on cast-iron trusses and became a concert hall and winter garden. Cuypers is also credited with the shop-and-house next door at no. 396, built for Stroucken. The complex was known as Maison Stroucken and was a favourite for political meetings; Ferdinand Domela Nieuwenhuis spoke to his voters here.

The halls later became cinemas and the Nieuwe De la Mar theatre. When the VandenEnde Foundation rebuilt the whole site as DeLaMar, opened in 2010, the old front was rebuilt, partly as a replica, with a glass façade rising behind and above it.

Next door, a bronze by Hildo Krop marks where the resistance set fire to the files of the German labour draft in January 1945, and where the occupier shot hostages in reprisal.

Look for:
- Cuypers's sandstone front, with round stair turrets, behind the glass
- the winged dog on the pediment over the old main door
- Krop's memorial at no. 404

title: Paleis van Justitie, the paupers' orphanage that became a court
summary: An orphanage of the 1660s for the city's poorest children, rebuilt in the 1820s as the Palace of Justice and dedicated to 'Law and Justice' in a line on its front. The court left in 2013; since May 2025 it is a luxury hotel.
body:
Behind this long classical front lies the Aalmoezeniersweeshuis, built in 1663–1665 for the poorest orphans of the city. In the 1820s it was rebuilt and widened into a Palace of Justice to a design by the city architect Jan de Greef, and on 4 October 1836 the courts moved in from the Prinsenhof.
