A line attributed to the poet Jacob van Lennep runs above the first-floor windows: under the rule of illustrious Willem, this institution was rebuilt and dedicated to Law and Justice.

The building did more than judge. From 1838 to 1863 the city library sat on the second floor on the canal side, and from 1833 to 1875 the left wing served as a garrison hospital. In 1950 the state bought the neighbours, including the city's home for children in its care on the corner of the Leidsegracht, built in 1864 and 1902; their interiors were stripped.

Most courts left for the Parnassusweg in 1990, but the Court of Appeal stayed after protests by its judges, until April 2013. After four years of building work the complex opened on 1 May 2025 as the Rosewood Amsterdam hotel.

Look for:
- the inscription to Willem above the first-floor windows
- the Corinthian pilasters on the three projecting bays
- on the Leidsegracht corner, the year 1902 with the Amsterdam arms and two lions, and the little corner turret

title: De Duif, the first Catholic church back on the street
summary: Built in 1796 as the first Catholic church on a public street in Amsterdam since the Reformation, rebuilt in 1857, and squatted by its own parishioners in 1974 when the bishop closed it. Open monthly, with organ concerts on a restored Smits organ.
body:
After the city turned Protestant, Amsterdam's Catholics worshipped in hidden churches. One was Het Vrede-duifje (the little dove of peace), built in 1671 by a master carpenter on the Kerkstraat. In 1796 its priest, Johannes Offerman, bought the site of a burned-down sugar refinery here and built a new church, the first Catholic church on a public street in Amsterdam since the Catholic city government was deposed. The church room lay on the first floor, above the presbytery, and kept the old nickname: De Duif.

In 1835 the neighbour at no. 754 pledged money for repairs in exchange for her own door into the church. In 1857 Theo Molkenboer replaced the building with the present church, its sandstone front following the Baroque church type of the Gesù in Rome. In 1886 the parish bought no. 754 and built a new presbytery there, again with direct access to the church.

In January 1974 the diocese closed De Duif. The parishioners occupied it and kept celebrating, and carried on as the ecumenical community De Duif, which still holds services here on Sunday mornings.

Now owned by Stadsherstel, it is open on the first Wednesday and third Sunday of the month (12:00–16:00), with organ concerts on the 1862 Smits organ once a month and every Sunday in summer.

Look for:
- the gilded dove in the pediment and "IN LOCO ISTO DABO PACEM" (in this place I will give peace)
- the presbytery of 1886 at no. 754, in a quite different style

title: Rath & Doodeheefver, the wallpaper palace
summary: The six-storey warehouse that the wallpaper firm Rath & Doodeheefver built on the Prinsengracht in 1911, nicknamed the Behangselpaleis (wallpaper palace). Behind it the firm swallowed half a block over thirty years, disguised as a row of small canal houses.
body:
In 1860 J.C. Doodeheefver started an upholstery business around the corner in the Tweede Weteringdwarsstraat. After his death his widow married his foreman, Friedrich Rath, and in 1890 Rath and his stepson founded Rath & Doodeheefver, importing wallpapers, among them designs from the Deutscher Werkbund and the Wiener Werkstätte. In 1911 the architect A. Jacot, known for the Maison de Bonneterie on the Rokin, gave them a warehouse with offices on the Prinsengracht, so tall it was nicknamed the Behangselpaleis.

The firm kept growing. In 1925–1928 H.D. Tabak doubled the canal front in the same style, and further wings followed on the Noorderstraat and the Reguliersgracht up to 1941. Those were made to look like separate older houses, some with spout gables, so that passers-by would not notice one business filling half the block. In the 1920s the firm sold artists' wallpapers by Jaap Gidding, Jacob Jongert and others, and Gerrit Achterberg named a poem after it. The company went bankrupt in 1998; its collection went to the Amsterdam Museum.

The building is seen from the street.

Look for:
- the colossal brick pilasters with flattened Ionic capitals on the canal front
- the frieze over the ground floor that once carried the firm's name, now covered in yellow tiles
- round the corner, the "old" fronts on the Noorderstraat and the Reguliersgracht that belong to the same complex

title: Garage De Hoofdstad, a car park from 1917
summary: A storage shed of 1914 that became one of the first city-centre garages for private cars, with Willem Noorlander's wavy brick front of 1917 on the Prinsengracht. More than a century on, cars still drive in under the bays.
body:
Around the First World War more and more people in the old cities owned a car, and the car needed a roof. On the Lange Leidsedwarsstraat the builder P. Leemhuis put up nine flats over a storage space in 1914. In 1917 Willem Noorlander added a front on the Prinsengracht for the N.V. Automobiel-garage Maatschappij: a garage entrance and a shop on the ground floor, six flats above, and on the yard behind four lock-up boxes and a workshop. In 1923 the yard got a roof of steel trusses with a glass ridge, and the shop was halved to make the drive-through easier.

The city register calls it an early, still experimental step towards the city parking garage, a type that reached its pre-war form on the Wijdesteeg in the early 1930s. Noorlander, who later designed the expressionist Ceintuur Theater, gave the front bays that run up three and four storeys and make the brick wall ripple, an odd duck among the narrow canal houses.

It is still a car park, now called De Hoofdstad.

Look for:
- the rippling bays on the upper floors, broad in the middle and narrow at the sides
- the hand-made wooden doors with forged nails in the porches to the flats
- the plain back front on the Lange Leidsedwarsstraat, where it all started

title: Hilmanhofje, a grieving father's almshouse
summary: An almshouse of 1875–1877 for single women, built in memory of a small son who died in 1864 by his father Johannes Hilman: bankrupt grain trader, heir, theatre fanatic, poet, early owner of a St Bernard and known to Amsterdam as Jan Goddome.
body:
Johannes Hilman (1802–1881), a baker's son, became a grain trader and went bankrupt in 1852. When his father-in-law died in 1859 he inherited a fortune, paid off his creditors and was rehabilitated. From then on he gave himself to the theatre and to poetry. He wrote verse and plays, sat on the city's theatre committee, had a plan for a new city theatre drawn up at his own expense (it was not liked), was among the first Amsterdammers to parade a St Bernard, and took mayor Fock to the stinking Looierssloot to hurry up its filling-in. His rough manners earned him the nickname Jan Goddome, after a curse.

His son Willem Hendrik, born in 1857, died in 1864. In 1871 Hilman asked the city for permission to build a hofje on the soon-to-be-filled ditch behind the Nieuwe Looiersstraat, named after the boy and meant for single women and widows. It opened in September 1877; two rows of one-room homes face each other across a narrow courtyard. Hilman lived around the corner at Reguliersgracht 114. He left the buildings and 125,000 guilders to the Reformed deacons; since 1882 the Magdalena Hodshon foundation has run it.

People still live here, so both fronts are seen from the street.

Look for:
- the cartouche over the gate: "Willem Hendrik Hilman's Stichting 1875"
- on the Fokke Simonszstraat side, the stone band "Ter zijner gedachtenis" (in his memory)
- the seam and different brick left of the gate, probably an older house taken in

title: Looiershofje, an almshouse made of 17th-century houses
summary: A small almshouse of 1828–1829 on the tanners' street, put together from houses of the 1660s: the gate runs through one of them. Its three wings round a courtyard carry their building dates in stones.
body:
The Nieuwe Looiersstraat, the new tanners' street, lies in the part of the 1660s city extension that was known as the Noortse Bos. A few of the more than two hundred weavers' houses built here around 1670 to a design by Philips Vingboons still stand.

The Looiershofje was founded in 1829 by making use of some of those old houses rather than pulling them down. Two narrow houses on the street, of the type the national register calls Noortse Bos, are dated to about 1665 and belong to the complex. The passage into the courtyard runs through no. 18, a 17th-century house turned into a gatehouse, with the date 1829 and a name stone above it. Behind it three wings of homes, with stones dated 1828 and 1829, stand round a courtyard; the back looks out on a fenced yard on the Fokke Simonszstraat.

It is lived in; the front and the gate are seen from the street.

Look for:
- the passage dated 1829 in no. 18, with the name stone above
- the old four-window house front dated 1665 in the row
- the small-paned sash windows of the old houses

title: Kaiser Wilhelm Schule, the German school of 1908
summary: A brick school of 1908 by Jan Stuyt for the German Kaiser Wilhelm Schule. In 1934 a paper called it a Nazi school, in the war the Dutch Nazi youth trained here, and today it is a primary school again.
body:
In 1908 five houses on the north side of the Nieuwe Looiersstraat made way for a large school. It was built for the Kaiser Wilhelm Schule of the Deutsche Schulverein (German School Association), named after the German emperor who reigned at the time.

The architect was Jan Stuyt (1868–1934), better known for Catholic churches, schools and convents across the country, among them the new St Bavo in Haarlem, designed with Jos Cuypers, and the St Agneskerk on the Amstelveenseweg. Here he kept it plain: a symmetrical brick front of three tall storeys, set back a little from the street so it would not overpower it, with the classrooms at the front and the corridors behind.

Then the school turned. In November 1934 the socialist weekly De Tribune called it 'a Nazi school in Amsterdam', where German and Dutch children were raised in the spirit of Hitler's Germany. From 1942 it was the central training school of the Jeugdstorm, the youth movement of the Dutch Nazi party. After the war a Montessori school moved in, followed by others. Today it is one of the two buildings of IKC De Kleine Reus, a primary school with after-school care.

Look for:
- the round-arched double door with five sandstone voussoirs and a beaded sandstone moulding
- the balcony over the door on sandstone volute brackets, with a wrought-iron railing
- the decorative wall anchors on the ground floor only

title: De Bont & Leyten's building, later the city's bathhouse department
summary: Built in 1911 for the royal sweets, chocolate and liqueur company De Bont & Leyten, taken over in 1930 by the city department that ran Amsterdam's public baths, washhouses and pools. A tiny octagonal turret sits on its corner.
body:
In 1911 the N.V. Koninklijke Nederlandsche Fabriek van Suikerwerken, Chocolade en Likeuren v/h De Bont en Leyten, a royal maker of sweets, chocolate and liqueurs, had this building put up on the corner of the Nieuwe Looiersdwarsstraat and the Nieuwe Looiersstraat. The architect, A. Salm GBzn (1857–1915), was a leading Amsterdam architect and chairman of the Maatschappij tot Bevordering der Bouwkunst, the main architects' society of the day.

It is much bigger than its neighbours, but by keeping to their three storeys and breaking the long front into parts, Salm made it fit in. In 1930 it was converted for the city's Dienst der Wasch-, Schoonmaak-, Bad- en Zweminrichtingen, the department for public washhouses, cleaning, baths and swimming pools. Since 1992 it has held a day nursery and offices.

Look for:
- the plastered panel over the ground floor in the middle of the long front, with the Amsterdam arms at both ends and a painted-out text
- the old iron swivel hoist on the recessed balcony on the south side
- the minute octagonal turret on the corner of the south front
- the big wooden cart gate on the right of the south front

title: Nicolaas Witsenkade, the houses on the old gasworks
summary: Until the 1880s coal barges unloaded here for the Hollandsche Gasfabriek. On its site rose some of the last new streets inside the canal belt, among them two rare neo-Venetian houses: one for a diamond dealer, one with tiles that sign its builders.
body:
The quay between the Pieter Pauwstraat and the Weteringplantsoen was once the Hollandsche Gasfabriek: coal ships at the quay, a gasholder, a coal shed and a little fire station. Around 1885 the city chose another gas supplier, and from 1891 a building company covered the site with three long blocks, some of the last new streets laid out inside the canal belt.

The houses facing the Singelgracht got the richest fronts. On the corner of the Pieter Pauwstraat, Eduard Cuypers built a house in 1889–1890 for the diamond dealer David Sanders, in a neo-Venetian style rarely seen in the Netherlands; the photographer Jacob Olie caught it under construction. A few doors along, H.G. Jansen, co-architect of the American Hotel, designed no. 32 in 1895 for an estate agent and a builder, in yellow brick with pink stone; the tiles under its gutter show trades, among them a hammer and compasses. At nos. 33–36 the same year, flats went up for the middle class, and the Pieter Pauwstraat got a plainer row with three shops.

All are private homes and offices, seen from the quay.

Look for:
- the gold stencilled ornament on pastel green on the top floor of no. 38
- the tile frieze with tools under the gutter of no. 32
- the green glazed rims round the windows of nos. 33–36, and the gable on the left that never got its twin on the right
- at Weteringschans 108, a second neo-Venetian house by Ed. Cuypers (1891), with painted blind windows

title: Sarphatistraat 7–13, survivors of a vanished row
summary: Three town houses of 1888 on Sarphati's boulevard, one in rare neo-Venetian style, are all that is left of a richly decorated row. Next to them stood a private women's clinic by Eduard Cuypers, broken up for firewood in the hunger winter of 1944–1945.
body:
The Sarphatistraat was the backbone of the plans of the physician Samuel Sarphati, who wanted to give Amsterdam boulevards like those of Paris and London. On its north side, by the Amstel, a row of richly decorated houses went up in 1888.

Three survive. No. 7 is by Eduard Cuypers in a neo-Venetian manner the national register calls rare. No. 9, for A. van Wezel, is faced in natural stone, its architect unknown. No. 11 was built for Thomas Vorstius, a banker who chaired the Queen Sophia Society for the Protection of Animals, by Van Rossem and Vuyk, the architects of Carré around the corner.

The corner at nos. 13–15 held a private clinic, also by Cuypers, for the gynaecologist Arthur Mendes de Leon, with turrets and plenty of ornament. Mendes de Leon soon outgrew it and moved on to the clinic that became the Boerhaave kliniek. In the hunger winter of 1944–1945 the building was pulled down and burned as firewood. In the 1950s a block of flats in a quietly historical style rose on part of the plot, keeping the clinic's old side wall. Nos. 1–3 and Cuypers's no. 5 were also replaced, no. 5 in 1972; only then were 7, 9 and 11 protected.

Look for:
- the stone balconies and loggias of no. 7
- the balcony across the whole front of no. 11
- the right-hand side wall of no. 13, left over from the clinic

title: The Ancient Order of Foresters' house, Sarphatistraat 8–10
summary: Two 1878 town houses that a British-born friendly society, the Ancient Order of Foresters, bought and merged in 1936 into its Dutch headquarters, behind a front sober enough for an order to recognise itself in. The Foresters left in 1976.
body:
The Ancient Order of Foresters, a friendly society of British origin, bought in 1927 no. 8, a town house of 1878 built at the same time as its neighbour no. 6, and had S. Vieyra convert it into a society building. When it also got hold of no. 10, the right wing of a three-house block by T. Sanders of the same year, Vieyra merged the two in 1936 and gave them the present front: five windows wide, solid and conventional, so close to the 1878 houses around it that it barely shows as a 1930s design. The city register suspects the order chose that look on purpose.

Inside came meeting rooms, a conversation room across the first floor and a caretaker's flat in the attic; a garden room of 1878 with neo-Renaissance decoration was kept almost whole.

In 1954 part of it was fitted out as a synagogue for the Liberal Jewish Congregation. By 1976 it was the order's head office, and that year the order decided to leave. The mental health service Mentrum was here in 2015; now the building is let as offices. You see the front from the street.

The ground has an older story. Before 1875 this was Lokaal Dalrust, a dance hall where Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels spoke in 1872.

Look for:
- the five-bay front of 1936 that blends in with the 1878 houses on either side
- the entrance in the middle bay, where the hall of the society building began

title: H.F. van Breemen, the peat dealer whose dredgers dug the Amsterdamse Bos
summary: A stone shopfront on the Lijnbaansgracht still carries the name of H.F. van Breemen, a dealer in peat, coal and coke whose smithy built steam-driven peat dredgers. One of his machines dug out the polder that became the Amsterdamse Bos.
body:
Across the stone shopfront of Lijnbaansgracht 296 runs a name in relief: H.F. VAN BREEMEN. He rebuilt this house in 1879, with a wide double door to his business between the house doors, and did the same to nos. 289 and 290 a few doors along.

Van Breemen traded in peat, coal and coke, and supplied fuel to schools and the city's poor-relief board. Around 1894 he was for a time polder master of the Middelveldsche Akerpolder, where peat had been dug since the 1870s. He also owned a smithy on the Haarlemmer Houttuinen that built peat dredgers: steam-driven machines that worked far faster than men dredging by hand. One of his machines was used to dig out the peat of the Rietwijkeroordpolder, now the Amsterdamse Bos, and of the Vinkeveense Plassen.

The three houses are private homes. See them from the quay.

Look for:
- H.F. van BREEMEN in relief over the middle door of no. 296
- the stone stair with wrought-iron rails to the house door on the left
- the carved consoles under the cornice and the round-topped dormer of nos. 289 and 290

title: Prinsengracht 808, the insurer's corner with a moral in tiles
summary: A corner building of 1906 for a life insurer from The Hague, with a tile panel at the door showing two roads through life, one insured and one not. The Hague's stork looks down from the turret, and the café on the corner is named after it.
body:
In 1906 the life insurance company 's-Gravenhage, a mutual society from The Hague, had the brothers Van Gendt build this corner block of shops, flats and offices where the Utrechtsestraat meets the Prinsengracht. It is a solid traditionalist building with a round bay window that rises into a little stepped-gable turret on the corner.

The insurer used the front to sell its product. In the round-arched porch on the Prinsengracht, between the two doors, a large tile panel shows two paths of life side by side: an insured life and an uninsured one. Over the arch a second panel carries the company's name between two Amsterdam coats of arms. Higher up, a tile panel in the turret's gable shows a stork, the emblem of The Hague. From 1916 the two lower floors were a piano showroom.

The corner is now a café, Onder de Ooievaar (under the stork), so you can sit beneath the bird with a beer; the floors above are homes and offices.

Look for:
- the tile panel of the insured and the uninsured life between the doors on the Prinsengracht
- 's-Gravenhage between two Amsterdam arms over the arch
- the stork in the turret's little stepped gable
- two carved heads under the corner bay

title: Paradiso, the free congregation's meeting hall
summary: Amsterdam's pop temple was never a church. It was built in 1879–1880 as the meeting hall of the Vrije Gemeente, a congregation that had walked out of the Dutch Reformed Church to believe without dogma. Hippies squatted it in 1967.
body:
Everyone calls Paradiso a former church, and it isn't. In 1877 the brothers Hugenholtz left the Dutch Reformed Church and founded the Vrije Gemeente (free congregation), which wanted no church dogma and saw itself as an association of equal members rather than a church with a minister who owns the truth. For it, G.B. Salm built this hall in 1879–1880, with advice from his son Abraham in Paris: a Romanesque entrance front on the Weteringschans and a half-round end towards the Singelgracht. Inside, cast-iron columns and galleries make the single hall look like a three-aisled basilica under a painted wooden vault.

The congregation left in 1965. In October 1967 about fifty hippies carried a love-in from the Vondelpark into the empty building, until the police ended it. The city, looking for room for the new youth culture, opened Paradiso in 1968; Pink Floyd and Captain Beefheart played in its first months. In the 1970s the stained glass gave way to mirrors and wooden panels; new windows by Hans van Houwelingen and Berend Strik went in in 1993.

Paradiso has bought the plot next door, empty for over a century, and in January 2026 presented plans for a renovation and extension, partly to cut noise for the neighbours.

Look for:
- the Romanesque entrance front with its paired round-arched windows
- the half-round end over the Singelgracht
- the empty plot beside it, where the extension is planned

title: Peper en Zout, the hated offices that became monuments
summary: Two villas built with nutmeg money stood here until the 1960s. The brick office towers by Frans van Gool that replaced them were called 'spit-ugly' and worse; in 2022 the city listed them against the owner's will.
body:
This stretch opposite the Rijksmuseum once carried on the row of villas along the Singelgracht. Nos. 26 and 28 were Groot Banda and Banda Neira, built in 1879 to a design by Coenraad Wiegand for A.M.L. Hartog, a nutmeg planter and trader from Banda Neira in the Moluccas, who had his name changed by royal decree to Hartog van Banda. After the war the villas decayed, and in 1963 the Philips pension fund and Maup Caransa bought the site.

The city wanted low buildings in the spirit of the villas; the owners wanted more. What went up from 1977 was Frans van Gool's design: two blocks on a concrete frame, clad in glazed hand-made brick, with rows of nearly square windows and backs that follow the curve of the water. Amsterdammers called them Peper en Zout, the salt and pepper set. Renate Rubinstein, Henk Hofland and others attacked them in the papers; Gerrit Komrij called them bastards of a marriage between conformity and mindless self-importance. Van Gool answered that his critics had judged before the buildings were finished, and Rem Koolhaas and Marte Röling admired his nerve.

Taste moved on. In December 2022 the city made them municipal monuments against the owner's will, confirmed by the Raad van State in November 2025. In the film The Hitman's Bodyguard (2017) they play a prison. They are offices.

Look for:
- the glazed brick, chosen because it barely weathers
- the windows that look square but are not

title: Commiezenhuisje, the excise post over a sewage pump
summary: Where the Weteringpoort stood until 1840, the city built a small classical office for its excise men in 1842. The tax barrier went in 1866; since 1987 the little house has been the lid on a pumping station that sends the old city's sewage west.
body:
Until 1840 the Weteringpoort stood here, one of the smaller city gates: really a passage through the rampart, with a long wooden bridge over the Singelgracht beyond. Many of the vegetables brought in along the Boerenwetering came through it, and at the gate the city levied excise, its tax on incoming goods. When the gate was pulled down because its upkeep cost too much, the excise men (commiezen) got this little house by Bas de Greef at the start of the bridge. A gate across the road made the spot known as the Weteringbarrière.

City excise at the gates was abolished in 1866 and the barrier went. The house was later used by the city's planting department. Since 1987 it has stood on top of a large sewage pumping station, which pumps waste water from the inner city to the treatment works in the west.

The crossing had a complicated life of its own: on old prints a timber bridge with two small drawbridges, then an earth dam with a wooden water barrier after the North Sea Canal changed the city's water levels, and a lock from 1878. The dam was cleared in 1896. The city saw no need for a new bridge, as the one in front of the Rijksmuseum lay 130 metres away.

Look for:
- the portico with two square pillars
- the white plaster with block patterns on the corners
- the lock beside it, still linking the Lijnbaansgracht and the Singelgracht

title: Industrieschool voor Vrouwelijke Jeugd, where girls learned a trade
summary: The first industrial school for girls in the Netherlands moved here in 1881. Its pupils helped make the cradle Amsterdam gave Queen Wilhelmina and made the flag first raised on the Dam for the February Strike in 1947. Today it is the entrance of the Barlaeus Gymnasium.
body:
In 1865 the Maatschappij tot Nut van 't Algemeen, the society for the public good, opened an industrial school for girls on the corner of the Herengracht and the Brouwersgracht, after a campaign by Mienette Storm-van der Chijs. The educator Elise van Calcar objected that a woman's calling was to bring up children. It was the first school of its kind in the country. Girls learned wood engraving, machine sewing, shoemaking, straw plaiting, bookkeeping, drawing and needlework, and from the start some were prepared for teaching.

The school grew fast and in 1881 moved into this building by A.L. (Dolf) van Gendt, with rooms for pharmacy, leather work, sewing machines and lace, and a flat for the headmistress. Pupils came in through the basement on the Zieseniskade at the back. Built for 200, it had 800 girls by 1949; in 1951 Herman Knijtijzer added a storey.

Pupils worked on the cradle designed by Karel de Bazel that the women and girls of Amsterdam gave the expectant Queen Wilhelmina in 1909, and made the February Strike flag designed by Pam Rueter, first raised on the Dam in December 1947. After the school reforms of the 1960s it became Akademie De Schans. Since 2002–2004 the building has been part of the Barlaeus Gymnasium next door, whose main entrance is now here.

Look for:
- Van Gendt's front with the extra storey of 1951 on top
- the old pupils' entrance on the water side, the Zieseniskade

title: De Nooteboome Uytkijk, a joiner's warehouse turned almshouse
summary: On the sharp point where the Lijnbaansgracht meets the Spiegelgracht, the joiners Jan and Fikko van Mekeren built a warehouse in 1724. A grandson left it as an almshouse, whose house rules banned quarrelling, drink, frying oliebollen for money and more than one cat a floor.
body:
The wedge-shaped building on the little square where the Lijnbaansgracht and the Tweede Weteringdwarsstraat run together began as a warehouse. In 1722 the carpenter and joiner Jan van Mekeren and his son Fikko bought the empty plot, and by 1724 a warehouse for their business stood here. It passed down the family until the grandson, also called Jan van Mekeren, owned the whole of it.

In 1774 this Jan and his second wife, Johanna Margaretha Okhuysen, laid down in their will that after both had died the warehouse should become a home for elderly members of the Reformed church, poor relatives from their own families first. Residents were to get peat, firewood, butter, coffee, tea, beer, meat, candles and potatoes, plus some cash, and subletting was strictly forbidden. Jan died in 1791 and the conversion followed. He also founded a second almshouse, De Eendracht, on the Overtoom.

The house rules of 1835 asked the residents, who in practice were always women, to live quietly, without quarrelling, fighting, swearing or drunkenness. No light after ten in the evening, no dogs, one or two little birds, and no more than one cat on each floor. Nor could anyone earn a living by baking waffles or oliebollen.

Since a restoration in 1974 it holds private homes and a shop.

Look for:
- the name over the double door on the Lijnbaansgracht
- the gable stone with a chair on the Tweede Weteringdwarsstraat side
- the ring of bollards around the building

title: Noordse Bos, the weavers' houses of 1670
summary: In 1670 the city gave free land to three charities to build 400 houses for cloth weavers from elsewhere, an early planned workers' housing scheme. The disaster year 1672 stopped it at 211. A corner house keeps the type; the orphanage that owned plots rebuilt others in the 1870s.
body:
In 1670 Amsterdam wanted to revive its flagging cloth trade and draw in skilled weavers, many of them Walloons. It gave free land in this new part of the city extension to three charities, the Burgerweeshuis (city orphanage), the two hospitals and the Leprozenhuis, to build 400 houses. Philips Vingboons drew a standard house: a near-square front under a shared roof, a tall cellar for spinners, and room for looms on the floor above and in the loft. Rents were capped, and at first only cloth workers from outside the city could rent. On 9 July 1670 the charities drew lots for the plots.

The disaster year 1672 stopped the scheme at 211 houses. Tenants fell behind or vanished, and in the end the charities were allowed to sell. The name Noordse Bos (Norwegian wood) is said to come from the Norwegian pine piles under the houses, though the explanation is disputed.

The Burgerweeshuis still owned land here two centuries later. Its surveyors, father and son Hendrik Moeton, replaced weavers' houses with the plain blocks at Vijzelgracht 14–16 (1876) and 10 (1885). Spiegelgracht 27, a corner house with a pothuis (a low lean-to at cellar level), is of the original type.

Look for:
- the corner of Spiegelgracht 27 and the Tweede Weteringdwarsstraat
- the three weavers' houses beside the Walenweeshuis, restored after the metro works made them subside in 2008
- the 1876 block filling the whole end of its street block on the Vijzelgracht

title: Walenweeshuis, the Walloon orphanage waiting for a future
summary: Adriaan Dortsman built this orphanage in 1669–1671 for children of the French-speaking Walloon church, with separate doors for boys and girls. After the French consulate and Maison Descartes left in 2016 it stood empty and decayed; a new owner announced a restoration in 2025.
body:
Protestant Walloons, French-speaking refugees from persecution, were welcome in 17th-century Amsterdam as skilled workers and for their trade links. Their orphans were not admitted to the regular orphanages, so the Walloon church ran its own, from 1631 in the Laurierstraat. In 1669–1671 it moved here, into a sober classical block by Adriaan Dortsman, the architect of the Ronde Lutherse Kerk. Boys and girls lived strictly apart, which is why there are two front doors; only the kitchen served both. Low wings for old men and old women were added on the Prinsengracht and Eerste Weteringdwarsstraat sides, and a school in the courtyard in 1866.

The orphanage stood at the heart of the new quarter of weavers' houses, and readily sent its girls to learn the trade in them.

The Walloon church used the building until 1967. From 1971 to 2016 it housed the French consulate and the cultural institute Maison Descartes. Then it stood empty. In October 2024 heritage campaigners pointed to cracks in the brickwork, rotting window frames and fences round almost the whole building. In March 2025 the new owner announced a restoration with offices that neighbours and other Amsterdammers should also be able to use.

Look for:
- the two door frames in the wide centre bay
- the rusticated brick strips on the corners
- the two chimneys with curved caps on the roof

title: Patisserie Holtkamp, an Amsterdam School bakery still baking
summary: A pastry baker has worked behind this front since 1886. In 1928 the shop got an Amsterdam School front and interior designed as one, and both survive: rare for a shop of that style, and rarer still in its original use. Since 1969 it is Patisserie Holtkamp.
body:
In 1880 the estate agent B.J. Meilink bought a house here at auction, made it into a shop and sold it to a pork butcher, L.J. van Gaasbeek, who opened in 1881. In 1886 George van Nie's cake and pastry bakery moved in. In 1928 Van Nie's son had the shop remodelled in the fashionable Amsterdam School style by F.M. Kramer, not to be confused with the far better known Piet Kramer, though the basic design is said to have come from Piet. In those years whole shop fittings were often designed along with such a front. What is unusual here is that front and interior have both survived and are still used by a bakery.

Since 1969 it has been Patisserie Holtkamp, which sells cakes, pastries and its own croquettes. It is open Monday to Friday 8:30–18:00 and Saturday 8:30–17:00.

Look for:
- the shop front in black polished stone and teak, with a brass-rimmed window
- the shop door of leaded glass, and the teak door to the flats with its tiny peephole
- the wrought-iron sign in the shape of a krakeling (a pretzel-shaped biscuit)
- inside, the original display cases and the painted band of waves with the clock set into it

title: Vijzelgracht 1, a 17th-century corner rebuilt in 1971
summary: By the 1960s this 17th-century corner house had been demolished to nothing and a bank wanted an office block on the site. Stadsherstel bought it in 1967 and rebuilt the bell gable from scratch; a gable stone with a red sheep honours the man who saw it through.
body:
The corner house appears on a map of 1675 and stood for almost three centuries. After the Vijzelgracht was filled in around 1933 it went downhill: it lost its bell gable, by 1942 only the ground floor with its wooden shop front was left, and in 1962 that was pulled down too. By then the whole corner counted as the rotten spot of the inner city, and there was a plan for a tall bank office on the site.

In 1967 Stadsherstel, the Amsterdam company that buys and restores old buildings, bought Vijzelgracht 1–5 and Prinsengracht 646–648, and the architect Gerard Prins reconstructed them. The corner house came back in its old form: a bell gable with corner scrolls and a curved pediment on top. Around May 1971 a gable stone reading Int root schaep (in the red sheep) went up on the Prinsengracht side, in memory of C.P. Schaap, an inspector of the city's monuments service who had worked hard to get the rebuilding finished.

The brown café Myrabelle has been on the corner since February 1971, with a painting of the street corner from that year behind the bar. Since 2018 the entrance of the Vijzelgracht metro station has been right in front of it.

Look for:
- the red sheep stone on the Prinsengracht side
- the bell gable with its curved top, all of it from 1971
- inside the café, the painted street corner behind the bar

title: The city's central kitchen for poor schoolchildren
summary: Built in 1871 as a public school for poor children, this building became in 1917 the city's central kitchen for school meals, with eighteen big cooking pots downstairs and a separate kosher kitchen upstairs. It was fired up again at the end of 1940.
body:
Openbare armenschool no. 23, a city school for poor children, opened here in 1871 with a gym and a teacher's flat. The first plan had no corridor: to reach the back classroom you walked through the front one. In 1885 the school got an extra floor, a central staircase and a walled playground on the plot next door, in line with the new rules of 1880 on hygiene in schools.

In 1917 the school closed and the building became the Centrale Keuken voor de Gemeentelijke Kindervoeding, the central kitchen where the city cooked meals for needy pupils of its public schools. Eighteen large cooking pots stood on the ground floor; upstairs four more were kept for ritually prepared food for Jewish children. The meals went on after the First World War, probably until 1940, when a newer central kitchen was ready on the Haarlemmerweg. At the end of that year the old kitchen here was put back into use, because the new one was needed as a public soup kitchen for the general population.

After the war the equipment was sold. From 1950 until the late 1970s the leather and rainwear maker Verha worked here, and in the 1990s the building was turned into two studios and eleven workshops.

Look for:
- the left-hand front door, which led to the teacher's flat upstairs
- the extra floor of 1885 on top of the low school

title: Havana, a cigar factory in a former stable
summary: A horse stable became a cigar factory in 1873, and from 1882 it was Petrus Alma's 'Havana'. Its front is almost all window, because cigar makers worked by daylight. After 1913 the publisher of the Wereldbibliotheek moved in; since 1985 it has housed a Spanish language centre.
body:
Cigar making long happened in ordinary houses; around 1900 the trade boomed and moved into buildings made for it. This one began in 1873, when a horse stable was converted into a cigar factory for two merchants from Koblenz, S.A.W. Ladner and H.J.L. Chardon. In 1882 Petrus Alma, who had started his business in 1868 in the Spuistraat, moved in and brought his factory's name with him: Havana.

The front is almost entirely window, since the cigar makers needed daylight, just like the diamond cutters in the big polishing works of the same years. Steel frames with thin glazing bars sit in arched openings, and the brickwork comes in two colours, with a projecting centre and corners.

In 1913 the rival firm C. Otto Roelofs took over Alma's business and the factory here closed. The Maatschappij voor Goede en Goedkope Lectuur, the society for good and cheap reading that published the Wereldbibliotheek books, then used the building until it moved to new premises in Sloterdijk in 1922. Clubs and a lampshade factory followed. Since 1985 the Spanish language and culture centre Molinos de Viento has been here, and in 2021 a photo and film studio had the ground floor.

Look for:
- the wide front of windows made for daylight
- the slender steel glazing bars
- the two colours of brick

title: Utrechtsestraat shop fronts, from a gilded pig to a cigar shop
summary: Around 1900 the old road to Utrecht became a smart shopping street, and four listed shops show it: an art nouveau front for a pork butcher called Het Vergulde Varken, a gift shop's glass and tiles, a tailor with shop windows upstairs, and a cigar shop a horse once crashed into.
body:
For centuries the Utrechtsestraat was the way out of town towards Utrecht. In the decades around 1900 it turned into a smart shopping street, and shopkeepers had the ground floors of ordinary houses rebuilt.

At no. 129 the contractor J.H. Box made a wooden shop front with art nouveau leaded glass in 1903 for a pork butcher, Het Vergulde Varken (the gilded pig). The last butcher closed in 1992, but the catchy lettering is part of the listed front. Across the street, no. 132 got an art nouveau front with leaded glass and Jugendstil tiles in 1901, for a seller of silverware and gifts. Later came a tea and milk salon, a dealer in electrical devices said to help against rheumatism and 'nerves', and since 1991 the fashion shop Angel Basics. Next door, the men's outfitter Nieberg had big shop windows put in on the first and second floors too, which is rare.

On the Prinsengracht corner, no. 104 was built in 1910 by Jacques van Straaten for the Utrecht cigar maker Hagen, which sold only through its own shops. In October 1924 a horse pulling a removal van over the bridge slipped and landed in its shop window. Hagen closed in 1934; there was still a tobacconist on the corner in 2018.

Look for:
- the lettering and glass of no. 129
- the tiles and glass of no. 132
- the upstairs shop windows of no. 134
- the stone festoons and balconies of no. 104

title: De Posthoorn, the house of Jos Brink and Frank Sanders
summary: A small bell-gabled house with a 17th-century core and the gable stone De Posthoorn, named in deeds of 1682. In the 1970s entertainer Jos Brink and Frank Sanders lived here and had it restored. Next door rises a 1935 garage block whose architect died before it was built.
body:
Before Amsterdam had street numbers, this house was known by its gable stone: De Posthoorn (the post horn), already named in deeds of 1682, though the national register dates the stone to the 18th century. Its resident then, the miller Meynert Rochus, is said to have put it up, but no link between him and a post horn has been found. The house has a 17th-century core and a bell gable with small side scrolls, and the hoisting beam now half hides the stone.

In 1957 it was restored and the ground floor lost its raised floor and double entrance. In 1976–1977 the residents, the actor, cabaret performer and television presenter Jos Brink and Frank Sanders, later his husband, brought in the restoration architect IJsbrand Kok and had to move out for the work. At a rebuilding in 1999 it still belonged to Jos Brink Producties.

The tall neighbour at no. 6–8 went up in 1935 for the garage owner J.J. van Breda: a car store on the ground floor and three flats above. Its architect, Cornelis Kruyswijk, who lived round the corner on the Frederiksplein, died on 10 January 1935 and probably never saw it.

Look for:
- the post horn stone just above the hoisting beam
- the old fronts leaning forward, as was usual, beside the plumb-straight block of 1935
- the bay window over three floors at no. 6, rare in this street

title: Villa Heineken, the brewer's house where Freddy was kidnapped
summary: Gerard Heineken had this villa built in 1891 across the water from his brewery and died two years later. It has been the company's head office since 1923, and on 9 November 1983 Freddy Heineken and his driver were kidnapped at its door.
body:
Gerard Adriaan Heineken, who in 1864 took over the brewery De Hooiberg and made Heineken of it, commissioned this villa from A.L. (Dolf) van Gendt in 1891, on a corner looking across the Singelgracht to his brewery on the Stadhouderskade. He did not enjoy it for long: he died suddenly in 1893, aged 51. His widow lived on here until 1923; since then it has been the company's head office.

At 18:56 on 9 November 1983 Freddy Heineken, then head of the company, and his driver Ab Doderer were kidnapped in front of this office. The gang, among them Cor van Hout and Willem Holleeder, held them in two soundproof cells hidden behind a false wall in a shed on an industrial estate in the western port area. A ransom of 35 million guilders was paid on 28 November, and two days later the police freed both men.

The house is a showy mix: half-timbering, Gothic spires and bands of stone in the brick, under a jumble of roofs topped by a steep pavilion roof with shingles, wrought-iron railing and a weathervane. It is an office, seen from the street.

Look for:
- the flower tiles in the arches over the windows, and two larger tile panels beside the entrance bay referring to trade and grain
- the original wrought-iron brackets of the porch canopy, and what is left of the old fence
- the former Heineken brewery across the water

title: Weteringschans 96, a children's clinic for the well-to-do
summary: In 1895 this house opened as a 'home for sick children' of well-off families, with about twenty beds, an outpatients' clinic in the basement and an operating room in the attic. A later patent office put up a stone saying Inventum Mutat Mundum.
body:
Amsterdam already had a children's hospital on the Sarphatistraat, open to every child and divided into three classes. The founders of this clinic, opened in 1895, wanted something else: a home for sick children of the well-to-do rather than a hospital, as the report of the opening put it. Here too the patients were divided over three classes. There were about twenty beds, an outpatients' clinic in the basement, an operating room in the attic, and a garden laid out for play.

The driving force was the paediatrician Israel Graanboom, who lived and practised next door at no. 98. The clinic closed around 1913, and the building was let as offices; a dentist, an ear, nose and throat doctor and Graanboom's own outpatients' clinic were among the tenants. Around 1929 the Bureau voor Technische Adviezen, a patent office run by the engineers Flesseman and Stigter, moved in. They or a successor put up a stone reading Inventum Mutat Mundum: inventions change the world.

The building stands among town houses of the 1890s on the site of the old Hollandsche Gasfabriek, and among them it is the odd one out in what it was built for.

Look for:
- the stone with Inventum Mutat Mundum
- the crowned pointed gable over the raised bay with the entrance
- the yellow brick accents and patterns in the red front

title: The Lutheran orphanage that lost its swan
summary: A notary's legacy paid for this Lutheran orphanage of 1883–1884, so that the orphans no longer had to live with the old people. Boys and girls were kept strictly apart. The swan, the Lutheran emblem, has gone from its dormer, and it is now flats.
body:
Amsterdam's Lutherans ran an orphanage from 1678, when the merchant Jan Geerkens let them use a house on the Lauriergracht. In 1811 the French occupiers claimed that building, and the orphans moved into the Lutheran deaconry house on the Nieuwe Keizersgracht, where they lived together with old people for more than seventy years. A legacy from notary Franke in 1881 at last made a separate orphanage possible, and A.L. (Dolf) van Gendt designed this one. Inside were dormitories, dining rooms and sitting rooms, with boys and girls strictly apart.

On the middle dormer stood a swan, the emblem of the Lutheran church, as a photo by Jacob Olie of 1890 shows; it is no longer there. In 1962 the home was named after Geerkens. It closed in 1985, served for a while as a shelter, and has since been divided into flats.

Its block is unlike the rest of the posh Weteringschans: next to the orphanage stand a former primary school of 1875–1880 and listed workers' houses on the Huidekoperstraat.

Look for:
- the middle dormer with its broken pediment and hoisting beam, where the swan stood
- the projecting centre bay with the entrance
- the rusticated strips that frame the centre

title: Weteringschans 231–251, where the builders moved in
summary: On the levelled rampart, architects and contractors built town houses to sell or let in 1890–1892, and some moved in: J.E. van der Pek, later a pioneer of Amsterdam's social housing, at no. 231, the Warners family at 243 and 245. A future prime minister lived at 251.
body:
After the city's ramparts were levelled, the Weteringschans filled up in the 1880s and 1890s with town houses built on speculation for well-off buyers. On this stretch, backing onto the Lijnbaansgracht, several of the builders kept a house for themselves.

The young architect Jan Ernst van der Pek designed nos. 231–233 in 1891–1892 as two houses holding probably about eight flats, let them himself, and lived at no. 231 from 1892 until his death in 1919, with a break around 1900; from 1903 with his wife Louise Went, who inspected working-class homes. Van der Pek went on to build Amsterdam's first homes under the Housing Act, on the Van Beuningenstraat in 1909, and the Van der Pekbuurt in Noord is named after him.

The contractor and architect Philip Andries Warners built nos. 243 and 245 in 1890–1891. He moved into 243 with his family, among them his son, the later architect F.A. Warners, and his father, the carpenter and estate agent Pieter Warners, became the first resident of 245.

Nos. 247–251 were built and let by the contractor H.D. van Voorthuijsen. At 251 lived the lawyer Theo Heemskerk, anti-revolutionary member of parliament and city alderman, until he became prime minister in 1908 and moved to The Hague.

All are private homes.

Look for:
- the two halves of Van der Pek's front, alike but not identical
- the rich neo-Renaissance fronts of 243 and 245
- nos. 247–251, three houses under one cornice, which lost their balustrade and pediment
